26Power supply faultyMinor/Major/Criticalinput power faulty or unstableGRDEV-8838, raised together with 15 on all four RFFEs. The LED spec also lists 26 with source eth1 under the FH LED (a vendor use of the ID).
27Power amplifier faultyMajor/CriticalPA faulty, unstable or broken; performance degraded or TX array not workingThe AAU LED spec lists 27 for mid-board/RFFE in the RF LED non-critical group. No bench case recorded.
29Transceiver faultCriticalmodule or port transceiver (SFP) fault (FH LED red heart blink)Class injected by the RF/Power/Transceiver group of the Common-AAU suite.
30Interface faultMajor/Criticalfault on one of the unit interfaces; source mb-N on the AAUNo bench case recorded.
2003, 2005vendor-specificas raisedvendor range (1000–65535); the LED spec lists them against the mid-board (RF LED red fast blink)Meaning not documented in our sources: ask the radio team before guessing.
5013 (BBU)BBU-side RRH alarmn/anot an RU fault-id: the BBU RRH manager's "RRH disconnected/connected" alarmIn the CM16 outage it was the only reaction to an RU reconnect; nothing re-sent the frequency config, so carriers stayed DISABLED.
Level 2 — where to read faults and how to read them
Where to read faults
# on the RU shell
tail -20 /run/media/mmcblk0p4/alarms.log          # raised / cleared, with fault-id, source, severity
tail -20 /run/media/mmcblk0p4/alarms_internal.log # internal detail behind the O-RAN alarm

# over NETCONF (netopeer2-cli, after connect)
get --filter-xpath /o-ran-fm:active-alarm-list

# identity / calibration files behind faults 12, 13, 16 (a 0-byte file = firmware dump problem)
ls -la /run/media/mmcblk0p4/O-RAN/eeprom_data /run/media/mmcblk0p4/O-RAN/default/eeprom_data \
       /run/media/mmcblk0p4/tx_calibration_eeprom.json
Reading an alarm correctly
• An alarm instance is the triple fault-id + fault-source + severity. The same ID can be active on several sources (for example 15 on rffe-0…rffe-3), and those are separate alarms.
• Affected objects decide the blast radius. When the affected objects are all carriers, the RU operations manager holds every TRX down until the alarm clears, so one critical file alarm can take the whole radio off air.
• Timing matters as much as the ID. 17 then 18 some minutes later is the normal PTP-loss story. 16 then 15 then 25 right after a firmware upgrade is the identity-loss story. 15 appearing exactly when carriers are reconfigured, with no other symptom, may be benign.
• Severity maps to the LEDs: non-critical IDs give green fast blink, critical ones red fast blink on the RU or RF LED; sync IDs go to the FH LED (LED01).

How the Common-AAU suite proves raise and clear: 23 test cases in six groups (Thermal, Config/File/SW, Unit/Reset/Reboot, Sync, RF/Power/Transceiver, HO/Soak) inject real triggers while a UE is attached and TCP data flows, check the alarm is raised, remove the trigger, check it clears and traffic recovers. One run: 17 pass, 3 fail, 3 skip in 3 h 28 min. The three fails were "alarm did not raise on injection", which pointed at the injection method, not the product.
Level 3 — triage rules from real RCAs, and spec details that trip people up
Triage rules that came out of real cases
1. Every boot, every unit, every chain at once (GRDEV-8838: 15 + 26 on all four RFFEs) means a common cause: firmware, thresholds or packaging. Four simultaneous hardware failures are far less likely.
2. Present on one branch, absent on another (GRDEV-9046: release branch only) means packaging or regression, not the unit. Compare the scripts that differ.
3. File alarms: check the file, then the source. For 12/13/16 look at the file size first. A 0-byte file with a readable physical EEPROM (a direct I2C read shows serial and revision) points at the firmware step that dumps it.
4. A BBU error can be the symptom of an RU fault: "failed to receive reply" on a NETCONF write was the RU FPGA (fault 15) crashing mid-RPC. Line up RU alarm timestamps with the BBU log.
5. RX-out-of-order is not always a broken receiver. On low band it was the ADC clipping at DSA 0 (a configuration problem fixed by DSA). On one B28 unit it was a genuine LNA/sensitivity fault. The test that separates them: does raising DSA move the over-range point without moving the noise floor? A real receiver fault shows up as poor sensitivity at any DSA.
6. Benign alarms exist. Count occurrences against carrier reconfigurations before calling a fault (the 38 unit-out-of-order lines equalled the number of reconfigurations).

Spec details that trip people up: fault 18 must not be reported during the normal initial synchronisation at start-up, so a fault 18 at boot deserves a second look: either sync took abnormally long or the RU is reporting outside the spec. The vendor range starts at 1000, so 2003/2005 carry no O-RAN meaning at all. Fault 24 (unit blocked) only exists if the RU supports the optional hardware-state feature.
Interview Q&A
Q: An AAU shows fault 12 "Critical file not found" on its b41 carriers only. What do you check?
A: Which file: the alarm source names it. In GRDEV-9046 it was tx_calibration_eeprom.json, never generated because start_transmission.sh chose the calibration route by matching hard-coded model names and the b41 sub-variant was missing. It appeared on the release branch only, which pointed at packaging, not the unit. The practical impact is an uncalibrated TX carrier, so output power cannot be certified.
Q: Fault 17 and then fault 18 appear some minutes apart. What happened?
A: The RU lost all sync inputs and went into holdover (17). When holdover could no longer keep the time within limits it declared freerun (18) and stopped RF. In our CMN_009/010 tests the gaps were about 3 min and 16–18 min after the PTP master port was disabled.
Q: Fault 15 "Unit out of order" is in the log 38 times after a conformance run. Is the unit broken?
A: Not necessarily. In our case every occurrence lined up with the framework tearing carriers down to reconfigure frequency or E-TM: the TRX chains go DISABLED, the LED manager raises unit-out-of-order, then the carriers come back. Count the alarms against reconfiguration events before filing a defect.
Q: What is the difference between fault-ids 20 and 1000+?
A: IDs 1–41 are the O-RAN common alarms with a defined meaning (20 = RX out of order). 1000–65535 is the vendor-specific range, so an ID such as 2003 has only the meaning the vendor documents.
Addition — fault catalogue from AAU bring-up: real root causes, confirm-with, fix
Triage top-down. Most lost time on these faults went into chasing a downstream symptom. One upstream problem (RU disk full, stale M-plane address in ornc, PTP not locked) manufactures a whole screen of misleading alarms. Check in this order: RU disk space, M-plane session and the address ornc uses, PTP state and clockClass, then cell/carrier state, then RF. These cases come from 4-/5-band AAU bring-up and lab test (see AAUBUP01 for the bring-up sequence).
SymptomReal causeConfirm withFix
RU NOT_PRESENT, RF TX 0; SSH (22) open but NETCONF (830) closedRU data partition (/dev/mmcblk0p4) 100% full of stale upgrade zips, so sysrepo cannot write and NETCONF diesdf -h on the RU, first, every timeDelete the stale upgrade zips, restart the M-plane
"FW Upgrade Failed" after about 16 sornc cannot subscribe to the software-download event because the RU M-plane session keeps cycling; the image is never downloadedNETCONF session state, and df (usually the disk-full case above)Stabilise the M-plane session; a 16 s failure never read the image, so do not blame it
Alarm panel shows alarms that are not real and misses real onesornc / RRH manager holding a stale RU M-plane address after RUs were renumberedCompare the address ornc uses with the RU's real M-plane addressRestart that ornc instance; take ground truth from the RU itself
Fault 16 with a healthy-looking unitIdentity backup O-RAN/eeprom_data has the wrong length. Healthy = board revision (4 chars, e.g. V2P1) + 15-char base serial = 19 charscat the file and count characters; check which source raised fault 16 in the active alarm list20 chars: index digit baked in and appended again at runtime: truncate -s 19 (do not reprogram or delete), clears on system-monitor restart. 15 chars: board revision missing: set revision then base serial with flash_eeprom, reboot. 19 chars but still raised: source is a midboard serial of zeros or a missing RFFE EEPROM JSON, separate fixes
Fault 18Points at the fronthaul SFP / sync path, not RFSFP type, seating, optical RX level (one case: RX fibre dark at -26.78 dBm)Reseat/replace SFP or fibre, recheck PTP lock
PTP never locks; every RU master port disabledptp4l bound to a port stuck in LISTENING because the fibre was moved to another physical port; clockClass 248 (free-run) makes ptpmgr disable all RU master portsptp4l port state and clockClassBind ptp4l to the port that really carries the fibre
PTP locks but clockClass is not 6Grandmaster disciplined from internet NTP with no GPS, so not traceableclockClass on the GM (6 = GPS-traceable)Give the GM a real GNSS reference
Fault 17 holdoverOften transient: one case held over 23 s and self-cleared, RU then LOCKED at clockClass 6Timestamped holdover durationDo not escalate a long holdover without timestamps

Availability about 95%, RFTX flappingU-PLANE-INVALID-PKT alarm: 933 RFTX flaps in 80 minutes gave 95.3% availabilityCount RFTX transitions in the DU log over a windowChase the invalid U-plane packets on the fronthaul

Fault 4 "Temperature too low" CRITICAL on a warm unitRFFE application checksum invalid, so every RFFE temperature read 0 °C; bisected to a one-day build window (GRDEV-10066)RFFE temperature readback all exactly 0Fix the RFFE application image; treat fault 4 as reportable to the radio team with its source
Known red herrings: RFFE temperature -128 appears at the same ~3% rate on healthy units (3.00% vs 3.06%), so it is not the fault; faults 15 and 25 next to an active fault 12 were stale lines left in alarms.log (GRDEV-9764): use the active alarm list, not the log file; Elastic @timestamp is ingest time, not measurement time, so replayed data looks like a live gap.

Alarm-suite lesson (RUREG01): grade the raise, the clear and the service action separately. In one release run raises were healthy, but faults 14 and 16 reset the RU where the matrix said "action continues", and a fault-18 trigger removed the fronthaul instead of the sync source, so fault 18 never appeared.
CM23 Three Product Defects Found by Conformance — GRDEV-8976 BW change, GRDEV-9046 fault-12 cal file, GRDEV-8838 false RFFE over-current, and how each was narrowed Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
A conformance campaign is built to measure a radio, but its most valuable output is often the product bugs it trips over on the way. This card follows three of them from the first odd symptom to the fixed build: a bandwidth change that the radio said it applied but did not, a calibration file that was never created on one band, and an over-current alarm that was not real. Each one is a small detective story, and the useful part is how the suspect list was cut down: which observation ruled out the unit, the test setup, or the configuration. Reuse the moves, not just the answers.
Level 1 — the three defects at a glance
DefectSymptomImpactRoot causeFix / status
GRDEV-8976 (Blocker, B28)M-plane BW change 10 → 15 MHz (same centre) shown in sysrepo/NETCONF, but the DFE channel filter stayed at 10 MHzedge PRBs stripped; SIB1 PDSCH CRC fails, UEs cannot attach; 100 % reproducibleruntime: filter reload only in the centre-frequency-change branch; reboot: filter sized from the personality default, not startup.xmlclosed as duplicate of GRDEV-8199; cherry-picked as ru-app PR #2064; verified 20 July
GRDEV-9046 (Critical, b41)CRITICAL fault 12 "Critical file not found" for tx_calibration_eeprom.json on n41 carrier-0 and -1, every b41 bring-upb41 carriers not TX-calibrated, so output power cannot be certifiedconfigure_flavour() in start_transmission.sh matched hard-coded model strings; the b41 sub-variant fell through to the RFFE calibration route and the file was never generatedPR #2068 (backport of GRDEV-8417): flavour from personality-app --flavour, match on b41/n41; verified on the 26 July build; in 2026.2.2
GRDEV-8838 (Critical, MidBoard V1.5)CRITICAL fault 15 "Unit out of order" + fault 26 "Power Supply Faulty" on all four RFFEs on every bootfalse CRITICAL alarms on every boot; critical faults with wide affected objects can hold carriers down, and the noise hides real faultsmid-board firmware v2.6 over-current supervision (status registers 0x03ED / 0x03EE read over I2C) reported an over-current that was not thereraised by the radio team, verified on an RCT bench unit; fixed in release 2026.2.2
Level 2 — how each one was narrowed, step by step
1. GRDEV-8976: "the config says 15 MHz, the radio still behaves like 10 MHz"
• First cut: is it the config layer? sysrepo and NETCONF both reported the new bandwidth, so the M-plane write had succeeded. The fault had to be below the datastore.
• Second cut: what does the signal path actually use? The DFE channel filter was still shaped for 10 MHz. With a 15 MHz carrier behind a 10 MHz filter the outer PRBs are cut off. SIB1 is scheduled across that region, so its PDSCH CRC fails and no UE can attach. That explains a "network" symptom from a "radio" bug.
• Third cut: which code path? Two routes set the filter, and both were broken in different ways. At run time lphy_config_device() was only called from the branch that handles a centre-frequency change; a width-only change keeps the centre, so it never ran. After an ruReset, lphy_config_init() sized the filter from the personality default instead of the startup.xml value, so there was no old-versus-new difference to trigger a reload either.
• Fourth cut: why only this branch? The PWK branch forked from develop on 22 June, after an LPHY refactor but before the GRDEV-8199 fix merged on 1 July. develop already had the fix; the release branch was never affected because it programs bandwidth by a different route. Same root cause as 8199, hence "Duplicate" and a cherry-pick (PR #2064).
• Proof: 10 → 15 MHz on all four B28 TX and RX array carriers, ruReset, filter reported "3xNR15MHz Configuration" with config_error 0. CM17 covers the boot-time bandwidth chain this sits on.

2. GRDEV-9046: "fault 12 on every b41 bring-up"
• First cut: unit or software? The alarm appeared on release/REL_2026.2.x but not on the PWK branch. A unit or provisioning problem would not care which branch is loaded; this followed the branch, so packaging or a regression.
• Second cut: who creates the file? The start-up script decides which calibration EEPROM to read by matching the model name. The b41 sub-variant under test was not in its list, so it fell through to read_calibration_eeprom rffe, and tx_calibration_eeprom.json was never produced.
• Fix design: do not whitelist models. Ask the personality for the flavour and match on the band family, which covers current and future b41 models.
• Why an RF engineer cares: an uncalibrated TX carrier is what a B41 power deficit looks like (the ~6 dB B41 shortfall discussed in GAIN_CAL/L28 appears with fault 12). Always read the alarm list before chasing a power miss.

3. GRDEV-8838: "every RFFE over-current on every boot"
• First cut: how many at once? Faults 15 and 26 on all four RFFEs simultaneously, every boot. Four PA supplies failing together at every power-up is implausible; a shared supervisor or firmware is the natural suspect.
• Second cut: where does the decision come from? The mid-board firmware (V1.5 board, FW v2.6) reads over-current status through registers 0x03ED / 0x03EE on I2C. Reading those registers directly separates "the supervisor claims over-current" from "the rail is actually overloaded".
• Status: fixed in the mid-board firmware delivered with release 2026.2.2 and verified on a bench unit. It was not an RCT-found bug, but the RCT verification record was the most detailed evidence on the ticket.
Level 3 — the reusable moves, and the framework bugs found alongside
The narrowing moves, generalised
MoveQuestion it answersUsed in
Check each layer's own viewDatastore says X; does the hardware register or filter say X?8976
Follow the unit vs follow the branchDoes the fault move with the hardware or with the software build?9046
Count the simultaneous failuresIs "all chains at once" more likely one common cause?8838
Read the raw register or fileIs the supervisor/file-generator lying, or is the physics real?8838, 9046 (and the 0-byte eeprom_data case in CM16)
Branch archaeologyWhen did this branch fork relative to the fix?8976
Prove with the failing scenariore-run exactly the triggering sequence (change, reset, read back)all three
The framework had bugs too. The same campaign fixed a set of automation defects, and none of them showed up in dry runs. They were found by comparing framework output with the analyser screen:
ruauto PRFramework defect
#675SEM per-segment index read the wrong segment
#679dynamic-range results written one column shifted
#678signal-generator external-trigger delay gated on vendor instead of duplex mode
#681PRACH re-offset never written or verified (eAxC read-back added)
#680PRACH statistics console not enabled
#695band-aware EIRP → TRP correction, plus B28 carrier read-back
#692carrier cycle made atomic around the gain write
Lesson: when a result surprises you, suspect the product, the setup and the tool, in that order of evidence rather than preference. Of 21 bugs raised by the RCT pair since April, only two belonged to this programme (9046 and 8976); the rest belonged to other flavours, the DU or platform boards. Filing against the right component is part of the job (see FWK3 for more framework failures).
Interview Q&A
Q: NETCONF shows the new bandwidth, but UEs stop attaching after an on-the-fly BW change. Where do you look?
A: Below the datastore: the value the signal path actually uses. In GRDEV-8976 the DFE channel filter stayed at 10 MHz while the carrier was 15 MHz, so the edge PRBs where SIB1 is scheduled were stripped and SIB1 failed CRC. The filter reload only ran on a centre-frequency change, and after reset it was sized from the personality default.
Q: A critical alarm appears on every bring-up with one software branch but not another. What does that tell you?
A: The fault follows the software, not the hardware: packaging or a regression. In GRDEV-9046 a start-up script whitelisted model names and missed the b41 sub-variant, so the TX calibration file was never generated.
Q: All four RFFEs report over-current at every boot. Hardware failure?
A: Very unlikely: four simultaneous failures at every power-up point to a shared cause. In GRDEV-8838 it was mid-board firmware supervision (read through I2C status registers) raising a false over-current, fixed in a later firmware release.
Q: How do you find bugs in the test framework itself?
A: Compare framework output with the instrument screen on a few points of every new measurement. That is how the SEM wrong-segment index, the shifted dynamic-range column and the never-written PRACH re-offset were found; dry runs had passed.
Energy measurement & energy saving (O-RAN)
CM21 O-RAN EPE Performance Measurements — the PM CSV decoded: enabling XML, row format, RFFE↔band mapping, real values and parser traps Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
Every board in the AAU has small meters on it: volts, amps, watts and degrees. O-RAN defines a standard way to switch those meters on and get the readings back as a CSV file every few minutes. These are the EPE statistics (Energy, Power and Environmental). Think of a smart electricity meter that emails you a spreadsheet every 5 minutes, with one row per quantity and one column group per board. This card shows how to switch EPE on, how to read one row, how the rows add up to band and flavour totals, and the traps found in a real archive of 14 power runs: a duplicated controller, sentinel values, missing minutes. USLEEP02 shows how these numbers are used in the uSleep test. CM14 explains why they never match a lab supply exactly.
Level 1 — what the O-RAN M-plane standard defines
Where: O-RAN.WG4.MP (the M-plane spec, v19 here), Annex B.5 "Energy, power and environmental statistics", plus clause 10 (performance management). EPE is measurement-group 4 (epe-stats). It is reported per hardware component, and the O-RU lists which objects it supports for each component class.
measurement-objectmeaningunit in the CSV
POWERpower consumed by the componentW
TEMPERATUREtemperature of the component°C
VOLTAGEsupply voltage of the component (added to B.5 in a later spec version)V
CURRENTsupply current of the component (added with VOLTAGE)A
RuleWhat it means in practice
epe-measurement-intervalone interval per measurement group. Each interval produces one min/max/avg set per object. We use 60 s.
Intervals are aligned to midnight(seconds since 00:00) mod interval = 0. So a 60-s block always starts at hh:mm:00, whenever you enabled it. Other sources must be binned on the same :00 grid.
First interval may be skippedif the RU had too little time to measure after activation, the first block can be missing
file-upload-intervalone CSV per upload interval (300 s → 5 one-minute blocks per file)
File nameC<start>_<end>_<name>.csv, where name = the ietf-hardware name, in practice the unit/board serial. Seen: C202604191300+0000_202604191305+0000_<serial>.csv
Row formatgroup id, object, start, end, then object-unit + object-unit-id + report-info (min, max, avg), repeated for every component in one line
Storagethe O-RU keeps files in its PM folder and deletes old ones itself. The PW FHGW writes them on the data partition /run/media/mmcblk0p4. Collect them before they rotate out.
Other measurement groups use the same CSV style (useful to recognise): 1 = transceiver-stats (optical RX/TX power per port), 2 = rx-window-stats (early/late/on-time fronthaul packets per eAxC), 3 = tx-stats, 4 = epe-stats, 5 = symbol-rssi-stats (time-domain RSSI per UL symbol at the antenna connector, in dBm). The spec's own EPE example is a PA temperature row: 4, TEMPERATURE, …, or-hw:O-RU-POWER-AMPLIFIER, PA1, min, 25, max, 44, avg, 33.
Level 2 — switch it on, then read a row
1. The enabling payload (the lab file Enable_EPE_Measurements.xml, sanitised). The file server in it is a dummy. The CSVs are simply collected from the RU partition.
<performance-measurement-objects xmlns="urn:o-ran:performance-management:1.0">
  <remote-SFTP-uploads>
    <remote-SFTP-upload-path>sftp://<file-server>:22/upload/path</remote-SFTP-upload-path>
    <password><password>REDACTED</password></password>
  </remote-SFTP-uploads>
  <enable-SFTP-upload>true</enable-SFTP-upload>
  <epe-measurement-interval>60</epe-measurement-interval>
  <file-upload-interval>300</file-upload-interval>
  <epe-measurement-objects><measurement-object>TEMPERATURE</measurement-object><active>true</active></epe-measurement-objects>
  <epe-measurement-objects><measurement-object>CURRENT</measurement-object><active>true</active></epe-measurement-objects>
  <epe-measurement-objects><measurement-object>POWER</measurement-object><active>true</active></epe-measurement-objects>
  <epe-measurement-objects><measurement-object>VOLTAGE</measurement-object><active>true</active></epe-measurement-objects>
</performance-measurement-objects>

# push it to each FHGW (same pattern as other RU XMLs)
netopeer2-cli> connect --host <fhgw-ip> --login <user>
netopeer2-cli> edit-config --target running --config=Enable_EPE_Measurements.xml
Two gotchas. (a) This payload uses the older leaf names remote-SFTP-uploads / enable-SFTP-upload. Newer spec versions use generic file-upload names, and sFTP or FTPES is chosen by the URI scheme. If an RU rejects the edit-config, check which YANG revision it implements. (b) The spec only lets you change an object's parameters (interval, report-info) while active=false. So to change the interval, set active false, edit, then set it true again.

2. Anatomy of one row (real B1B3 file, 0 % allocation, B1 and B3 carriers on):
4, POWER, 2026-04-19T13:00:00+00:00, 2026-04-19T13:01:00Z, or-hw:O-RAN-RFFE,
   O-RAN-RFFE0, min,37.7600, max,37.7600, avg,37.7600,   ... O-RAN-RFFE7, min,36.4400, max,37.7600, avg,37.3200,
   O-RAN-RFFE-CONTROLLER, O-RAN-RFFE-CONTROLLER0 , min,47.6000, max,47.6000, avg,47.6000,
                          O-RAN-RFFE-CONTROLLER1 , min,47.6000, max,47.6000, avg,47.6000,
   O-RAN-B1, min,174.8000, max,177.4000, avg,176.0933,  O-RAN-B2, min,177.3600, max,181.3200, avg,179.1200
FieldExampleNote
group id4epe-stats
objectPOWERone row each for TEMPERATURE, CURRENT, POWER, VOLTAGE → 4 rows per minute
start / end13:00:00+00:00 / 13:01:00Z60-s block on the :00 grid. Note the two different UTC notations in one row.
object-unitor-hw:O-RAN-RFFEPW hardware class for the RF front-end boards. A second unit follows: O-RAN-RFFE-CONTROLLER
object-unit-id + report-infoO-RAN-RFFE0, min,x, max,y, avg,z8 RFFE entries, then CONTROLLER0 and CONTROLLER1 (with a trailing space in the id!)
band totalsO-RAN-B1, O-RAN-B2POWER rows only: per-band sums, derived rather than measured
3. How the totals are built. This was checked to the milliwatt against the archive:
B1B3 flavour, one minute, POWER row
Per RFFE: POWER = VOLTAGE × CURRENT exactly (40.0 V × 0.944 A = 37.76 W). Each band total = its RFFEs + an equal share of CONTROLLER0.
FlavourO-RAN-B1O-RAN-B2Rails seen (V)Real check
B1B3 (mid-band)B1 = RFFE0–3 + ½ CTRL0B3 = RFFE4–7 + ½ CTRL0RFFE 40.0 · CTRL 11.9152.29 + 23.80 = 176.09 ✓
B8B20B28 (low-band)RFFE0–3 (B8 in these runs) + ½ CTRL0RFFE4–7 (B20/B28 slot) + ½ CTRL0RFFE 48.1 · CTRL 11.9B2 idle: 4 × 3.126 + 17.255 = 29.76 ✓
B7B41 (B41 here)RFFE0–3 + all of CTRL00 (RFFE4–7 read 0)RFFE 45.5 · CTRL 11.9183.13 + 41.65 = 224.78 ✓
Flavour power = O-RAN-B1 + O-RAN-B2 = Σ RFFE0–7 + CONTROLLER0 (once). AAU power = the sum of the three flavours, from three files written by three FHGWs. For KPIs use the per-minute avg, not min/max (the mentor's rule, and the spec's intent).

4. Typical values from the archive
QuantityB1B3B7B41B8B20B28
CONTROLLER0 (FHGW + mid-board 12 V rail)11.9 V × 4.0 A ≈ 47.6 W3.5 A ≈ 41.7 W2.9 A ≈ 34.5 W
one RFFE, carriers on, 0 % alloc0.91–1.01 A → 36–40 W0.88–1.14 A (TDD, jumpy)0.91–1.04 A → 44–50 W
one RFFE, PAs off≈ 1 current step (~0.03 A → ~1.3 W)≈ 0RFFE4–7: 0.065 A → 3.1 W (idle leakage)
RFFE temperature, warm, 0 % alloc45–54 °C——
flavour total, all PAs off (RUN1)≈ 54 W≈ 39 W≈ 62 W → AAU ≈ 155 W
Level 3 — traps found in the real archive (and how to parse safely)
1. CONTROLLER1 is a mirror. Its voltage, current and power are identical to CONTROLLER0, and its temperature reads 0. Adding both double-counts 35–50 W per flavour, about 120 W for the AAU. Use CONTROLLER0 only, or simply use B1 + B2.
2. Sentinel values = failed sensor read. In one 100 %-load scenario the whole low-band flavour reported VOLTAGE/CURRENT 6553.5 (= 0xFFFF × 0.1), POWER -1310.71, band totals -655.355, and all temperatures 0. A naive sum gave a negative AAU power. Treat V > 100, I > 100 or P < 0 as invalid. Do not replace them with 0, which would fake a saving. Re-run or exclude the flavour. The GRDEV-9526 work (CM14) later fixed several RU-side PSU read failures of exactly this kind.
3. Isolated zero samples. Watch for min = 0 while avg > 0, e.g. B41 RFFE0 min 0.000, max 1.139, avg 0.922 A. One dropped sample drags the average down. It was most common on the B41 (TDD) flavour. Keep the avg, but flag minutes with min == 0 and check that they do not cluster in one test arm.
4. Missing blocks. In one run, 11 of 20 files held 4 one-minute blocks instead of 5. Always align by the row's start timestamp, never by file index × 5. Also expect the first block after enabling to be missing.
5. Parsing details. The start time uses +00:00 and the end time uses Z. Object ids can carry a trailing space ("O-RAN-RFFE-CONTROLLER0 "). Walk the tokens as (id, "min", v, "max", v, "avg", v) groups rather than using fixed column numbers, because the POWER row is longer (it adds B1/B2).
6. Resolution. The RFFE current moves in steps of about 0.0325 A. At 40 V that gives POWER values of 36.44 / 37.76 / 39.04 / 40.36 / 41.64 W, which is ≈1.3 W per step. The controller current resolves 0.1 A (≈1.2 W). So an "idle 1.27 W" RFFE is one LSB, not a real leakage measurement. A per-flavour ΔP below a few watts in one minute is within resolution. The uSleep or RoP saving you claim must be well above it, averaged over many minutes.
7. Know the boundary before comparing with a lab supply. In the April–May 2026 archive every POWER value is plain rail V×I and the band totals are plain sums, so no PSU-loss correction is visible. The lab supply measures the whole chassis at its DC input. Two real comparisons:
ComparisonPM (CSV)Lab DC supplyGapWhy
B1B3 CSV only vs whole AAU, all PAs off≈ 60 W≈ 205 W≈ 145 Wthe other two flavours (≈ 100 W by their own PM) + PSU conversion / common board (≈ 45 W)
same, 0 % allocation≈ 361 W≈ 507 W≈ 146 Wsame constant offset: a boundary, not an error
same, 100 % allocation≈ 719 W≈ 865 W≈ 146 Wsame
all three flavours, 0 % (RUN13)≈ 353 W≈ 405 W≈ 52 W (13 %)PSU loss + common board outside the CSV scope
single flavour active, 0 % (B41 / LB runs)155 / 198 W206 / 250 W≈ 51 Wnear-constant ≈ 50 W offset at light load
Later builds add a factory PSU-efficiency LUT to chassis-level EPE POWER (GRDEV-9526; see CM14). Always record which build produced the CSV before comparing runs.

8. Validation recipe. Bin every source (PM avg, get-PSU 1-s samples, lab supply) on the same 60-s grid anchored to :00. Drop minutes with sentinels, zero-min or too few samples. Trim the warm-up. Report PM − reference per flavour and for the AAU, as a mean and a worst case. This is the same method GRDEV-9526 used, with 91 aligned windows.
Interview Q&A
Q: An RU's EPE CSV gives O-RAN-B1 = 176 W, but the four RFFEs of band 1 only add up to 152 W. Is the file wrong?
A: No. The band total also includes a share of the RFFE-CONTROLLER (the 12 V FHGW + mid-board rail): half of 47.6 W on a two-band flavour, all of it on the single-band B41 flavour. Flavour power is B1 + B2, which equals the sum of all RFFEs plus CONTROLLER0 once.
Q: Your summed AAU power comes out ~120 W higher than get-PSU. What is the first thing you check?
A: Double counting of RFFE-CONTROLLER1. It mirrors CONTROLLER0 for V/I/P, and its temperature reads 0. Summing both adds 35–50 W per flavour. After that, check for mixed builds and for summing min/max instead of avg.
Q: A PM file shows 6553.5 V and -1310.71 W. What happened and how should automation treat it?
A: 0xFFFF × 0.1 is a failed sensor read (a sentinel), not a measurement. Mark the minute or the whole flavour as invalid, exclude it and report the gap. Never coerce it to 0 W: that would look like a huge energy saving.
Q: Why must the lab supply and get-PSU be binned on hh:mm:00 boundaries?
A: O-RAN aligns PM measurement intervals to midnight (seconds mod interval = 0), so each 60-s EPE block runs from :00 to :00. If another source uses free-running minutes from when the script started, you compare different time windows. During warm-up or load changes that shows up as fake error.
Q: PM and the lab DC supply differ by a near-constant ~50 W at light load. Error or boundary?
A: Mostly boundary. The CSV sums rail outputs (RFFE rails + 12 V controller rail) as V×I. The lab supply sees the chassis input, including PSU conversion loss, the common board and cabling. A constant offset points to a boundary difference. An error that grows with load points to the efficiency model, which is what GRDEV-9526 calibrated.
CM22 O-RAN Network Energy Saving Toolbox — carrier sleep, TRX control, Advanced Sleep Modes, deep hibernate, max-power control, and where PW uSleep/RoP fit Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
O-RAN gives the DU a standard set of energy-saving switches for the radio. They range from "turn one carrier off" to "put the whole radio to sleep for hours". Picture an office building at night. You switch off one floor (carrier deactivation), unplug half the desk lamps (TRX control: switch off some antenna elements), put the PCs into standby (advanced sleep modes), lock the whole building until morning (deep hibernate), or cap the thermostat (max output power control). PW's uSleep is like motion-sensor lights that flick off between footsteps: much faster, decided inside the RU, and invisible to the DU. PW's Reduced Output Power (RoP) is the thermostat cap. This card maps each standard technique, how you test it, and where the PW features fit.
Time-scale of each technique (illustrative, log axis)
Bars show typical sleep or hold durations, not exact spec limits. Faster techniques save less per event but can be used during traffic. Slower ones save more but need the carrier or unit to be idle.
Level 1 — the toolbox in O-RAN.WG4.MP clause 20 (all optional for the O-RU)
Each technique is advertised as a feature in o-ran-wg4-features.yang, and the O-RU exposes capability containers that the controller reads at start-up. If the feature is not advertised, the DU must not use it.
TechniqueFeature flagCommanded byWhat is switched offWake-up / exit
Carrier deactivation(base) + ENERGYSAVING for power-stateM-plane: [tr]x-array-carrier/active = INACTIVEC/U-plane processing of that carrier. With energy-saving-enabled=true and no active carrier, the O-RU may also power down carrier circuitry and may stop C/U/S functionsset ACTIVE again. If the S-plane was stopped, re-activation takes an implementation-dependent time.
Carrier SLEEP (since v14)—M-plane: active = SLEEP (state stays READY)array elements, but only if every carrier sharing those elements is also asleepset ACTIVE; elements are re-enabled for the carrier
TRX control, C-planeTRX-CONTROLC-plane commands from the DUselected array elements, e.g. 32 of 64 in massive MIMO, for a defined or undefined timeadvertised wake-up-duration (µs; the DU converts it to slots for its SCS)
TRX control, M-planeMPLANE-TRX-CONTROLM-plane: antenna-bitmask or antenna-bitmask-index on the largest arrayarray elements, until the next commandasynchronous. The O-RU sends mplane-trx-control-ant-mask-update when done.
Data-layer controlMPLANE-DATA-LAYER-CONTROLM-plane: energy-sharing-groups-disabledprocessing hardware shared by a group of endpoints (FPGA blocks, cores)remove the group id; a notification follows when the hardware is awake
Advanced Sleep Modes (ASM)ADVANCED-SLEEP-MODEC-plane Section Type 4 commandsa fraction of O-RU processing, per sleep-mode typewake-up-duration + wake-up-duration-guaranteed; optional ST8 "ready" message; emergency wake-up
Deep hibernateDEEP-HIBERNATEM-plane RPC <deep-hibernate> with hibernate-timeC/U/S and M-plane. Controllers must close their sessions, and call-home stops.timer expiry → full restart, restart-cause = DEEP-HIBERNATE-RESTART
Max output power controlMAX-POWER-CONTROLM-plane: max-power-level-index per tx-array, or carrier-max-power-reduction per tx-array-carriernothing is switched off. The PA can be re-biased for a lower maximum while the DU caps the PRBs.index 0 = normal; the O-RU confirms with a max-power-level-used notification
States you will read back (o-ran-hardware):
StateValues and rules
power-state (read-only, ENERGYSAVING)AWAKE: initial state; used whenever any carrier is active or energy-saving-enabled is false. SLEEPING: the M-plane is alive, C/U/S may be stopped. UNKNOWN: optional.
admin-statelocked: all carriers are forced INACTIVE/DISABLED and RF emission must stop. Requests to set ACTIVE must be rejected, and antenna-line/ALD power is off. unlocked: initial state after reset.
hardware-state-change notificationsent on any change of admin, oper, usage, power or availability state. The subscriber should then read the state with a get.
Common capability container for TRX control and ASM: ST8-ready-message-supported, sleep-duration-extension-supported, emergency-wake-up-command-supported (RPC <emergency-wake-up> followed by a notification). For every sleep-mode type the O-RU reports wake-up-duration and whether it is guaranteed. For the lightest type (SLEEP_MODE_0) it must be guaranteed = TRUE. If not guaranteed, the value is only a minimum.
Level 2 — how a test engineer verifies each technique
Step 0: discover, don't assume. Read o-ran-wg4-features and the capability containers (trx-control-capability-info, asm-capability-info, energy-saving-capability-common-info, supported-max-power-level, max/min-hibernate-time-duration). A feature that is not advertised is a "not applicable" result, not a fail.
TechniquePositive testNegative / rule testMeasure
Carrier deactivationACTIVE → INACTIVE: state goes to DISABLED (may pass BUSY); with ES enabled and no active carrier, power-state becomes SLEEPINGwith energy-saving-enabled=false, re-activation must be immediate. With it true, measure the re-lock time if the S-plane was stopped.ΔP per flavour (get-PSU / PM / lab supply), time to READY
Admin locklock: all carriers INACTIVE, no RF on the analyseredit-config ACTIVE while locked → must be rejectedspectrum analyser shows no carrier
M-plane TRX controlapply a mask from the advertised list, expect the mask-update notificationthe list must contain the all-ones mask. The mask must target the largest array. The C-plane mask must be all-ones before an M-plane command, and vice versa.per-element power (RFFE01 isolation method), ΔP
ASM / C-plane TRXsleep and wake inside the advertised wake-up-durationemergency wake-up RPC → notification; while asleep, delay measurement, connectivity check and sync must keep workingfirst-symbol EVM after wake-up, ΔP
Deep hibernateall carriers INACTIVE → RPC accepted → notification with hibernate-time → sessions closed → silent → restart at expiryRPC with any carrier active → rejected with a reason. hibernate-time outside min/max → rejected.restart-cause = DEEP-HIBERNATE-RESTART, watts while hibernating
Max power controlset index n: max-power-level-used notification, output drops by array-max-power-reductionDU order: cut scheduled power before increasing the reduction. Do not raise power before the notification when decreasing it.output power, ACLR/EVM at the new cap, ΔP
Power measurement uses the same triad as USLEEP02: get-PSU per FHGW (1-s samples → 1-min mean), the EPE CSV (CM21) and a lab DC supply (PWR01). All three are binned on the same :00 minute grid. Always check that ΔP is well above the sensor step (≈1.3 W per RFFE current LSB).
Level 3 — where PW uSleep and RoP fit, and what the data says about the ceiling
uSleep is vendor-internal. The FPGA detects all-zero symbols in the DL IQ and drops the PA enable line (TX_EN AND MC_EN on the RFFE; see RFFE02, USLEEP01), with a fixed advance before the next occupied symbol. No O-RAN message is involved and the DU does not know it happens. The nearest standard idea is a C-plane sleep of the lightest type (SLEEP_MODE_0, guaranteed wake-up). But standard sleeps are commanded by the DU for whole array elements over slots. uSleep is autonomous and data-driven, per symbol. The price is a first-symbol quality risk, so EVM on the symbol after a gap is always part of the test.

RoP (3 / 10 dB) corresponds to MAX-POWER-CONTROL. The standard adds two things PW testers should copy. (1) The DU must keep the IQ level below the reduced maximum (a CUS-plane input-level restriction), otherwise the PA clips at its new bias. (2) Changes must be ordered and confirmed by notification. RoP tests should therefore check ACLR/EVM and DPD re-convergence after each change, not just output power (M13, GRDEV-7438).

How much can each lever remove? Real 3-flavour AAU numbers (EPE PM sums from the power-run archive, CM21):
StateAAU (PM sum)Which lever reaches it
all carriers active, 0 % allocation (control channels only)≈ 353 Wbaseline for idle-hour savings
all PAs off, electronics alive≈ 155 Wcarrier deactivation / PA shutdown. uSleep can recover part of the ≈ 200 W of PA bias at 0 % load, limited by the symbols that stay occupied.
12 V rail alone (FHGW + mid-board)≈ 47 + 42 + 34 ≈ 123 W, near-constant in every runonly deep hibernate or data-layer control, which stop processing, touch this
lab supply vs PM at light load+≈ 50 WPSU conversion and common board. No RU technique removes it, but it shrinks as the load drops.
So, on this hardware: symbol and carrier techniques act on the ~200 W PA share. The ~120 W of always-on digital electronics needs the hibernate or data-layer class of technique. Night-time strategies usually combine carrier deactivation with deep hibernate. One more trap: with energy-saving enabled and the S-plane stopped, the first carrier activation after sleep waits for PTP re-lock. If a test script expects immediate READY it will report a false failure (CM16 activation chain).
Interview Q&A
Q: Name the O-RAN M-plane energy-saving techniques and the one that also stops the M-plane.
A: Carrier deactivation (and carrier SLEEP), RF channel switch-off via C-plane or M-plane TRX control, data-layer control, Advanced Sleep Modes, deep hibernate and maximum output power control. Deep hibernate is the one that stops C/U/S and then the M-plane. The O-RU restarts when hibernate-time expires, with restart-cause DEEP-HIBERNATE-RESTART.
Q: The DU sends deep-hibernate while one carrier is still active. What must the O-RU do?
A: Reject the RPC and include the reason in the error message. All tx and rx array-carriers must be deactivated first. This is a good negative test case.
Q: How is PW uSleep different from O-RAN Advanced Sleep Modes?
A: ASM is commanded by the DU over the C-plane, using advertised sleep types and wake-up durations, and works at array or processing level. uSleep is decided autonomously inside the RU FPGA per empty OFDM symbol, and gates the PA enable line. It is transparent to the DU and not part of any O-RAN interface.
Q: What is the standard counterpart of Reduced Output Power, and what extra obligation does it place on the DU?
A: MAX-POWER-CONTROL, per tx-array index or per carrier reduction in dB. The DU must restrict scheduled PRBs so the IQ level stays below the reduced maximum. It must lower power before increasing the reduction, and only raise power after the max-power-level-used notification confirms a smaller reduction.
Q: Why might carrier re-activation be slow after an energy-saving period, and how do you guarantee it is instant?
A: With energy-saving-enabled=true and no active carrier the O-RU may go SLEEPING and stop the S-plane. Re-activation then waits for sync. Setting energy-saving-enabled=false keeps the O-RU AWAKE and ready to activate immediately.
Site integration, commissioning & acceptance
CM24 Site Hardware, Power & Earthing — BBU/DU ↔ RRU/AAU ↔ feeder/jumper ↔ TMA ↔ antenna + RET, the -48 V power plant, earthing/lightning and installation rules, with correct typical specs Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
A cell site is a chain of boxes and cables that all have to be right: a baseband unit doing the digital work, a radio making RF power, cables, sometimes a small amplifier at the top of the mast, and the antenna. Behind it sit two things people forget until they fail: the power plant (mains, rectifiers, a -48 V battery bank, maybe a generator) and the earthing and lightning protection that keep people and equipment safe. Older sites ran a thick coaxial feeder up the tower; modern ones run only fibre and DC power to a radio next to the antenna, or to an AAU that combines both. This card gives the honest typical numbers for each block and the installation rules that prevent later alarms.
Three generations of the same site
Each RF joint is a future VSWR or PIM risk; each DC and earth joint is a future power or surge fault.
Level 1 — RF blocks and typical values (always check the datasheet)
BlockRoleTypical values
BBU / DU (+CU in 5G)Baseband, scheduling, protocol stack-48 V DC, 19-inch rack or cabinet; GNSS/PTP sync input. CU–DU is F1 over Ethernet (midhaul), not CPRI.
RRU / RUDAC/ADC, up/down-conversion, PA, LNA, duplexer2T2R/4T4R, e.g. 2×40 W or 4×60 W per band; fronthaul CPRI or eCPRI / O-RAN 7.2x; IP65
AAURadio + antenna array + beamforming32T32R/64T64R at 3.5 GHz typical; fibre + DC only. Used for LTE TDD massive MIMO too, not "5G only".
Main feederGround radio ↔ mast topLoss per 100 m at ~900 MHz / ~2 GHz: 1/2" ≈ 7 / 11 dB; 7/8" ≈ 4 / 6 dB; 1-5/8" ≈ 2.5 / 4 dB. Thicker = lower loss but lower maximum frequency (1-5/8" ≈ 2.5–2.7 GHz, 1/2" ≈ 8 GHz).
JumperShort flexible link at each end1/2" superflex, 1–3 m, ≈0.2 dB/m at 2 GHz. Jumpers are 1/2" in practice, not 1-5/8".
TMAUL low-noise amplifier at the antennaUL gain ≈12 dB, NF ≈1.2–2 dB, DL insertion loss ≈0.3–0.5 dB, bypass on failure; powered by ≈7–30 V DC on the coax via bias-tee (not -48 V).
Diplexer / combinerSeveral bands share one feeder or portInsertion loss 0.2–0.5 dB, cross-band isolation typically ≥50 dB; a same-band hybrid combiner costs ≈3 dB.
RETRemote electrical tilt motorAISG 2.0: RS-485 on an 8-pin connector, 9.6 kbit/s, 10–30 V DC; range often 0–10° or 2–12°, 0.1° steps (see CM08).
ConnectorsThe #1 fault location7/16 DIN ≈25–30 N·m; 4.3-10 ≈5 N·m (screw type); N ≈1.4–1.7 N·m. Low-PIM types on multiband FDD sites. Details: A14.
Return loss is positive and higher is better: RL 20 dB ≈ VSWR 1.22. Writing "RL ≤ -20 dB is good" mixes RL with S11. TMA and feeder loss: 3.5 dB of feeder before a 2.5 dB-NF radio gives a system NF of about 6 dB; a 12 dB / 1.5 dB-NF TMA at the top brings it to about 2 dB (Friis, see NF3). An RRU at the mast top gets about 3 dB without a TMA, which is why TMAs have mostly disappeared.
Level 2 — power plant and earthing
DC power chain: AC mains (230/415 V) → AC distribution (MCB, surge protector) → rectifier modules → DC distribution (breakers/fuses) → loads. A battery bank floats on the same -48 V bus (positive side earthed), and a generator (DG) or solar covers long outages.
ItemTypical values
Rectifier modulesSwitch-mode, input ≈90–290 V AC, output -48 V nominal (adjustable ≈-42 to -58 V), hot-swappable 25–100 A modules, efficiency ≥92–96 %, PF ≥0.98
Battery string4 × 12 V VRLA blocks (or 24 × 2 V cells) = 48 V nominal; float ≈2.25 V/cell = ≈54 V per string; low-voltage disconnect (LVD) at ≈43–44 V protects the batteries
Battery lifeKeep at 20–25 °C; VRLA service life roughly halves for every ≈10 °C above that
GeneratorAutomatic mains-failure (AMF) panel starts it and switches over; weekly test run, log running hours
Site earthCommonly specified <5 Ω; stricter operators or tower/lightning systems ask for 1–2 Ω. Follow the operator spec.
Sizing example. Load: 3 RRUs × 600 W + baseband and transport ≈ 1.8 kW = 3.6 kW → 75 A at 48 V. Battery for 4 h: Ah ≈ P × h / (V × usable fraction) = 3600 × 4 / (48 × 0.8) ≈ 375 Ah → choose 400 Ah (2 strings × 200 Ah). Rectifiers: load 75 A + battery recharge at about 0.1 C (40 A) = 115 A → three 50 A modules plus one spare (N+1).

Earthing and lightning: every frame, rack, radio, cable tray and SPD bonds to one earth bus bar, which connects to the earth pit or ring electrode. The lightning system is air terminal → straight down-conductor → earth electrode. Feeders and DC cables get earthing kits at the top, at the bottom of the tower and at the building entry. Surge protectors go on the AC input, on DC lines to tower radios, and on GNSS and RF lines. Measure earth resistance with a 3-point fall-of-potential tester (potential probe at about 62 % of the current-probe distance), preferably in the dry season, and repeat it regularly.
Level 3 — installation rules that prevent tomorrow's alarms
RuleTypical value / practice
Bend radius, coaxSingle bend ≈10–15 × outer diameter: 1/2" ≈125 mm, 7/8" ≈250 mm, 1-5/8" ≈400–500 mm (datasheet); superflex jumpers ≈30–40 mm
Bend radius, fibrePatch cords ≈30 mm static; outdoor/armoured cable ≈15–20 × diameter; never kink
WeatherproofingSelf-amalgamating tape + PVC tape over it (or a cold-shrink kit) on every outdoor connector; drip loop below connectors
SegregationPower apart from signal and fibre; cross at 90°; UV-resistant ties, not over-tightened; seal unused glands
LabellingBoth ends of every cable: sector, port, band (e.g. "S1-RRU1-ANT-P1"); crossed sectors are the classic mistake that every RF test misses
DC to tower radiosSize for voltage drop: 12.5 A over 60 m of 2 × 6 mm² copper drops ≈4.4 V, so a battery at 44 V delivers ≈39.6 V to the radio, near the bottom of a typical -36 to -57 V input range
Outdoor SFPsIndustrial temperature grade (-40 to +85 °C) in radios; commercial 0–70 °C modules fail in summer or winter
GNSS antennaClear sky (≥120° cone, ideally full), away from metal and other antennas, arrester at the building entry; accept at ≥4 satellites and C/N0 ≥30 dB-Hz
Common errors in training material: TMAs are not fed -48 V and their gain is not 20–40 dB; mmWave radios are AAUs with no feeder, and n78 (3.5 GHz) is not mmWave; the RRU/AAU link to the DU is fronthaul, not F1; a "passive RRU" does not exist; a rural site usually needs less downtilt than a dense urban one, not more.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why do modern sites rarely use TMAs?
A: The RRU or AAU sits within a few metres of the antenna, so less than about 1 dB of loss precedes the receiver. A TMA recovers feeder loss on the uplink; with no long feeder there is little to recover, and it adds a failure point and DL insertion loss.
Q: How is a TMA powered, and how do you know it is working?
A: The radio or a bias-tee puts DC (typically 7–30 V) on the coax. The radio watches the DC current and raises a TMA alarm if it leaves the expected window, and the TMA falls back to bypass. The idle UL RSSI also rises by roughly the TMA gain, which must be entered in the configuration.
Q: Size the battery for a 3.6 kW site that needs 4 hours of backup.
A: 3.6 kW at 48 V is 75 A. 3600 × 4 / (48 × 0.8) ≈ 375 Ah, so fit 400 Ah (two strings of 200 Ah). Also size the rectifiers for load plus recharge current (≈115 A) with one spare module, and remember that cold batteries deliver less capacity.
Q: A tower radio reboots only during mains failures. Why?
A: Voltage drop. On battery the bus falls towards 44–46 V, and the IR drop in a long, thin DC cable takes the radio below its minimum input voltage. Check the cable cross-section against the load current and length; the fix is a thicker cable or a DC booster.
Q: Why is site earthing tested in the dry season?
A: Soil resistivity is highest when dry, so that is the worst case. A value that meets the limit only after rain will fail when it matters.
CM25 On-Site Path Verification — VSWR/return-loss sweep, distance-to-fault, PIM, fibre (loss budget, OTDR) and microwave backhaul checks: procedures, maths and pass criteria Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
Before a site goes live, the engineer proves that the "pipes" are clean: the RF path from radio to antenna, and the transport (fibre or microwave) back to the network. A line sweep sends a signal into the cable and measures how much comes back — a good path swallows almost everything. Distance-to-fault (DTF) uses the same data to show where a reflection happens, like sonar. For fibre, an optical power meter and an OTDR do the same job with light. For microwave, the received level must match the link design. Every trace is saved; it becomes the reference for all later maintenance.
Level 1 — the RF numbers
VSWRReturn lossReflected powerMismatch lossTypical meaning
1.1026.4 dB0.2 %0.01 dBexcellent (single component, good connector)
1.2220.0 dB1 %0.04 dBgood complete antenna line
1.3017.7 dB1.7 %0.07 dBcommon acceptance limit for antenna + feeder
1.5014.0 dB4 %0.18 dBmarginal: a common minimum pass line and alarm region
2.009.5 dB11 %0.51 dBfault: find and fix
3.006.0 dB25 %1.25 dBradios reduce power or shut down (L28)
Γ = (VSWR−1)/(VSWR+1); RL = −20·log₁₀|Γ|; mismatch loss = −10·log₁₀(1−Γ²). The operator method statement sets the limit: VSWR ≤1.5 is a common floor, and many require ≤1.3–1.4 for the antenna line. Theory: M02.
Feeder loss hides reflections: a fault behind 3 dB of cable looks 6 dB better at the bottom because the signal crosses the cable twice. A sweep can pass at ground level while the top joint is poor. That is why DTF is corrected for cable loss.
Reading a DTF trace (return loss vs distance)
Small regular peaks are connectors. A big peak mid-run means a kink, crushed section or water. The last big peak is the antenna. A clean line sits around 25–30 dB between joints.
Level 2 — procedures: RF sweep, DTF, PIM, fibre and microwave
Line sweep / DTF (cable and antenna analyser):
  • Lock the cell or switch off TX for that port. The sweep is a passive, TX-off test: the analyser replaces the radio. Never connect an analyser to a transmitting port.
  • Set the frequency range of the band on that port. Calibrate open–short–load at the end of the test lead, including the adapter you will use.
  • For DTF enter the cable type: velocity factor (foam feeder ≈0.88, superflex jumper ≈0.82–0.83) and loss per metre.
  • Sweep RL/VSWR for the whole line, then DTF. Save both per port with site, sector and port in the file name. Reconnect, torque and weatherproof.
DTF maths: d = vf·c·t/2. Resolution Δd ≈ 1.5×10⁸·vf/span(Hz): about 0.13 m for a 1 GHz span, about 1.3 m for a 100 MHz span. Maximum range = (points − 1) × Δd. A wrong velocity factor places the fault at the wrong height (0.80 instead of 0.88 is a 10 % error).
Symptom → cause: all bands high → common cable, jumper or connector; one band only → antenna element, diplexer/filter or RET section; reading changes with weather or touch → loose or wet connector; very low RL (<5 dB) → open, short or crushed cable.
PIM: two 20 W (43 dBm) tones in the TX band, measure the third-order product in the RX band. A common site limit is ≤−150 to −153 dBc. Tap connectors lightly during the test; a jumping reading means a loose joint (PIM01).

Fibre (fronthaul and backhaul): inspect and clean every connector with a scope first, then check continuity (visual fault locator), optical power with a meter, and the OTDR trace. Never mix APC (green, 8° angle) with UPC connectors. Never look into a live fibre.
ItemTypical value
Singlemode attenuation≈0.35 dB/km at 1310 nm, ≈0.21 dB/km at 1550 nm; splice ≤0.1 dB; mated connector ≤0.5 dB
Common SFPs1310 nm "LR/LX" ≈10 km; 1550 nm 40–80 km; 850 nm multimode ≈300–550 m; CWDM/DWDM for shared fibres. Radio SFPs must be industrial temperature grade.
Loss budget example10G LR: Tx min ≈−8.2 dBm, Rx sensitivity ≈−14.4 dBm → 6.2 dB budget. A 3 km link with 4 connectors and 2 splices ≈1.05 + 2.0 + 0.2 = 3.25 dB → ≈3 dB margin.
Pass checkRx power (read from the SFP digital diagnostics) inside the module window with margin to sensitivity and overload; no CRC/BER errors
Microwave backhaul: align the antennas by peaking the received signal level (RSL) on azimuth and elevation (avoid locking onto a side lobe), then set polarisation and check cross-polar discrimination if XPIC is used.
CheckTypical acceptance
RSL vs designWithin about ±2–3 dB of the planned value (typical RSL −30 to −60 dBm, depending on hop)
Fade margin / availabilityFade margin ≈20 dB or more; design availability 99.95–99.999 % depending on hop role
Service testsEthernet service activation (ITU-T Y.1564 or RFC 2544): throughput, latency (a few ms per hop), loss, jitter; an error-free soak (often 24 h)
Protection1+1 switchover and adaptive modulation steps verified; alarms reach the NMS
Level 3 — pitfalls and expert habits
  • Sweep in-band only. An antenna is matched only in its passband, and a diplexer or TMA reflects everything outside its filter. An out-of-band "fail" means nothing.
  • The aggregate number can hide one bad joint. A line that passes RL overall but shows a 20 dB spike halfway still needs fixing, because that joint will get worse.
  • AAU sites have no external RF path to sweep. Checks move to fronthaul optical power, the radio's built-in VSWR and antenna-calibration results, and UL noise per branch.
  • Radio-side cross-checks need no instrument: idle UL noise per PRB (LTE, ≈−119 to −116 dBm: −121.4 dBm thermal in 180 kHz plus receiver NF); RX branches within ~2–3 dB of each other; UL noise that rises with DL load points to PIM.
  • OTDR habits: use a launch (and tail) cable so the first connector is not hidden in the dead zone. Measure splices from both directions and average, because a single direction can show "gainers".
  • Microwave rain fade grows sharply above ≈10 GHz. A link that passes on a dry commissioning day can fail its availability target in the rainy season if it was accepted with low margin.
  • Keep every trace. A later DTF or OTDR trace compared with the acceptance baseline shows exactly what changed and where to climb.
Corrections to common training sheets: RL values are positive (a joint "at RL 28 dB" is healthy; printing "−28 dB" means S11). A sweep is not done while transmitting at low power. VSWR 1.0–1.5 is not "excellent" for a full line: 1.5 is only 14 dB RL.
Interview Q&A
Q: Convert VSWR 1.5 to return loss. Is it good?
A: Γ = 0.5/2.5 = 0.2, so RL ≈ 14 dB, with 4 % of the power reflected and 0.18 dB mismatch loss. The loss is small, but for a new installation it is only marginal. Many operators want RL ≥ 17–18 dB (VSWR ≈1.3) for the antenna line.
Q: A sweep from the bottom of a 60 m feeder passes, but the site drops calls in rain. What next?
A: Run DTF with the correct velocity factor and cable loss, and compare it with the baseline. Feeder attenuation masks a bad joint at the top in the aggregate RL. Check UL noise per branch in wet and dry conditions, and do a PIM test. Water in a top connector is the usual cause.
Q: Why must the velocity factor be right?
A: DTF converts round-trip time to distance using the propagation speed in the cable. A 10 % error puts you metres away from the real fault on a tall tower.
Q: Rx optical power on a fronthaul link is −13.8 dBm with an LR SFP. Pass?
A: It is within the window but only about 0.6 dB above the ≈−14.4 dBm sensitivity, so there is no margin. Clean and inspect the connectors, check for tight bends and bad splices with the OTDR, and aim for several dB of margin before accepting.
Q: What proves a microwave hop is correctly aligned?
A: RSL within a couple of dB of the planned value on both ends (not a side lobe, which reads 20 dB or more lower), expected cross-polar discrimination, and an error-free service test at the planned capacity.
CM26 Node Bring-up & Datafill — software, licence, initial config, IP/VLAN plan, clock, S1/NG and X2/Xn links, PCI/TAC/ARFCN/neighbours: correct ports and formulas, and the symptom of each wrong digit Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
Once the hardware is installed and powered, the node has to be brought to life and told who it is. It needs the right software and a licence for its features, an identity and management address, a tidy IP/VLAN plan, an accurate clock, working links to the core (S1 or NG) and to its neighbours (X2 or Xn), and finally the radio datafill: PCI, TAC, frequency and neighbour lists. Most bring-up faults are simply one wrong digit in this data, so the skill is knowing which symptom each mistake produces.
Bring-up order
Level 1 — the standard numbers (several training sheets get these wrong)
InterfaceProtocolPort
S1-MMES1AP over SCTP36412
X2-CX2AP over SCTP36422
NG-C (N2)NGAP over SCTP38412
Xn-CXnAP over SCTP38422
F1-C / E1F1AP / E1AP over SCTP38472 / 38462
S1-U, X2-U, N3, Xn-U, F1-UGTP-U over UDP2152
PTPIEEE 1588 over UDP or Ethernet319/320 or EtherType 0x88F7
O-RAN M-planeNETCONF over SSH830
IdentityLTENR
PCI0–503 (168 groups × 3)0–1007 (336 × 3)
TAC16 bit24 bit
Node IDeNB ID 20 bit (macro)gNB ID 22–32 bit (part of the 36-bit NCI)
FrequencyEARFCN: FDL = FDL,low + 0.1·(N − Noffs)NR-ARFCN (3–24.25 GHz): F = 3000 MHz + 15 kHz·(N − 600000)
Frequency accuracy±0.05 ppm (wide area)±0.05 ppm (wide area) — not ±0.01 ppm
TDD phase±1.5 µs to a common reference (3 µs cell to cell)same
Worked frequencies: B3 EARFCN 1650 → 1805 + 0.1·(1650 − 1200) = 1850 MHz DL (UL EARFCN 19650 = 1755 MHz). B1 EARFCN 300 → 2140 MHz. EARFCN 6300 is Band 20 (806 MHz), not a Band 3 channel. NR-ARFCN 636000 → 3000 + 0.015 × 36000 = 3540 MHz (n78). Use the test PLMN 001/01 in labs, never a real operator code.
Level 2 — each bring-up step and its classic mistakes
Software and licence. Check the current version and hardware → download the package → verify the checksum (SHA-256/MD5) → back up the running configuration → load → activate → verify version, alarms and cells → commit. Committing only after verification keeps an automatic fallback to the previous release; never interrupt power during a load. Licences are bound to the node serial number and software release; "invalid licence" usually means the wrong serial or release, and an expired licence can take a cell down (see CM04 for RU firmware).
Initial configuration. Change default passwords, disable insecure services (Telnet, SNMPv1/v2c with the "public" community; use SSH and SNMPv3), set management IP, gateway, DNS, NTP, site identity and timezone, point alarms and traps to the EMS, then back up the configuration.
IP/VLAN plan. One subnet and VLAN per traffic type, e.g. OAM, control plane (S1-C/X2-C/NG-C/Xn-C), user plane (S1-U/N3), sync (PTP/NTP), with about 20 % spare addresses and a loopback for management. Do not carry traffic on VLAN 1, prune the trunk allowed list, and remember IPsec overhead when choosing the MTU.
Clock. GNSS (1PPS + 10 MHz) or PTP (IEEE 1588v2, telecom profiles G.8275.1 with full on-path support or G.8275.2 partial) for phase; SyncE gives frequency only; NTP gives time of day only, never radio-grade frequency or phase. Verify: source LOCKED, holdover not active, offset within limits (CM11, L20).
SymptomUsual cause
Ping to core OK, SCTP never comes upWrong peer IP or port, firewall allows ICMP but blocks SCTP, C-plane VLAN mismatch, IPsec tunnel down
SCTP up, S1/NG Setup FailurePLMN or TAC not configured on the MME/AMF, unknown or duplicate eNB/gNB ID (read the failure cause)
Attach OK, no dataGTP-U path blocked, MTU/fragmentation with IPsec, wrong APN/DNN on the test SIM
X2/Xn down to one neighbourPeer IP or ID wrong, not configured on the peer, port blocked; always check from both ends
HO fails only towards the new cellMissing neighbour relation, PCI collision/confusion, wrong ARFCN in the relation
Cell unlocked but invisibleCell barred flag, sync not locked (TX gated), ARFCN outside the test UE's bands
Level 3 — radio datafill rules that the planning tools enforce (and training sheets forget)
  • PCI collision: two neighbouring cells with the same PCI. PCI confusion: one cell has two neighbours with the same PCI, so a handover can go to the wrong one. Both must be avoided.
  • Mod rules: in LTE keep co-site and adjacent cells on different PCI mod 3 (PSS and CRS positions) and different PCI mod 30 (uplink reference-signal sequence groups). In NR use different mod 3 (PSS) and mod 30 (uplink DMRS). The simple pattern X, X+1, X+2 for three sectors of one site satisfies mod 3.
  • No PCI values are "reserved" by 3GPP — a rule like "never use PCI 0 and 1" is an operator habit at most.
  • TAC design: a tracking area that is too large overloads paging; one that is too small causes TAU/registration storms. Keep high-handover clusters in one TA and avoid TA borders along highways and railways.
  • Neighbours: intra-frequency, inter-frequency and inter-RAT relations; ANR can add them automatically but initial lists come from the plan. Typical A3 settings: offset about 1–5 dB, hysteresis 1–3 dB, time-to-trigger 160–480 ms (TTT is chosen from a fixed list from 0 to 5120 ms). An A3 offset of −6 dB would trigger on a weaker neighbour, so treat such values in a plan with suspicion.
  • Cell parameters: bandwidth (LTE 1.4–20 MHz, NR FR1 up to 100 MHz), TX power per port (e.g. 43 dBm = 20 W for an LTE 20 MHz carrier; always within the radio rating and the RF plan), antenna ports, cell range, SSB position (NR), barred flag.
For an RU test engineer this is the field twin of the lab set-up: the same frequency, power and sync parameters that RCT verifies (CM16 shows how a carrier is activated inside the node).
Interview Q&A
Q: SCTP to the MME is ESTABLISHED but S1 Setup keeps failing. Where do you look?
A: At the S1 Setup Failure cause and the identities it carries. The PLMN and TAC must be configured on the MME, and the eNB ID must be allowed and unique. Transport is already fine because SCTP is up.
Q: Which ports would you open on a firewall for X2 and Xn?
A: SCTP 36422 for X2AP and SCTP 38422 for XnAP, plus UDP 2152 for GTP-U data forwarding. 36412 (S1AP) and 38412 (NGAP) are the core-facing ports that people copy by mistake.
Q: Convert EARFCN 1650 and NR-ARFCN 636000 to frequencies.
A: EARFCN 1650 is in Band 3: 1805 + 0.1 × (1650 − 1200) = 1850 MHz downlink. NR-ARFCN 636000 is in the 3–24.25 GHz range: 3000 + 0.015 × (636000 − 600000) = 3540 MHz.
Q: Why is NTP not enough to synchronise a TDD cell?
A: NTP delivers time of day with millisecond-level accuracy over the network, and no frequency reference. TDD needs ±1.5 µs phase alignment and ±0.05 ppm frequency, which require GNSS or PTP with suitable network support (plus SyncE if used).
Q: Explain PCI confusion with an example.
A: Cell A has two neighbours, B and C, which both use PCI 150. When a UE reports PCI 150, cell A cannot tell which one is meant and may prepare the handover towards the wrong cell. The fix is to re-plan one of the two PCIs.
CM27 Commissioning Tests & Acceptance Gates — SCFT, SSV, alarm tests, then PAT / ATP / SAT / PAC / FAC: checklists, example pass criteria, ATP report outline and rejection reasons Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
After bring-up, two questions remain: does every cell really work? and will the customer accept it? The first is answered by commissioning tests: attach, data, voice, handover, then a drive around the site. The second is a set of formal gates, each with a checklist, pass criteria and a document pack, ending in a signature. The names change from operator to operator — PAT, AT, SAT, ATP, PAC, FAC — but the logic is the same: no evidence, no acceptance, and every open issue has an owner and a date.
From installed to accepted
Level 1 — the commissioning tests
TestHowTypical target (example; the contract decides)
Attach / registrationTest UE per cell, repeated attemptsAll attempts successful
PingTo a core-side server, e.g. 100 pings of 32 bytes, both directions where possible0 % loss; RTT within design (commonly <30–50 ms)
ThroughputUDP/TCP (iPerf-type) DL and UL near the cell in good RFA set share of the theoretical peak for bandwidth, MIMO and UE category; backhaul must not be the limit
VoiceVoLTE/VoNR (or CSFB) MO and MT, emergency-call routing check where requiredSetup success 100 % in the sample; setup time a few seconds; MOS ≥3.5
SMSMO and MT100 %
HandoverSector to sector (intra-site), to each neighbour, LTE↔NR where deployedAll successful in both directions, no ping-pong
NSA / SA specificEN-DC: SgNB addition and NR leg throughput; SA: registration, PDU session, Xn handoverNR leg added and carrying data
Alarm testSimulate faults: pull a fibre, open the cabinet door, switch mains to batteryEach alarm arrives at the NMS with the right severity and time, then clears
SCFT (single cell function test) runs these per cell next to the site. SSV (single site verification) is the drive test: RSRP/SINR per sector match the prediction, each PCI appears in the direction of its azimuth (this catches crossed feeders), and handovers work to real neighbours (method: PT18).
Level 2 — acceptance gates, checklist and document pack
Gate (common names)Run byProves
Installation / site QAInstaller + customer QABuild matches design: civil, mounting, cabling, earthing, labelling, weatherproofing
Pre-acceptance (often "PAT")Vendor / project teamEverything above plus configuration, links, alarms and SCFT; all critical and major issues closed
ATP / AT (acceptance test)Vendor executes, customer witnesses or samplesThe agreed test list and pass criteria in the ATP document
SAT / SSV / cluster acceptanceCustomer + optimisation teamCoverage, capacity and mobility in the live network; failover (power, link) behaviour
PAC (provisional acceptance)CustomerSite may carry commercial traffic; minor items on a punch list
FAC (final acceptance)Customer, after a KPI observation periodKPIs stable, punch list closed, documents complete; often a payment milestone and warranty start
AreaWhat is checkedExample criterion
Power & earthRectifier output, battery backup time, changeover to DG, earth resistanceDC within range; backup as designed; earth <5 Ω or operator value
RF path (CM25)VSWR/RL per port, DTF, PIM, azimuth, tilt, RET calibrationVSWR ≤1.5 (often ≤1.3–1.4); PIM ≤−150 dBc; azimuth ±5°
TransportLink up, optical/RSL levels, latency, loss, capacityError-free, latency within design
SyncGNSS/PTP stateLOCKED, no holdover
AlarmsActive list after testsNo critical/major open; every remaining alarm explained
O&M and securityEMS reachability, config backup, software version, passwords changed, certificatesAll present
KPIs (FAC)Availability, accessibility, retainability, mobility, throughput over days or weekse.g. availability ≥99.5 %, setup success ≥98 %, drop rate ≤1–2 %, HO success ≥98 %
ATP report outline: project and site information; references (design, bill of quantities, drawings); test environment (hardware and software versions, tools with calibration dates); test cases with results (pass / fail / partial / not applicable); KPI summary; issues and actions; attachments (sweep, DTF, PIM, OTDR, earth and drive-test reports, alarm snapshot, configuration backup, photos); sign-off sheet. The as-built drawings and a clear punch list are what reviewers check first.
Level 3 — how acceptance goes wrong
  • Conditional acceptance: minor items → accept with a punch list and dates; major items (open critical alarm, KPI miss, safety defect) → fix and re-test. Classify honestly: marking a site PASS with majors open contradicts the gate rule and returns as a dispute later.
  • Top rejection reasons: missing or inconsistent documents (a photo that does not show the label, traces not saved per port), high earth resistance, unsealed connectors, poor cable management, crossed sectors found in the drive test, configuration that differs from the plan, incomplete O&M handover.
  • Separate the site from the cluster: a new site can miss drop or handover targets because of a neighbour's tilt or a missing relation. Break KPIs down per neighbour relation before accepting the blame.
  • Pre-run everything: the customer usually witnesses a sample of cells. Run the full set yourself first so the witnessed run is a formality.
  • Numbers come from the contract: generic material often quotes different targets for the same KPI (>95 % on one page, ≥98 % on another). Always use the KPI annex of the contract.
  • Lab-to-field chain: field ATP is the last link after lab RCT and conformance (L37). Margins shown in the lab (ACLR, EVM, sensitivity) are what keep field KPIs stable through temperature and ageing.
Interview Q&A
Q: What is the difference between SCFT and SSV?
A: SCFT tests each cell's functions next to the site in good RF: attach, data, voice, SMS, intra-site handover. SSV is a drive test around the site that checks the footprint per sector, PCI versus azimuth and handovers to real neighbours. It catches crossed feeders and overshooting, which SCFT cannot see.
Q: What is the difference between PAC and FAC?
A: Provisional acceptance lets the site carry commercial traffic while minor punch items stay open. Final acceptance comes after a KPI observation period, once every item and document is closed. It is usually tied to payment and the start of the warranty.
Q: The drive test shows sector B's PCI in sector C's direction. What happened, and how do you prove the fix?
A: Crossed feeders or fibres, or a wrong cell-to-radio mapping in the configuration. Correct the cabling or mapping, then repeat the PCI-versus-azimuth drive and the per-branch RSSI check, and attach the new results to the punch-list item.
Q: How do you test alarm integration during commissioning?
A: Create real conditions: pull a fronthaul fibre, open the cabinet door, switch mains off so the site runs on battery. Confirm that each alarm reaches the NMS with the correct severity, object and timestamp, and that it clears when the condition is removed.
Q: Your new site misses its drop-rate target, but its radio and transport are clean. What next?
A: Break the drops down by cause and by neighbour relation. Drops often cluster on handovers to one neighbour (missing relation, PCI conflict, the neighbour's tilt). Fix it or document it as a cluster issue, so the site is not rejected for a problem it did not cause.
CM28 Site Alarm Triage, Maintenance & Field Safety — severity/response matrix, bottom-up triage (power → transport → sync → hardware → RF → config), first checks, preventive maintenance and safety rules Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
When a site misbehaves the NOC sees a list of alarms, often dozens at once. Most are consequences of one root problem: when mains power fails and the batteries run out, the transport drops, the cells go down and the core complains too. The first-line engineer finds the lowest broken layer — power, transport, sync, hardware, RF path, then configuration — fixes it, and watches the rest clear. Good sites also need preventive maintenance so alarms do not happen, and every visit must be safe. Radio-internal fault IDs are covered in CM20, RU fault behaviour in L28, automatic recovery in CM02 and cabinet/environment inputs in CM10.
Triage order
Level 1 — severity, response time and the alarm families
Severity (X.733)MeaningTypical response (set by the SLA)Examples
CriticalService lostImmediately (≈0–15 min to start)Cell or site down, power failure, transport link down
MajorDegraded or at riskWithin hoursHigh VSWR, GNSS lost (holdover), fan failure, rectifier module fault, high packet loss
MinorNo service impact yetSame or next working dayTemperature warning, optical power low, door open, battery warning
WarningInformation or trendPlannedLicence expiry warning, configuration change
FamilyTypical alarmsWhat follows if ignored
PowerMains failure, rectifier fault, battery discharging, DC low/high, LVD operated, radio under-voltageSite runs on battery for its backup time, then drops
TransportSFP LOS/LOF, optical Rx low, Ethernet down, MW RSL low or high BER, S1/NG or X2/Xn SCTP down, GTP-U path failureCells may be disabled or barred when the core link is lost; handovers fail when X2/Xn is down
SyncGNSS antenna fault or no satellites, PTP unlocked, holdover active or expiredCells stay up in holdover for a vendor-dependent time; after that TDD cells normally stop transmitting
HardwareBoard or radio fault, fan failure, over-temperature, fronthaul link down, radio unreachableRadio or cell down, PA power reduced for protection
RF pathVSWR high, TMA current out of range, RET fault or not calibrated, RX branch imbalance, UL interferenceOutput power cut back (VSWR), poor uplink, edge drops
Level 2 — triage matrix: first checks and frequent root causes
AlarmRemote first checksOn-site checksFrequent root causes
VSWR highWhich port and band; value and history; does it follow rain or DL power; other branches normal?Jumpers and connectors at both ends, weatherproofing, sweep + DTF vs baseline (CM25)Loose or wet connector, damaged jumper, antenna or diplexer fault, unterminated port
S1/NG downPing gateway and core, SCTP state, recent changes, other sites on the same routerTransport LEDs, SFP optical power, patch cordsTransport outage, IP/VLAN or firewall change, core-side outage or configuration
SFP LOS / optical lowRx power trend: sudden drop = break, slow drift = dirt or ageingClean and inspect, meter reading, swap SFP, OTDRDirty connector, tight bend, wrong SFP type, fibre cut
MW link degradedRSL and modulation history, weatherAlignment, ODU cable and connectorsRain fade, misalignment after wind, new obstruction, interference
GNSS / PTP unlockedSatellites and C/N0, PTP master reachable, time in holdoverAntenna sky view, cable, arrester, waterObstruction, cable fault, grandmaster or boundary-clock fault, path asymmetry
Mains fail / DC lowMains status, battery voltage trend, rectifier modules, generator startDC at rectifier and at radio, breakers, terminalsGrid outage, failed rectifier, aged batteries, generator did not start, DC cable voltage drop
Cell down (no lower alarm)Admin state, licence, cell config, radio ready, sync gatingRarely neededCell left locked after work, licence expired, configuration error, radio not ready (CM16)
Handling loop: acknowledge → read the details (object, time, severity) → correlate with related alarms → find the root cause → fix → verify the service (call, ping, throughput) → confirm the alarm cleared by itself → record the cause and action.
Level 3 — correlation, maintenance and field safety
Correlation habits:
  • The first alarm in time in the lowest layer is usually the root cause. Check NTP first: clock skew between systems breaks the time line.
  • VSWR that follows weather or time of day points at water or a connector changing with temperature. Compare DTF with the acceptance trace.
  • High UL noise without VSWR is interference or PIM. PIM follows your own DL load (PIM01).
  • A flapping alarm (raised and cleared many times per hour) means a marginal level: optical power, DC voltage or VSWR near its threshold. Fix the margin, do not filter the alarm.
  • Most outages follow a change. Ask "what changed?" (software, parameters, transport work) before climbing. Useful RCA tools: 5 Whys, fishbone and Pareto (a few alarm types usually cause most of the downtime).
Preventive maintenance (typical intervals; operators set their own):
IntervalTasks
Daily/weekly (remote)Alarm and KPI review, battery-discharge events, sync state
MonthlyVisual inspection, connectors and weatherproofing, VSWR/RSSI trend, optical levels, rectifier and DC voltages, filters and fans, generator test run
QuarterlyBattery capacity or backup-time test, terminal cleaning, antenna mounting and RET check, software and log review
Yearly / dry seasonEarth resistance measurement, lightning system inspection, tower and bolt audit
Field safety — never skip:
  • RF exposure: stay out of the main beam of live antennas and AAUs; lock or power down the sector (or follow the site RF exposure zone plan) before working in front of it (L33).
  • Working at height: trained climbers only, full-body harness, double lanyard with 100 % tie-off, tools tethered or in a bag, no climbing in high wind, rain or lightning.
  • Electrical: lock-out/tag-out, verify that voltage is absent, insulated tools. DC plants deliver very high short-circuit currents: insulate tools and remove rings and watches near battery terminals.
  • Batteries: ventilate battery rooms (VRLA can release hydrogen when overcharged), use eye protection, and have an eyewash and spill kit ready.
  • Fibre: never look into a fibre or connector; invisible laser light can damage the eye. Use a power meter or scope with a filter.
Corrections to common training sheets: an S1 or X2 link is SCTP, so a successful ping does not prove it — check the association and the setup procedure. X2 uses port 36422 and Xn 38422 (not 36412). LTE has no soft handover (that was UMTS). The LTE periodic TAU timer is T3412 (T3212 is a 2G/3G timer).
Interview Q&A
Q: The NOC reports 40 alarms on a site at once. How do you start?
