A: Sort by time and by layer. Take the earliest alarm in the lowest layer (power, then transport, then sync), fix that and watch whether the others clear. Most of the list is usually consequences.
Q: A VSWR alarm appears every morning and clears by midday. Likely cause?
A: A connector or jumper that lets in moisture, or whose contact changes with temperature: dew at night, drying and expansion during the day. Check the weatherproofing and compare DTF with the acceptance trace to find the joint.
Q: GNSS is lost but the cells are still on air. Is that OK?
A: Only for a while. The clock is in holdover and stays within limits for a vendor-dependent time. Fix the GNSS before holdover expires, because TDD cells normally stop transmitting once phase accuracy can no longer be guaranteed.
Q: Ping to the MME works but the S1 alarm stays. What else do you check?
A: The SCTP association (a firewall may pass ICMP but block SCTP 36412), the peer addresses configured on both ends, and the S1 Setup result. A PLMN or TAC mismatch fails at the application layer even when transport is fine.
Q: Why is preventive maintenance worth the truck roll?
A: Most site outages come from slow degradation: ageing batteries, drying weatherproofing, clogged filters, drifting optical levels. Finding them on a planned visit is much cheaper than an outage, and trend data (VSWR, optical Rx, battery backup time) shows which sites to visit first.
Cloud-native RAN platform
CM29 Cloud-Native RAN Platform — Kubernetes for vRAN, CPU pinning/isolation, huge pages, DPDK/SR-IOV, NUMA, RT kernel: what goes wrong and how to check Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
A virtualised or cloud-native RAN runs the baseband (DU/CU) as software containers on ordinary servers orchestrated by Kubernetes. The catch: the physical layer has hard deadlines — an LTE subframe or NR slot is processed in well under a millisecond, and fronthaul packets must arrive inside a microsecond-scale window (CM19). A normal Linux server is tuned for average throughput, not for "never late". So the platform is carefully bent into a real-time machine: dedicated CPU cores nobody else may touch, huge memory pages so lookups are fast and predictable, DPDK and SR-IOV so packets bypass the kernel, everything placed on the same NUMA node, and a real-time kernel. When one of these is wrong, the RAN does not crash neatly — it produces rare late slots, HARQ failures and throughput dips that look like radio problems. This card is generic (no specific product).
What a correctly placed DU looks like on a dual-socket server
Level 1 — the building blocks
BlockWhat it doesHow it is configured (typical)Symptom if wrong
CPU isolationRemoves cores from the general scheduler, stops timer ticks and RCU callbacks on themKernel cmdline isolcpus=, nohz_full=, rcu_nocbs=, irqaffinity= (housekeeping only); tuned "realtime" profilePeriodic latency spikes, late slot processing
CPU pinning in k8sGives the pod exclusive whole coreskubelet CPU Manager static policy; pod QoS Guaranteed (requests = limits, integer CPUs)Threads share cores with other pods → jitter
NUMA alignmentKeeps CPU, memory, NIC and accelerator on one socketkubelet Topology Manager single-numa-node; Memory ManagerExtra 100s of ns per access, unpredictable throughput
Huge pagesLarge (2 MB/1 GB) pages → few TLB misses, memory pre-reserved for DPDKKernel default_hugepagesz=1G hugepagesz=1G hugepages=N; pod requests hugepages-1GiDPDK/L1 fails to start ("cannot allocate memory") or pod pending
DPDKUser-space poll-mode NIC drivers, no interrupts, no kernel copiesVF bound to vfio-pci; dedicated poll cores (show 100% CPU by design)Packet drops, rx_missed errors
SR-IOVSplits a physical NIC into virtual functions handed directly to podsSR-IOV network device plugin + CNI, Multus for secondary interfaces; VF VLAN/trust/spoof-check settingsNo fronthaul interface in pod, VLAN mismatch, VF lost after reboot
Real-time kernelPREEMPT_RT: almost everything preemptible → bounded latencyRT kernel package, RT thread priorities (SCHED_FIFO) for L1 threadsWorst-case latency tens-hundreds of µs
Power/BIOSStable frequency, no deep sleepDisable deep C-states, fix P-state/turbo policy, disable SMT if required, SR-IOV/VT-d on in BIOSWake-up latency, frequency wobble
TimingPTP to the NIC hardware clock, then system clockptp4l (G.8275.1 profile) + phc2sys, often in a dedicated pod/daemonRU out of sync, carrier not activated (CM11/CM16)
AcceleratorsOffload LDPC/turbo FECDevice plugin exposes accelerator VFs; bound with vfio-pciCPU overload or decode failures
Level 2 — how to check a node (commands you will actually run)
# kernel & isolation
cat /proc/cmdline                      # isolcpus / nohz_full / hugepages present?
cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/isolated
lscpu | grep -i -E "numa|socket|thread"
numactl -H                             # memory per NUMA node

# huge pages
grep -i huge /proc/meminfo
cat /sys/devices/system/node/node0/hugepages/hugepages-1048576kB/free_hugepages

# NIC / SR-IOV / DPDK
cat /sys/class/net/<pf>/device/sriov_numvfs
cat /sys/class/net/<pf>/device/numa_node
ip link show <pf>                      # VF list, VLAN, trust, spoofchk
dpdk-devbind.py --status               # which VFs are on vfio-pci
ethtool -S <pf> | grep -i -E "drop|miss|err"

# Kubernetes view
kubectl describe node <node> | grep -A12 -i allocatable   # cpu, hugepages-1Gi, sriov/fec resources
kubectl get pod <du-pod> -o jsonpath="{.status.qosClass}"  # must be Guaranteed
cat /var/lib/kubelet/cpu_manager_state                    # exclusive CPU sets

# real-time quality
cyclictest -m -p95 -t -a <isolated-cpus> -D 1h -q      # worst-case latency
grep -E "ctxt|intr" /proc/stat; cat /proc/interrupts      # IRQs landing on isolated cores?
turbostat --quiet sleep 10                                # C-state residency, frequency
pmc -u -b 0 "GET TIME_STATUS_NP"                          # PTP offset, master

Acceptance ideas: cyclictest over 1–24 h on isolated cores with worst-case latency within the RAN vendor's budget (typically low tens of µs); zero rx_missed on fronthaul VFs at full cell load; PTP offset stable within tens of ns; after a node reboot all of the above come back automatically (VF count, hugepages, bindings) and the DU pod re-schedules to the same aligned resources.

Level 3 — what goes wrong in real deployments
  • "Rare late slot" syndrome: throughput fine in short tests, then a few HARQ failures per hour and occasional UL CRC bursts. Root causes: an IRQ (e.g. storage or management NIC) migrated onto an isolated core by irqbalance, a kernel worker thread, or a monitoring agent exec-ing into the pod. Fix: pin IRQs to housekeeping cores, disable irqbalance or ban isolated cores, keep agents off RT cores.
  • Cross-NUMA placement: the pod got cores on socket 0 but the SR-IOV VF or FEC card sits on socket 1 (the device plugin did not report NUMA or Topology Manager was "none"). Symptom: higher CPU load per cell and load-dependent jitter.
  • Hugepages fragmented: 1 GB pages must be reserved at boot; allocating at runtime often fails after uptime. Pod stays Pending with "insufficient hugepages-1Gi".
  • SR-IOV lost on reboot: VFs created by a manual echo into sriov_numvfs disappear after reboot; the DU pod then cannot start. Use the operator/daemon that re-creates VFs, and include a reboot in every acceptance run.
  • Firmware/driver mismatch: NIC firmware, kernel driver and DPDK PMD versions must be a supported combination; PTP hardware timestamping in particular breaks silently.
  • SMT/hyper-thread siblings: pinning an RT thread to one logical CPU while its sibling runs something noisy — allocate full physical cores (CPU Manager option "full-pcpus-only").
  • Throttling: CPU CFS quota applied to a Guaranteed pod on older setups causes micro-throttling; check cpu.stat nr_throttled.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why does a DU pod need Guaranteed QoS?
A: Only Guaranteed pods (requests = limits, integer CPUs) get exclusive cores from the kubelet static CPU Manager; without exclusivity RT threads share cores and miss slot deadlines.
Q: What do isolcpus, nohz_full and rcu_nocbs do?
A: isolcpus removes cores from the general scheduler, nohz_full stops the periodic tick on them when a single task runs, rcu_nocbs moves RCU callbacks off them — together they remove OS noise from RT cores.
Q: Why DPDK plus SR-IOV for fronthaul?
A: SR-IOV gives the pod a hardware NIC function directly; DPDK polls it from user space with no interrupts or kernel copies, which keeps latency low and predictable at high packet rates.
Q: How do you check NUMA alignment for a running DU?
A: Compare the pod's exclusive CPUs (cpu_manager_state) with lscpu NUMA mapping, and the numa_node of the NIC PF and accelerator in sysfs; all should be on the same node, and Topology Manager should be single-numa-node.
Q: Throughput dips a few times an hour on a vRAN cell — first checks?
A: cyclictest on the RT cores, /proc/interrupts for IRQs on isolated cores, C-state/frequency with turbostat, NIC drop counters, PTP offset history, and whether any other process was scheduled on those cores.
Addition — DU server BIOS profile, the two O-Cloud host stacks, and BMC recovery
A concrete BIOS profile (from a lab DU bring-up guide for Ice Lake / Skylake-class servers) — the "Power/BIOS" row of Level 1 made specific:
BIOS areaSetting for a vRAN DU serverWhy
Start point"Restore Optimized Defaults" (Save & Exit), then change only the items belowknown baseline; vendor defaults differ per board
CPUHyper-Threading on, Intel VT on, AES-NI on, prefetchers onthe DU pinning plan assumes sibling threads exist; VT/VT-d for SR-IOV passthrough
Power policyPower technology Custom, BIOS controls EPB, energy-perf bias = Maximum Performancestop the CPU trading latency for power
P-statesSpeedStep on, Turbo on, Energy-Efficient Turbo off, Hardware P-states offthe OS (tuned profile) controls frequency, not the hardware governor
C-statesAutonomous core C-state off, C6 report off, C1E off, package C-state limited to C0/C1deep-sleep exit latency would land inside a slot deadline
T-statesSoftware-controlled T-states offno throttling by clock modulation
PCIeSR-IOV support enabledwithout it no VFs can be created for fronthaul
After a BIOS change, verify from Linux: turbostat should show almost no C6 residency on RT cores and a steady frequency. Some FOCOM releases can correct BIOS settings automatically through an optional BIOS service package installed on the FOCOM server.

Two O-Cloud host stacks in PW labs: Ubuntu + EKS-Anywhere (Ubuntu 24.04 nodes, k8s 1.35, RT kernel 6.4 from release 2026.3) and SUSE SL-Micro + RKE2 (cilium CNI, SUSE Edge images). The real-time tuning above applies to both; only the provisioning path differs — FOCOM builds either kind from bare metal (see CM37, CM38).

BMC / IPMI is the recovery path. When a node no longer boots or loses its network: open the BMC remote console, mount an install ISO as virtual media, power-reset and pick the virtual drive from the boot menu (F11 on many boards). Get the BMC address with ipmitool lan print on the console if unknown, and keep it on a reachable management VLAN — FOCOM itself provisions servers through the BMC (Redfish/IPMI), so a BMC that cannot be reached also blocks re-provisioning.
Addition — the production RT kernel: patch order, the self-IPI spike, the cmdline set and how new kernels regress
The production RT kernel in practice. The DU/RCT servers run a PREEMPT_RT kernel (5.15.160-rt77) built as .deb packages (make deb-pkg) inside a pinned Docker toolchain. Patches go on in a strict order: upstream RT patchset, then the local source patch, then rt-sched-*.patch files in lexical filename order. The later patches were generated against the post-RT tree, so reordering breaks the hunks; name future files 01-, 02- so they sort correctly. Keep the upstream RT tarball pristine and put every local fix in its own file.

The self-IPI latency spike. The RT scheduler pushes runnable RT tasks to other CPUs by chaining an IPI across the CPUs in the overload mask. The scan could pick the CPU that was already running the handler and send an interrupt to itself. On x2APIC that is a write to the self-IPI MSR (0x83F); it fires at hardware-interrupt level and preempts everything, including the highest-priority SCHED_FIFO thread. On dense RT deployments it appeared as unexplained latency spikes on isolated cores, exactly what PREEMPT_RT is meant to prevent. The fix (a backport of an upstream scheduler change) skips the current CPU when walking the mask. Lesson: if an isolated, top-priority core still shows rare spikes, look for interrupts no priority can mask.

NVMe queue cap. Stock NVMe creates IO queues per possible CPU, so a high-core host gets many MSI-X vectors and per-CPU queue contexts. A local patch adds a total_io_queues module parameter (e.g. modprobe nvme total_io_queues=8, or write it under /sys/module/nvme/parameters/) so operations can cap it without a rebuild.

Shared kernel command line for the RT hosts:
Cmdline parameterWhy it is there
idle=poll, intel_idle.max_cstate=2Keep cores out of deep C-states; wake-up latency from deep sleep is a jitter source
intel_iommu=on iommu=ptIOMMU needed for vfio-pci (DPDK VFs), pass-through mode for host devices so normal I/O pays no translation cost
mitigations=off, nosoftlockupRemove speculative-execution mitigation overhead and soft-lockup warnings from 100%-busy poll cores
rcu_nocb_poll, rcutree.kthread_prio=99Offloaded RCU callbacks polled by kthreads that run at high RT priority
hugepagesz=1G hugepages=32Pre-reserved 1 GB pages for DPDK and L1
isolcpus=managed_irq,domain,<list> plus nohz_full and rcu_nocbs with the same listEvery core except 2 housekeeping cores per socket isolated, tickless and free of RCU callbacks
irqaffinity=<housekeeping cores>Device interrupts kept on the housekeeping cores
Validating a new kernel: diff, do not trust. A 6.4 RT kernel was built from one vendor source package for two distributions. Of 11,241 config lines only 31 differed, and the RT settings were identical (PREEMPT_RT, NO_HZ_FULL, RCU_NOCB_CPU, RCU_BOOST, HZ_250). Yet the review still found three regressions in one build:
• Module signing lost: the signing-key path was blanked and sign-all was unset, so modules were unsigned; NIC drivers (i40e/iavf) were also side-loaded out of tree, tainting the kernel. Nothing failed at boot because signature enforcement was off, which is exactly why nobody noticed.
• No MAC security module: AppArmor had dropped out of the LSM list while the command line still disabled SELinux, leaving only classic Unix permissions.
• CPU frequency governor: the "performance by default" option was dropped, so the governor must be set to performance at runtime and checked after every upgrade; a powersave governor on RT cores is a latency source.
Method: diff /boot/config-* and /proc/cmdline between the old and new kernel, and check module taint, active LSMs and the governor on a booted box before declaring the kernel equivalent.
Addition: SMT sibling pairing, the "second NUMA node" myth, and reserving housekeeping cores
Finding the sibling of a logical CPU. On the single-socket Xeon DU/PHY test hosts seen in the lab, logical CPU n and n + (logical count / 2) are the two hardware threads of one physical core: on a 48-thread host the pair of 2 is 26, on a 64-thread host the pair of 2 is 34. That is a common enumeration, not a law — always confirm on the host:
lscpu -e=CPU,CORE,SOCKET,NODE          # CORE column: same number = siblings
cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu2/topology/thread_siblings_list   # e.g. "2,34"
numactl --hardware                      # how many NUMA nodes really exist
docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.CpusetCpus}}' <container>       # what a container was given
Give a real-time workload whole physical cores = both siblings. Example on a 64-thread host: physical cores 2–7 = logical 2-7,34-39. If you give only 2–7, another workload scheduled on 34–39 shares the same execution units and caches and steals cycles from your PHY thread. A DU configuration with CPU_LIST=2,34 is exactly "core 2 and its sibling".

Misconception to avoid: the upper half of the CPU numbers (e.g. 32–63) is not a second NUMA node on a single-socket host — they are sibling threads on node 0. numactl --hardware settles it in one line.

ARM DU CPUs without SMT (Octeon-class): no siblings to pair, allocate sequential physical cores. On every host type reserve cores 0–1 (and, on x86, their siblings) for the OS, SSH, the container runtime and interrupts — never hand every core to the workload, or the node becomes unreachable under load.

Host settings seen on these test hosts: 1 GiB huge pages (24–48 per x86 host; 512 MB pages on the ARM hosts), vm.overcommit_ratio 50%, minimal swap.
Addendum — kubectl shorthands, the 5G pod set, deployment workflow order and LLS-C3 checks on a worker node
Everyday kubectl shorthands used on vRAN worker nodes (all pods live in namespace pw):
alias kg='kubectl get pods -n pw'          # list pods + status
alias kd='kubectl describe pod -n pw'      # kd <pod>
alias kdel='kubectl delete pod -n pw'      # pod respawns with DEFAULT config: manual edits are lost
ke() { kubectl exec -n pw -it "$1" -- bash; }   # ke <pod>: shell inside the container
Typical pod set on a 5G worker node:
PodRole
bbuvBBU manager / OAM for the node
cunode01 / dunode02CU and DU stack instances (numbered per node)
phynode02, 03 ...One 5G PHY per cell / RU
netconM-plane: NETCONF client towards the RUs
ptpmgrptp4l / phc2sys management (status files under /run/ptpmanager)
rscmgrResource manager (CPU / VF / accelerator allocation)
xdbsrvr, ciph-appData-store server and ciphering application
Orchestrated deployment order (REST, via the deployment service or Postman): create an empty deployment (name = ID = worker node, CSAR version, manifest ID = the access build, device ID with HW class, OUI and the server serial from dmidecode -s system-serial-number) → PUT the OAM address → executeWorkflow "deploy" target platform → PUT backhaul / global settings → deploy vBBU manager → deploy vNode services. Three workflows, always in that order; a failure in one blocks the next.
Address planning: one 5G E2E node needs at least 7 IP addresses (OAM, vBBU, cell/service addresses ...); reserving a contiguous block per node and encoding the OAM address in the host name avoids collisions.
LLS-C3 bring-up check: when RU and DU fronthaul both hang off a PTP grandmaster / xHaul switch, both ports must be in the same (private) VLAN. If the RU never gets its fronthaul address from the vBBU, check that VLAN and the switch MAC table (is the RU MAC learnt on the right port?) before touching the pods. On the RU, the on-time packet counter should equal the total received; any early/late counts point to timing (CM19).
CM30 Upgradability & Resilience — rolling/in-service upgrade, NIC & RU firmware, multi-node cluster failure, geo-redundant SMO, load profiling Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
A mobile network is expected to stay up 24/7, yet its software changes every few weeks and its hardware eventually fails. Upgradability is about changing software and firmware — baseband pods, NIC firmware, radio-unit firmware — with the least possible outage and a guaranteed way back. Resilience is about surviving failures — a crashed process, a dead server, a lost data centre for the management system — and recovering automatically. Load profiling tells you how much headroom you really have before either of these becomes dangerous. This card collects generic patterns and, most importantly, how to test them. See CM04 (RRH firmware upgrade), CM29 (the platform), ZT4 (NSA resilience tests).
Level 1 — upgrade types and what they cost
What is upgradedTypical methodService impactRollback
CU / management microservices (stateless or replicated)Kubernetes rolling update (maxUnavailable / maxSurge), Helm upgrade, canary on a subset of sitesNone to seconds if replicas > 1 and state is externalHelm rollback / previous image tag
DU (real-time L1/L2 pod)Replace pod; usually no surge possible because the second copy would need the same SR-IOV VFs, FEC and RU linkCell outage of seconds–minutes unless a standby DU/node or an overlapping cell carries the usersRe-deploy previous version; keep old image cached on the node
Host OS / kernel / RT tuningDrain node (cordon), upgrade, reboot, uncordonAll pods on that node move or stopA/B boot partitions or re-image
NIC / accelerator firmwareVendor NVM update tool, then reboot or device resetNode outage; must match driver + DPDK versionPrevious NVM image; test compatibility matrix first
RU firmwareO-RAN M-plane software management: software-download → software-install into the inactive slot → software-activate → resetCarrier off only during reset/re-activation (minutes)RU falls back to the other slot if the new image fails to boot / call home
SMO / EMS (management)Active–standby or multi-replica, upgrade standby first then switch overManagement gap only; traffic unaffectedSwitch back to the old side
Level 1 — resilience building blocks
  • Process/pod level: liveness/readiness probes, restart policies, PodDisruptionBudgets so voluntary operations never take all replicas; SCTP (S1/NG/X2/F1) re-establishment after restart.
  • Node level: pods reschedule to healthy nodes — except hardware-bound DU pods, which need a pre-provisioned standby node with the same NIC/FEC/fronthaul reach (N+1 pooling).
  • Cluster control plane: 3 (or 5) control-plane nodes; etcd needs a majority (quorum = ⌊N/2⌋+1), so 3 nodes survive 1 failure, 5 survive 2. Losing quorum freezes changes but running pods keep running.
  • Geo-redundancy of management/SMO: two sites, data replicated (synchronous for small RPO, asynchronous across long distance), a witness/arbiter to avoid split-brain, defined RTO (time to restore service) and RPO (data you may lose). Network elements must reconnect to the surviving site automatically (multiple NETCONF call-home / VES endpoints, DNS or VIP switchover).
  • RU level: dual software slots, watchdogs, supervision (M-plane keep-alive; RU stops transmitting if supervision is lost — CM05).
Level 2 — how to test it
TestHowPass criteria to record
Upgrade under trafficUEs with continuous DL/UL + VoLTE/VoNR calls; run the full upgrade procedureOutage duration per cell (from UE logs / counters), calls dropped, time to KPI recovery, no config loss
RollbackUpgrade, then roll back; also upgrade to a deliberately broken imageAutomatic fallback works, same config and KPIs as before
RU firmware failureInterrupt power during software-install; corrupt imageRU boots from the old slot, calls home, carrier re-activates (CM04/CM16)
Pod killkubectl delete pod / kill -9 main process for each microserviceRecovery time, SCTP links back, UEs re-attach, alarms raised and cleared
Node failurePower-off or drain a worker; power-off a control-plane nodePods reschedule (non-DU), DU fails over to standby if designed, etcd quorum kept
Network partitionCut links between sites or between cluster nodesNo split-brain, one side stays active, clean re-sync when the link returns
Geo switchoverPlanned and unplanned switchover of SMO/EMSRTO/RPO within target, all NEs reconnected, PM/FM data gap bounded
Soak / load profile72 h+ at busy-hour load with mobility and attach stormsCPU per core, per-slot processing time percentiles, memory growth (leaks), no crashes

Load profiling: build a traffic model (users per cell, active ratio, attach/HO/paging rates per hour, throughput mix), run it at 50/80/100/120% of target, and record the worst core and the 99.9th-percentile L1/L2 processing time — averages hide the late slots that matter. The headroom left at 100% is what upgrades, failovers (where one node absorbs another's load) and traffic peaks will consume.

Level 3 — pitfalls learned the hard way
  • "Zero-downtime" that isn't: rolling updates of a stateful service without externalised state drop sessions; readiness probes that turn green before SCTP links are up send traffic to a pod that cannot serve it.
  • Version skew: during a rolling upgrade old and new versions run together — interfaces (internal APIs, config schema, database migrations) must be backward compatible for at least one version.
  • Firmware compatibility matrix: a NIC firmware upgrade that works with the new driver but not the old one turns a rollback into an outage. Always test the rollback path, not only the upgrade.
  • Standby DU never tested: failover capacity exists on paper but the standby node has a different BIOS, NIC firmware or VF setup. Periodic scheduled failover drills catch it.
  • Split-brain in geo-redundancy: both sites become active after a link cut and both push configuration to network elements. A witness in a third location or strict fencing is mandatory.
  • Memory leaks show only in soak tests; a service that grows 50 MB/day will be OOM-killed weeks later at busy hour. Track RSS trends, not snapshots.
  • Alarm storms during upgrades hide real faults; suppression windows must be scoped and must end automatically.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why can't a DU be upgraded with a normal Kubernetes rolling update?
A: A surge copy would need the same exclusive hardware (SR-IOV VFs, FEC, fronthaul link to the RU) on the same node, which is already in use. So a DU upgrade means a short cell outage unless a standby DU/node or overlapping coverage takes the users.
Q: How does O-RAN RU firmware upgrade stay safe?
A: Via M-plane software management: download and install into the inactive slot, then activate and reset. If the new image fails to boot or connect, the RU falls back to the previous slot.
Q: How many control-plane nodes do you need to tolerate one failure?
A: Three — etcd needs a majority (2 of 3). Five nodes tolerate two failures.
Q: What are RTO and RPO?
A: RTO is the maximum time to restore service after a failure; RPO is the maximum amount of data (time window) that may be lost. Geo-redundancy design and replication mode are chosen to meet both.
Q: What would you record in an upgrade-under-traffic test?
A: Per-cell outage duration, dropped calls/sessions, KPI recovery time, alarms raised/cleared, configuration integrity after upgrade, and the same metrics for rollback.
Addition — RU A/B flashing practice and the regression bisect method
RU A/B slots in daily practice (PW RU, script path). Outside the M-plane flow, lab engineers flash with the RU upgrade script: it writes the inactive slot, flips selected_slot and reboots, so the previous build stays as the fallback (design details and power-cut rules: CM36).
rm -rf image_upgrade                      # stale-extract trap: if the folder exists, unzip is skipped
                                          # and the OLD files are flashed without any error
yes | bash RU_upgrade.sh <build>.zip
md5sum <slot BOOT / image files>          # compare with the build manifest
cat /etc/rfsoc_fru_detail.txt             # running version, commit, branch, timestamp
# afterwards: delete upgrade zips and image_upgrade from the RU data partition - they accumulate
Also expect the RU M-plane address to change after a version change; re-find it before the next step.

Regression bisect — "halve the date range". When a feature works on an older build and fails on the latest, flash a build from the middle of the range, test, and keep the half that contains the change. Record per build in one table: availability state, carrier activation, the actual pass criterion (SSB seen / UE attaches), plus any new faults. Three rules keep it reliable: (1) verify what is running, not what you think you flashed; (2) mark a point uncertain if the unit is unstable (e.g. periodic watchdog reboots) rather than forcing a verdict; (3) when several regressions overlap, pick builds that isolate the one you are chasing — a later, worse failure can mask it. Six flashes took a six-week window down to six days and one FPGA change: the full worked case is CM40. Keep the A/B fallback in mind — each bisect flash leaves the previous build one slot away, so a bad point costs one reboot, not a re-image.
O-RAN in depth — C/U-plane, RIC, SMO, O-RU/O-DU, sync
CM31 O-RAN C/U-Plane Packet Anatomy — eCPRI header, eAxC, section types 0/1/3/4/5/6/7, section fields and IQ compression (BFP, µ-law, modulation compression) with a bandwidth worked example Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
The DU and the RU talk on the fibre in two kinds of short Ethernet packets. A C-plane packet is the work order: "in slot 7, symbols 2–13, PRBs 0–272 of antenna stream 3, use beam 12, and the IQ will be 9-bit block-floating-point". A U-plane packet is the parcel itself: the compressed IQ samples for those PRBs. Both are wrapped in an eCPRI header that says what kind of message it is and which antenna stream (eAxC) it is for. Once you can read these headers in Wireshark, most "RU transmits garbage / nothing" problems stop being a mystery. CM15 covers the four planes and CM19 the timing windows; this card opens the packet itself.
Anatomy of an O-RAN 7.2x fronthaul packet (own drawing)
Field widths from O-RAN.WG4.CUS.0 (C/U-plane chapters) and eCPRI v2.0 §3.1. The 4-byte eCPRI common header is followed by 4 bytes of PC_ID/RTC_ID + SEQ_ID.
Level 1 — headers, message types and the section types
eCPRI common header (4 bytes): revision (4 bits, =1), reserved, C (concatenation) bit, message type (8 bits) and payload size (16 bits). Then 2 bytes of stream ID and 2 bytes of sequence ID. O-RAN uses only a few eCPRI message types:
eCPRI msg typeNameO-RAN use
0IQ dataU-plane — the ID field is called PC_ID and holds the eAxC
2Real-time control dataC-plane — the ID field is called RTC_ID and holds the eAxC
5One-way delay measurementoptional: measure fronthaul delay (feeds the CM19 window calculation)
1, 3, 4, 6, 7bit sequence, generic data, memory access, remote reset, eventnot used by the O-RAN CUS spec
eAxC (extended antenna-carrier) is a 16-bit ID split into DU_port / BandSector / CC / RU_port. The bit width of each part is not fixed by the standard: the RU learns it from M-plane bitmasks (o-ran-uplane-conf e-axcid). A DU and RU using different bitmasks silently misroute or drop every packet. SEQ_ID holds an 8-bit sequence number per eAxC (lets the RU spot lost or out-of-order packets), an E bit and a sub-sequence for fragmentation (O-RAN normally sends E=1, no fragmentation).

O-RAN application header (common to C and U): dataDirection (1 = DL/Tx, 0 = UL/Rx), payloadVersion (=1), filterIndex (0 = normal channel filter; other values select, for example, a PRACH filter), frameId (8 bits, SFN mod 256), subframeId (4 bits), slotId (6 bits, slot within the subframe) and startSymbolId (6 bits). This is the air-interface timestamp: the RU puts the IQ on exactly that symbol.
Section typePurposeKey extra fields
0Unused PRBs / symbols — the RU may blank them (idle or guard periods)timeOffset, frameStructure (FFT size + SCS), cpLength
1The workhorse: almost every DL and UL channel with the normal numerology (PDSCH, PDCCH, SSB, PUSCH, PUCCH, SRS…)udCompHdr + per-section sectionId, startPrbc, numPrbc, reMask, numSymbol, beamId
3PRACH and mixed numerology — PRACH uses its own SCS and FFT, so the RU needs a separate gridtimeOffset, frameStructure, cpLength, udCompHdr + per-section freqOffset (24 bits, half-SCS units)
4Slot-level common configuration (added in later CUS versions; used, for example, by some energy-saving commands — see CM22)version dependent
5UE scheduling information so a Category B RU can compute beam weights itselfueId instead of beamId
6Per-UE channel information (channel estimates) for RU-side weight calculationueId, regularisation factor, I/Q channel samples per antenna
7LAA / LBT support (unlicensed spectrum)LBT parameters
Level 1 — IQ compression — why 9 bits is enough
The U-plane compression header udCompHdr is one byte: udIqWidth (4 bits; 0 means 16) and udCompMeth (4 bits). It is either sent in every section (dynamic) or agreed once over the M-plane (static, then it is absent from the U-plane).
udCompMethMethodPer-PRB parameter (udCompParam)Notes
0No compressionnone16-bit I and Q: 12 RE × 2 × 16 bit = 48 bytes per PRB
1Block floating point (BFP)1 byte: 4-bit shared exponentthe common choice; one exponent for all 24 I/Q values of the PRB
2Block scaling1 byte scalerfixed-point scaling instead of an exponent
3µ-law1 byte (shift / sign)logarithmic companding, like telephone audio
4Modulation compressionnone in U-plane (scale in C-plane extension)DL only, Cat B: sends constellation indices, not IQ
5, 6BFP / modulation compression with selective RE sendingas above + RE masksend only the REs actually used
Worked example (BFP 9-bit): one PRB = 1 byte exponent + 24 × 9 bits (27 bytes) = 28 bytes instead of 48, a 42% saving. For a 100 MHz, 30 kHz carrier (273 PRBs, 28 000 symbols/s): uncompressed 273 × 48 B × 28 000 × 8 = 2.94 Gbit/s per eAxC stream; with BFP-9 273 × 28 B × 28 000 × 8 = 1.71 Gbit/s (before headers, full load). Four DL layers at BFP-9 are therefore about 6.9 Gbit/s — a 10 GbE link is tight, 25 GbE is comfortable. The cost is a small EVM contribution (quantisation noise), usually well under 1% at 9 bits.
Level 2 — how to read and test it
Capture: mirror the fronthaul port (or tap the DU NIC) and open the pcap in Wireshark, which has both an eCPRI dissector and an O-RAN FH CUS dissector. In the dissector preferences set the eAxC bitmasks, the udCompHdr mode (static or dynamic) and the static bit-width, otherwise the decoded fields look random.
Filters that pay off quickly
ecpri.type == 2                      # C-plane only
ecpri.type == 0                      # U-plane only
oran_fh_cus.sectionType == 3         # PRACH C-plane
oran_fh_cus.frameId == 12 && oran_fh_cus.slotId == 1
eth.type == 0xaefe && vlan.id == <fh-vlan>
Checks for an RU bring-up or conformance run (see CM16 and CM23 for real cases):
  • Every U-plane section has a C-plane section with the same eAxC, sectionId and symbol, sent earlier (CM19 windows).
  • SEQ_ID increments by one per eAxC with no gaps — gaps mean drops in a switch or NIC queue.
  • frameId/subframeId/slotId advance consistently with the PTP time — a constant offset of whole slots means an SFN/time-offset configuration error, not an RF fault.
  • udIqWidth / udCompMeth match what the RU advertised in its M-plane capabilities and what was configured in uplane-conf.
  • PRACH (ST3): frameStructure SCS and FFT, cpLength, timeOffset and freqOffset match the PRACH configuration index and msg1-FrequencyStart in SIB1 — otherwise the RU samples the wrong band and PRACH detection fails.
  • Guard/idle symbols of TDD special slots appear as ST0 (if used) or simply have no section.
Level 3 — pitfalls that look like RF faults
Symptom at the RF port / KPIReal cause in the packetsHow to prove it
Constant EVM of several %, ACLR fine or slightly high, on every channelBFP bit-width mismatch (DU sends 9-bit, RU decodes as another width) or static/dynamic udCompHdr mismatchDecode one PRB by hand: exponent + 24 mantissas must fill exactly (1 + 27) bytes
Carrier ACTIVE but no RF powereAxC bitmask mismatch — RU discards all packets as "unknown stream"; or wrong VLANRU fronthaul counters: rx packets arriving but "unknown eAxC" / dropped increasing
PRACH never detected, all else fineST3 freqOffset / timeOffset / filterIndex wrong, or UL PRACH eAxC not mappedCompare ST3 fields with the PRACH config; look for U-plane UL packets on the PRACH eAxC
Periodic bursts of DL BLERLate C/U-plane packets outside the RU receive window (CM19) or sequence gaps under loadRU window counters (on-time / early / late) and SEQ_ID gaps vs time
Beam test shows the wrong directionbeamId table in the RU (loaded over M-plane) differs from the DU's beam indices; or ef=1 extension 1 weights with wrong bit-widthRead the RU beam table; decode section extension 1
Section extensions (ef bit = 1) add optional detail. The ones you meet most: ext 1 (explicit beamforming weights), ext 4 and 5 (modulation-compression parameters), ext 6 and 12 (non-contiguous PRB allocations), ext 10 and 11 (grouped / flexible beam weights for many eAxCs). An RU that does not support an extension must reject it — check the RU capability list before blaming the DU.

Modulation compression (Cat B, DL only): instead of IQ, the DU sends the constellation-point index (for example 2 bits per RE for QPSK) plus a scaling factor and constellation shift in the C-plane. Fronthaul load then drops roughly in proportion to bits-per-symbol, which is why massive-MIMO RUs support it. It cannot be used for UL, because the received signal is no longer on a clean grid.

Expert note: numPrbc = 0 means "all PRBs of the carrier", and startPrbc counts from the lowest PRB of the carrier (not from Point A). reMask = 0xFFF means all 12 REs; splitting one PRB between two beams with complementary reMasks is legal and is how some DMRS/data multiplexing is done.
Further reading
techplayon — O-RAN fronthaul section types · techplayon — what is eCPRI · techplayon — fronthaul C/U/S/M planes and protocol stack
Specs: O-RAN.WG4.CUS.0 (C-plane / U-plane chapters, compression annex); eCPRI Specification v2.0 §3.1–3.2; related cards CM08, CM15, CM19, L30, CM22.
Interview Q&A
Q: What is the eAxC and why does a mismatch kill the carrier?
A: The eAxC is the 16-bit stream ID in every C/U-plane packet (the eCPRI PC_ID/RTC_ID field). It splits into DU port, band-sector, component carrier and RU port, with bit widths set per RU by M-plane bitmasks. If the DU and RU use different widths, the RU maps packets to the wrong stream or drops them, so the carrier is ACTIVE with no RF.
Q: Which section type carries PRACH, and why is it special?
A: Section type 3. PRACH has its own subcarrier spacing and FFT size, so the C-plane must also carry frameStructure, cpLength, timeOffset and a freqOffset (in half-SCS units) telling the RU where to put its PRACH filter.
Q: How much does 9-bit BFP save, and what does it cost?
A: A PRB goes from 48 bytes (16-bit I/Q) to 28 bytes (1-byte exponent + 24 × 9 bits), about 42% less. The cost is quantisation noise: a small EVM contribution, normally well under 1%.
Q: Difference between Section type 1 and 5/6?
A: ST1 says "these PRBs, this beamId". The beam weights are pre-computed or tabled. ST5 and ST6 give a Category B RU the UE scheduling or channel information so it can compute the weights itself.
Q: The RU shows high EVM on every channel but the RF chain calibrates fine. What do you check on the fronthaul?
A: The compression settings: udIqWidth and udCompMeth in the U-plane (dynamic) or the static setting in uplane-conf, against the RU capability. Then decode one PRB by hand. Also check for late packets and SEQ_ID gaps.
CM32 Near-RT RIC & E2 — E2AP setup / subscription / indication / control, E2SM-KPM and E2SM-RC, xApps, test ladder and integration pitfalls Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
The near-real-time RIC is a small software platform that sits next to the RAN and runs plug-in apps called xApps. Each xApp watches the network (for example PRB usage per cell or throughput per UE) and may nudge it (move this UE, give that slice more PRBs). The wire between the RAN and the RIC is E2. Think of E2 as a subscription service: the RAN first lists what it can offer, the xApp subscribes to what it wants, and the RAN then sends reports or asks for decisions. It is "near-real-time" because the loop is 10 ms to 1 s — slower than the MAC scheduler, faster than a human or the SMO. CM07 gives the one-paragraph idea; this card is the protocol and how to test it.
E2 life cycle — setup, subscribe, report, control (own drawing)
Procedures from O-RAN.WG3.E2AP. REPORT is fire-and-forget; INSERT suspends the procedure in the node until the RIC answers with CONTROL (or a timer expires).
Level 1 — the pieces and the procedures
E2 nodes are O-CU-CP, O-CU-UP, O-DU and O-RAN-compliant O-eNBs. Transport is SCTP over IP; messages are ASN.1 (aligned PER) E2AP, and the payload inside is defined by an E2 Service Model (E2SM). E2AP is the envelope; the E2SM is the letter.
ClassProcedureWho startsWhat it does
GlobalE2 SetupE2 nodeAnnounces node ID, component configuration and the list of RAN functions (each = RAN function ID + E2SM OID + revision + definition)
GlobalRIC Service Update / Querynode / RICAdd, modify or delete RAN functions after setup
GlobalE2 Node Configuration UpdateE2 nodeTells the RIC about configuration changes (for example new F1/NG connections)
GlobalE2 Connection Update, Reset, Error Indication, E2 RemovaleitherHousekeeping: extra TNL associations, clear all subscriptions, report protocol errors, tear down
FunctionalRIC Subscription (+ Delete, Delete Required, Modification)RIC (for an xApp)Event trigger + list of actions (REPORT, INSERT, POLICY) on one RAN function
FunctionalRIC IndicationE2 nodeDelivers REPORT data or an INSERT request
FunctionalRIC ControlRICPushes a decision or command; ACK or FAILURE with cause
FunctionalRIC Query (newer)RICOne-off read of node information without a subscription
Service models you will meet:
E2SMPurposeTypical content
KPM (Key Performance Measurement)MonitoringMeasurements named after TS 28.552 counters, e.g. DRB.UEThpDl, RRU.PrbUsedDl, RRC.ConnMean; per node, per cell, per slice or per UE; granularity period set in the subscription. Report styles 1–5: node-level, single UE, condition-based UE-level, common-condition UE-level, multiple UEs
RC (RAN Control)ControlStyles REPORT, INSERT, CONTROL, POLICY, QUERY over areas such as radio bearer control, radio resource allocation (slice PRB quotas), connected-mode mobility (handover), radio access control, dual connectivity, carrier aggregation, idle-mode mobility
NI (Network Interface)MonitoringCopies of messages seen on X2, Xn, F1, NG, S1, E1
CCC (Cell Configuration and Control)ConfigRead and change node/cell configuration through E2 (newer)
LLC (Lower-Layer Control)ControlDU-level, faster control (newest, check support)
Level 2 — RIC platform and how to test E2
Inside the near-RT RIC (O-RAN.WG3.RICARCH): E2 termination (SCTP + E2AP decode), subscription manager (merges duplicate subscriptions from several xApps), a shared data layer with RAN and UE information bases, conflict mitigation (two xApps must not fight over the same parameter), xApp management (onboard, deploy, scale — xApps are containerised microservices), plus A1 and O1 terminations toward the SMO (CM33).

Test ladder for a new E2 node:
  1. Transport: SCTP association up (INIT / INIT-ACK / COOKIE), heartbeats flowing; the RIC endpoint is <ric-e2t-ip> on the configured SCTP port.
  2. E2 Setup: every RAN function the node claims is in the accepted list. A rejected function usually means an E2SM version or OID the RIC does not know.
  3. Subscription: a KPM REPORT subscription with a periodic trigger (for example 1 s granularity, 10 s report period) returns SUBSCRIPTION RESPONSE with the action admitted. "Action not admitted" plus a cause is a capability mismatch, not a transport problem.
  4. Indication: reports arrive at the expected period; the timestamps and the number of granularity periods per report are correct.
  5. Cross-check values: compare KPM values with the node's own OAM counters (CM21-style PM files) for the same window. Differences are usually granularity, aggregation (sum vs mean) or unit (kbit/s vs bit/s), not a bug.
  6. Control: send an RC CONTROL (for example handover of a test UE to a target cell) and verify the RRC Reconfiguration in the UE log and the CONTROL ACK. Also send an invalid control and expect CONTROL FAILURE with a sensible cause.
  7. Robustness: restart the E2 node or the RIC; the node must redo E2 Setup, and the RIC must re-subscribe (or the node must keep subscriptions, depending on the product — know which).
Tools: Wireshark decodes E2AP (and several E2SMs if the ASN.1 plug-ins are installed); the O-RAN Software Community RIC and open-source E2 simulators are the usual lab counterpart.
Level 3 — timescales, conflicts and real pitfalls
LoopTime scaleWhere it runsExample
Real-time< 10 msDU MAC scheduler / L1per-slot scheduling, link adaptation, HARQ
Near-real-time10 ms – 1 sNear-RT RIC xApps over E2traffic steering, slice PRB quotas, interference mitigation
Non-real-time> 1 sNon-RT RIC rApps in the SMO (CM33)policy, ML training, energy-saving schedules
Pitfalls seen in integration:
  • E2AP / E2SM version skew — node on one E2AP version, RIC on another. Setup may succeed but subscriptions fail to decode. Always compare the versions both sides advertise.
  • RAN function ID vs OID — the ID is local to the node, the OID identifies the service model. An xApp that hard-codes the ID breaks on another vendor's node.
  • Conflicting control — a mobility xApp and the node's own SON (or a second xApp) change the same handover offsets; the network oscillates. Conflict mitigation and clear ownership of parameters are needed.
  • INSERT timeouts — if the RIC answers too late, the node continues with its default behaviour. Measure the RIC round trip under load before relying on INSERT.
  • Per-UE reporting load — UE-level KPM for hundreds of UEs at 100 ms granularity is a lot of E2 traffic and CPU on the CU/DU. Size it.
  • Time alignment — KPM timestamps come from the node clock. Unsynchronised clocks make cross-node correlation meaningless.
Further reading
techplayon — what is the E2 interface · techplayon — E2SM-RC RAN control procedures · techplayon — 5G RIC overview
Specs: O-RAN.WG3.E2GAP (general aspects), O-RAN.WG3.E2AP, O-RAN.WG3.E2SM-KPM, O-RAN.WG3.E2SM-RC, O-RAN.WG3.E2SM-NI, O-RAN.WG3.RICARCH; 3GPP TS 28.552 (measurement names); related cards CM07, CM21, CM33.
Interview Q&A
Q: What is the difference between E2AP and an E2 service model?
A: E2AP is the generic protocol (setup, subscription, indication, control) carried over SCTP. The E2SM defines what is inside those messages for one RAN function, e.g. KPM for measurements or RC for control. One E2AP, many E2SMs.
Q: REPORT vs INSERT vs POLICY actions?
A: REPORT: the node sends data and carries on. INSERT: the node pauses a procedure (for example a handover decision) and waits for the RIC's CONTROL. POLICY: the RIC installs a rule the node applies by itself whenever the trigger occurs.
Q: KPM throughput from the RIC differs from the gNB PM counter by 10%. Bug?
A: Probably not. First check that the window, granularity period, aggregation (mean vs sum over UEs) and units are the same, and whether the KPM covers the same cells or slices. Only a difference that remains after aligning these is a real finding.
Q: Why is a near-RT RIC loop limited to about 10 ms at the fast end?
A: Transport and processing: E2 over SCTP/IP, ASN.1 encode/decode and xApp logic add milliseconds. Anything faster (per-slot scheduling) has to stay inside the DU. Newer lower-layer service models push the limit down but do not replace the scheduler.
Q: After a CU restart the xApp stops getting reports. What do you check?
A: That E2 Setup ran again after the restart and whether the RIC re-subscribed. Subscriptions are usually lost with the node context. Then check the subscription manager and the xApp's own reconnect logic.
CM33 SMO, Non-RT RIC & rApps — the A1 / O1 / O2 / R1 interfaces, VES alarms and PM files, what to test on each, and control-loop traps Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
If the near-RT RIC (CM32) is the shift supervisor on the factory floor, the SMO is head office. It configures every network function, collects alarms and performance files, upgrades software, and — through the non-real-time RIC inside it — sets goals and policies that change over seconds, hours or days. Apps that run on the non-RT RIC are called rApps. The SMO talks to the RAN over four interfaces with short names: A1 (policies to the near-RT RIC), O1 (management of CU/DU/RIC), O2 (the cloud that hosts them) and, inside the SMO, R1 (rApps to the platform). The RU is managed over the fronthaul M-plane instead (CM15, CM16).
SMO and its interfaces (own drawing)
Architecture per O-RAN.WG1 architecture description; interface names A1, O1, O2, R1, E2 as defined by the O-RAN ALLIANCE.
Level 1 — the four interfaces at a glance
InterfaceBetweenProtocolCarries
A1Non-RT RIC → near-RT RICREST (HTTP + JSON); the near-RT RIC is the A1 serverA1-P declarative policies; A1-EI enrichment information (external data); A1 ML model management (newer)
O1SMO → O-CU, O-DU, near-RT RIC (and O-eNB)NETCONF/YANG (3GPP NRM, TS 28.541) over SSH/TLS for configuration; VES events (JSON over HTTPS) for faults, heartbeat and streaming PM; file transfer (SFTP/HTTPS) for bulk PMFCAPS: provisioning, fault, performance, trace (incl. MDT), file and software management, heartbeat
O2SMO → O-CloudO2ims (infrastructure management services) and O2dms (deployment management services, often a Kubernetes profile)Inventory of servers/accelerators, cloud alarms, deploy/scale/heal CNFs such as the DU and CU
R1rApps → SMO / non-RT RIC frameworkService-based REST APIsService registration and discovery, data access (e.g. O1 PM data), A1-related services, AI/ML workflow, O1/O2-related services
OFH M-planeO-DU or SMO → O-RUNETCONF/YANG (o-ran-* models), call homeRU configuration, alarms, PM, software (CM15, CM20, CM21)
A1 policy vs configuration: an A1 policy is a goal, for example "keep average DL throughput of UEs in slice X above 10 Mbit/s in these cells" or "prefer cell Y for this UE group". It has a policy type (a JSON schema), a scope (UE, UE group, cell, slice, QoS flow) and statements (objectives and resources). The near-RT RIC tries to meet it with its xApps and reports a status such as ENFORCED or NOT_ENFORCED. It is not persisted in the RAN node and does not change node configuration directly — that is O1's job.
Level 2 — what to test and how
O1 fault path (alarm test): an alarm raised in a CU/DU (or RU via the DU) must reach the SMO as a VES fault event with the right severity, source and specific problem — and the clear must arrive too. Testing only the node-local alarm list (see CM20, AUTO10) misses broken VES forwarding, wrong severity mapping and missing clears.
O1 heartbeat: VES heartbeat events at the configured interval; the SMO should raise "heartbeat missed" when you block them.
O1 PM: file-based PM is XML (3GPP measurement-file format) or CSV, typically every 15 minutes; check file naming, begin/end time, counter names (TS 28.552) and that the collector picks the file up. Streaming PM goes over VES with a much shorter period.
O1 configuration: NETCONF on TCP 830 (SSH); call home uses TCP 4334 for SSH and 4335 for TLS (RFC 8071). Verify <get-config>/<edit-config> on the NRM objects, candidate/commit if supported, and that a rejected edit returns a meaningful rpc-error.
# quick NETCONF sanity from a lab host (netconf-console style tool)
netconf-console --host <du-oam-ip> --port 830 -u <user> --hello          # capabilities, YANG modules
netconf-console --host <du-oam-ip> --port 830 -u <user> --get-config -x /ManagedElement
# credentials come from the lab vault, never from scripts
A1: create a policy instance of a supported type (PUT), read its status (GET), delete it, and check that an invalid JSON body is refused with HTTP 400. Then check the effect in KPIs, remembering that a policy is best-effort.
O2: the SMO must see the O-Cloud inventory (nodes, NICs, FEC accelerators) and be able to deploy and remove a DU/CU CNF; a node failure should raise an O2 alarm and trigger re-deployment if configured (CM29, CM30).
Level 3 — control loops, rApps and design traps
Example rAppInputs (via R1)Output
Energy savingO1 PM (PRB usage, traffic per hour)O1 config (cell/carrier sleep schedules) or A1 policy to an energy xApp (see CM22)
Coverage & capacity optimisationPM, MDT/trace, drive-test dataTilt/power changes via O1 (RET via the RU M-plane)
Traffic steering / slice SLAPM + enrichment infoA1 policies (QoS targets, cell preferences) for near-RT xApps
Anomaly detectionAlarms, PM trendsTickets / alarms to the operator, no network change
ML life cycle: the non-RT RIC can train a model on O1 data, then deploy it as an rApp (non-RT inference) or push it to an xApp (near-RT inference) and keep monitoring its accuracy. A model trained on one cluster may not fit another — watch for drift.

Traps:
  • Two masters: an rApp changing a parameter over O1 while an xApp controls the same behaviour over E2 (or local SON) causes oscillation. Decide parameter ownership up front.
  • Hierarchical vs hybrid RU management: in hybrid mode the SMO and the DU both have NETCONF sessions to the RU; they must not write the same leaves. Know which mode your deployment uses before debugging "config reverted" issues.
  • PM granularity: a 15-minute PM period cannot validate a 1-second control loop — use streaming PM or E2 KPM for fast checks.
  • Time: VES and PM timestamps depend on NTP on the OAM side (separate from PTP for the radio). Wrong NTP makes alarms appear out of order.
Further reading
techplayon — what is the O1 interface · techplayon — O-RAN reference architecture · techplayon — 5G RIC · techplayon — cloud RAN orchestration and management
Specs: O-RAN.WG1 architecture description; O-RAN.WG2.A1GAP / A1AP / A1TD; O-RAN.WG2.R1GAP / R1AP; O-RAN.WG10.O1-Interface; O-RAN.WG6.O2-GA&P; 3GPP TS 28.532, TS 28.541, TS 28.552; IETF RFC 6241 (NETCONF), RFC 8071 (call home); related cards CM07, CM15, CM20, CM22, CM29, CM32.
Interview Q&A
Q: What is the difference between A1 and O1?
A: A1 carries goals: declarative policies and enrichment data from the non-RT RIC to the near-RT RIC, which tries to meet them with xApps. O1 carries management: NETCONF configuration, VES alarms and heartbeat, PM files and software for the CU, DU and near-RT RIC. A1 never configures a node directly.
Q: Is the O-RU managed over O1?
A: No. The O-RU is managed over the Open Fronthaul M-plane (NETCONF with o-ran YANG models), either through the O-DU (hierarchical) or directly from the SMO (hybrid).
Q: What are rApps and how do they differ from xApps?
A: rApps run on the non-RT RIC in the SMO, use R1 services and work on loops longer than 1 s (policy, optimisation, ML training). xApps run on the near-RT RIC and act over E2 in 10 ms to 1 s.
Q: How would you test the alarm path end to end?
A: Trigger a real fault (for example pull a fibre or force a PTP loss), then check: node-local alarm raised, VES fault event at the SMO with the right severity and source, then the clear event after recovery, both with correct timestamps. Also test the heartbeat-missed alarm.
Q: What does O2 add that O1 does not cover?
A: Management of the cloud platform itself: inventory of servers and accelerators and life-cycle management of the CNFs (deploy, scale, heal). O1 manages the RAN function inside the container, O2 manages the container and the host.
CM34 O-RU Category A vs B, O-DU Internals, 5G FAPI (P5/P7) and L1 Acceleration (look-aside vs inline) — who does what, fronthaul maths and DU failure signatures Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
A 7-2x O-RAN base station has two boxes doing the physical layer. The O-DU is a server that does the heavy maths (channel coding, modulation, scheduling). The O-RU is the radio that turns frequency-domain samples into RF. Where exactly the cut sits decides the RU category: a simple Category A RU gets samples that are already precoded for each antenna, a smarter Category B RU does the precoding itself, so far fewer streams cross the fibre. Inside the DU, the MAC talks to the PHY through a standard API called FAPI, and the most expensive PHY job — LDPC decoding — is usually offloaded to an accelerator card, either "look-aside" (only that job) or "inline" (the whole PHY pipeline). CM08 introduces split 7.2x and CM29 the server platform; this card goes inside the boxes.
Split 7-2x and the RU categories (own drawing)
Category definitions from O-RAN.WG4.CUS.0; DL shown, UL is the mirror image.
Level 1 — Category A vs Category B, and who does what
Category A O-RUCategory B O-RU
PrecodingNot in the RU — the DU sends precoded streamsIn the RU — the DU sends layers plus precoding / beam information
Fronthaul streamsOne per antenna port (or per beam)One per MIMO layer
Typical productsSmall cells, 2T2R / 4T4R / 8T8R macro RUs, analog-beam FR2 RUsMassive-MIMO 32T32R / 64T64R AAUs
C-plane features usedST1 / ST3 with beamId from a predefined tablePlus section extensions for weights, ST5/ST6 so the RU can compute weights, modulation compression (DL)
RU complexity / costLowerHigher (precoding hardware, weight calculation, more memory)
Split 7-2x function split: the O-RU does iFFT/FFT, cyclic prefix, PRACH filtering, digital beamforming, IQ (de)compression, DFE (DUC/DDC, crest-factor reduction, DPD) and the RF front end. The O-DU does high-PHY (CRC, LDPC/polar coding, rate matching, scrambling, modulation, layer mapping, and precoding for Cat A), MAC and RLC; the O-CU does PDCP, SDAP and RRC.
O-DU building blockRole
COTS server CPU (isolated, pinned cores)L1 high-PHY threads, L2 MAC/RLC, DPDK poll-mode drivers — see CM29
FEC / L1 accelerator (PCIe card, or on-die in some CPUs)LDPC encode/decode, rate matching; for inline cards the whole L1
Fronthaul NIC with PTP hardware timestampingeCPRI to the RU (SR-IOV virtual functions), and the PTP slave or boundary clock (CM35)
Midhaul NICF1 toward the O-CU
Level 1 — FAPI — the MAC ↔ PHY contract
5G FAPI (Small Cell Forum SCF 222) lets a MAC from one vendor drive a PHY from another. Messages are grouped in two families:
FamilyMessagesWhen
P5 (configuration)PARAM.request/response (PHY capabilities), CONFIG.request/response (cell config: carrier, SSB, PRACH, TDD pattern), START.request, STOP.request/indication, ERROR.indicationAt cell set-up; PHY state IDLE → CONFIGURED → RUNNING
P7 (per slot)SLOT.indication (PHY tick), DL_TTI.request (PDCCH, PDSCH, SSB, CSI-RS PDUs), UL_TTI.request (PUSCH, PUCCH, PRACH, SRS), UL_DCI.request, TX_Data.request (the transport blocks), RX_Data, CRC, UCI, RACH and SRS indicationsEvery slot: 1 ms at 15 kHz, 0.5 ms at 30 kHz, 0.125 ms at 120 kHz
nFAPI (SCF 225 for 5G) carries the same messages over a network between a VNF (MAC) and a PNF (PHY), i.e. split 6. Newer SCF documents add a P19 family for RF and digital front-end control. In an O-RAN DU the FAPI boundary is usually inside the same server (shared memory), but logging it is the best way to see what the scheduler asked the PHY to do.
Level 2 — L1 acceleration and how to check the DU
Look-asideInline
What goes to the cardSelected functions only (LDPC encode/decode, rate (de)matching), via an API such as DPDK BBDevThe whole high-PHY pipeline; the card also terminates the fronthaul
Data pathCPU → PCIe → card → PCIe → CPU for each jobMAC hands FAPI to the card, IQ leaves the card directly
ProsFlexible, PHY software stays on the CPU, easy upgradesLowest latency, fewest CPU cores, lower power per cell
ConsPCIe round-trips, more CPU cores, latency jitter under loadLess flexible; the card vendor's PHY features define what you get
O-RAN WG6 defines an Acceleration Abstraction Layer (AAL) so a DU application can use different accelerators through a common interface.

Health checks on a DU host (generic, adapt to your product):
lspci | grep -i -E "acc|fec|processing accelerator"   # accelerator present?
dpdk-devbind.py --status                             # FEC VF bound to vfio-pci, FH VFs bound?
ethtool -T <fh-if>                                    # hardware timestamping for PTP
# DU logs: count late DL_TTI / "slot missed" / FAPI ERROR.indication per minute
# FEC counters: enqueued vs dequeued jobs, queue-full events
Test angle: run a full-buffer DL/UL test and step MCS up. A collapse at high MCS while the L1 cores are not at 100% usually means the accelerator queue is saturated, the BBDev VF was not bound (software LDPC fallback, if any, is far slower), or the card firmware is mismatched — not an RF fault. UL CRC failures that appear only at high PRB load with good SINR point the same way.
Level 3 — failure signatures and expert notes
SignatureLikely causeFirst check
FAPI ERROR.indication "SFN out of sync" or "slot error" burstsMAC late in sending DL_TTI/UL_TTI — CPU jitter, non-isolated cores, NUMA crossingCM29 checklist, cyclictest latency, core isolation
PHY stuck in CONFIGURED, never RUNNINGCONFIG.request rejected (unsupported TLV, bad TDD pattern or PRACH config)CONFIG.response error codes and the PARAM capability list
Throughput ceiling far below theory, CPUs idleAccelerator saturated / VF not bound / wrong queue countFEC counters, dpdk-devbind, accelerator configuration file
Cat B RU: beams wrong or MU-MIMO gain missingWeights or ST5/ST6 information missing or late; wrong antenna calibrationDecode C-plane extensions (CM31), RU calibration status
Cat A 8T8R: fronthaul link saturates at peakStreams per antenna × BFP width exceeds link rateRedo the CM31 bandwidth maths; use 25 GbE or higher compression
Why Cat B scales: a 64T64R RU serving 16 layers at 100 MHz and BFP-9 needs about 16 × 1.7 = 27 Gbit/s of DL fronthaul as Cat B, but about 64 × 1.7 = 110 Gbit/s as Cat A (using the per-stream figure from CM31). That factor of four is why massive MIMO uses Category B.

UL is harder: for Cat B UL, the RU combines antennas into layers before the fronthaul, so the DU loses per-antenna data. Advanced receivers (interference rejection across antennas) then need either channel information in the RU or a split variant; this is an active area in O-RAN WG4.
Further reading
techplayon — O-RU reference architecture · techplayon — O-DU reference architecture · techplayon — 5G FAPI · techplayon — L1 accelerator card
Specs: O-RAN.WG4.CUS.0 (RU categories, split 7-2x); O-RAN.WG7 white-box hardware specs; O-RAN.WG6.AAL-GAnP (acceleration abstraction layer); SCF 222 (5G FAPI PHY API), SCF 225 (5G nFAPI); 3GPP TS 38.211 §6.3 / §7.3 (layer mapping, precoding); related cards CM08, CM15, CM29, CM31.
Interview Q&A
Q: What is the difference between a Category A and a Category B O-RU?
A: Cat A does not precode: the DU sends one precoded stream per antenna port or beam. Cat B precodes in the RU, so the DU sends only MIMO layers plus beam or channel information. Cat B cuts fronthaul load for massive MIMO but makes the RU more complex.
Q: Name the main FAPI P7 messages and their timing.
A: SLOT.indication, DL_TTI.request, UL_TTI.request, UL_DCI.request, TX_Data.request, then RX_Data, CRC, UCI, RACH and SRS indications. They are sent every slot, so the period follows numerology: 1 ms at 15 kHz, 0.5 ms at 30 kHz.
Q: Look-aside vs inline acceleration?
A: Look-aside offloads only chosen functions such as LDPC via an API like BBDev, and data returns to the CPU. Inline runs the whole high-PHY on the card, which also drives the fronthaul. Inline gives lower latency and fewer cores; look-aside is more flexible.
Q: UL throughput collapses at high MCS but SINR is excellent. RF or DU?
A: Probably the DU. Check the FEC accelerator queue counters, whether the BBDev VF is bound, core isolation and late-slot or FAPI error counts before touching the RF.
Q: Why does split 7-2x put iFFT in the RU but coding in the DU?
A: Frequency-domain IQ of only the used PRBs is much smaller than time-domain samples (option 8/CPRI), and it can be compressed. Coding and scheduling need pooling and flexibility, so they stay on the DU server.
Addition: a FAPI dialect frozen on the June 2019 SCF 222 — how it deviates and why it matters
"FAPI-compliant" always needs a version. The 5G PHY used here took its message header from a third-party PHY drop based on the June 2019 SCF 222 (FAPI v3); in 2022 the team chose to freeze on that header rather than take the vendor's later, more spec-aligned update. Real stacks therefore speak a dated FAPI dialect, and the deviations matter when you mix MACs, PHYs or decoders.
AreaSpecification (SCF 222)This implementation
Config messages (P5)fields are TLVs (tag/length/value), may be sent piecemeal and in any order in the pre-started stateone ordered CONFIG.request struct: carrier, cell, SSB, PRACH, SSB table, TDD table, measurement, beamforming and precoding tables (the TLV classes exist but are not used for config)
Message headera top-level header (number of messages + reserved) plus a per-message headerone 8-byte header per message: phy_id, message_id, message_length, spare (16 bits each)
Cell configphy_cell_id as uint8widened to uint16 — 0–1007 does not fit in 8 bits
PRACHFD-occasion fields per tableadds totalnum_ra_preambles; RACH.indication adds ra_rnti after the preamble index
SSB tableper tableadds ssb_case
DL / UL PDUsper tableDLSCH PDU adds max layers / modulation order / PRBs and rate-match patterns and omits dlTbCrc; PUSCH PDU adds pusch_id and group/sequence-hopping flags; CSI-RS PDU replaces the precoding/beamforming block with a list of DLSCH PDU indices
PARAM tablesfull capability listsseveral truncated (trailing members missing)
Debug use: when a Wireshark FAPI decode, a third-party MAC or a test tool disagrees with the PHY, check the implementation struct (the generated header), not the spec table. The generated dissector in PHYCI01 is built from that same header, so it decodes the dialect correctly; a generic SCF 222 dissector will mis-parse CONFIG.request and any PDU with added fields.
CM35 S-Plane Sync Topologies LLS-C1…C4 and PTP Telecom Profiles (G.8275.1 / G.8275.2) — clock classes, time-error budget, and ptp4l / phc2sys / pmc checks when an RU will not lock Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
Every radio in a TDD network must switch between transmit and receive at the same instant, and the antennas of one RU must be aligned to tens of nanoseconds. The O-RAN S-plane delivers that time over the same Ethernet as the IQ, using PTP (IEEE 1588) and usually SyncE. There are only four ways to wire it — the LLS-C1 to C4 topologies — and two telecom PTP profiles. On Linux-based DUs the tools are ptp4l, phc2sys and pmc. CM11 and L20 explain why sync matters and FWK4 how the RU is measured; this card is the topology, the profile settings and the command-line checks you run when an RU will not lock.
The four O-RAN lower-layer split (LLS) sync topologies
From the S-plane chapter of O-RAN.WG4.CUS.0. In C2 and C3 the switches should be telecom boundary clocks (T-BC) for full on-path support.
Level 1 — topologies, profiles and the numbers that matter
TopologyTiming source for the RUWhen usedWatch out for
LLS-C1The O-DU, directly (point-to-point fibre)Small sites, DU next to RUDU must itself be well synchronised (GNSS or network PTP)
LLS-C2The O-DU, through one or more PTP-aware switchesDU hub feeding several RUsEach switch adds error; DU acts as a boundary clock
LLS-C3A grandmaster in the fronthaul network; DU and RU are both slavesThe most common lab and field set-upGM clock class, switch profile support, DU and RU on the same domain
LLS-C4Local GNSS (PRTC) at the RUWhere fronthaul cannot carry timingGNSS antenna/cabling at every RU; holdover on GNSS loss
ITU-T G.8275.1ITU-T G.8275.2
Network supportFull on-path: every node is a T-BC (or T-TC)Partial: PTP-unaware nodes allowed
TransportEthernet (Layer 2) multicast, EtherType 0x88F7IPv4/IPv6 UDP unicast (ports 319/320) with negotiation
Destination MAC01-1B-19-00-00-00 (forwardable) or 01-80-C2-00-00-0E (non-forwardable)n/a (unicast IP)
Domain number24 by default (24–43)44 by default (44–63)
Message ratesSync 16/s, Delay_Req 16/s, Announce 8/sNegotiated; Sync up to 128/s
FrequencyNormally combined with SyncE (physical-layer frequency)SyncE optional
Fronthaul useThe usual choiceUsed where not every hop is PTP-aware; accuracy then depends on the unaware hops
Targets: TDD cells must be within 3 µs of each other (TS 38.133 §7.4), i.e. about ±1.5 µs to a common reference; ITU-T G.8271.1 gives a network limit of max|TE| ≤ 1.1 µs at the end application interface. Inside one RU, TS 38.104 §6.5.3 limits time-alignment error to 65 ns for MIMO / Tx diversity, 130 ns for intra-band contiguous CA and 260 ns for intra-band non-contiguous CA (FC05). Budget pieces: PRTC-A ±100 ns; each T-BC adds a constant time error of up to ±50 ns (class A), ±20 ns (class B) or ±10 ns (class C) per G.8273.2.

255Slave-only clock
Level 2 — linuxptp checks on a DU or test host
ptp4l runs the PTP protocol on a NIC port and steers that NIC's hardware clock (PHC). phc2sys copies time between the PHC and the Linux system clock. pmc queries the running ptp4l. ts2phc disciplines a PHC from a GNSS 1PPS (grandmaster or LLS-C4 style).
# 1. hardware timestamping present?
ethtool -T <fh-if>            # need hardware-transmit / hardware-receive and a PTP Hardware Clock index

# 2. G.8275.1 slave (key lines of the config file; linuxptp ships a G.8275.1.cfg example)
[global]
dataset_comparison        G.8275.x
G.8275.defaultDS.localPriority 128
domainNumber              24
network_transport         L2
ptp_dst_mac               01:1B:19:00:00:00
logSyncInterval           -4      # 16/s
logMinDelayReqInterval    -4
logAnnounceInterval       -3      # 8/s
announceReceiptTimeout    3
clientOnly                1       # slaveOnly in older versions
ptp4l -f g8275_1.cfg -i <fh-if> -m

# 3. healthy output: servo state s2, offsets of a few ns to tens of ns, steady path delay
ptp4l: master offset   -7 s2 freq  +1520 path delay   612
ptp4l: master offset    4 s2 freq  +1531 path delay   611

# 4. system clock follows the PHC (-w waits for ptp4l and takes the UTC offset from it)
phc2sys -s <fh-if> -c CLOCK_REALTIME -w -m -n 24

# 5. query state
pmc -u -b 0 -d 24 'GET PORT_DATA_SET'           # portState SLAVE
pmc -u -b 0 -d 24 'GET CURRENT_DATA_SET'        # offsetFromMaster, meanPathDelay, stepsRemoved
pmc -u -b 0 -d 24 'GET PARENT_DATA_SET'         # grandmaster identity and clockClass
pmc -u -b 0 -d 24 'GET TIME_STATUS_NP'          # master_offset, gmPresent
pmc -u -b 0 -d 24 'GET TIME_PROPERTIES_DATA_SET' # currentUtcOffset (37 s), ptpTimescale
Servo states: s0 = unlocked, s1 = clock stepped, s2 = locked (s3 = locked and stable in newer versions). Repeated s1 steps mean the clock keeps jumping — find out why before testing anything else.
RU side (M-plane o-ran-sync): read sync-state (LOCKED / HOLDOVER / FREERUN), ptp-status lock-state, the configured ptp-profile, domain-number, the multicast MAC choice and the accepted-clock-classes list. An RU refuses a grandmaster whose clockClass is not in that list, even if packets arrive perfectly.
Level 3 — why it will not lock — real causes
SymptomCauseFix / proof
RU stays FREERUN, no PTP packets countedDomain mismatch (24 vs 44), wrong VLAN, or the switch drops the multicast MACCapture on the RU port: filter eth.type == 0x88f7; compare domainNumber in the header
Packets arrive, RU still UNLOCKEDGM clockClass 248 (GM has no GNSS yet) or not in accepted-clock-classespmc GET PARENT_DATA_SET; fix the GNSS antenna or the accepted list
Locked but a constant offset of hundreds of nsPath asymmetry: a PTP-unaware switch, different fibre lengths per direction, or a media converterError ≈ asymmetry / 2 (10 m of extra fibre one way ≈ 50 ns asymmetry ≈ 25 ns error); use T-BCs, set delay-asymmetry compensation
Offset jumps of tens of µs under trafficPTP not prioritised: PTP queued behind eCPRI in a switchPut PTP in the highest-priority queue (see L30); check switch profile support
System time 37 s offUTC/TAI offset not applied (PTP runs in TAI)phc2sys -w, or check currentUtcOffset and ptpTimescale
phc2sys offset wanders although ptp4l is stablechronyd/ntpd also steering CLOCK_REALTIME, or two ptp4l instances on one PHCStop the competing service; one owner per clock
PTP works on the PF but not in the DU podSR-IOV VF without PHC access or timestampingRun ptp4l on the PF (or a dedicated timing pod) and share time; CM29
Holdover: when the reference is lost the clock free-runs on its oscillator and the clockClass it advertises drops (6 → 7 → 140…). An RU in holdover keeps transmitting until its own drift budget is exceeded, then raises a timing alarm and may stop radiating. The alarm timing is product-specific (AUTO10 lists the measured holdover and free-run fault times for one AAU). FWK4 shows how holdover drift is measured.

Correction to older notes: G.8275.2 is not simply "±1 µs"; its accuracy depends on how many PTP-unaware hops there are and how asymmetric they are, while G.8275.1 accuracy is set by the number and class of T-BCs.
