Interview Q&A
Q: Explain LLS-C1 to LLS-C4.
A: C1: the DU times the RU directly over a point-to-point link. C2: the DU is master through PTP-aware switches. C3: a grandmaster in the fronthaul network times both DU and RU, which are both slaves. C4: the RU has its own GNSS and needs no timing from the fronthaul.
Q: G.8275.1 vs G.8275.2?
A: G.8275.1: full on-path support, Layer-2 multicast, domain 24 by default, every node a boundary clock, normally with SyncE. It is the fronthaul default. G.8275.2: partial support, IP unicast, domain 44 by default, for networks with PTP-unaware hops; accuracy depends on those hops.
Q: ptp4l shows s2 and 10 ns offsets, but the RU is 300 ns off at the antenna. How is that possible?
A: ptp4l only sees its own offset from its master and assumes a symmetric path. An asymmetric link, such as a non-PTP switch or unequal fibre lengths, gives a constant error of half the asymmetry that no servo can see. Measure 1PPS against a reference (FWK4) and use boundary clocks or asymmetry compensation.
Q: What does clockClass tell you and why does the RU care?
A: It tells you the grandmaster's state: 6 = locked to GNSS, 7 = holdover in spec, 248 = free-running. The RU only accepts classes in its configured accepted-clock-classes list, so a GM without GNSS (248) is refused.
Q: Which pmc commands do you run first?
A: GET PORT_DATA_SET (is the port SLAVE?), GET CURRENT_DATA_SET (offsetFromMaster, meanPathDelay), GET PARENT_DATA_SET (which GM and its clockClass), and GET TIME_PROPERTIES_DATA_SET (UTC offset, timescale).
Addition: sync_manager on FHGW-based RUs — what it applies, default class list, holdover and the alarm chain
On the FHGW-based RUs PTP is not run by ptp4l but by the clock vendor's PTP stack; the M-plane process sync_manager sits between it and sysrepo. It reads status from the stack and publishes it under o-ran-sync, and pushes configuration changes down only when a value differs from what the stack already has.
o-ran-sync leaf it appliesDefault in the startup XML
ptp-config/domain-number24
ptp-config/accepted-clock-classes6, 7, 135, 140, 150, 160, 165, 248, 255
ptp-config/ptp-profileG_8275_1 (hard-coded in the code)
g-8275-1-config/multicast-mac-addressFORWARDABLE (NON_FORWARDABLE also supported)
g-8275-1-config/delay-asymmetry0
reporting-period (PTP and SyncE), synce-config acceptance-list-of-ssm, ssm-timeoutfrom configuration
Note the default class list: it accepts 248 and 255 (free-running / slave-only grandmasters). So with this startup file an RU can lock to a GM that has no GNSS — good for a bench without a GNSS antenna, misleading in a timing test. Check the list the DU actually pushed before concluding anything about GM quality.

States and holdover: LOCKED (corrected from PTP packets) → HOLDOVER (TCXO, or SyncE-assisted) → FREERUN (local TCXO/XO only). Without SyncE, holdover expires after 1000 s.
Operational data per source port: lock-state, clock-class, grandmaster identity, steps-removed, priority1/2, current UTC offset, time- and frequency-traceable flags, two-step flag; for SyncE: lock-state and quality level.
Alarm chain: a notification thread watches lock changes; on FREERUN or HOLDOVER it sends a PTP sync-fail / sync-error message to system-monitor, which raises the fault-manager alarm and changes the LED. If the LED and the alarm disagree with o-ran-sync:sync/sync-status, look at this chain, not at the network.
Addition — lab grandmaster on the vBBU: slave-port check, GM firmware upgrade and the one-step / two-step BC
  • Lab grandmaster bring-up: enable the GM's timing Ethernet ports (disabled → static), configure PTP on the port facing the BBU with the G.8275.1 values above.
  • Which server port is the slave? On the vBBU the port the GM is cabled to must be the one declared as the "GM interface" when the FOCOM cluster was created (CM38/CM39). Check with cat /run/ptpmanager/tx/status on the OAM side: that port must show as slave. If it does not, move the GM cable to the slave port rather than reconfiguring.
  • GM firmware upgrade: the GM must be idle; upload the package, it reboots by itself and PTP is lost for about 2 minutes — downstream RUs go into holdover. Re-check the GM PTP settings afterwards even though they should survive.
  • Our BC deployment: a two-port server acting as a boundary clock is one-step on the upstream (slave) port and two-step on the downstream (master) port towards the radios. G.8275.1 itself bans unicast and VLAN-tagged PTP.
  • Scope trick: 1 PPS out of the clock on an oscilloscope in infinite-persistence mode shows a clock that is "walking" as a smeared edge — a quick visual holdover/drift check (FWK4 for the measured version).
2G platform
G2PHY01 2G PHY Modem — TX/RX chain (CRC, conv. coding, puncturing, GMSK/8-PSK, blind detection, MLSE/RSSE), legacy CWS DSP/JESD platform & debug hints Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
The 2G PHY is a classic GSM baseband modem running in software: the transmitter adds CRCs, convolutional coding, puncturing and interleaving, maps bits into bursts and modulates them (GMSK, or 8-PSK for EDGE); the receiver does the reverse with a channel estimator and a Viterbi-based equaliser. On the older CWS platform the baseband ran on CEVA DSPs talking to a third-party RF board over JESD; on the FHGW the same 2G PHY drives the RU over a split-8 (time-domain IQ) fronthaul.
Level 1 — transmit chain
BlockGSMEDGE
CRC6 / 8 / 14-bit (e.g. g = D⁶+D⁵+D³+D²+D+1)header 8-bit, data 12-bit (coded separately)
Convolutional coderate ½, TCH/F polynomials G0 = 1+D³+D⁴, G1 = 1+D+D³+D⁴rate ⅓ mother code (adapted from TCH/H)
Tail bits4 (or 6) zero bitsdata: 6 zeros; header: tail-biting
Puncturing—fixed 3GPP patterns set the code rate (decoder unchanged)
Interleavingspread over 4 or 8 bursts against fadesover 4 bursts
Mapping156.25-symbol bursts with training + guardsame
ModulationGMSK, BT = 0.3, constant envelope (PA-friendly)8-PSK, 3π/8 rotation, shaping filter
Level 1 — receive chain
8 → 1 sample/symbol down-sampling (with anti-alias pre-filter) → de-rotation (8-PSK) → blind detection GMSK vs 8-PSK (training correlation) → channel estimation & burst sync (sliding correlation with the training sequence) → prefilter (matched filter; plus noise whitening for 8-PSK) → MLSE/RSSE Viterbi equaliser with soft outputs → de-mapping, de-interleaving, de-puncturing (punctured bits = erasures) → Viterbi channel decoding (M-state sub-optimal for long codes) → CRC. Soft outputs carry reliability, so the decoder can trust strong bits more than weak ones.
Level 2 — legacy CWS 2G platform (how the samples moved)
  • RF board and RF FPGA from a third-party vendor; baseband on CEVA DSPs; IQ over a JESD serial link.
  • DL: 4 TRX chains in parallel; the DSP over-samples ×8; because the RF FPGA is LTE-based, 2G is resampled to the LTE 3.84 MS/s grid with a Farrow filter and shifted to its RF channel with an NCO. UL is the mirror, with a mux for two-antenna diversity.
  • An “IQ counter” block raises a DSP interrupt per GSM frame in each direction (RX and TX), spaced to create the 3-slot RX→TX offset the standard requires.
  • IQ arrives in FPGA containers: 4 TRX per antenna port, 4 IQ pairs per TRX per container.
  • Hunt-mode calibration: the first sample of the DMA buffer may not be aligned to the JESD super-frame, so DSP and FPGA exchange a known in-band sequence; if alignment fails within 1 s of the first RX frame the PHY goes to PHY_STOP.
Level 3 — what this means when you debug a 2G RCT failure
  • Good RSSI but no CRC passes → suspect sync/hunt alignment, wrong slot/TRX mapping or the 3-slot offset, not the RF.
  • CRC passes on GMSK, fails on 8-PSK → equaliser/prefilter or blind-detection issue (8-PSK is far more sensitive to ISI and phase noise).
  • Degradation only at high Doppler (RA250/HT100) → channel tracking within the burst; the training sequence sits mid-burst for this reason.
  • Spectrum/ORFS failures → ramp shaping and the GMSK/8-PSK shaping filters (see G2TX01 for the PvT mask trap).
Interview Q&A
Q: Why does GSM use GMSK?
A: Constant envelope: the PA can run near saturation efficiently, and the Gaussian pre-filter (BT = 0.3) keeps the spectrum compact within 200 kHz.
Q: What does the training sequence give the receiver?
A: Burst timing (sync) and the channel impulse response, which the matched filter and Viterbi equaliser use to remove multipath ISI.
Q: Why soft outputs from the equaliser?
A: They carry how reliable each bit decision is, so the convolutional decoder weights strong bits more — typically 1–2.5 dB better than hard decisions.
Q: What is hunt-mode alignment on the CWS platform?
A: A start-up handshake in which DSP and RF FPGA exchange a known sequence to find the true start of the JESD super-frame in the sample buffer; without it every burst is mis-timed.
Software update
CM36 RU Software Update redesign (GRDEV-9274 HLD) — stable updater + installer in the package, board types, M-plane flow, write order, exit codes Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
Today two different programs install RU software — fw_manager for M-plane installs and ru-upgrade.sh for the command line and Recovery — and the install code lives in the image already on the unit. That creates a chicken-and-egg problem: a bug in the installer can only be fixed by a new image, but the buggy installer has to install that image. It also writes whatever BOOT.BIN it is given, and a BOOT.BIN built for another board type can brick the unit (it stops before U-Boot, so no fallback; only a site visit recovers it). The GRDEV-9274 design splits the job: a small stable updater on the unit checks the package and runs an installer that ships inside the package. A fix to the install logic now arrives with the release that needs it, and one package can serve several board types (NGC is the first new one).
Status: a high-level design (wiki revision 7, Nov 2026), not yet shipped — details may change.
New install path
The updater checks; the installer writes. U-Boot activation variables are written only by the activate and confirm scripts.
Level 1 — the package
Same zip name (PWAAU-ubuntu-<release>-<label>[-signed].zip), same image_upgrade/ folder. A package is new-format when it contains install.sh.
File in image_upgrade/LegacyNew formatPurpose
manifest.xml, md5sum.txt✓✓MD5 of BOOT.BIN, image.ub, rootfs.tar.gz — kept so every older installer still works on a PW board
BOOT.BIN, image.ub, rootfs.tar.gz✓✓boot chain for one board type, kernel, root file system (PW files stay in rootfs)
sha256sum.txt (+ .sig)✓SHA-256 of every other file; signed on secure builds — covers the manifest too
install.sh, install.conf, ru-pcb.sh✓the installer and its contract (contract=2, time_limit ≤ 240 s)
pcb/pw.files, pcb/<pcb>.tar.gzfrom the first non-PW boardlist of PW-only files, and one archive per other board type (e.g. ngc)
Board types: the installer reads the board label from the running device tree (pw,pcb-type) and checks it against hardware reads; on a mismatch, or if the package has no archive for that board, it refuses with exit 37 before writing anything. On a non-PW board it unpacks rootfs.tar.gz without the files in pcb/pw.files, then unpacks pcb/<pcb>.tar.gz (its own BOOT.BIN, device trees, bitstreams, personalities, clock plans).
Level 2 — the M-plane flow and the install itself
#O-RAN requestWhat happens on the unit
1software-downloadfw_manager downloads the zip into RAM (/var/volatile) over SFTP/HTTPS → download-event
2software-installfw_manager runs ru-upgrade.sh -M; the reply sets sw-install-timeout = 300 s → install-event with the mapped exit code
3software-activateru-software-activate.sh N: refuses a slot that is not VALID (exit 48); sets bootcount=0, upgrade_available=1, selected_slot=N in that order → activation-event
4resetoperations_manager reboots; U-Boot boots selected_slot and counts boots — after 4 failed boots it falls back to Recovery
5(110 s after start)ru-confirm-update.sh clears bootcount then upgrade_available — only on the first good boot of the activated slot
StepInstall write order (installer)Why
0every check and refusal first (lock, signature, SHA-256, pending slot, board type, RAM)a refusal changes nothing
1unset slot record and MD5 record; remove sw-inventory.json, p1 BOOT000N.BIN and any legacy image000N.ub; flushfrom here the slot is “not VALID”
2write the slot (rsync from RAM, or stream); flush
3write p1 BOOT000N.BIN; flushthe BootROM reads it, so it lands only after the slot it boots
4write /etc/pw-install/sw-inventory.json last (temp name, rename, flush)the slot becomes VALID only when everything is on the eMMC
Activation state = three U-Boot variables (selected_slot, upgrade_available, bootcount). Only the activate and confirm scripts write them, one fw_setenv call each, in an order that keeps a power cut between calls safe. The install never writes them, and it refuses a slot that is already activated and waiting for a reboot (exit 41) — so a failed install can never change the slot that boots.
Slot status is derived each time: a slot with sw-inventory.json is VALID when p1 BOOT000N.BIN and /boot/image.ub match the SHA-256 stored in it (a boot file changed afterwards → INVALID).
Level 3 — staging, time budget, exit codes and what to test
PathWheneMMC writes
RAM staging → rsyncMemAvailable ≥ 1.1 × unpacked size + 256 MiB (≈ 590 MiB package)only the difference: rsync -aHAX --numeric-ids --checksum --no-whole-file --inplace --delete-before --omit-dir-times (no -S)
StreamRAM short (2 GB unit with radio up), or -wempty the slot and unpack once
p4 stagingnever (rejected)would write the tree twice on the same eMMC
Time budget: the O-RU controller waits 300 s; the installer gets at most 240 s; the rest is the checks and the legacy records. Measured on bench units: unpack into RAM with the radio running 16.2 s, rsync checksum compare 7.9 s, stream path without the write 22.9 s; a full stream write is not timed yet (target ≤ 100 s on a 2 GB unit with traffic). Two real watchdog resets drove the design: a long uninterruptible I/O wait (GRDEV-8761) and RAM staging without a reserve on a 2 GB unit.
BlockMeaningExamples
0done
1xthe command is wrong10 path unreadable · 15 target is the running slot · 18 not root
2xthe package is damaged21 zip cannot be listed · 22 checksum fails · 23 sha256sum.txt changed after signing
3xthe package does not fit this unit30 not a zip · 31 file not listed · 32 wrong signing · 34 no matching key · 35 legacy package on non-PW · 37 wrong board type · 38 slot too small
4xthe unit is not ready40 install lock held · 41 target slot pending activation · 45 RSA_EN unreadable · 47 partition cannot be made writable (or read-only after a file-system error) · 46 eMMC write-protect (reserved for phase 2) · 48 slot not VALID
5xthe installer run50 time limit (installer killed) · 51 crash / unknown code · 52 installed but the legacy records failed
6xfailed after the first writeslot left not VALID; the unit keeps booting its current slot
Exit-code rule: 1x–4x are refusals before any write (slot, records and activation untouched); 6x means something was written and the slot is not VALID. Compatibility: every older installer (fw_manager 2025.2–2026.3, command line 2026.2–2026.3, Recovery ru-golden 16+) installs a new-format package on a PW board as a legacy package; a non-PW unit can never install a release older than its first.
Test angles for validation: every caller installs (CLI, M-plane, both Recoveries, older installers); each wrong package is refused with the right code and changes nothing; kill / Ctrl-C / power-cut during an install leaves the unit bootable; activate during an install (40) and activate the running slot (cancels a pending activation); same build re-installed; downgrade and back; a 2 GB unit with the carrier up survives the install with no reset. Known risks: a good image falls back if its M-plane apps cannot stay up past the watchdog silence limit in each of 4 boots, and a power cut before the 110 s confirm counts as a failed trial boot; a downgrade loses configuration made in the newer release (e.g. the call-home address). See also CM04 (RRH firmware upgrade) and OPS3 (FHGW bring-up).
Interview Q&A
Q: What is the chicken-and-egg problem in RU software upgrade?
A: The install code runs from the image already on the unit, so a bug in it can only be fixed by a new image — which that buggy code must install. Shipping the installer inside the package fixes it.
Q: Why can a wrong BOOT.BIN brick an RU when a wrong root file system cannot?
A: BOOT.BIN holds the FSBL and U-Boot device tree built for one board; if it hangs before U-Boot, the slot/Recovery fallback (which lives in U-Boot) never runs. A bad slot is caught by U-Boot’s boot counter.
Q: In what order does the installer write, and why is sw-inventory.json last?
A: All checks first, then unset the records and remove the inventory, write the slot, write p1 BOOT000N.BIN, and finally the inventory file. The slot becomes VALID only once all data is flushed, so a power cut never leaves a VALID-looking half slot.
Q: What do exit codes 3x and 6x tell you?
A: 3x: the package does not fit the unit (format, signing, board type, size) and nothing was written. 6x: the installer failed after its first write — the slot is not VALID, but the unit still boots its current slot.
Q: How does the unit avoid booting a broken new slot forever?
A: Activation sets upgrade_available=1; U-Boot counts boots and falls back to Recovery after 4. The confirm script clears the flag 110 s after the first good boot — later than the wd-manager silence (88 s) + transport (20 s) limits, so a boot that is about to be reset by the watchdog is still counted.
Update from the wiki HLD (revision 7, Nov 2026) — corrections, the stable rules R1–R9, CLI, inventory file, tests T1–T24
Corrections applied above (from wiki revision 7): confirm delay 110 s (not 50 s), board-type hardware reads now live in ru-pcb.sh inside the package, active write-window refusal is 47 (46 is reserved for phase 2), and write step 1 also removes a legacy image000N.ub. The activation-event a controller sees carries fw_manager’s own code (0 success, 127 refused/failed) with the reason in text, not the script’s exit code.

The stable updater rules R1–R9 — the contract every later release must keep:
RuleWhat it fixes in place
R1 lock/run/ru-upgrade.lock for the whole run; held → 40 for install or activate of slot 1/2; confirm and Recovery activation wait for it; the activate script gets it as --lock-fd
R2 package checkssigning vs RSA_EN, signature of sha256sum.txt (keys in /etc/pw-install/keys/), SHA-256 of every listed file (22), any unlisted file (31) — all before the installer runs, nothing unpacked
R3 / R4running slot taken from the mounted root; never install into the slot selected_slot names (41)
R5 installer runonce, own process group, ≤ 240 s; timeout → SIGTERM, SIGKILL after 10 s → 50; Ctrl-C/SIGTERM to the updater → 130/143 after the group is gone
R6 legacy recordswhile the other slot is old-format: md5 record, slot record, then p1 image000N.ub copy (failure → 52, slot stays VALID)
R7 exit mapinstaller codes 10–49 and 60–69 pass through; anything else → 51
R8 legacy installerold-format packages go to legacy-package-installer.sh from the running image; only a pw (or missing) board label installs, else 35
R9 activation orderother slot: bootcount=0 → upgrade_available=1 → selected_slot=N · running slot (cancel): selected_slot=N → upgrade_available=0 → bootcount=0 · Recovery: selected_slot=0 → upgrade_available=0 → bootcount=0 · confirm writes only if upgrade_available=1 and running = selected
Command line
ru-upgrade.sh [-M] [-w] [-n] [-F] [-x] <zip|package-dir> <slot 1|2>   # -v prints version 3.0.0
  -M  called by fw_manager (M-plane)      -w  force the stream path
  -F  allow a signed package on an unfused board (never unsigned on a fused one)
  -x  unpack into /var/volatile/sw_mngmnt/ex/ and install nothing   (-s removed → 16)
ru-software-activate.sh [--lock-fd <fd>] <0|1|2>
ru-confirm-update.sh            # no arguments, run by fw_manager
# logs: upgrade.log and slot-install.log on p4, rsync change list in upgrade-rsync.log
The slot inventory file (slot status is derived from it, never stored: VALID if both SHA-256 match):
/etc/pw-install/sw-inventory.json (in the slot, written last)
{ "vendor", "product_code": "AAU", "build_id", "build_name", "build_version",
  "files": [ {"name":"BOOT.BIN","version", "path":"BOOT000N.BIN","sha256"},
             {"name":"image.ub","version", "path":"/boot/image.ub","sha256"}, … ] }
Board type (ru-pcb.sh): the label pw,pcb-type from the device tree must agree with read-only hardware reads (copper PHY id, optical module ID byte, board-controller alias); disagreement, an unknown board, or no pcb/<label>.tar.gz → 37. Nothing caches it — it is read every run.
Power-cut rule: a power cut on an already accepted slot must never roll back (boots of an accepted slot are not counted). The flip side: a slot that later fails at every start-up loops without reaching Recovery — a reboot-loop alarm is an open item.
What changes for testers vs today: upgrade_available is set at activation (so CLI installs now get boot-count rollback too); fw_manager no longer unpacks the zip, writes U-Boot variables or refuses re-installing the same build; the confirm writes only on the first good boot; p4 staging is gone; CLI installs get the 240 s limit; activating the running slot is allowed and cancels a pending activation.

Open item: an old-format package with no md5sum.txt — install or refuse is still to be decided.
Addition — bridge release, frozen contract data, phase 2 batch writes, downgrade limits and install details (HLD rev 7 + bridge design)
TopicDetail not covered above
Bridge releaseAn old-format release that already carries the new thin updater (GRDEV-10349). A unit older than the first bridge must install a bridge before it can take any new-format package. Once shipped, the bridge freezes the updater and its data contracts in the field — they can never change again, which is why the R1–R9 rules are written as a permanent contract.
Frozen data (contract 2)U-Boot sw_inventory_dataN (colon-separated, VALID/INVALID) and sw_inventory_md5_dataN, the p1 names BOOT000N.BIN / image000N.ub, and /etc/pw-install/manifest.xml in the slot. A new-format package has no top-level BOOT.BIN or image.ub; /boot/image.ub comes from rootfs-v2.tar.gz. Contract 2 replaced a three-phase contract 1 that never shipped.
Two phasesPhase 1 (GRDEV-10528): updater, installer contract 2, legacy installer, activate/confirm scripts, sw-inventory. Phase 2 (GRDEV-6613): the three U-Boot variables written in one fw_setenv -s batch, the legacy uboot.env retired, p1 and the standby slot read-only outside their write windows. Why the batch matters: with single calls, a power cut after upgrade_available=0 but before selected_slot changes would boot the other slot with no boot count and no fallback.
Old-format slot statusNo sw-inventory.json → status comes from sw_inventory_dataN; with no record at all the slot is EMPTY if p1 has no BOOT000N.BIN and the root holds only lost+found, otherwise INVALID.
Board labelpw,pcb-type sits at the root of the running base device tree ("pw" on the current board). An NGC (3U VPX) board needs the board-controller hardware read (GRDEV-9214) before it can install.
  • RAM-need check without writing: the installer reads the gzip ISIZE field (last 4 bytes = uncompressed size). The 1.1 factor covers 4 KiB block rounding (measured 1.035×). RAM staging without this check once tripped the 45 s hardware watchdog on a 2 GB unit.
  • I/O priority: ionice -c 2 -n 7 was dropped — the eMMC uses the mq-deadline scheduler, which ignores I/O priority; the install runs at nice 10 instead.
  • Measured delta between two releases: 1678 files and 344 MiB of a 577 MiB tree. rsync omits -S because with --inplace sparse handling can leave old bytes under a trailing run of zeros (test T10).
  • After a refusal, fw_manager keeps the downloaded zip so the install can be retried without a new download.
  • Boot counting only while pending: U-Boot counts boots (bootlimit 4 → Recovery) only while upgrade_available=1. An accepted slot that later fails at every start loops in place; the mitigation is the reboot-loop alarm of the Reboot Event subsystem.
  • Downgrade limits: back to any release from REL_2025.2.x (the first with image_upgrade/). An old vendor .tar.bz2 package is refused with 30, a pre-release zip with 31. After a downgrade, an older fw_manager shows a new-format slot without records as EMPTY and refuses to activate it — rule R6 exists to write those records. Configuration made only in the newer release (e.g. the call-home address) is lost.
  • After a command-line upgrade through an older updater, fw_manager keeps showing the previous build name until the slot is reinstalled.
  • Each install ends with fstrim (GRDEV-10462) so the eMMC gets freed blocks back.
  • Lab flashing with the upgrade script and the stale image_upgrade trap: CM30; a bisect that relied on A/B slots: CM40.
Hands-on: the same upgrade from the DU with netopeer2-cli — subscribe, download, install, activate, reset
The flow above is what the O-RU controller automates. On a bench you can drive the same four O-RAN RPCs by hand from the DU with netopeer2-cli — useful to reproduce an upgrade failure step by step and see each notification.
# on the DU (the RU's fronthaul eth1 address: from the DU's DHCP leases, serial console or SSH via eth0)
netopeer2-cli
> connect --ssh --host <ru-eth1-addr> --login <user>
> subscribe --filter-xpath /o-ran-software-management:*      # see every SW-management notification

> user-rpc --content software-download-<build-id>.xml
  reply: status STARTED (+ a notification-timeout)
  notification: download-event  file-name image_upgrade-<build-id>...  status COMPLETED   (sFTP into p4)

> user-rpc --content software-install-slot2.xml               # only the NON-running slot
  notification: install-event  slot-name swSlot2  status COMPLETED  (checksum check + extract)

> user-rpc --content software-activate-slot2.xml
  notification: activation-event  slot-name swSlot2  status COMPLETED  return-code 0

> user-rpc --content reboot.xml                               # O-RAN reset RPC - activation alone runs nothing new
The RPC files are small XML bodies in the urn:o-ran:software-management:1.0 namespace: download carries remote-file-path (an sftp URI) plus the server's public key and credentials; install and activate carry slot-name (swSlot1 / swSlot2; swRecoverySlot is the factory slot). CI builds publish a ready-made software-download file with each build. If the RU cannot reach the artifact server directly, give it a path through the DU with an SSH local port-forward bound to the DU's fronthaul link-local address, and point the download URI at that.

What is inside the package
FileContents
BOOT.BINFSBL (fsbl.elf) + PMU firmware (pmufw.elf) + FPGA bitstream (system.bit) + ATF (bl31.elf) + U-Boot (u-boot.elf) — so the FPGA image travels inside BOOT.BIN
image.ubcompressed kernel + device tree
rootfs.tar.gzapplications, libraries, configuration
manifest.xmlvendor, product code, build id, software version, boot file name and its checksum
Inventory first: the client reads /o-ran-software-management:software-inventory and compares build-name/version with the manifest, so it only downloads when the slot content differs. Factory default can be restored by activating the recovery slot + reset, or by a 10 s press of the hardware reset switch. On this platform the 8 GB eMMC is split into four 2 GB partitions: three for software images, the fourth for logs, configuration and the downloaded package.

Bench tips: keep the subscribe session open in a second window, timestamp each notification, and on any failure collect fw_manager's log before retrying. The 110 s confirm described above still applies after the reset — do not power-cycle the unit during that window.
Cloud platform — FOCOM
CM37 FOCOM as the Admin Server for EMS (release 7.5) — web server + Harbor, EKS-A provisioning API, kubeconfig, pwcloudctl EMS install Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
FOCOM (O-Cloud manager) installs Kubernetes clusters on bare-metal servers. In release 7.5 the same FOCOM server is used as the admin server for the EMS cluster: it serves the OS images (web server), holds the container images (Harbor registry, air-gapped), provisions an EKS-Anywhere cluster (up to 3 control-plane nodes, HTTPS supported) through a REST API, and is then the place you run kubectl and the pwcloudctl tool that installs the PW EMS products. See CM29/CM30 for the cloud-native RAN platform around it.
Level 1 — what you need and the order of work
FOCOM server: 8 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 240 GB disk, FOCOM ISO for release 7.5. Addresses: one per node, plus Tinkerbell, OAM, northbound/control-plane and southbound IPs (and one extra free southbound IP for the EMS load balancer).
  1. Install the offline dependency package on FOCOM (install-pwctl-dep-on-focom.sh), log out and in.
  2. Start the web server (pwfocomctl -a host-web-server --web-server-ip <focom>) and put the Ubuntu OS image and the HookOS kernel/initramfs under /opt/pw/focom/images/eks-a/.
  3. Start Harbor (pwfocomctl -a deploy-harbor-registry -registry-ip <focom>, port 8888), download the EKS-A and PW image bundles and pwfocomctl -a upload-harbor.
  4. Change the k8s cluster network now if needed — it must be done before provisioning.
  5. Create and provision the cluster through the API (next block) — 20–60 min depending on node count.
  6. Use the EMS kubeconfig on FOCOM, check kubectl get nodes, then install the EMS products with pwcloudctl.
Level 2 — the provisioning API (FOCOM HTTP :9021 / HTTPS :9022)
CallPurpose
POST :9021/api/v1/smoclusters/<cluster>create the cluster definition (nodes, networks, images)
POST …/<cluster>/eksprovisionstart provisioning (bare-metal install via Tinkerbell)
POST …/<cluster>/cancelcancel a running provision
GET …/<cluster>cluster definition
GET …/<cluster>/clusterstatusprovisioning progress by stage
FieldMeaning / tip
id, focomadminip, harborip, osimage, webserverurl, airgapsetup name (lower case, starts with a letter), FOCOM IP, Harbor (FOCOM :8888), Ubuntu image, FOCOM web server (:9443 for HTTPS), air-gapped install
servers[].hardwareinventoryper node: hostname, vendor, BMC (IPMI) IP and login, MAC of the connected OAM port (from the IPMI page, LAN1/LAN2), OAM IP/mask/gateway/DNS, label type=cp or type=worker, disk (/dev/sda or nvme0n1)
networkingOAM IP, Tinkerbell IP, control-plane IP; oamvlanid only for VLAN-tagged setups; oammtu
k8sversion, ntpaddress, additionalIPpathKubernetes 1.27, NTP list, optional extra network file for the nodes
Enable the cluster on FOCOM: sudo chown -R ubuntu:ubuntu /opt/pw/focom/eksa/pwfocomctl-1.0.0/eksa-network-deployment/eks-anywhere/ems/<cluster>/<cluster>/, export KUBECONFIG=<that kubeconfig>, kubectl get nodes → control-plane and worker nodes Ready. Node SSH uses the key generated during cluster creation.
Level 3 — installing EMS with pwcloudctl, and the traps
tar xvf pwcloudctl-<version>.tar.gz
# edit pwcloudctl-<version>/environments/values.yaml
./pwcloudctl --action update-values -platform eksa -cluster kubernetes-admin@kubernetes --file <values.yaml>
./pwcloudctl --action get-values -cluster kubernetes-admin@kubernetes
./pwcloudctl --action install          # (--action destroy to uninstall)
values.yaml keySet it to
platform / profileeksa / e.g. dev
containerRepoHarbor on the cluster southbound side, <SB IP>:8022/library
airGapRepoUrlthe FOCOM/admin registry, <admin IP>:8888
pwcloud_northbound_lb_ipthe EKS-A control-plane IP (unless the customer wants another)
pwcloud_southbound_lb_ipa free IP in the southbound range — not the host’s own SB IP
  • FOCOM and the SMO/EMS cluster must be time-synchronised (NTP) — certificates and provisioning fail otherwise.
  • Cluster name: lower case, starting with a letter. MAC = the OAM port that is actually cabled. Disk device must be guessed per server type (HP usually /dev/sda).
  • pwcloudctl -a update-eksa-network failing → create ~/.ssh/known_hosts for the admin user and retry.
  • Default Harbor/node credentials from the guide must be changed on any shared setup.
Interview Q&A
Q: What role does FOCOM play for EMS in 7.5?
A: It is the admin server: it hosts the OS images and an air-gapped Harbor registry, provisions the EKS-Anywhere cluster on bare metal through its REST API, and is where kubectl and pwcloudctl are run to install EMS.
Q: Which two API calls install a cluster?
A: POST /api/v1/smoclusters/ with the node and network definition, then POST …//eksprovision; track it with GET …/clusterstatus.
Q: What is the southbound load-balancer IP and what is the common mistake?
A: A spare IP in the southbound range that the EMS load balancer takes; using the host’s own southbound IP clashes with it.
Q: Provisioning stalls on one node. What do you check first?
A: The MAC in the node entry (must be the cabled OAM port from the IPMI page), the BMC address/credentials, and the disk device name; then clusterstatus for the failed stage.
Update — release 2026.3 EKS-A admin flow (tarball install, certificate, pre-install-smo, k8s 1.35)
What changed for the EKS-A admin from release 2026.3 (live build Nov 2026).
  • FOCOM install is now one tarball on a vanilla Ubuntu 22.04 VM: sudo ./install-pw-focom.sh (~15 min, one automatic reboot; log out/in afterwards for the docker group). Verify with cat /opt/pw/focom/FOCOM_SERVER_INFO and systemctl status focom-api-server mongod. The FOCOM server OS itself stays on 22.04.
  • Certificate first: from 2026.1.0-201 self-signed certificates are refused. Generate one on the internal dev-cert portal: product FOCOM, RSA 2048, CN = SAN = admin IP (second SAN if NB and SB use different IPs); pass it as zip, as p12 with its password, or pre-load it in /opt/pw/focom-cert/.
  • One command replaces the separate web-server, Harbor and upload steps of the 7.5 flow above:
    pwfocomctl -a pre-install-smo --focom-ip <admin-ip> --focom-dir-url=<release>/focom-packaging/focom/ \
   --pwems-dir-url=<release>/pwems-product-packaging/ --cert-path <admin-ip>.zip     # ~35 min here, 50–100 min typical
    No internet on the admin: pwfocomctl -a download --option=smo … on another FOCOM, copy into ~/focom_downloads, rerun with --skip-download=yes. If pre-install fails, rerun it; if files are corrupt, empty ~/focom_downloads and rerun.
  • Cluster body: k8sversion = 1.35 and the new osimage (the "Kubernetes 1.27" in Level 2 applies to 7.5 only). Upgrading an existing admin = install the new tgz and re-upload images.

Kubernetes / EKS-A1.27–1.28 / v0.181.35 / v0.25.2

Expected result of a good build: eksctl-anywhere v0.25.2, kubectl 1.35.2; 16/16 downloads checksummed; web server 9443 with the PW CA cert; Harbor 8888 with 10 healthy containers and ~50 eks-anywhere repos; ~49 GB disk used.
Known issues (2026.3.2): apt is blocked on the admin because the bundle misses a few OS packages — FOCOM is not affected; 7 optional eks-anywhere package bundles fail to push to Harbor (HTTP 400) — cluster images are complete. HP DL20 Gen11 boot loop during provisioning (second reboot returns to iPXE): press F11 and boot the Ubuntu disk.
Shared-admin rule: one EKS-A provision at a time per admin (SUSE admins allow two). Building both admin types, the EKS-A vs SUSE comparison and sizing: CM38. Using the cluster for a 4G vBBU: CM39.
Cloud platform — FOCOM admin servers & vBBU bring-up
CM38 FOCOM Admin Servers for EKS-A and SUSE Edge — building the admin VM (tarball vs MGT ISO + kexec), certificates, cluster API, sizing and parallel limits Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
FOCOM (the O-Cloud manager) is the server that turns bare HP servers into Kubernetes clusters. For the EMS/SMO and for vBBU setups it also acts as the admin server: it serves the OS images over HTTPS, holds an air-gapped container registry (Harbor), drives the bare-metal install through a REST API, and keeps the kubeconfig and SSH keys of every cluster it builds. From release 2026.3.2 a lab runs two flavours side by side: an EKS-A admin (Ubuntu 22.04 + the FOCOM tarball, provisions EKS-Anywhere clusters) and a SUSE MGT admin (SL-Micro 6.1 + RKE2, built from a per-host ISO, provisions SUSE Edge clusters). An EKS-A FOCOM cannot provision SUSE clusters and vice versa. This card shows how both admins are built as OpenStack VMs, how they differ, how a cluster is created, and how many jobs one admin can run in parallel. CM37 covers the EKS-A EMS install in detail; CM39 uses these admins to bring up a 4G vBBU; AUTO17 covers OpenStack VM basics.
Figure — one-time admin build (left four boxes) and per-setup cluster bring-up (right three)
The first four steps are done once per admin server. Every new setup only repeats the last three, with its own cluster name, IPs and node list.
Level 1 — EKS-A admin vs SUSE MGT admin at a glance (release 2026.3.2)
AspectEKS-A adminSUSE MGT admin
Host OSUbuntu 22.04 (vanilla cloud image) + FOCOM tarballSL-Micro 6.1, installed from a per-host MGT ISO
Admin Kubernetesnone on the admin (EKS-A tools only: eksctl-anywhere v0.25.2, kubectl 1.35)RKE2 v1.32.4 single node, cilium CNI, Rancher UI
Target clustersEKS-A, k8s 1.35, osimage ubuntu-1.35.4-pw-1.0.gz (Ubuntu 24.04 nodes)SUSE Edge, osimage = edge network raw image (~7.5 GB)
VM size used8 vCPU / 16 GB / 240 GB8 vCPU / 32 GB / 400 GB (guide minimum 8 / 16 / 450)
FOCOM installinstall-pw-focom.sh from a tgz, ~15 min, one rebootbaked into the ISO (Focom RPM is an ISO build field)
Certificateseparate step: PW dev CA cert, passed as zip/p12mgmt-IP cert built into the ISO (/opt/pw/certs)
Images + registrypwfocomctl -a pre-install-smo (~35 min here, 50–100 min typical)pwfocomctl -a preload-edge-airgap-resources + download the edge raw image
PortsAPI 9021/9022, web 9443, Harbor 8888API 9021/9022, web 9442/9443, Harbor 8022, Rancher
Cluster API/api/v1/smoclusters/<name> → eksprovision/api/v1/suseclusters/ (EMS) or susevbbuclusters/ (vBBU) → suseprovision
Login modelubuntu user; cluster SSH key generated at createroot key-only (key from the ISO build); smoadmin user for EMS work
Parallel jobs per admin1 provision, 1 upgrade2 provisions, 5 upgrades (Modify)

Both admins use the same lab rules: HP servers only (iLO / Redfish power control), single node or 3 masters + 1 worker; one IP per node plus a Tinkerbell IP (EKS-A), a control-plane / northbound IP and a spare southbound load-balancer IP — book a block of about ten per setup. Cluster name: lower case, starts with a letter, unique.
Level 2 — building the two admin servers
A. EKS-A admin VM
  1. Check project quota first (Compute → Overview: instances, vCPU, RAM, volumes). Flavour disks do not use volume quota; only explicit volumes do.
  2. Launch from the vanilla Ubuntu 22.04 cloud image, no new volume, 8 vCPU / 16 GB / 240 GB, external network. Do not use the automation image with Python 3.10 pre-installed — its Docker/pip packages conflict and the FOCOM install fails (see AUTO17).
  3. Set an initial login through the cloud-config box (password, no expiry, SSH password auth) — change it after first login.
  4. If the root disk was not grown automatically: parted /dev/vda resizepart 3 100%, pvresize, lvextend -l +100%FREE, resize2fs (online, no reboot).
  5. Install FOCOM from the release tarball, then verify:
tar -xvf pw-focom-setup-<version>.tgz
cd install-pw-focom && sudo ./install-pw-focom.sh   # ~15 min, reboots once (cgroup change)
# log out / in: the ubuntu user is now in the docker group
cat /opt/pw/focom/FOCOM_SERVER_INFO
systemctl status focom-api-server mongod
Releases up to 2026.1 needed two tarballs (dependency package first, then FOCOM); 2026.3 does both phases in one script.
B. Certificate (EKS-A only — SUSE has it in the ISO)
From 2026.1.0-201 self-signed certificates are refused. Generate one on the internal dev-cert portal: product FOCOM, RSA 2048, CN = admin IP, SAN 1 = admin IP (add SAN 2 if northbound and southbound use different IPs). Three ways to hand it over:
OptionHow
ZIP--cert-path <ip>.zip (no bundle password)
PKCS#12--cert-path <name>.p12 --openssl-cert-pass <pass>
Pre-loadedunzip to /opt/pw/focom-cert/, rename CA → ca.crt, key → tls.key, cert → tls.crt, run without cert options

C. Images, web server and Harbor (EKS-A) — one command replaces the old separate web-server / Harbor / upload steps:
pwfocomctl -a pre-install-smo --focom-ip <admin-ip> \
   --focom-dir-url=<release>/focom-packaging/focom/ \
   --pwems-dir-url=<release>/pwems-product-packaging/ --cert-path <admin-ip>.zip
Good result: 16/16 downloads with checksums OK, web server on 9443 with the PW CA cert, Harbor on 8888 with 10 healthy containers and ~50 eks-anywhere repos, ~49 GB disk used. Without internet on the admin, run pwfocomctl -a download --option=smo on another FOCOM, copy to ~/focom_downloads and add --skip-download=yes.
D. SUSE MGT admin — ISO build
Create the VM first (any temporary Ubuntu, 8 vCPU / 32 GB / 400 GB) and a 17 GiB empty volume attached as /dev/vdb. Note the IP and MAC — they go into the ISO. Then run the Jenkins job suse-mgmt-iso-builder (Build with Parameters, release branch, x86_64; ~1.5 h, ISO ~14.6 GB, sha256 in the log):
FieldWhat to put
hostNameletters, digits, hyphens only
mgmtIP / mgmtSubnet / mgmtGatewaythe VM's own address, prefix length and gateway (from the OpenStack network page)
dnsAddress / ntpServerlab DNS / NTP
diskType/dev/vda on OpenStack and Proxmox, sda on KVM, nvme0n1 on bare metal
mgmtMacAddressthe VM port MAC (Instance → Interfaces)
k8sPodsCidr / k8sServicesCidrempty = defaults
sshKeysyour public key — the only way in, root has no password
focomRpmURL of the FOCOM RPM for the release (can be upgraded later)
focomAuth / buildPurposedevelopment / internal for lab builds
suseConnectRegCode / EmailIDSUSE registration — take from the internal builder page, never leave empty
The ISO contains the management container images and charts, the edge-image chart, Harbor images, the SR-IOV CRD/chart, Python modules and the FOCOM RPM. A private registry plus Hauler (embedded registry and file server storing OCI artifacts) is used because Hauler cannot serve nested registry names or Helm charts directly.
E. SUSE install with dd + kexec (no ISO boot on OpenStack)
# on the temporary Ubuntu, as root
curl -sS -o suse-mgmt.iso <ISO link> && sha256sum suse-mgmt.iso
dd if=suse-mgmt.iso of=/dev/vdb bs=4M conv=fsync && sync
sgdisk -e /dev/vdb && partprobe /dev/vdb   # fix backup GPT, re-read table
mount -o ro /dev/vdb1 /mnt                       # the larger partition
apt install kexec-tools                          # answer "No" to the reboot hook prompt
kexec -l /mnt/boot/x86_64/loader/linux --initrd=/mnt/boot/x86_64/loader/initrd \
  --append="cdinst=1 console=ttyS0,115200 console=tty0 security=selinux selinux=1 net.ifnames=0 \
  ignition.platform.id=metal loglevel=0 root=install:CDLABEL=INSTALL rd.kiwi.oem.installdevice=/dev/vda"
umount /mnt && kexec -e          # jumps into the SUSE installer, which overwrites /dev/vda
SUSE is up in ~3 min (watch the OpenStack console); SSH as root with your key and wait ~10 min for kubectl get pods -A. Then start Harbor and the web server and fetch the edge OS image:
pwfocomctl -a preload-edge-airgap-resources -openssl-cert-pass <pass> [--cert-path <new cert>]
mkdir -p /opt/pw/focom/images/suse-edge && cd /opt/pw/focom/images/suse-edge
curl -O <release>/network-x86-alsmicro6-1-non-rt-prod-<date>.raw      # ~7.5 GB
curl -O <same>.raw.txt && sha256sum -c <image>.raw.txt
pwfocomctl -a update-rpm-on-suse --rpm-path <pw-focom.rpm>   # later FOCOM upgrade
Make sure the project security group allows the FOCOM ports (9021/9022, 9442/9443, 8022) in and out.
Level 2 (cont.) — creating a cluster through the FOCOM API (Postman collection "SMO API 2026.3")
StepEKS-A adminSUSE admin (EMS / vBBU)
CreatePOST /api/v1/smoclusters/<name>POST /api/v1/suseclusters/<name> or /susevbbuclusters/<name>
Start…/<name>/eksprovision…/<name>/suseprovision
ProgressGET …/<name>/clusterstatusGET …/<name>/clusterstatus
Stop / removePOST …/<name>/cancelPOST …/<name>/delete
  • Fixed per admin: focomadminip, harborip (EKS-A :8888, SUSE :8022), webserverurl (:9443 HTTPS, :9442 HTTP on SUSE), osimage, airgap = yes, vendor = HP. SUSE adds product = EMS and focommultiinterfaceip.
  • Per node (servers[].hardwareinventory): hostname, iLO IP / MAC / login, MAC of the cabled OAM port (LAN1 or LAN2 on the iLO page), OAM IP / mask / gateway / DNS, labels type=cp or type=worker, disk /dev/sda or nvme0n1.
  • Optional active/standby bond on SUSE: mac = primary NIC, bond_slave_mac = standby NIC — FOCOM rejects the body if they are equal; leave empty for no bond.
  • Networking: oamip (= first master on single node), workercpip (control-plane / northbound IP), Tinkerbell IP on EKS-A, optional VLAN and MTU; additionalIPpath points to a YAML on the admin only when NB and SB are on different networks.
  • Single node: cluster id = hostname. Multi-node: different hostnames per node. Use a real NTP server — with a wrong BIOS clock the time never syncs and certificates fail.
After provisioning (20–60 min by node count) take ownership of the cluster folder and use its kubeconfig:
# EKS-A: /opt/pw/focom/eksa/pwfocomctl-1.0.0/eksa-network-deployment/eks-anywhere/ems/<name>/<name>/
# SUSE (as smoadmin, new SSH session): /opt/pw/focom/eksa/pwfocomctl-1.0.0/susemicro-network-deployment/ems/<name>/
sudo chown -R smoadmin:smoadmin <cluster dir>
export KUBECONFIG=<cluster dir>/<kubeconfig>
kubectl get nodes        # SUSE nodes show v1.32.4+rke2r1, Ready
Node SSH uses the key generated at cluster creation (ssh-eks-key-<name> / edge-key). For EMS on SUSE, values.yaml uses platform = suse and the air-gap registry on port 8022.
Level 3 — sizing, parallel limits, pitfalls and a real build
Sizing rules (server sizing calculator, valid up to FOCOM 2027.1): host = sum of FOCOM VMs + reserve, 1 vCPU = 1 hardware thread, no CPU overcommit; VM disks are thin but only grow, so budget full size. At most 4 FOCOMs per platform, counted at the upgrade peak. Every upgrade needs a FOCOM on the current release and one on the target release; after the upgrade the old one is deleted (FOCOM is stateless — the new one becomes the admin with the kubeconfigs and keys). Hence the peak is the first upgrade window.
FOCOM VM rolevCPU / RAM / diskParallel jobs per FOCOM
EKS-A "fresh": admin for DC + vBBU, provisions SMO8 / 16 GB / 450 GB1 provision
EKS-A "upgrade": vBBU (+ vBSC, RIC on VM), no SMO4 / 16 GB / 200 GB1 provision, 1 upgrade
SUSE (any role)8 / 16 GB / 450 GB2 provisions, 5 upgrades (Modify)
KVM host reserve2 threads / 4 GB—
Most parallelism the 4-FOCOM cap allows: EKS-A 4 deployments or 2 upgrades (1 while a deployment runs); SUSE 8 deployments or 10 upgrades (5 with a deployment). Vendor minimums for comparison: EKS-A admin 4 CPU / 16 GB / 30 GB; SUSE Edge management 4 CPU / 16 GB recommended — FOCOM adds Harbor, images and bundles on top. A shared lab admin therefore runs one EKS-A provision at a time and at most two SUSE provisions; announce start and end to the team.

Pitfalls
  • Empty licence fields shift the ISO parameters. A real build failed with "User 'root' must have either a password or at least one SSH key": the empty registration fields moved every later value one slot, so the SSH key was lost. Fill every field.
  • Never rebuild, snapshot-relaunch, re-IP or detach interfaces of the SUSE admin — IP and MAC are inside the OS image. Keep the 17 GiB ISO volume until the first setup works so you can reinstall without a new 1.5 h build.
  • Harbor port mix-up: SUSE is 8022, EKS-A is 8888 — wrong port in harborip or airGapRepoUrl gives image-pull failures late in provisioning.
  • Healthy SUSE admin still shows one cilium-operator Pending (single node, expected) and systemctl --failed listing mgmt-stack-setup-watcher and pw-apply-iptables (finished one-shots, harmless).
  • EKS-A admin known issues in 2026.3.2: apt blocked because the bundle misses a few OS packages (FOCOM unaffected); 7 optional eks-anywhere package bundles fail to push to Harbor (HTTP 400) — cluster images are complete.
  • HP DL20 Gen11 boot loop during EKS-A provision: second reboot goes back to iPXE — press F11 and pick the Ubuntu disk.
  • pwcloudctl -a update-eksa-network failing → create ~/.ssh/known_hosts for the admin user; pre-install-smo errors → rerun, or clear ~/focom_downloads and rerun.
Real build (Nov 2026, release 2026.3.2): EKS-A admin ready in about an hour (15 min install, 35 min pre-install, 49 GB used); SUSE admin: 1.5 h ISO build (the first build failed on the licence-field shift), 3 min kexec install, ~50 min to a Ready node with 84/85 pods Running, Harbor 8022 and web server 9442/9443 answering HTTP 200 with the PW dev CA cert, edge image checksum OK, 63 GB used of 400 GB. A routed design (admins and target servers on different subnets) was not yet tested.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why does a lab need both an EKS-A and a SUSE FOCOM?
A: Each FOCOM family provisions only its own platform: EKS-A FOCOM builds Ubuntu/EKS-Anywhere clusters, the SUSE MGT builds SL-Micro/RKE2 edge clusters. Setups of both kinds need both admins.
Q: How do you install SUSE on an OpenStack VM that cannot boot an ISO?
A: dd the MGT ISO onto a spare 17 GiB volume, mount its install partition, kexec-load the installer kernel and initrd with the install-device argument pointing at the root disk, then kexec -e.
Q: The SUSE admin needs a new IP. What do you do?
A: You cannot just change it: IP and MAC are built into the ISO. Build a new ISO with the new values and reinstall (keeping the ISO volume makes that quick).
Q: How many vBBU provisions can one admin run in parallel?
A: EKS-A: one provision (and one upgrade). SUSE: two provisions or five Modify upgrades. Upgrades also need a second FOCOM on the target release.
Q: Provisioning works up to the image pull and then fails. First checks?
A: Harbor port in the body (8888 vs 8022), certificate CN/SAN matching the admin IP, NTP sync between admin and nodes, and the web-server URL port.
CM39 4G vBBU Bring-up on a FOCOM Cluster — cluster provision, BBU clean-up, ACS Platform Redeploy, BBU_MultiCA certificate, vBBU → vNode → eNodeB → cells Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
A 4G vBBU in the lab is a Kubernetes cluster on an HP server, built by FOCOM (CM38), with the LTE software deployed on top by ACS (the PW management system). Getting "cells on air" therefore crosses three tools: FOCOM builds the cluster on bare metal, the BBU OAM shell is where you clean old deployments, read the kubeconfig and install the certificate, and ACS holds the device tree (Platform → vBBU → vNode → eNodeB → vNode deployment → cells). Most failures are ordering mistakes: deploying a vNode onto a platform ACS cannot reach, or a vBBU with the old certificate. This card gives the order, the values that matter and the first checks when something stalls. The RU side (O-RAN split 7.2x, discovery) is in CM42 and CM36.
Figure — order of work from bare metal to cells on air
Steps 1–4 prepare the platform (FOCOM, OAM shell, ACS). Steps 5–9 are ACS device objects, each Save and Deploy before the next.
Level 1 — what you need before you start
  • Hardware: HP server with iLO (Redfish power and virtual media) — single node, or 3 masters + 1 worker. The PTP grandmaster must be cabled to a known NIC port (default expectation: the first port, ens1f0).
  • Addresses: one per node + Tinkerbell + control-plane/northbound + southbound LB; for the vBBU a further small manual range for the CP/UP interfaces and one GTP-U address. Book a block of about ten in the team IP sheet before you start.
  • Names: cluster name lower case, starts with a letter, unique on the admin. vNode name <BBU serial>-01-4G.
  • Software: the LTE build you want to run (its version string goes into vNode and eNodeB), the matching platform manifest in ACS.
  • Slot: EKS-A admin runs one provision at a time, SUSE admin at most two — agree the slot in the team group, announce start and end, and never install or change anything on the shared admin VMs.
  • Time: cluster provision 30–45 min, then wait for the platform pods after the redeploy; the ACS objects themselves are quick form fills.
Level 2 — step by step
1. Cluster in FOCOM. Fill the Postman cluster body (iLO IP and login, OAM IP and the MAC of the cabled OAM port, Tinkerbell IP, control-plane IP, the admin's fixed values from CM38), check the setup name, create, then start provisioning and poll clusterstatus (30–45 min).

2. Clean the BBU before reusing a server: log in to the OAM shell, undeploy running pods and delete the deployment; in ACS delete the old vBBU, eNodeB, vNode and service so the new objects do not collide with stale ones.

3. Platform Redeploy. ACS → Create Device → Platform Redeploy. ACS needs the cluster kubeconfig as one escaped string, so print it from the OAM home directory:
python3 -c "f=open('.kube/config');content=f.read();f.close();content=content.strip();print(repr(content))"
Paste the output into ACS, select the platform manifest, save, and wait until the platform pods are Running.
4. BBU certificate. On the internal dev-cert portal choose product BBU_MultiCA, RSA 2048, CN = BBU serial number, SAN 1 = OAM IP; download the zip, copy it to OAM, then:
cd /opt/pw-config/ipsec_cert/Certificates/Certificate00/EndEntityCert/
rm -f *
cp ~/<CN>/Certificates/Certificate00/EndEntityCert/* .
ls -l            # expect ca.crt  cert.crt  key.crt
kdel --all       # restart all pods so they load the new cert
5–9. ACS objects (each Save and Deploy before the next):
ObjectValues that matter
vBBU — globalNTP = local loopback (default); M-plane aggregation ticked; 3 ms shift not ticked
vBBU — networkone network named common: subnet, mask, gateway of your setup; a booked manual IP range for CP/UP; GTP-U range of a single address
vNodeservice type LTE, hosting vBBU = the one just created, name <serial>-01-4G, version = your LTE build, sim / heartbeat / stats-interval profiles
eNodeBeNB ID and TAC unique per setup; OM PLMN 001/01 (test PLMN) plus a secondary PLMN; version = build; template default; deployment eNodeB BIDI: CP IP and U-plane IP both on network common
vNode deploymentRAT mode 7_2 (O-RAN split 7.2x RU), max carriers 2, max bandwidth 40 MHz, no extra interfaces; select the pre-filled RRH entry (2 carriers, 2 antennas)
Cellsper cell EARFCN, cell ID, PCI, band, bandwidth; radius auto; carrier index 1 → Save and Deploy
Level 3 — where it breaks and why
  • Provision fails: PTP grandmaster not on ens1f0. The vBBU cluster template expects the GM on the first port. Find the real GM port from the iLO page / cabling, update the body and run create again. If the GM is on ens1f0, check from the iLO console that the OAM IP is reachable — next suspect is the OAM MAC (must be the cabled LAN port).
  • Kubeconfig paste rejected or platform never deploys: the file was pasted raw. ACS needs the single-line repr() form with escaped newlines; strip trailing whitespace first.
  • Pods healthy but S1/IPsec or M-plane fails: old certificate. CN must be the BBU serial and SAN the OAM IP; the three files must replace (not sit beside) the old ones, and the pods must be restarted with kdel --all.
  • IP clash: the manual CP/UP range and GTP-U address must be free and outside the cluster/LB addresses — always book them in the IP sheet.
  • Cells deploy but do not radiate: check the vNode deployment RAT mode (7_2), carrier count and bandwidth against what the RU publishes (RRH entry, CM42), then RU-side carrier state (CM40 shows a no-SSB RCA).
  • Shared admin etiquette is part of the procedure: a second parallel EKS-A provision on one admin breaks both; never modify the admin VMs.
Interview Q&A
Q: What do you check first when a vBBU cluster provision fails?
A: Whether the PTP grandmaster is on the first NIC port (ens1f0); if not, fix the body and recreate. If it is, check OAM reachability from the iLO console and the MAC of the cabled OAM port.
Q: Why does ACS need the kubeconfig printed with repr()?
A: The ACS field takes one string; repr() produces a single line with escaped newlines and quotes, so the YAML survives the paste.
Q: Which certificate does a vBBU use and how is it applied?
A: A BBU_MultiCA end-entity cert (RSA 2048, CN = BBU serial, SAN = OAM IP); the ca/cert/key files replace those in the EndEntityCert folder and all pods are restarted.
Q: What does RAT mode 7_2 in the vNode deployment mean?
A: The eNodeB drives an O-RAN split 7.2x radio unit over eCPRI fronthaul; together with max carriers 2 and 40 MHz it must match the RRH capabilities.
Q: Why clean the BBU before reuse?
A: Old deployments and ACS objects (vBBU, eNodeB, vNode, service) keep names and IPs; new objects then fail or bind to stale resources.
Addendum — build a BBU image locally and side-load it into the vBBU cluster (rollout and rollback)
When you need to try a BBU code change on a lab vBBU before it goes through CI, you can build the BBU image yourself and side-load it into the cluster's containerd, then point the existing deployment at it. Kubernetes keeps the previous ReplicaSet, so one command rolls back.
1. Build (inside the docker build container, in the core repo's vru directory):
export BLD_ARCH=x86 BLD_OS=ubuntu
export BRANCH=$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD) COMMIT_ID=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
export PW_BUILD_EPOCH=$(date +%s) BUILD_NUMBER=$(date +%s) COVERITY_BUILD=0 USER=<you>
./build.sh            # -> vru/out/pw-bbu-<tag>.k8s.tgz
For an incremental build, comment out the make clean line in build.sh. DEV_BUILD=1 appends your user name to the tag.
2. Copy and import — the tarball is gzip-compressed but ctr import wants a plain tar, so stream it through gunzip:
scp vru/out/pw-bbu-<tag>.k8s.tgz <server>:/tmp/
gunzip -c /tmp/pw-bbu-<tag>.k8s.tgz | sudo ctr -n k8s.io images import -
sudo ctr -n k8s.io images ls | grep pw-bbu | tail -1     # lands as docker.io/library/pw-bbu:<tag>
3. Re-tag to the path the deployment expects (the registry prefix is site-specific — read it from the deployment):
sudo kubectl get deployment bbu -n pw -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'
sudo ctr -n k8s.io images tag docker.io/library/pw-bbu:<tag> <registry>/pw/bbu/pw-bbu:<tag>
4. Roll it out, verify, and know the way back (namespace pw, container bbu-container):
sudo kubectl set image deployment/bbu bbu-container=<registry>/pw/bbu/pw-bbu:<tag> -n pw
sudo kubectl rollout status deployment/bbu -n pw
sudo kubectl get pods -n pw | grep bbu
sudo kubectl rollout undo deployment/bbu -n pw          # rollback
A helper script (deploy-bbu.sh <server> [image-tarball]) wraps steps 2–4.
Traps: importing into the wrong containerd namespace (must be k8s.io, or kubelet never sees the image); a tag that does not match the deployment's registry path makes the pod try to pull from the registry and fail (ImagePullBackOff) — re-tag locally, and keep the image pull policy in mind; the side-loaded image exists only on that node, so on a multi-node cluster the pod must land there; and a later platform redeploy from ACS replaces your image with the manifest version — note what you loaded so results are traceable.
Addendum — field notes: virtual CD-ROM for iPXE, one address for C- and M-plane, watching provisioning
  • Older servers and iPXE: on some Cascade Lake platforms the network boot of the installation ISO only worked after a virtual CD-ROM was mounted manually from the BMC; if the server never picks up the image, check this before debugging the provisioning service.
  • C-plane vs M-plane address: on one release manifest M-plane aggregation was disabled, and the eNB deployment info had to carry the same C-plane address for both C-plane and M-plane; otherwise the radio was not managed.
  • Watching provisioning: follow the provisioning API service journal (journalctl -u <focom api-server unit> -f) and poll the cluster-status API until the cluster is reported ready, rather than guessing from the BMC console.
Bring-up RCA & RU discovery
CM40 RCA: n78 RU at 100 MHz — no SSB while 40 MHz works: Fault 15/25 reboot loop, on-the-fly config loss, config-id persistence, build bisect to an FPGA datapath change Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
A real root-cause analysis on an n78 TDD radio unit: with a 40 MHz carrier the UE attaches, at 100 MHz it never even sees the SSB (the sync block every UE must find first). Because the symptom did not change with any DU PRACH setting, it was a downlink problem, not a RACH one. The investigation found three overlapping regressions in the RU develop builds — a Fault 15/25 reboot loop, a corrupted base config file (Fault 14) and the real SSB break — plus two test-method traps that could have sent the team the wrong way. It ends in a build bisect that pinned the break to one FPGA change, and a frequency explanation: a 100 MHz carrier shifted +70.74 MHz from the DAC centre reaches the edge of what the new datapath carries. Use it as a template for any "works at one bandwidth, fails at another" case. Fault IDs: CM20; A/B slot flashing: CM30 and CM36.
Figure — develop-build bisect at 100 MHz (green = UE attaches, red = no SSB)
May-18 is uncertain (watchdog reboots every ~7 min). Jun-11 adds Fault 14 (DEGRADED); Jun-17 adds the Fault 15/25 reboot loop, which hides the SSB question entirely.
Level 1 — the facts in one table
BuildAvailabilityTX carrier activates?Result at 100 MHz
May-5 / May-14NORMALyesUE attaches (3 UEs with valid TA and CSI at 100 MHz)
May-20 / May-26NORMALyes, config_error 0, correct centreno SSB — the real regression
Jun-11DEGRADED (Fault 14)yesno SSB; base_startup.xml malformed
Jun-17 (latest)FAULTY (Fault 15 + 25)neverno SSB; reboot loop
  • Fault 15 "Unit out of order" (CRITICAL, source FPGA) — datapath bring-up failed; availability FAULTY, Operational 0, carrier never TX-on.
  • Fault 25 "Reset Requested" — the RU asks the DU for a reboot; Fault 15 clears only after that reboot.
  • Fault 14 "Configuration file corrupted" (MAJOR) — /etc/configs/base_startup.xml had four top-level elements and no single root; a strict parser stops with "junk after document element". Availability DEGRADED, carrier still works.
  • Fault 23 "FPGA SW update failed" (MINOR) twice at install time — an early clue that the FPGA image deserved suspicion.
  • Ruled out by A/B between 40 and 100 MHz: DFE channel filter (NR100MHz correctly loaded), carrier gain (0→1 in both), "Skip Init of Filter" (present in both), PRB registers, centre frequency.
Level 2 — the method, step by step
1. Compare states, time-correlated. Collect DU pod logs (bbu, DU stack, fronthaul server, PHY, PTP manager) and RU logs (fhgw.log*, alarms.log on the RU data partition) for each state: same build at 40 MHz, same build at 100 MHz, an older build at 100 MHz. Confirm both sides run UTC and the skew is small (here < 0.5 s), then pin the bandwidth-switch moment from the fronthaul server's eAxC/bandwidth configuration lines — last 40 MHz line, first 100 MHz line.

2. Build a cross-side A/B table per signal: RU FPGA alarm, availability (MSG_CMD_AVAIL_NORMAL/FAULTY), operational state (OPER_ENABLE), DU rrhmgr messages ("RRH Ready / L1 Done" = cell on air), RU reboots, channel filter, carrier gain. Anything identical in both columns is ruled out.

3. Confirm the reboot protocol live instead of trusting a static log window. A manual RU reboot at 100 MHz reproduced the whole loop:
RU  fault-manager      Fault 25 - Reset Requested
DU  rrhmgr             RRH Reboot is required; ALARM 5034 "Reset Requested by Ru"
DU  rrhmgr → oammgr    UNI_RRHMGR_RRH_REBOOT_CMD
DU  ornc               processRebootReq → Sending WatchdogReset rpc
RU  operations-manager Executing GPIO Reboot sequence
So the RU does not reboot blindly: it requests a reset and the DU commands it over NETCONF. An earlier reading "no DU reboot command seen" was just a log window that missed the send. A second, unrelated trigger also exists: wd-manager: supervision Stopped Working → watchdog GPIO reboot when the supervision daemon dies — it briefly drops the cell and makes attach tests flaky.
4. Read alarm state, not alarm text. A DU line re-reporting alarm 5013 "RRH got disconnected" every 60 s turned out to be a periodic re-report in the CLEARED state (4 raises vs 142 clears in the window) — not an active disconnect.

5. One good boot proves nothing. On the Jun-17 build some boots came up clean at 100 MHz and ran for two hours; others looped. And "cell up" in logs is not "SSB on air" — confirm with a UE or a spectrum analyser.

Test-method traps found on the way
TrapWhat happenedFix
On-the-fly config shrinks on rebootRU rewrote on_the_fly_configs.json with only the carrier block (1734 B → 653 B), dropping the RE-offset and all 16 endpoint entries pushed by the DUDo not rely on the RU to persist DU-pushed RE-offset/endpoints; diff the file before and after reboot
Endpoint config-id persistsOne carrier's 4 RACH endpoints sat at config-id 1 (PRACH 1.25 kHz, long format) instead of default 3 (30 kHz short). Deleting the OTF JSON did not reset the startup XML — the ids survive regenerationDefault the startup XML endpoint ids (keep the device's own MAC, never push the template MAC) before comparing DU builds
RU clockRU clock restarts near the last boot time and jumps to UTC only when PTP relocks (1–2 min)Correlate early-boot events with the DU clock
"RCT passes"The bring-up test runs at a centred frequency where a 100 MHz carrier sits ±50 MHz from the DAC centreA passing test at another frequency is not a control
Level 3 — the root cause, the bisect and the flashing practice
Every RU configuration value was correct. Registers and LPHY logs were read back live at 100 MHz:
Read-back on the broken build (devmem, carrier active)ValueExpected
DL buffer RB_X_RE_PER_ANT, both CCs, 4 antennas0xCCC273 PRB × 12 = 3276
O-RAN UL ul_rb_per_ant (reset value 0x20)0x111273
max_prb_per_frame0x111273
LPHY logchannel filter + mixer loaded for 100 MHz, 120 NR filter coefficients, also on the runtime CCF update path100 MHz
Frequency placement explains the edge. The NCO shift is carrier centre minus the band-centre f_ideal set once at device open (3700.74 − 3630 = +70.74 MHz); there is no guard on the carrier edges. A 100 MHz carrier at that offset spans up to +120.74 MHz from the DAC centre:
CarrierOffset from DAC centre (f_ideal 3630 MHz)Lower edgeUpper edgeResult
40 MHz @ 3700.74 MHz+70.74 MHz+50.74+90.74 MHzworks
100 MHz @ 3700.74 MHz+70.74 MHz+20.74+120.74 MHzno SSB
100 MHz centred (bring-up test)≈ 0−50+50 MHzworks
Bisect ↔ commit agreement. The May-14 (works) → May-20 (broken) window holds exactly one downlink-relevant change: GRDEV-5111 (FPGA PRB register definitions, regenerated FPGA↔SW bindings) which also bumped the FPGA bitstream (DMA data-width change, IQ record). Tx-power and LTE phase-compensation changes in the window were ruled out. Conclusion: the datapath (DDC / data width / sample rate at a large NCO offset) no longer carries a 100 MHz carrier that far from the DAC centre. Proposed decisive test: RU-only bring-up (startup XML + array-carrier activation, no DU) at 3700.74 MHz on latest develop — failing there but passing centred exonerates the DU and U-plane completely.

Bisect rules that kept it honest:
  • Halve the date range each step; record availability, carrier activation and SSB/attach per build in one table.
  • Use a build where the carrier activates to study the SSB; the Jun-17 Fault 15 loop fails earlier and masks it.
  • Mark results uncertain when the unit is unstable (May-18 rebooted every ~7 min from a supervision-daemon crash) — and note weekends with no builds.
  • Read the running build from /etc/rfsoc_fru_detail.txt (software version, commit, branch, timestamp), not from what you think you flashed.
Flashing for a bisect (A/B slots, see CM30/CM36):
rm -rf image_upgrade                     # else unzip skips extraction and STALE files are flashed
yes | bash RU_upgrade.sh <build>.zip    # writes the inactive slot, flips selected_slot, reboots
md5sum <slot BOOT / image>              # compare with the build manifest.xml
cat /etc/rfsoc_fru_detail.txt            # confirm version + commit
# afterwards: remove upgrade zips and image_upgrade from the data partition (they accumulate)
The RU M-plane address changes on every version change — re-find it from the vBBU pod ARP table. Separately, the malformed base_startup.xml (Fault 14, May-26 → Jun-11) and the Fault 15 never-activate mode are their own regressions and need their own tickets.
Interview Q&A
Q: The carrier is READY/ACTIVE with config_error 0 but the UE sees no SSB. Where do you look next?
A: Downstream of activation: the DL datapath (gain, TX enable, DPD, DDC/sample-rate), the DU U-plane, and where the carrier sits relative to the DAC centre — not the M-plane configuration.
Q: Fault 25 is raised on the RU. What happens next?
A: The DU rrhmgr raises alarm 5034 and issues a reboot command; ornc sends the WatchdogReset RPC and the RU does a GPIO reboot. Fault 15 clears only after that reboot.
Q: Why did the team default the startup XML before comparing DU builds?
A: Endpoint config-ids written by the on-the-fly JSON persisted in the XML (RACH config-id 1 instead of 3). Left in place, they would confound the DU comparison; the device MAC must be kept.
Q: Why is "40 MHz works" not proof the RU is fine at 100 MHz?
A: At the same centre the 100 MHz carrier extends 30 MHz further from the DAC centre (to +120.74 MHz); a datapath limit shows only at the wider span.
Q: One clean boot at 100 MHz after a fix — done?
A: No. The failure was intermittent per boot; repeat reboots, confirm SSB with a UE or analyser, and check stability over time.
CM42 How the BBU Discovers and Records an RU — fronthaul DHCP vendor classes, recovery-image detection, RRH DB entry (endpoint types, power window, build-signing flag) Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
Before a BBU can put a carrier on an O-RAN radio unit it has to find it and describe it. The RU boots, asks for an address on the fronthaul link with DHCP and says who it is in the vendor-class option; the BBU's fronthaul DHCP server answers with an address and, in option 43, the controller address the RU should call home to. The RU then opens its NETCONF M-plane session and publishes its capabilities (bands, carriers, power limits, which signal types each antenna/carrier endpoint can carry, whether the image is signed). The RRH manager turns all of that into one RRH database entry, which ACS and the DU scheduler later read. When something is wrong in that chain — a recovery image, a missing endpoint type, a pinned lease — the symptom shows up much later as "carrier setup failed" with no clear reason. This card is the map for reading that entry. See CM39 for the vBBU side and CM36 for software slots.
Figure — discovery chain from RU power-on to the RRH database entry
Each arrow is a place where a wrong match silently changes what the BBU believes about the RU.
Level 1 — the identifiers that matter
ItemValue / meaning
DHCP option 60, production imageo-ran-ru2/PW
DHCP option 60, recovery (golden) imageo-ran-ru2/PWRecovery — same first 12 characters as production
DHCP option 43vendor-encapsulated options; sub-option 0x81, length 4 = the call-home controller address (one link-local slot per RU class)
Server files on the BBU/opt/pw/etc/dhcpd-fh.conf (classes, pool, lease times), /opt/pw-config/dhcpd-fh.leases, service dhcpd-fh
Vendor tablerrh_vendor_data.json — per vendor type: login, call-home address and flags used by orannetconf
Running build on the RU/etc/rfsoc_fru_detail.txt — software version, commit, branch
  • Endpoint types tell the BBU what each carrier/antenna can carry. PXSCH (Tx/Rx): 0 = LTE, 4 = NR 30 kHz, 7 = LTE + 2G (Option-8 carrier); a B1 LTE/NB-IoT carrier in a sample entry publishes 2. PRACH: 103 = NR format 0 + NR 30 kHz format B4 (GreenRAN n78), 104 = adds NR format 1, 105 = LTE format 0 only; 100 / 101 = LTE and NB-IoT PRACH.
  • Stored as one string per band/carrier/antenna, "Tx,Rx,Rach, " — the trailing comma and space are a legacy quirk kept so every row parses the same.
Level 2 — configure, read and test
Pin an RU to one fronthaul address (lab trick)
  1. Back up dhcpd-fh.conf and dhcpd-fh.leases first.
  2. In the pool, set the range start and end to the same address.
  3. Shorten the leases (defaults are a week, 604800 s): min/max 600 s, default 20 s — so the change takes effect quickly.
  4. Empty the leases file except its header and server-duid line.
  5. systemctl restart dhcpd-fh, then reset the FHGW / RU so it asks again.
Reading the RRH DB entry
RRH DB field groupWhat to check in debug
AutoDiscovered, Active, SerialNum, MfrModelName, HwClassIdthe BBU found the unit you think it found (model name selects the per-model power JSON)
FhEthIface, PTPEnablewhich BBU NIC port the RU sits on, PTP on
num_of_bands, BandIdN_BandNumber / NumberOfCarriersband list as published; unused slots read 0
BandIdN_MaxTxPower / MinTxPowerper-band power window — ACS shows both and its validator keeps every carrier inside it
BandIdN_CCc_AntA_Tx / Rx / Rach (/ RachNBIot)_EndpointTypesignal types per endpoint (Level 1)
NumTx/RxAntennas, fh_split_option, ru_supported_category, num_ru_portssplit 7 (7.2x) vs 8, category A/B, port count
BuildSigningEnforcedsecure-boot image flag (below)
M-plane address/MAC, fronthaul address, OcwsBaseVersionreachability and software baseline
EthInterfaces[].AssignedBBU NIC role per port: Fronthaul, GM, GMPlusFH or Backhaul (the OAM port)
Quick tests: boot an RU into its golden slot and watch which DHCP class it lands in and what orannetconf does; compare the endpoint-type strings with the band (n78 should read "4,4,103"); check MinTxPower is present for every active band before testing 2-carrier power (see DACG01 for the DAC/digital-gain split).
Level 3 — real gaps found in this chain
  • Recovery RU looked healthy. The fronthaul dhcpd matched only the first 12 characters of option 60, so o-ran-ru2/PWRecovery fell into the production class, got the production call-home slot and the normal NETCONF setup ran. The golden image has no lower PHY configured, so TX setup failed with no clear diagnostic. Proposed fix (GRDEV-853): a separate class matching 20 characters (and the production class explicitly excluding it), its own call-home slot, a new vendor type GREENRAN_RECOVERY in orannetconf that skips signal-path / carrier / TX setup but keeps the RU reachable for software recovery, and a new PW-specific "RU in recovery mode" alarm to the RRH manager — deliberately not reusing O-RAN fault 15, so operators can tell "RU broken" from "RU waiting for firmware" (CM02, CM20).
  • Non-GreenRAN RUs publish no endpoint types (or talk LRCP instead of O-RAN), so the column was empty and the PHY/scheduler had nothing to use. GRDEV-7657 derives defaults in rrhmgr from the capability message: n77/n78/n79 → "4,4,103" (aligned with GreenRAN B78; first drafts used 104), any other band → "0,0,105"; with fronthaul split Option 8 on bands 3 and 8, carrier 0 = 2G (Tx/Rx 7) and carrier 1 = LTE (0), PRACH stays 105. Other 30 kHz NR bands (n41, n40 …) still fall to the LTE default — a known gap.
  • Secure boot flag. The RU publishes read-only build-signing-enforced under module-capability, derived at runtime from a -signed suffix on the software version in /etc/rfsoc_fru_detail.txt (false if absent or unreadable). The RRH manager stores it (default false) so ACS can choose a signed or unsigned build; a failed checksum on download/install is reported as fail-reason INTEGRITY_ERROR.
  • Two-carrier power window. If disabling one carrier pushes the other below the band minimum, the RU keeps the surviving carrier on and raises TX-out-of-order (MAJOR) plus configuration fault 11 with the carrier gain as source.
Interview Q&A
Q: How does the BBU tell a recovery-image RU from a production one?
A: By the DHCP option 60 vendor class: o-ran-ru2/PW vs o-ran-ru2/PWRecovery. The server must match enough characters (20) to separate them.
Q: What does option 43 carry for an O-RAN RU here?
A: Vendor-encapsulated options with the call-home controller address the RU opens its NETCONF M-plane session to.
Q: An n78 RU from another vendor shows empty endpoint types. What happens and what is the fix?
A: PHY/scheduler have no signal-type info; rrhmgr now fills defaults from band and split — "4,4,103" for n77/78/79.
Q: How do you force an RU to always get the same fronthaul address in the lab?
A: Back up the files, set the pool range start = end, shorten lease times, clear the leases file, restart dhcpd-fh and reset the RU/FHGW.
Q: Where does build-signing-enforced come from?
A: The RU derives it from a -signed suffix in its software version string; rrhmgr stores it in the RRH entry and ACS uses it to pick the build.
RU platform — sync, PM, storage, integration
PTPSTEP01 PTP Time-Step Resilience — why a clock step leaves the RU "LOCKED, no alarms" with a broken cell, and how the FPGA pps_aligner detects it and re-aligns DL/UL/PRACH without a reboot Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
An RU keeps two kinds of time. The time of day (ToD) comes from PTP and drives the TDD on/off gate and the O-RAN slot counters. The data paths (DL playout, UL capture, PRACH framing) are started once and then just count samples. If PTP steps the clock (for example after a fault on the BBU grandmaster side), the gate and counters jump to the new PPS, but the data paths keep their old phase. Nothing compared the two, so the RU stays "LOCKED, no alarms" while the cell quietly breaks: RAR lost in the first DL slot after UL, Msg3 CRC failures, wrong preamble IDs, PUSCH loss. Restarting the DU or PHY does not help; before this fix, only an RU reboot did.

The fix is an FPGA block called pps_aligner. It measures the PPS phase against the 10 ms frame counter at every PPS, adds up the net shift M, and when |M| is larger than about 1.5 µs it mutes DL, waits for the clock to settle, and restarts DL, UL and PRACH on one common frame tick, without a reboot and without reprogramming any DFE IP. See CM11 (timing and SFN), CM35 (PTP profiles and lock checks), CM19 (fronthaul windows) and SPLANE01 (S-plane verification).
Why a clock step breaks the cell
The TDD gate follows the new PPS; the data paths keep the phase they were started with.
Level 1 — the mechanism and the numbers
  • Field symptom 1: on a customer n78 Mini Metro, after a BBU PTP fault, RAR in slot 6 (first DL slot after UL) was not decoded for more than 8 hours. SIB and paging in slots 0–2 were fine. RU: LOCKED, no alarms.
  • Field symptom 2: at another customer, no RAR, Msg3 CRC failures, wrong preamble ID and PUSCH loss. DU/PHY restarts did nothing; an RU reboot fixed it.
  • Root cause: the kernel PTP driver (xlnx_ptp_adjtime) steps the RU ToD. The TDD gate and slot counters re-align at the next PPS. DL playout (rd_addr_gen), UL capture (sync_enable_logic) and PRACH framing do not. The data paths start at the first array-carrier update, which is not gated on PTP lock.
  • M = net PPS shift against the data paths since they started, modulo 10 ms. DCO steering of the DSPLL does not change M (sample clocks and timer move together). A step undone by an equal step gives M = 0; a pair that does not cancel leaves the residual. A step of an exact multiple of 10 ms is a blind spot.
  • Pass limit: TDD cell phase sync must be within 3 µs between cells (TS 38.133 §7.4.2), so about 1.5 µs per cell. Hence mis_thresh = 184 cycles = 1.497 µs (one 122.88 MHz cycle = 8.138 ns). jump_tol default = 2 cycles (16 ns).
