  • FDD has no TDD gate, so it is exposed only through the DL buffer margin and the fronthaul timing windows.
Level 2 — detect, re-align, and test it on the bench
Detection. At every PPS, pps_phase_mon measures where the PPS falls on the 10 ms frame counter (rollover 1,228,800 cycles, wrapped to ±5 ms). Once armed (first valid DL beat) it adds these offsets into M. Steps before DL starts, such as the first PTP lock, are not counted.
Offset (base 0xA0002000)RegisterWhat it holds
0x00mon_cfgreset 0x00B81702: jump_tol[3:0], clr[4], mute_thresh[15:5], mis_thresh[31:16]
0x04mon_statusarmed, misaligned, jump_sticky, mis_sticky
0x08jump_cntPPS jumps seen since armed
0x0Clast_offsetlast PPS offset, signed cycles
0x10net_offset (M)accumulated net shift, signed cycles
0x14realign_cfgreset 0x371E0453: en 1, mute_en 1, tmo_frames 5, n_stable 4, hold_max 30, dl_stale_sym 7, retry_max 3
0x18realign_statusstate[2:0] (1 WATCH, 2 HOLD, 5 EXEC, 7 FAIL), mute[3], fail_sticky[6], fail_hold[7], realign_cnt[31:24]
0x1Crealign_retryretries used
Before Nov 2026 these registers sat in rf_gpio at 0xC4–0xD4. A new ru-app on an old FPGA image hangs on its first read of 0xA0002000, so FPGA image and ru-app must match.

Re-align FSM: OFF → WATCH → HOLD → ARM → REQ → EXEC → RELEASE (or FAIL).
  • If |M| > 1.5 µs, DL is muted with zeros at once; TVALID stays high so no DFE IP sees a gap.
  • Wait for N = 4 clean PPS, then raise the request about 33 µs (one guard) after a frame tick.
  • Every path restarts on the same frame tick Tc from its own boot delay (DL iq_read_delay ≈ 0.95 ms, UL rx_delay ≈ 9.988 ms on n78). M is re-based to 0 at Tc + 2. No DFE IP is reset or reprogrammed.
Lab procedure (RU + DU running an RCT test + signal analyser triggered on the RU frame-tick output):
# step the clock by hand
systemctl stop splane-ptp-supervisor
#   step /dev/ptp0 with clock_adjtime(ADJ_SETOFFSET), e.g. +/-10 us  (= -/+1229 cycles)
systemctl start splane-ptp-supervisor
devmem 0xA0002010          # net_offset M (signed cycles)
devmem 0xA0002008          # jump_cnt

# force a re-align (expect within ~20 ms: realign_cnt +1, M = 0, PRACH back at boot TA)
devmem 0xA0002014 32 0x371E0457
# detection only, re-align disabled
devmem 0xA0002014 32 0x371E0452
Always write the whole 0x14 / 0x00 word: force and clr share the register with every setting, so a partial value silently changes the timeouts too.
Level 3 — outage cost, failure path, PRACH trap and measured results
Outage cost on n78 (for a step bigger than 1.5 µs):
  • DL off air ≈ 4.011 s (4 s hold-off + up to 10 ms to Tc + 1.24 ms restart).
  • About 10 ms without PUSCH U-plane, one UL frame (3 TBs lost in the lab).
  • PRACH back ≈ 30–40 ms after Tc, after about 2 missed occasions.
  • Steps of 1.5 µs or less are not re-aligned by design (inside the TDD budget). FDD variants are not muted; DL is cut for only about 11 ms.
Failure path. If a path does not acknowledge within tmo_frames, the controller retries up to retry_max = 3. If the last retry fails, or the PPS keeps jumping past hold_max, it sets fail_sticky. RU SW then raises fault 15 UNIT_OUT_OF_ORDER plus fault 25 RESET_REQ with source "PPS-ALIGN" (see CM20 for fault-ids). Both clear when a later re-align passes its PRACH checks.

No alarm on a jump or a good re-align — a time jump clears active alarms on the RU, so alarms would be lost anyway. Evidence is only a log line in /var/log/fhgw.log with the prefix "PPS aligner:" (for example re-align count, duration, retries, M before re-base) and PM counts in the ps-health object pw-ps:PS-PPS-REALIGN (jumps, re-aligns, retried, failures).

PRACH trap. A re-align that moves the frame grid sets PRACH IP ISR bit 4 (Frame Error, 0x10) once. SW must clear it with a raw write of exactly 0x10 — a read-modify-write would clear every set bit. If Frame Error returns on the next poll, the re-align counts as failed. be_rearm_status.rearm_cnt advances once per PRACH re-anchor.
MeasurementResult
Forced re-align, TDD DL edgemoves by M (+260 ns and −155 ns seen)
PUSCH after each re-align100% CRC pass; TA shifts by M (M = +81 cycles → −656 ns)
PRACH during a held +3 µs stepTA +2995 ns, 99.9% detection kept
DL EVM (b3b7)0.41–0.50% before, 0.41–0.52% after
Held step of 2–3 µsbreaks PUSCH on that bench (decodes only within ≈ ±1.3 µs)
Troubleshooting rule: if a TDD cell loses RAR / Msg3 / PRACH after a PTP event while the RU says LOCKED, read net_offset (0xA0002010) and jump_cnt before touching RF. Non-zero M or rising jumps points to this mechanism.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why can an RU show PTP LOCKED and no alarms but still lose RAR?
A: A ToD step moves the TDD gate and slot counters to the new PPS, but DL/UL/PRACH data paths keep their original phase. The offset M makes the head of the first DL burst after UL go out with the gate closed, so slot-6 RAR is lost while lock status is fine.
Q: Why does DSPLL/DCO frequency steering not cause this problem?
A: Steering moves the sample clocks and the timer clock together, so the relative phase M does not change. Only a time step (adjtime/settime) creates M.
Q: Where does the 1.5 µs threshold come from?
A: TS 38.133 requires TDD cells to be within 3 µs of each other; split per cell that is about 1.5 µs. 184 cycles × 8.138 ns = 1.497 µs.
Q: What does a re-align cost and why mute DL first?
A: About 4 s DL off air on n78, one UL frame of PUSCH and ~2 PRACH occasions. Muting stops the RU transmitting into UL slots of neighbours while it is misaligned.
Q: Why is a 10 ms step a blind spot?
A: M is measured modulo the 10 ms frame, so a step of an exact multiple of 10 ms looks like zero, though SFN would be wrong.
CM43 O-RU Performance Management end to end — pm_manager's nine measurement families, CSV groups, the ROP rendezvous, RU → DU (RRHmgr) → ACS/Kibana delivery and its timing rules Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
Every 15 minutes (by default) the O-RU writes a CSV of performance counters: optical module readings, fronthaul packet timing, transmit and receive power, energy use, Ethernet counters and a few vendor extras. The DU fetches the file, bundles it with the antenna-tilt (RET) data, and hands the bundle to the ACS parser, which feeds a Kibana index. If any link in that chain is wrong — a bad interval, a race at the end of the reporting period, a counter read from the wrong place — the dashboard shows gaps or plausible-looking but wrong numbers. This card walks the whole chain from the pm_manager daemon on the RU to the dashboard. CM21 decodes the EPE CSV rows in depth; CM14 covers power self-reporting against a reference meter; CM33 covers SMO PM files in general.
PM delivery chain
Each hop can lose or distort data; check them in order.
Level 1 — the daemon and its nine families
pm_manager is one of 22 M-plane managers on the RU (about 20k lines of C, 14 threads). It owns the o-ran-performance-management YANG module. Nine measurement families map to CSV group ids:
CSV groupFamilyObject / unit
1TransceiverSFP DDM readings, per port number
2RX-Windowper eAxC id — on-time / early / late / corrupt / total (+ C-plane _C variants)
3tx-statsTX_TOTAL only
4EPE (energy, power, environment)per RFFE, controller, FHGW0, plus O-RAN band rows (see CM21)
8TSSIdBFS
9RSSIdBm
11Ethernetfronthaul MAC counters
1000DPD statsvendor
1001PS Healthvendor (deliberately not 12, which O-RAN would allocate next)
RX-Window vs Ethernet: RX-Window answers "is the DU's timing right?" (eCPRI packets only, see CM19); Ethernet answers "is the link healthy and loaded?" (every L2 frame). RX_DUPL exists in the YANG model but is not implemented — expect it absent or zero.
Level 2 — timing rules, conversions and how to check a file
Phase 1 timing rules
  • All measurement intervals are 900 s; counters start when the config is accepted.
  • The first CSV is longer than 900 s — a full 900 s plus the time since accept. It is never shorter, so do not flag it as a bad file.
  • Statistics reset every interval; nothing accumulates across intervals.
  • Upload success → local CSV deleted. Upload failure → kept up to 24 h, oldest deleted first.
  • Filename: C<start>_<end>_<serial>_ru-module.csv. report-info tokens are lowercase (max / min / first / latest / freq / avg).
  • The config leaf is enable-SFTP-upload, not the SRS name enable-file-upload — a config built from the SRS text is rejected.
Power conversions
TSSI_dBFS = 10*log10(raw) - 93.039
RSSI_dBFS = 10*log10(raw) - 84
RSSI_dBm  = RSSI_dBFS + adc_dbfs_adj[adc]
averages are taken in the linear domain (inside the log), not on dB values
Misconception: TSSI 0.00 dBFS means full scale, not zero power. A total read failure is therefore floored to the noise sentinel (−93.04 dBFS), never left at 0.

Quick checks
  • On the RU: ls /O-RAN/PM/ — files that pile up mean upload is failing (they live up to 24 h).
  • On the DU: look for the stats_…-S<serial>_<ts>.tgz bundle with CSV, RET JSON and the 0-byte xfer_complete marker; no marker = ACS will not parse it.
  • In Kibana, filter greenran-stats by RrhSn and count families per ROP; a missing family for every ROP of a boot is the rendezvous bug below.
  • The PM config from RRHmgr is fixed and not field-changeable; if nothing arrives, first confirm all RRH configs/activations completed (it is pushed ~5 min after).
Level 3 — real defects and the Phase 3 automation
  • ROP rendezvous (GRDEV-9044). Producer threads and the file writer raced at the reporting boundary, so whole families could be dropped for an entire boot. Fix: producers seal each boundary and consumers wait with a bounded grace. Intervals that do not tile the reporting period still miss the rendezvous (92 of 119 legal values) — use the recommended intervals.
  • Ethernet 78× under-report. Counters were first read from Linux netdev, which only sees traffic forwarded to the processing system, not eCPRI handled in the FPGA. They matched only at idle. Rebuilt on the FPGA MAC block. Lesson: prove the source sees the physical quantity before building on it.
  • EPE robustness. A unit-presence mask from the personality makes absent RFFE slots report 0.0 instead of flooding I2C errors; a two-pass outlier filter drops temperature samples more than 10 °C from the baseline; the frequency table is optional (GRDEV-9549).
  • Open risk GRDEV-9113: RX/transceiver KPIs stopped at midnight on the 4-band AAU. Fix is on develop; acceptance needs a ≥ 24 h soak that crosses midnight.
  • Phase 3 E2E (GRDEV-9582), two Robot suites: (a) all six enabled groups (rx-window, epe, transceiver, ethernet, rssi, tssi) reach the SMO each ROP, and EPE matches the RU operational value digit for digit (mW→W); (b) EPE band power vs an external DC supply over a load ladder. The pass rule is that the two agree on the idle→max delta, not that power rises — on band 3 with uSleep off both were flat (EPE +0.87 W, DC +0.27 W). With a 300 s PM window each rung must dwell ≥ one window (≈ 45 min per ladder).
  • Bench gotchas: oran-cli callback port "Address already in use" on back-to-back runs; re-add the DU→runner route after a pod restart; on multi-carrier park the other cells and judge traffic by delivered DL > 0; use the framework UE-attach keyword, not hand-rolled adb.
Interview Q&A
Q: The first PM CSV after config covers 1,140 s. Is that a bug?
A: No. Counters start on config accept and the first file is a full 900 s interval plus the time since accept; it is never shorter than 900 s.
Q: RX-Window and Ethernet counters disagree. Which do you trust for what?
A: RX-Window counts only eCPRI packets against the reception window — it tells you whether DU timing is right. Ethernet counts every L2 frame at the MAC — it tells you link health and load. They measure different things.
Q: Why did the Ethernet counters under-report 78× under load?
A: They came from Linux netdev, which sees only PS-forwarded frames; eCPRI is handled in the FPGA. The fix read the FPGA MAC block.
Q: A TSSI value reads 0.00 dBFS. What does that mean?
A: Full scale, not silence. Failed reads are floored to −93.04 dBFS so they cannot be mistaken for full-scale power.
Q: How would you validate the EPE power report end to end?
A: Compare the idle→max delta of EPE band power with an external DC supply across a load ladder, dwelling at least one PM window per rung; pass if the deltas agree.
EMMC01 RU eMMC Wear, Logs in RAM & Power-Cut Safety — wear counters, write amplification, what writes (GRDEV-10352), residual risks and the read-only active slot Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
The RU stores its software, configuration and logs on an 8 GB eMMC chip — flash memory that wears out after a fixed number of erase cycles per block. A study of field and lab units (GRDEV-10352) found that an idle RU was writing about 8 GB a day, mostly log lines and status dumps. Because flash rewrites whole pages and blocks, every small synced log line costs far more flash than its text size. At that rate the chip reaches its rated life in roughly 1–1.5 years. The fix moved logs and other runtime churn into RAM and saves them to flash only once per orderly shutdown; idle writes fell about 4,000×. This card explains how to measure wear, what writes, what can still wear the chip out (boot loops, lab log modes), what a power cut can still break, and the follow-on design that makes the running root file system read-only. Related: CM36 (software update), CM30 (upgradability), CM20 (fault-ids).
RU write path
Each layer can multiply the bytes: a 150-byte log line can cost ~15 KiB of flash.
Level 1 — the chip, the layout and the three wear counters
  • Chip: SanDisk iNAND 7250, 8 GB: mostly MLC rated 3,000 erases per block, plus a small SLC area (30,000 erases) that absorbs small writes first. Some FHGW v2.1 boards carry a Macronix 8 GB MLC part (GRDEV-1470) that reports wear only through JEDEC fields.
  • Sizes: flash page ~16 KiB, erase block ~4 MiB; Linux sees 512 B sectors, 4 KiB ext4 blocks, 512 KiB erase groups, 7.28 GiB user area. "Block" is ambiguous — a flash block is ~1,024× an ext4 block.
  • Partitions: p1 = BOOT*.BIN, kernels, U-Boot env; p2 / p3 = A/B root file systems (slot 1 / slot 2, ~974 MiB each, an image takes ~790 MiB); p4 = shared data that survives upgrades (logs, RU_LOG, configs). Slot 0 is the golden Recovery initramfs.
  • Counter 1 — Linux (/proc/diskstats, ext4 KiB written, /proc/<pid>/io write_bytes): how much the RU writes; says nothing about wear.
  • Counter 2 — JEDEC EXT_CSD life-time estimate A (SLC) and B (MLC) plus Pre-EOL: coarse 10% steps (0x01–0x0A); one step = 300 MLC erase cycles.
  • Counter 3 — vendor Device Report (CMD62 + CMD63): erase counts per area and lifetime host writes in 100 MiB units (verified as 104.86 MB, not 100 MB). One MLC erase ≈ 0.03% of life. The datasheet SLC field offsets are off by 4 bytes (4 / 108 / 120 are correct).
Level 2 — measuring a write rate, what writes, and the fix
Measure: take two reads of the same chip (match the eMMC serial) 1–3 days apart with no reboot between them; per partition use /proc/diskstats, per process write_bytes in /proc/<pid>/io. Then:
write amplification (WAF) = flash bytes written / host bytes written
years to 100% wear     = 100 x (GB per 1% wear) / (MB per day / 1000) / 365
Measured: WAF 2.8–7.2 over unit lifetimes (median ≈ 4); small synced log writes give 7–12, a boot loop ≈ 13, large installs ≈ 1. Endurance was 33–86 GB of host writes per 1% wear (median 55), i.e. about 3–8 TiB total. Worst unit: 869 GiB written used 27.9% of life (837 of 3,000 erases).
Writer (idle unit, before fix)Approx. per dayWhy
systemd-journald (persistent journal)~4.8 GiB (≈ 60%)two managers logged every sensor reading
sync-timing driver log~1.4 GiBopened and closed its log file for every message
operations-manager carrier JSON dumps~1.1 GiB96 dumps a minute
dhclient lease DB~0.6 GBrewritten every 4–5 s when no DHCP server answers
tcpdump S-plane PTP capture~0.3 GiBcontinuous pcap
sysrepo pipes/locks, logrotate state~130 MB + ~110 MBruntime state on flash; logrotate state every 120 s
Why ~100× for journald: 47 MiB/day of log text (≈150 B a line) became 4.8 GiB of flash writes — ×6 from journal fields and metadata (~0.9 KiB a line) and ×16 because each changed 4 KiB page is written whole (~15 KiB per line).

Fix (PR 616 and follow-ups):
  • /var/log is a 256 MiB tmpfs; the journal lives in /run/log/journal (RuntimeMaxUse=64M).
  • At an orderly shutdown ru-log-flush --reason=… --deadline=15 saves logs to p4/logs/boot-<N> (newest first, last 20 archives, ≤ 512 MiB). Old p4 paths still work through bind mounts and symlinks.
  • Read a saved journal with journalctl --file …; journalctl -b -1 shows nothing now.
  • Debug "eMMC log mode" is enabled by creating p4/logs/emmc.enable — never leave it on in the field.
  • dhclient lease, sysrepo runtime files and logrotate state moved to RAM; noatime on all eMMC mounts (relatime wrote 856 KB in 30 idle minutes, noatime 0). Side effect: the DHCP client ID becomes a DUID-LL from the eth1 MAC, so a reservation keyed on client ID needs one update.
  • PR 633 keeps the newest journal lines first; PR 639 shows writes and wear in the login banner.
Result: idle writes fell from ~6.6 GiB/day to ~1.6 MiB/day (≈ 4,000×). A typical day (idle + one boot ≈ 9 MB + one log archive ≈ 20 MB + one update a month) is ≈ 60 MB/day — under 1% wear a year even at the worst measured endurance.
Level 3 — residual risks, power cuts and the read-only root
ScenarioWear per year (worst endurance)
Before the fix, idle≈ 77% (dead in under 1.5 years)
After the fix, idle≈ 0.02%
Typical day after the fix≈ 0.7%
Boot loop, one boot every 144 s≈ 62% (a bench looped 779 times in 63 h and used 1.8% of rated life)
"eMMC log mode" left on≈ 39% (≈ 1.3 years to end of life)
fhgw.log 64 KiB tail kept on p4 every 300 s / 60 s / 10 s0.21% / 1.0% / 6.2%
Whole log synced every 5 s (old PetaLinux behaviour)7.3–7.6%
  • A unit at 144% of rated life still ran with no uncorrectable errors, but its read-reclaim count was 27–100× the others — wear shows up first as background work, not errors.
  • Trim: nothing sends DISCARD today (fstrim.timer off, no discard mount option), so garbage collection copies dead data. GRDEV-10462 adds one fstrim at the end of each install; each DISCARD (up to 74 MiB) stalls eMMC I/O because there is no command queue engine.
  • Update writes: RAM staging with rsync --inplace --no-whole-file wrote 36–189 MB vs 134–250 MB for whole-file rsync (see CM36).
  • Power-cut, eMMC side: reliable write on, 4 MB cache flushed FIFO, so a cut loses only writes in flight. The Macronix alternate has a 256 KB non-FIFO cache with BKOPS off, so cached writes can be lost out of order.
  • Power-cut, Linux side: write-back cache with FUA, no nobarrier, so fsync and ext4 commits are durable; after 779 unclean resets ext4 replayed clean. In RAM-log mode a cut loses that boot's logs — only alarms.log on p4 survives. Crash Record (pstore, GRDEV-10558) keeps the panic report and last 256 KiB of fhgw.log across a panic or watchdog reset; Reboot Event (GRDEV-9680) reports the real restart cause to the SMO instead of POWER-ON for every restart.
  • What a cut can still break: sysrepo .startup files are rewritten in place without fsync. A torn file means only some modules rebuild — NACM, users, keys and the NETCONF server do not load and the unit can become unreachable. The most frequent window is the call-home copy on every DHCP renewal. Operator on-the-fly changes are baked into startup only on a planned reset, so the first boot after a cut runs the older config. Proposed: atomic store (temp, fsync, rename, fsync dir), skip unchanged call-home copies, bake before import, e2fsck -p on p4 before mount, and a power-cut soak (GRDEV-8662).
  • Read-only active slot (GRDEV-6615 HLD): today a rollback does not return to a known image, hand edits survive reboots unseen, and upgrades lose state kept in the slot. Design: ro on the / line of /etc/fstab; each written path keeps its FHS name but is backed by tmpfs (if the boot recreates it) or a p4 bind (if it must persist). Trap: dhclient-script's wait_for_rw() reads the fstab / line — kernel ro with fstab rw loops forever, DHCP never completes and the unit never calls home. The active slot is also mounted rw a second time under /run/media/mmcblk0p2|3, so root=…ro alone protects nothing. p1 is now fsck'd before mount (GRDEV-10409) after a repair on a mounted p1 truncated uboot.env.
  • Validation angles: read wear counters before and after every soak; track per-process write_bytes to catch a regressing writer; keep boot-loop tests short; after the RO change a missed writer fails with EROFS (check systemctl --failed); a missing p4 is silent because of nofail.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why can 47 MiB of log text wear the flash like 5 GiB?
A: Journal metadata adds about ×6 and the kernel writes each changed 4 KiB page whole on every sync, about ×16 more; flash then adds its own write amplification.
Q: Why use the vendor erase count instead of the JEDEC life-time field?
A: JEDEC reports in 10% steps (300 erases each), too coarse to see a trend in days; the vendor Device Report gives exact erase counts and host writes.
Q: What field risk remains after logs moved to RAM?
A: Boot loops (~62% of life a year at one boot per 144 s) and a lab eMMC log mode left enabled (~39% a year); both must be flagged early.
Q: Why is root=...ro on the kernel command line not enough for a read-only root?
A: fstab still says rw, which makes dhclient-script wait forever, and the slot is mounted rw a second time under /run/media, so it is still writable.
Q: After a power cut a unit is unreachable over NETCONF but boots. What would you suspect?
A: A torn sysrepo .startup file — written in place without fsync — so NACM, users, keys or the NETCONF server failed to load.
CM44 Flavour E2E Integration Playbook — B41 TDD and B8 + B28 low band: model names, antenna maps, BoB power settings, the acceptance matrix and known stack limits Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
A "flavour" is one band combination of the AAU (for example B41 TDD, or the B8 + B28 low band). Before a flavour is released it goes through an end-to-end integration: a real DU and core, a breakout box (BoB) and RF chamber, commercial UEs, and a fixed list of acceptance tests — reboot recovery, coverage to cell edge, link adaptation, upgrades, deliberate alarms, peak throughput and long stability runs. This card collects what two integrations (B41 and B8 + B28) taught: how the bench is wired, which model name and antenna map each flavour uses, why the bench power settings are deliberately tiny, the acceptance matrix you can reuse as a test-plan template, and the stack limits that look like RU faults but are not. Related: OPS3 (re-offset formula, model flash), CM26 (bring-up and datafill), CM27 (acceptance gates), CM20 (fault-ids), G2RUN01 (2G on the FHGW).
Level 1 — bench setup, model names and antenna maps
  • 10 Gb/s multimode fibre with matched SFP types at both ends; FHGW + BoB + chamber + RF combiners.
  • Model name written into EEPROM with flash_eeprom (option 9, then 20) — it selects the personality, so a wrong name means the wrong band/port map.
  • First firmware install by hand: ru-upgrade.sh <zip> <slot_id> (slot 0 = install to the inactive slot); every later install only from ACS.
FlavourModel name (EEPROM)Antenna / port map
B41 TDDIntegrity-ME-0-B1B3B8B41-00-2antennas 1–4 on TX/RX 5–8, alternating ±45° polarisation
B8 (low band)…B1B3B8B41-00-1 (4-band) or …B1B3B8B28n41-00-1 (5-band)TX 1/2/5/6, RX 3/4/7/8
B28 (low band)same unit as B8TX 3/4/7/8, RX 1/2/5/6 — TX and RX interleave across the two low bands
Level 2 — bring-up settings and the acceptance matrix
B41 bring-up before ACS supported BW and re-offset: set the BW in startup.xml channel-bandwidth (Hz) and the PRACH re-offset per BW:
LTE BWPRACH freq offsetre-offset (no CA)
5 MHz141284
10 MHz374308
15 MHz627908
20 MHz8611220
X        = (PRACH offset - MAX_PRB/2) + 3
ReOffset = 288 * X - 12          # e.g. 20 MHz: X = 86 - 50 + 3 = 39 -> 11220
BoB bench power: P0 Nominal PUSCH = −70 dBm, Carrier Tx Power = −18 dBm. On low band the max/min power per antenna advertised in SIB1 / RU capability is cut by editing max/min-power-per-antenna in the -oran.json personality: B8 44.7 / 34.7 → 6 / −4 dBm, B28 46 / 36 → 1 / −9 dBm (applied after cell creation by the release script). Why: otherwise the UE's UL power control assumes a 45 dBm macro site and transmits far too hot for a cabled bench.

Acceptance matrix (reusable as a template):
  • Recovery after phy-pod, vnode-pod and RRH reboot — 100 iterations each.
  • Cell centre → edge with attenuation down to −110 dBm, per BW.
  • UL link adaptation (TPC, PHR, target SINR) and DL link adaptation (RI, TM, efficiency in ltestats).
  • Firmware upgrade and downgrade from ACS.
  • Deliberate alarms: fault ids 1, 2, 4, 11, 12, 16 (see CM20).
  • Max throughput for 1 h (UDP + TCP) per BW; 8 h stability per BW; low and high EARFCN.
Results: B8 + B28 — 26 / 26 pass on B28 (B8 limited to 5/10 MHz); B41 — 13 pass, 2 fail (different-frequency test and alarm implementation).
Level 3 — stack limits that look like RU faults
ObservationReal causeWhat to do
Control-channel decode poor with several UEs on B41no dynamic CFI on TDD in the stackCFI 1 for one UE, CFI 2 for more
PRACH / special-subframe change has no effectonly PRACH config index 4 and SSF config 2 / 6 take effectstay on those configs
UL throughput capped at 10 MHzUL RBs split per UL slot (45 and 32 RB)stack limit, not RF — note in report
TA reads 4 instead of 0 on a cabled benchthe 20 µs N_TA offset of TDD (see NTA01)expected; do not chase cable delay
CQI and DL throughput dip at EARFCN 41390top-of-band behaviour, still passes KPIrecord, keep testing low/high EARFCN
Alarm time wrong at ACSwrong timestamp in the alarm messageone of the two B41 failures
Only 2 DL layers on low bandFHGW supports 4, low-band commercial UEs do 2not an RU defect
B8 + B28 inter-band CA untestedUEs lack the CA combinationflag as a coverage gap
Lessons for the next flavour:
  • Write the antenna map and model name into the test plan first; interleaved TX/RX ports on the low band make a single swapped cable look like a dead RFFE.
  • Always lower advertised max power for a cabled bench, or UL power control and PHR results are meaningless.
  • Separate stack limits (CFI, PRACH configs, UL RB split, UE layers) from RU defects in the report so the RU is not blocked for something it does not own.
  • Low/high EARFCN runs catch band-edge issues that a mid-channel test never shows.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why reduce max power per antenna to a few dBm on a BoB bench?
A: SIB1 and RU capability otherwise advertise a ~45 dBm site and the UE sets its UL power for that path loss; on a cabled bench that over-drives the receiver and distorts PHR/TPC results.
Q: Compute the PRACH re-offset for 10 MHz LTE with PRACH offset 37.
A: X = 37 − 25 + 3 = 15; ReOffset = 288 × 15 − 12 = 4308.
Q: A B41 bench shows TA = 4 with a short cable. Fault?
A: No — TDD adds the 20 µs N_TA offset, which shows up as a small fixed TA.
Q: Name the main blocks of a flavour acceptance matrix.
A: Reboot recovery loops, centre-to-edge coverage, UL/DL link adaptation, ACS upgrade/downgrade, deliberate alarms, 1 h peak throughput, 8 h stability, low/high EARFCN.
Q: Why might B8 + B28 CA be untested even though the RU supports both bands?
A: The commercial UEs did not support that inter-band CA combination, so there was no way to exercise it.
Addition — 4-band AAU physical, power and fronthaul facts, first link-up checks and campaign gotchas
The 4-band AAU as hardware. Inside are three independent FHGWs (B1/B3, B41, B8 — B28 on the 5-band variant) plus a midboard; four RFFEs per mid-band antenna and two per low-band antenna. Each FHGW has its own fibre and its own management path, and its band personality is factory-set per slot — you cannot swap bands just by re-flashing. Model strings follow Integrity-ME-0-B1B3B8B28n41-00-X (board revision V2P1); an RU on release N with a DU on develop N+1 is a normal campaign mix.
TopicWhat to know
Mechanics~3 m × 1 m, ~150 kg; all cabling from the bottom/back; conducted access by removing a 4-screw cover and using metal jigs that expose per-RFFE TX/RX ports
Powerone PSU input rated up to 3 kW, ~2.5 kW sustained with all four bands transmitting; DC cable AWG 4–6, properly crimped (thinner is a fire hazard); stand it on a non-conductive mat until the enclosure is fitted
Coolingone band is fine on lab air-conditioning; all bands at once needs an external high-flow fan or it thermally shuts down
Fronthaulthree FH fibres to three ports of one Intel E810 4×25G NIC on the DU; the fourth port of the same NIC carries PTP from the GM (LLS-C1, single GM); OAM/backhaul on a 10 G switch port so throughput tests are not capped
FW check / installflash_eeprom option 4 = board revision, 10 = model; stage the zip under /run/media/mmcblk0p4/upgrade/; ru-upgrade.sh <zip> 0 installs to the opposite slot
First link-up checklist (per FHGW): each enumerates as a separate linkable unit, registers as an O-RAN client, gets a DHCP address from the BBU pod (CM42), is reachable, and ornc_debug shows PTP / PA / carrier status. For LLS-C1 each RU is set as a PTP master entry in the ptp-manager configuration. B41 CFI was forced from 2 to 1 for the campaign (more PDSCH symbols) — set over the M-plane from DU/SMO, never by editing XML on the RU.
GotchaConsequence / handling
UEs cannot do 4×4 on B8measure B8 throughput as 2×2
Cell bandwidth changetriggers an automatic RU reboot (chip workaround; see CM17)
B1, B3 and B41 share an antenna portone external attenuator hits all three bands — handover tests need two units or digital per-FHGW attenuation
One RFFE lostup to 6 dB less on a mid-band antenna (3 dB low band) and a skewed beam — check every RFFE (AAUUPG01)
Unused RFFE portsterminate them and keep high-power attenuators in line
16-test E2E plan themes: first link-up, vNode constellations, maximum performance, mobility, VLAN multiplicity, IPsec through a firewall, PTP holdover, fibre pull/reconnect, AAU cold boot (calibration persistence), DU pod restart, RU firmware upgrade and rollback, and a 24 h VoLTE run.
CM41 Integrity RU Feature Map — six feature families, test tiers (CI / Nightly / Weekend), E2E vs tmRCT, per-flavour applicability and model-name families Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
The Integrity RU has grown dozens of features — secure boot, M-plane, PTP handling, PA protection, uSleep, IQ record/playback and more — across seven band "flavours". The feature map is the single table that says, for each feature: which Jira epics delivered it, which test tier runs it (CI, Nightly, Weekend & Regression), whether it is tested end to end with a DU and UE or in test-mode RCT (tmRCT, the RU alone with instruments), and which flavours it applies to. Before planning a campaign or signing off a release, use it to answer: "is this feature covered, at which tier, by which test type, on which flavour?" Gaps in the map are gaps in validation. Related: CM44 (flavour integration playbook), PTPSTEP01 (PTP time jumps), CM43 (performance metrics), EMMC01 (storage).
Level 1 — six feature families
FamilyFeatures in it
1. Platform, boot & securitysecure boot, TPM, serial-port login, startup time, SW upgrade, midboard bootloader upgrade, RU recovery, supervision, personality
2. Management & O&MM-plane (O-RAN compatibility), CLI manager, alarms, logs, performance metrics, LEDs, e-tilt, configurable VLAN
3. Sync & fronthaul transportS-plane and sync, external sync source, PTP time-jump handling, FHGW daisy chain (L2 switch), Mini Metro single fibre, raw IQ streaming to DU
4. RF & signal processingPA protection, temperature compensation, AGC, array phase calibration, DL equaliser, configurable CP removal, reduced carrier power, DPD GUI via DU, IBIT connectivity test
5. Power & thermalpower consumption, uSleep, carrier/band shutdown, power derating, warm-up temperature handling
6. Test, debug & sensingIQ recording, IQ playback, embedded RCT, fake PTP, spectrum analyser
Each row also records the delivering epics, the tiers ticked and the test type. Rough pattern: management, sync and boot features lean on E2E (they need a DU and M-plane peer); RF features (PA protection, temp comp, phase cal, DL EQ, CP removal) and debug tools lean on tmRCT; many RF features are tested in CI and Weekend but skipped in Nightly. A feature row with no epic, or with no tier ticked, is a flag to investigate.
Level 2 — tiers, test types and per-flavour scope
TierBandwidthsChannelsPurpose
CI20 MHz (50 MHz on N78)middle onlyfast gate on every change
Nightlytwo BWs per test, rotating from test to testtwo of bottom/middle/topbreadth over time without a full run
Weekend & Regressionevery BWbottom, middle and topfull coverage before release
Test types. E2E = a real DU, core and UE (max throughput, variable-attenuation coverage test). tmRCT = the RU in test mode measured by instruments: EVM (max RBs and 1 RB), ACLR, output power, UL sensitivity, UL dynamic range (max − min input), PRACH, MRC and RSSI. Each test row lists the RATs (4G, 5G, NB-IoT, 2G + 4G, 2G standalone) and the flavours it runs on.
Flavour (build id)Notes
B1B3 (b0103)LTE 5–20 MHz; 2CC on B1 and on B3
N78 (n78 / n78l)40 / 50 / 80 / 100 MHz; long PRACH format 0; 3 extra TDD patterns; 2CC at 40 / 50 MHz; its own test table (CI at 50 MHz)
B3/4 + 7 Mini Metro (b0307 / b0407)5–20 MHz; 2CC on B3, B4 and B7
Low band (b0828: B8 / B28)5–20 MHz; 2G applicable on B8 (and B3)
B41 (b41)LTE only, 5–20 MHz (see CM44)
n255 (NGC)NGC platform; tested at 10 MHz only
n101 (FRMCS)railway band, 10 MHz only
How to read a row: for "ACLR" on non-N78 flavours CI runs 20 MHz middle; Nightly runs two of the BWs at two of the three channels; Weekend runs 200 kHz (2G/NB-IoT), 5, 10, 15 and 20 MHz at bottom, middle and top. A band-edge failure (for example ACLR at the top channel) can therefore escape CI and appear only in Nightly or Weekend — check which tier last covered that BW/channel before calling a regression.
Level 3 — model names, personality symlinks and how to use the map
Model names follow Integrity-<ME|MM>-<variant>-<bands>-00-<index>. The final index picks which band group of a multi-band unit the personality describes.
Example model nameWhat it means
Integrity-ME-0-B1B3B8B41-00-0macro-type unit, variant 0, bands B1B3B8B41, personality index 0 = the B1B3 group
Integrity-ME-0-B1B3B8B41-00-1same hardware, index 1 = the B8 group
Integrity-ME-0-B1B3B8B41-00-2same hardware, index 2 = the B41 group
Integrity-MM-0-B3B7B78-00-1Mini Metro, variant 0, the N78 group
  • One master personality per band group. When the same band group appears under another model name, the file is a symbolic link to the master — saves space and keeps one source of truth. Consequence: editing a symlinked personality on a lab unit changes every model name that points to it.
  • Planning a campaign: list the features touched by the change, look up their tier and type, and add Nightly/Weekend runs for any feature that CI covers only at mid-channel or only E2E.
  • Release sign-off: any row with an epic Done but no tier ticked is untested functionality; any flavour marked "not applicable" must really lack the feature (for example extra PRACH formats only on N78).
  • Common trap: 2G rows (2G + 4G and 2G SA) apply to B3 and B8 only; n255 and n101 run 10 MHz only — a "missing result" on other combinations is expected, not a failed run.
Interview Q&A
Q: What is the difference between E2E and tmRCT testing?
A: E2E uses a real DU, core and UE and measures user-visible behaviour (throughput, coverage); tmRCT puts the RU in test mode and measures RF conformance (EVM, ACLR, power, sensitivity, PRACH, RSSI) with instruments.
Q: Why can a top-channel ACLR failure appear only at the weekend?
A: CI runs only the middle channel at one BW; Nightly rotates two BWs and two channels; only Weekend & Regression runs every BW at bottom, middle and top.
Q: What does the last digit of an Integrity model name select?
A: Which band group of a multi-band unit the personality describes, e.g. -00-0 B1B3, -00-1 B8, -00-2 B41 on the B1B3B8B41 hardware.
Q: Why are personalities symlinked?
A: One master file per band group avoids duplicates and drift; other model names reusing that group link to it.
Q: How would you use the feature map before a release?
A: Check every changed feature has a tier and test type, that band-edge and all-BW coverage happened in the latest Weekend run, and that rows with delivered epics but no tests are raised as gaps.
CM45 RU DVT CLI — access, roles and platform/OAM commands (system, sync, clocks, FRU, sensors, power, midboard, AISG, alarms) Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
Besides the O-RAN M-plane, every RU has a lab/DVT command line — ru-dvt-cli, served by cli-manager — that lets a validation engineer read and poke the platform directly: software and hardware identity, PTP/SyncE lock, clock routing, temperatures and power rails, the midboard MCU, the AISG antenna-tilt bus, LEDs and GPIOs, and even raise a fault on purpose to test alarm handling. This card covers the access model and the platform/OAM commands; RF-path commands (DPD, uSleep, IQ playback, sensing) are covered in RUCLI01. Related: CM14 (power monitoring), CM35 (PTP checks), CM20 (fault-ids), EMMC01 (eMMC health), CM18 (MCU flashing).
Level 1 — access, roles and limits
  • Telnet service on port 8888; one session at a time, 3 login attempts. Credentials are lab-controlled and not reproduced here.
  • Three built-in roles: root (all commands), operator (USER commands only), rfal (USER + RF-alignment commands).
  • Parser limits: 10 arguments, 2,048 characters per line, 250 commands, history of 10,000.
  • Command set grew from 204 to 232 between June and September 2026: 18 added and 27 renamed to kebab-case (getrammem → get-ram-mem, get-ptplockstate → get-ptp-lock-state). Old scripts with the old names fail with "unknown command" — update automation when moving releases.
  • The command table depends on the unit: at boot is_5band_aau() reads the personality/EEPROM; a 5-band AAU loads aau_Command[], other units load asCommand[]. A command "missing" on one unit may simply not exist for that variant.
Level 2 — platform and OAM commands
AreaCommandsNotes
Systemget-sw-info, get-sys-uptime, get-ram-mem, get-rom-info, get-emmc-health, rebooteMMC health shows pre-EOL and life-time estimates (see EMMC01)
Syncset-domain-number <24-44>, set-accepted-clock-class <0-255>, get-ptp-lock-state, get-synce-lock-state, get-synce-status, get-synce-ssm-timeoutalso PTP/SyncE reporting intervals and multicast MAC selection 0/1
Clock I/Oexternal-10mhz-1pps-enable/disable, gps-10mhz-1pps-enable, 1pps-input-to-rfsoc 0|1, 1pps-output-external 0|1input: 0 = external/GPS, 1 = Si5518; output: 0 = from RFSoC, 1 = from Si5518
FRUget-hw-fru, get-sw-fruvariant (43 / 45 / 48), board revision, TRX / RU / QPAM / cavity serials; SW version and Vivado build. set-* identity commands are password-gated
Sensors & powerget-temp, get-temp-threshold <id> <sovl|suvl|bovl|buvl>, get-current, get-voltage, get-power, get-ina-threshold, get-psu-data, get-vdd-data, set-vdd-datawarn / fault thresholds e.g. 85 / 95 °C with hysteresis; VDD = 50 V PA rail
Alarmstrigger-alarm <fault id> <1|0>raise / clear a fault to test fault management end to end
A quick health sweep after bring-up or before a long soak:
get-sw-info ; get-hw-fru ; get-sw-fru      # right image, right variant?
get-ptp-lock-state ; get-synce-lock-state   # locked before any RF test
get-temp ; get-psu-data ; get-vdd-data      # thermal and power baseline
mb-get-alarm ; mb-get-rffe-appver           # midboard happy, FW pairing correct
get-emmc-health                             # wear before/after a soak
Level 3 — midboard, ALD and the traps
Midboard / ALD commandUse
mb-set-mode <0 NORMAL|1 CALIBRATION|2 BOOTLOADER|3 RESET> <col>threshold and AISG set commands work only in CALIBRATION mode
over-temp / over-current threshold + hysteresis get/setB3 has its own over-current registers from MB FW v2.6
mb-get-alarm, mb-get-hw-revisioncurrent MCU alarms and board revision
mb-get-rffe-appver / bootverconfirms FHGW / MB / RFFE firmware pairing; 0xFFFF = not present
mb-get-reset-logMCU reset cause (EEPROM 0x0580)
mb-upgrade-firmware, mb-get/set-addr-valueMCU upgrade (see CM18 for SWD recovery) and raw register access
AISG RET: mb-set-aisg-tilt-ant <tilt> <col> <ant>AS platform only; ALD serial /dev/ttyPS1 at 9600 / 38400 / 115200 baud; install date, bearing, sector, gain (dBi), beamwidth, mech/min/max tilt in tenths of a degree
LEDs, AD5141 pot, GPIO, IO expanders, get-eth-info eth0..2LED green/red 1–3 brightness 0–255; digital pot 0–255; GPIO export/direction/read/write
BT small-cell commandsbias DAC 0–255, EEPROM, PSU — only on a low-power AAU
  • Clock routing trap: 1pps-input-to-rfsoc and 1pps-output-external change where the RFSoC takes its PPS from. Leaving the input on the Si5518 after a GPS/external test means the unit no longer follows the PTP-disciplined path you think it does — record and restore the setting.
  • Calibration mode trap: threshold and AISG writes silently fail (or are rejected) in NORMAL mode; switch to CALIBRATION, write, then return to NORMAL so protection logic runs again.
  • Firmware pairing: mismatched FHGW / MB / RFFE versions cause odd alarms; mb-get-rffe-appver showing 0xFFFF for a slot means the RFFE is absent or not answering, not "version 65535".
  • Alarm testing: trigger-alarm exercises the full fault path (RU → M-plane → DU/SMO) without breaking hardware — use it for alarm acceptance tests (see CM20, CM44), and always clear with 0 afterwards.
  • Power numbers: CLI rail readings, PM EPE values and an external meter use different sensors and models; expect small differences (see CM14, CM43). Do not poll get-psu-data while a PM interval is being measured — a concurrent read can zero that minute.
  • Single session: a forgotten telnet session blocks automation; close sessions cleanly in scripts.
Interview Q&A
Q: An old test script fails with "unknown command get-ptplockstate". Why?
A: In 2026 the CLI renamed 27 commands to kebab-case; the new name is get-ptp-lock-state.
Q: A command exists on one RU but not on another of the same release. Why?
A: cli-manager loads a different command table by variant: is_5band_aau() picks aau_Command[] for the 5-band AAU and asCommand[] for others.
Q: How do you test alarm reporting without causing a real fault?
A: trigger-alarm 1 raises it through the normal fault path; trigger-alarm 0 clears it.
Q: Why would a midboard threshold write not take effect?
A: Threshold and AISG set commands need the midboard in CALIBRATION mode (mb-set-mode 1 ).
Q: What does 0xFFFF from mb-get-rffe-appver mean?
A: The RFFE is not present or not responding; it is not a valid version.
Addition: ru-mb-cli origins, the command families, and what the midboard does on its own
The midboard commands above started life as a separate CLI, ru-mb-cli, derived from ru-dvt-cli. The same source builds for a Raspberry Pi bench midboard (build flag RPI_MIDBOARD) and for the radio (GR_RRH_MIDBOARD), so midboard firmware and commands could be tested on a Pi before a radio existed. On units that still carry it, reach it from the RU shell with telnet localhost 7788 and list everything with help -a. Every command takes a column argument (midboard 0 or 1).
FamilyCommands (examples)
Midboard identity / FWmb-get-bootloaderver, mb-get-appver, mb-upgrade-fw <file>
Midboard healthmb-get-temperature, mb-get-alarms (per column)
RFFE health (RFFE 0–7)mb-get-rffe-temperature, mb-get-rffe-current, mb-get-rffe-alarms, mb-reset-rffe
PA / LNA per antenna (0–3)mb-set/get-pa-state, mb-set/get-lna-state
Modemb-set/get-mode: 0 normal, 1 calibration, 2 bootloader, 3 reset
AISG antenna datatilt, min/max/mechanical tilt, operating band, gain, beamwidth, sector id, base-station id, installer id, bearing, install date, HW revision, product number, serial number (set and get)
Protection thresholdsover-temperature and over-current threshold + hysteresis (set and get)
Raw accessmb-set-addr-value (register read/write)
Autonomous behaviour worth knowing when you test: the PA follows the Tx array-carrier (enabled on activate, disabled on deactivate) and the LNA follows the Rx array-carrier; midboard and RF-board alarms are handled with a watchdog; midboard firmware is upgraded at RRH boot when needed; AISG runs over RS485. So a manual mb-set-pa-state can be undone by the next carrier activation — for a PA-off test, deactivate the carrier rather than fight the automation.
RU boot, bring-up & upgrade
RUBOOT01 O-RU Boot Chain — BootROM → U-Boot → systemd → M-plane apps → call-home, golden fallback, and where the boot seconds go Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
When an O-RU is powered on it climbs a ladder: first the chip's own ROM picks a boot image, then a chain of small loaders hands over to U-Boot, U-Boot works out what kind of radio this is and which software slot to boot, Linux starts, systemd brings up the network and the M-plane applications, and finally the RU calls home to the DU/SMO, which pushes carriers and the sync profile. Only after PTP/SyncE lock and the carriers move to READY is the radio transmitting.

Two things make this ladder worth knowing for validation. (1) If the active slot keeps failing to boot, the unit drops to a golden / recovery image that has no M-plane at all, so the DU simply never sees it. (2) The first boot after a software upgrade is much slower than a warm boot, because the new slot starts with an empty sysrepo datastore and must install ~72 YANG models; the metric that matters is time from power-on to SYNC_LOCKED. See CM15 for the high-level RU lifecycle, CM36 for how slots are installed and activated, and RBTCAUSE01 / CRASH01 for reboot causes.
Figure — O-RU boot ladder from power-on to OPERATIONAL
Solid path = normal boot of slot 1 or 2. Dashed red = fallback when the active slot repeatedly fails to boot.
Level 1 — the boot chain, stage by stage
Stage 0 — hardware chain. The BootROM/CSU reads the multiboot register and loads a boot image from eMMC partition 1:
Multiboot offsetBoot imageRoot file system
1BOOT0001.BINslot 1 = mmcblk0p2
2BOOT0002.BINslot 2 = mmcblk0p3
0BOOT0003.BIN + golden.ubrecovery / factory fallback
Each BOOT.BIN runs FSBL → PMU firmware → ATF (BL31) → U-Boot. Partition p1 holds the boot images and the kernel FIT images (image0001.ub, image0002.ub, golden.ub); p2/p3 are the A/B root file systems; p4 is the data/staging partition.

Stage 1 — U-Boot is the only board-identity authority. It reads the model name from the EEPROM (I2C offset 0xa2), maps model → flavour via a generated file /boot/map/flavor-by-model/<model>, reads three MAC addresses, and passes ru.model= ru.flavor= ru.eth0/1/2= plus root=/dev/mmcblk0p2|p3 on the kernel command line. Kernel and applications only read these values. bootcmd tries mmc_boot twice, otherwise triggers recovery; bootlimit=4 failed boots of an activated slot send the unit to recovery.

Stage 2–4 — Linux and systemd. The kernel uses the DTB to bring up FPGA IP nodes, I2C, EEPROM, hwmon and the PTP chip, mounts the active slot and starts systemd. The M-plane comes up in a strict order:
UnitTypeWhat it does
mplane_initoneshotinstalls the O-RAN YANG models into sysrepo and seeds the startup datastore (first boot of a slot only)
network-bringuponeshoteth0 up; enables the SFP transmitter via GPIO, sets FPGA line-rate/FEC, polls the GT-ready register until it reads 0x3, then eth1 + management VLAN up
mplane-appsforkingresolves the personality startup XML, patches MACs, loads it into sysrepo, launches 16 manager daemons
wd-managernotifysoftware watchdog for the managers: WatchdogSec=45, FailureAction=reboot
netopeer2-serverforkingNETCONF server on port 830
vlan-discoveryexecvlan_scan on eth1, DHCPv4/v6, then nw_manager performs the call-home to DU/SMO
The 16 managers launched by launch_apps() (start-stop-daemon, one PID file each), in order: nw, led, user, fw, sync, file, supervision, log, radio, fault, system-monitor, operations, pm, ald, beam, agc. Documents that say "~21 managers" also count netopeer2, wd-manager, vlan_scan, personality-app and post-app.

Stage 5–6 — call-home and configuration. The DU/SMO reads the RU capabilities, pushes carriers, tx/rx-array-carriers and the sync/PTP profile; PTP/SyncE lock, carriers go DISABLED → READY, the RU sends RRH-Ready and becomes OPERATIONAL.
Level 2 — operations-manager start-up and how to time a boot
What operations-manager does at start-up (this is where RF state is set, so it explains many "radio looks wrong after reboot" cases):
  • apply the personality (flavour data, U-plane change hooks)
  • tx_power_init and the dynamic-VDD worker
  • read FPGA capabilities, then reset the DFE, LowPhy and SMEC register blocks
  • wait if a firmware upgrade is in progress, then calibration_init, set NCO frequencies, initialise micro-sleep
  • read the RF EEPROM file (band-specific calibration data)
  • connect to sysrepo, log ruReset(POWER_ON) — this only records the power-on reason, it does not reboot
  • start threads: keep-alive, array-carrier update / failure / notification, TDD monitor (low-power TDD units), dynamic VDD
  • subscribe to o-ran-operations, o-ran-processing-element and o-ran-uplane-conf, then copy startup → running
Measuring boot time on the bench (the validation metric is power-on / reboot → SYNC_LOCKED, measured on the first boot after an upgrade and on a warm boot):
systemd-analyze                       # kernel + userspace totals
systemd-analyze blame | head -20      # slowest units (mplane_init should top the list on a first boot)
systemd-analyze critical-chain mplane-apps.service
journalctl -b -u mplane_init -u mplane-apps -u netopeer2-server -o short-monotonic
cat /proc/cmdline                     # ru.model= ru.flavor= ru.eth*= root=/dev/mmcblk0pN
fw_printenv selected_slot bootcount upgrade_available
Reading the result: a first boot after upgrade where mplane_init takes ~2 minutes is expected on images that install YANG at boot; the same unit warm-booting should be far faster. If a unit keeps rebooting about a minute after the managers start, look at wd-manager (45 s watchdog) and the DU supervision timer before suspecting the radio.
Level 3 — boot-time budget, acceleration options and pitfalls
Where the first-boot seconds go (first boot into a freshly installed slot, total 170.5 s): mplane_init YANG install 117 s (69%), everything else 28 s, a fixed sleep before netopeer2-server 16 s, mplane-apps 8.8 s. The install runs one sysrepoctl -i per model for ~72 models, and it is paid on every upgrade, not only at first flash, because the new slot has an empty datastore.
ApproachTotal bootmplane_initBoot → SYNC_LOCKEDCatch
One sysrepoctl call per model (baseline)3:02.7117 s213.5 sslow on every upgrade
Option 1: one batched install on the unit1:31.727.4 s103.3 sall-or-nothing: one bad model (a truststore gap in o-ran-certificates) failed the call and the M-plane never came up
Option 2: bake the sysrepo datastore at image build1:07.4 (−63%)2.9 s77.3 srootfs build +15:48 unless a prebake cache is used
Option 2 keeps integrity by construction: the bake stores a fingerprint (checksum of every staged .yang + module list) and is reused only on an exact match; a verify script fails the build if a referenced model is missing. The skip is gated on an init marker, so an image without a bake simply provisions itself on the unit as before. The module set changes rarely, so a cache serves almost every build.

Costs baking cannot remove (paid on every boot): sr_connect() ~0.53 s per process × ~16 managers ≈ 8.5 s; applying the NACM module (ietf-netconf-acm, ~1800 lines of rules) 4.5–5 s.

Pitfalls
  • Ordering bug = reboot loop. mplane-apps must Require mplane_init: a manager that subscribes before the YANG modules and startup datastore exist fails, M-plane supervision is never answered, and the DU reboots the RU again and again.
  • Recovery looks like a dead RU. The golden image has no netopeer2/sysrepo, so the DU sees no call-home. Check over SSH or serial console; /proc/cmdline and the multiboot offset tell you which image you are in.
  • Identity comes only from U-Boot. A wrong flavour or MAC after an EEPROM edit is fixed in the EEPROM, not in a rootfs file; the kernel command line is the truth.
  • Bake vs factory reset. A factory-reset path that restarts netopeer2 before the datastore is re-provisioned leaves M-plane down; include factory reset in boot tests.
  • Power cuts during the trial boot after activation count as failed boots toward bootlimit (see CM36).
Real case: on one build the batched-install option made boots twice as fast in the lab, but the very first unit with a slightly different YANG set never brought up its M-plane because one model failed and took the whole batch with it — the reason the team chose build-time baking, which has no runtime failure mode.
Interview Q&A
Q: Walk me through an O-RU boot from power-on to OPERATIONAL.
A: BootROM/CSU reads the multiboot register and loads BOOT000N.BIN; FSBL, PMU firmware, ATF and U-Boot run; U-Boot reads model and MACs from the EEPROM, picks the slot and boots the kernel; systemd runs mplane_init, network-bringup, mplane-apps (16 managers), netopeer2 and vlan-discovery; the RU calls home, the DU pushes carriers and sync config; PTP/SyncE lock and the carriers go READY.
Q: What happens if the new software slot will not boot?
A: U-Boot counts boots of the activated slot; after bootlimit (4) it falls back to recovery (BOOT0003.BIN + golden.ub). Recovery has no M-plane, so you reach it only by SSH or serial console.
Q: Why is the first boot after an upgrade slower than a normal reboot?
A: The new slot has an empty sysrepo datastore, so mplane_init installs ~72 YANG models one by one (about 2 minutes). Baking the datastore into the image at build time cuts the whole boot by about 63%.
Q: Which boot metric would you put in a test plan?
A: Time from reboot to SYNC_LOCKED, on a first boot after upgrade and on a warm boot, on the same unit and grandmaster. It covers software start-up, call-home, configuration and sync together.
Q: Where does the RU get its model and flavour from?
A: Only from U-Boot, which reads the EEPROM model, maps it to a flavour and passes ru.model / ru.flavor / MACs on the kernel command line. Everything later only reads those values.
AAUBUP01 Bringing up a 4-/5-band AAU from zero — 12 gated stages, 40-port cabling math, midboard and model-number gates Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
A 4-band or 5-band Integrity-ME AAU is several radios in one box: a high-band section (B1/B3/B41) and a low-band section (B8/B28), fed by three fronthaul fibres and exposing 40 RF connectors. Bringing one up on a conducted bench is not hard, but it has many steps, and an early mistake shows up much later as a confusing symptom. A missing attenuator looks like a weak uplink. A wrong model number looks like a frequency problem. A full RU disk looks like a dead M-plane.

The method is a gated sequence of 12 stages. You do not move on until the current stage is proven, so when something breaks you only have one place to look. Think of it as a pre-flight checklist: it is boring, and it is the reason the plane lands. This card is the checklist with the reasons behind each gate. For the AAU itself see M10 and AAUCTL01; for the fault IDs you may meet on the way see CM20.
RF cabling of a 40-port AAU into a 12-port chamber
Drawn from the bring-up procedure. Loss values are nominal; check splitters against their datasheet and measure cables per build.
Level 1 — the 12 gated stages
Work strictly in order. Do not cable RF before the unit is identified, and do not enable RF before the pre-RF checklist (Level 2) is complete.
#StageWhat you do and checkWhy the gate exists
1Identify the unitAAU serial (label, or the DU radio inventory if the label is gone), FHGW version against the test plan, RFFE / low-band filter serials photographed before cabling hides themEvery later fault report and M-plane record keys off the serial
2DC power3 kW 48 V supply, short 4-6 AWG red/black run, polarity checked at the AAU terminals, supply left OFFReversed polarity is not field-recoverable; a weak bench supply cannot hold the inrush
3Connectivity3 x 10G multimode fibres server to FHGW, each carrying C/U-plane + M-plane + PTP, plus a server-to-grandmaster link and out-of-band consoleOne fibre per radio section; a missing fibre means a missing radio
4RF labellingRead the printed bracket labels first; use the port map only where a label is unreadable, then re-label physicallyThe printed label on that unit is authoritative
5RF cablingAttenuator at every port, then combiner/splitter, then chamber; cap every unused portMost "RF problems" later are really this stage
6Power upSwitch on, check the AAU appears in the radio inventory, run orncrrh_dbg on the BBU: expect 3 ornc clientsFewer than 3 clients = a fibre, SFP or radio is not online
7RU SW + midboard FWCheck midboard HW revision, app version and bootloader; pick the upgrade path; check RFFE healthAn out-of-range midboard app makes the RU upgrade abort
8Model numberThe trailing digit of the model number selects which bands the board advertisesWrong model = EMS rejects the EARFCN
9vBBUCertificates, FOCOM registration, deployment input, deploy; every pod Running with no restartsA crashing certmgr usually means certs were not copied
10vNode in EMSRAT mode LTE_Option_7_2 (default is Option 8), Associated RRH ID from orncrrh_dbg, antennas 4 for 4T4R (default 2)Two defaults that silently produce the wrong vNode
11CellEARFCN inside an advertised band, RRH ID and RRH Carrier Index set, Carrier Tx Power is total carrier power, not SIB2 EPREEMS will not save without RRH ID and carrier index
12UE + trafficAttach, IN_SERVICE, bidirectional traffic, record RSRP/SINR/CQI/RI/MCS/BLER, spot-check path lossThis is the baseline every later test compares against
Level 2 — software, model number and the pre-RF checklist
Midboard version gate (stage 7). From the midboard CLI (cli-manager, then telnet to local port 8888) read mb-get-hw-revision 0, mb-get-appver 0 and mb-get-bootloaderver 0, and compare /etc/rfsoc_fru_detail.txt with the image you expect. Versions are hex: high byte major, low byte minor, both read as decimal, so 0x0206 is 2.6 and 0x020b is 2.11. The HW revision often reads "DEFAULT HW REV" because it was never programmed; then infer the generation from the app version.
Midboard HWRequired MB app versionIf out of range
V1.42.1 or 2.2 (0x0201 / 0x0202)Firmware GUI first (path B), then the RU upgrade
V1.52.6 or later (0x0206+); 2.5 / 2.6 / 2.11 fineExactly 2.9 (0x0209): flash the bootloader first (path C)
anye.g. 1.3 (0x0103)The RU upgrade aborts with "failed to identify the midBRD version"
PathWhenTool
A — CLIMB app already in rangeupgrade.sh on the RU
B — firmware GUIV1.4 with MB app out of rangevendor firmware-update GUI over an I2C server
C — bootloader firstV1.5 with MB app 2.9GUI "boot only", then the FHGW image
D — ACSevery later upgrade once the first is doneACS web UI
RFFE health after any upgrade: mb-get-rffe-current <1-4> <band>, mb-get-rffe-temperature <1-4> <band> and mb-get-alarm 0. An empty reply means that RFFE is not reachable. Never cut power to the AAU or the console host mid-flash: it can disconnect the RFFEs.

Model number (stage 8). Format Integrity-ME-0-<bands>-<hwrev>-<flavour>. Each radio in the AAU has its own board and its own model number, and the last digit decides which band group that board advertises:
Trailing digitFlavourBands advertised
-0b0103B1 / B3
-1b082028B8 / B28
-2b41B41
The HW revision field changes the B28 span, not the band set: revisions -00 and -01 have the limited-span filter and advertise B28A (UL 703-733 / DL 758-788 MHz); -02 has the full filter and advertises full B28 (UL 703-748 / DL 758-803 MHz). Read and set it with the RU flash_eeprom tool (option 10 read, 9 set, 11 read back all board details), reboot, and confirm orncrrh_dbg still lists the RU.

Three fronthaul clients (stage 6). orncrrh_dbg inside the BBU pod lists one ornc client per fronthaul link with the RRH ID in brackets. Record those IDs: they are what you pick as Associated RRH ID on the vNode and RRH ID on the cell, and what epe-stats and alarms key off. An RU missing from the list is usually fault 16 "unit unidentified" (CM20), not cabling.

Pre-RF checklist (all must be true before RF is enabled): serial recorded with its source; FHGW version matches the plan; DC polarity verified; labels read from the unit; 40 attenuators fitted at the AAU ports; no TX port on an RX splitter; 12 chamber feeds present and labelled (8 HB + 4 LB); unused connectors capped; connectors torqued; sample path loss matches the expected ~36 / ~33 dB plus cable; 3 ornc clients and PTP locked; midboard app in range; RFFE 1-4 reply and no midboard alarm; model number matches the band.
Level 3 — the traps that cost the most time
1. Path loss is your cabling test. With 30 dB at the port and ~6 dB in a 4:1 combiner, a high-band path should read about 36 dB plus cable; low band about 33 dB plus cable. A path 30 dB too low means a missing attenuator (and risk to the analyser or the AAU front end). A path a few dB high often means a loose connector or a port on the wrong group. Measure a sample of feeds before trusting any RF number. In one lab case a forgotten external attenuator left in one band's path made the uplink about 150x weak while downlink looked normal; removing it gave DL ~220 / UL ~50 Mbps.

2. The same part is a combiner and a splitter. On TX, four ports go into the 4:1 part and one comes out to the chamber. On RX, the chamber feeds the same part type and it fans out to four ports. The part marking does not say which way you used it, so it is easy to cable an RX group backwards.

3. Wrong model number = phantom RF problem. EMS answers with "EARFCN value ... not within the range of available rrh bands" and quotes the bands the board does advertise. If it quotes B8 and B28 ranges while you wanted B3, the board is the -1 flavour. Fix the EEPROM model number, reboot, retry. Do not start debugging the radio.

4. Two EMS defaults are wrong for this bench. RAT mode defaults to Option 8; set LTE_Option_7_2 for O-RAN split 7.2. Allocated antennas defaults to 2; set 4 for a 4T4R high-band cell. Neither causes an error at save time.

5. vBBU addressing must be self-consistent. The M-plane address must sit inside the manual IP range, the GTP-U range must not overlap it, and every network name must match the network block. A mismatch gives a vBBU that deploys but never talks to the RU.

6. The RACH discriminator for "no attach". Run lteStats showuerachinfo while a UE is trying (always with a subcommand and < /dev/null; with no subcommand it drops into an interactive prompt and hangs). Preambles but no Msg3 means the cell hears the UE but the uplink RF path is broken: check RX cabling and attenuators. Zero preambles while the UE reports strong RSRP means the UE refuses to transmit: core, PLMN or barring, not RF. Zero preambles and the UE sees nothing means the cell is not really radiating.

Real case. A B41 cell would not come up on an otherwise healthy radio. The EARFCN put the carrier centre on the wrong antenna-port pair; moving from EARFCN 40375 to 40620 brought the cell up at 20 MHz 2T with about 128 Mbps DL. Lesson: compare the configured carrier centre with what the RU actually supports before blaming the radio.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why is the bring-up done as gated stages rather than "cable everything and power on"?
A: Because upstream mistakes create misleading downstream symptoms. If each stage is proven before the next, a failure points at one stage. For example, an EMS EARFCN rejection after a proven RF chain points at the model number, not the cabling.
Q: A 40-port AAU feeds a 12-port chamber. Walk me through the cabling and the expected loss.
A: Every port gets its own 30 dB attenuator at the AAU connector. High band has separate TX and RX: four ports per group go through a 4:1 combiner (TX) or 1:4 splitter (RX), about 6 dB, so 32 ports become 8 chamber ports at about 36 dB plus cable. Low band is duplexed: two ports per group through a 1:2 splitter, about 3 dB, so 8 ports become 4 chamber ports at about 33 dB plus cable.
Q: EMS refuses your B3 EARFCN and lists B8 and B28 ranges. What is wrong?
A: The radio board is programmed with the -1 (b082028) flavour model number, so it advertises B8/B28. Set the model number with the -0 flavour (B1/B3) in the RU EEPROM, reboot, check the RU is still listed by orncrrh_dbg, and retry.
Q: The RU upgrade aborts with "failed to identify the midBRD version". What do you check?
A: The midboard app version with mb-get-appver. V1.4 needs 2.1/2.2 and V1.5 needs 2.6 or later. If it is out of range, upgrade the midboard app with the firmware GUI first; if a V1.5 board is exactly on 2.9, flash the bootloader first.
Q: A UE cannot attach. What is the single most useful counter?
A: The RACH preamble count from showuerachinfo while the UE tries. Preambles without Msg3 = broken uplink RF path. No preambles with strong RSRP = UE refusing to transmit (core/PLMN/barred). No preambles and no cell seen = cell not radiating.
AAUUPG01 Multi-band AAU Upgrade Paths — the midboard version gate, GUI / bootloader flashing, ACS, and RFFE health checks Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
A multi-band Integrity-ME AAU is not one firmware image but several: the FHGW (RFSoC board, Linux + ru-app), the midboard (MB) that manages the RF front ends, and four RFFEs per band group, each with its own bootloader and application. The normal upgrade (CLI or ACS) only works if the midboard is already on a firmware version the new ru-app recognises — the midboard version gate. Units that left the factory with an old or awkward midboard version need a detour through a Windows flashing GUI first. This card explains how to read the versions, which of four paths to take, how to prove the RFFEs survived, and the mistakes that leave a midboard "missing".
Related: CM04 (A/B bank upgrade theory, LRCP RRHs), CM36 (RU software update redesign), FHGWBOB01 (slots and ru-upgrade.sh), RUCLI01 (cli-manager RF commands), SERNO01 (midboard vs board revision, fault 16).
Choosing the upgrade path
Two inputs decide the path: midboard hardware generation and the midboard application version.
Level 1 — what you are upgrading and the version gate
Read the versions from the midboard CLI
/usr/bin/cli-manager &          # start the CLI manager on the FHGW
telnet localhost 8888
mb-get-hw-revision 0       # V1P4 / V1P5, or "DEFAULT HW REV" = never programmed (common)
mb-get-appver 0            # MB application version, hex
mb-get-bootloaderver 0     # MB bootloader (ru-app does not check this one)
Hex: high byte = major, low byte = minor, in decimal. If the HW revision is not programmed, infer the generation from the app version.
CLI valueVersionMeaning
0x0201 / 0x02022.1 / 2.2V1.4 midboard, in range
0x02062.6V1.5 midboard, in range
0x02092.9V1.5, bootloader must be upgraded first (Path C)
0x020b2.11V1.5, latest (result of Path C)
0x01031.3out of range — upgrade aborts (Path B first)
The gate. Before installing, the RU software runs check_midboard_app_version(): V1.4 needs MB app 2.1/2.2, V1.5 needs ≥ 2.6. Anything else ends with "failed to identify the midBRD version → aborting upgrade". Note: mb-get-hw-revision is the midboard revision, not the board revision stored in the FHGW EEPROM (SERNO01).
Level 2 — the four paths step by step
Path A — CLI. Copy the PWAAU-…zip to the unit and run ./upgrade.sh <zip> 0 (0 = install to the inactive slot), then watch the upgrade log. Prove the result with cat /etc/rfsoc_fru_detail.txt (software version, branch, commit) and mb-get-appver 0.
Path B — GUI (V1.4 out of range). A Windows NUC on a debug port runs the approved flashing GUI and talks I2C over TCP to the FHGW:
  • In /etc/configs/personalities/<model>-pw.json set midboard-config → "is-available": false and reboot, so ru-app releases the midboard.
  • Start the I2C-over-TCP server on the FHGW (TCPI2CServer_t, it listens on port 64890), connect the GUI; it shows the current BOOT/APP versions of each RFFE and the midboard.
  • Start: RFFE 1–4 then the midboard are flashed in turn (~50 min). Then set "is-available": true again and reboot, and check mb-get-appver 0.
Path C — V1.5 on MB 2.9. Same GUI set-up, but choose upgrade order "BOOT Only" (15–20 min); expect RFFE BOOT 2.2 and midboard BOOT 2.3 when it finishes. Re-enable the midboard, install the current FHGW image (Path A or D), then wait 5–10 min: the image upgrades the midboard 2.9 → 2.11 and the midboard then pushes RFFE app 2.6 → 2.8 in the background.
Path D — ACS. Upgrade section → type System → upload the .tgz to the inventory → Download to RRH → Activate. Use it for every upgrade after the first.
RFFE health check after any path
mb-get-rffe-current <rffe 1-4> <band>       # every RFFE, every band
mb-get-rffe-temperature <rffe 1-4> <band>   # MCU, monitor ADC, TX path sensors
mb-get-alarm 0
# empty or error reply = that RFFE is unreachable
Typical healthy temperatures in one example were ~68–77 °C across the sensors of an RFFE. Compare RFFEs with each other: one outlier or one silent RFFE is the finding.
Level 3 — troubleshooting and pitfalls
SymptomCauseAction
"failed to identify the midBRD version → aborting upgrade"MB app outside the gatePath B (V1.4) to reach 2.1/2.2
V1.5 on 2.9 fails to take the new imageknown 2.9 bootloader incompatibility (2.5/2.6/2.11 unaffected)Path C
GUI cannot connectI2C server not running, is-available still true, or wrong addressfix and retry
Midboard undetected after the GUI workis-available left falseset true, reboot
RFFEs missing after flashingpower or NUC interrupted mid-flashfind which RFFE with current/temperature, re-flash it
Rules. Never remove AAU power or shut the NUC during any flash — RFFEs can drop off. Use only the approved GUI version. A failed midboard step can masquerade as an RF fault later (missing RFFE = up to 6 dB less on a mid-band beam, see CM44), so the health check is part of the upgrade, not optional.
Interview Q&A
Q: mb-get-appver returns 0x020b. What version is that?
A: High byte 0x02 = 2, low byte 0x0b = 11, so 2.11 — the latest V1.5 midboard application.
Q: An upgrade aborts with "failed to identify the midBRD version". What next?
A: The midboard app is outside the accepted range for its hardware generation. Bring it into range with the GUI path (B) first, then upgrade normally.
Q: Why set the midboard is-available to false before using the GUI?
A: So ru-app releases the midboard and the GUI can own the I2C bus through the TCP bridge. Forgetting to set it back leaves the midboard undetected.
Q: How do you prove all RFFEs survived a firmware upgrade?
A: Query current, temperature and alarms for every RFFE on every band through the midboard CLI; any empty reply marks an unreachable RFFE.
FHGWBOB01 FHGW on a Breakout Board as a Bench Radio — personalities, BoB provisioning, the DU→RU power chain, conducted UE cabling and the traps that cost days Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
The Integrity FHGW (fronthaul gateway — the RFSoC board inside the AAU) can be run on its own on a bench, with a Breakout Board (BoB) in place of the RFFEs and midboard, as a small conducted 7.2 O-RU for a vBBU cell. That is an excellent bench radio, but the board does not know it is on a bench: its model name picks a personality written for a full AAU, which expects midboards, RFFEs and ~46 dBm of output. Left alone, the unit raises critical faults, reset-loops, or refuses every carrier. This card is the end-to-end recipe that a team arrived at the hard way: choose the personality, provision the BoB, understand the DU→RU power chain (why cell power must equal the RU capability), cable a conducted UE simulator correctly, and recognise the traps that each cost a day or more.
Related: OPS3 (FHGW + DU bring-up recipe), CM44 (flavour playbook, BoB bench power), CM42 (how the BBU records an RU), SERNO01 (fault 16 / EEPROM), CAL01 (dummy TX calibration — not needed on a BoB), NBXG01 (NB-IoT on the same bench).
The DU→RU power chain on a BoB bench (numbers from a real capture)
The only value a human chooses is the cell Carrier Tx Power. The RU advertises its capability; ornc on the DU subtracts and sends a carrier gain.
Level 1 — personalities, BoB provisioning and the power capability
1. The model name decides everything. The band and capabilities are chosen by a model string in the board EEPROM (e.g. Integrity-ME-0-B1B3-00; it is also the hostname, so the shell prompt tells you which personality booted). At boot it selects a set of files from /etc/configs/personalities/ (~130 files on a universal build):
FileWhat it holds
<model>-startup.xmlcarriers, bands, channel bandwidth, antennas and the debug-Ethernet address (differs per model so several FHGWs in one AAU never collide)
<model>-hw.jsonper-band calibration; /etc/configs/hardware.json is re-symlinked to it on every boot
rfdc-<flavour>.txtRF data converter (RFSoC DAC/ADC/DSA) setup for the band group
<model>-oran.jsonO-RAN capability: split 7, CAT_A, port counts, static 9-bit compression, min/max power per antenna
<model>-pw.jsonboard config including midboard presence (is-available)
2. BoB provisioning. A shipped script, /etc/scripts/update_bob_universal.py, makes a full-AAU personality fit a bare board: zeroes adc_dbfs_adj, marks midboards unavailable (mb/is-available false), forces every DSA to 0 dB, resets rx gain-correction and writes the real BoB power capability (each file backed up with a timestamp). For FHGW + BoB only — it damages hardware if an RFFE is attached. Advertised power per antenna (min = max − 10 dB):
Bandmax-power-per-antennamin-power-per-antenna
B17.3 dBm−2.7 dBm
B38.3 dBm−1.7 dBm
B86.0 dBm−4.0 dBm
B281.0 dBm−9.0 dBm
B412.0 dBm−8.0 dBm
3. Facts worth memorising.
  • The FHGW is a 7.2x Category-A O-RU; the split is a property of the RU, the DU deploys the matching PHY (RAT mode LTE_Option_7_2 selects the -o7 images; default is Option 8).
  • max-power-per-pa-antenna still shows the AAU figure (~47.7) after provisioning — irrelevant on a BoB (no PA). Check max-power-per-antenna.
  • A BoB unit should never need dummy TX calibration (CAL01). Calibration faults on a BoB mean a provisioning step was missed.
  • The FHGW has separate TX and RX connectors — no duplex dividers are needed (unlike a duplexed RRU bench).
  • On a bench with no PTP source, fault 18 (FREERUN) is expected until the DU is up; PTP then arrives over the fronthaul (LLS-C1), so eth1 must show carrier.
Level 2 — model change, provisioning order, verification, cabling and slots
A. Change the model (band personality). Order matters:
# 1. back up the EEPROM (partition 2 holds this unit's factory gain calibration)
cat /sys/bus/i2c/devices/i2c-1/1-0054/eeprom > /run/media/mmcblk0p4/eeprom_before.bak
# 2. write the model name with flash_eeprom (option 9 = write model, 10 = read back, 20 = exit)
# 3. delete the cached config of the OLD model BEFORE the first boot
rm -f /run/media/mmcblk0p4/on_the_fly_configs.json
sync; reboot          # boot 1 regenerates the cache
reboot                # boot 2 uses it
# 4. verify
hostname                                  # new model name
uptime                                    # > ~5 min = no watchdog reset loop
ls -l /etc/configs/hardware.json          # points at the new -hw.json
tail -20 /run/media/mmcblk0p4/alarms.log  # no new 15 / 25 / 2005
Skipping the cache delete gives faults 15/25 and endless reboots. A band-suffixed build (e.g. an n78-only package) carries only that band's personalities: after a model change it reset-loops instead of coming up — install a universal build first. Rollback = same procedure with the old name.
B. Provision, then align the cell — in this order.
  • Bring the cell up first (the 27.8 dBm form default still activates against the AAU capability).
  • Run update_bob_universal.py --dry-run, then apply it (it asks three confirmations) and reboot so the new capability is re-advertised.
  • Check the RU really advertises the BoB values: sysrepocfg -X -d operational -x /o-ran-module-cap:module-capability | grep -E 'band-number|power-per-antenna' → B1 7.3 / −2.7.
  • Set the EMS cell Carrier Tx Power = capability (7.3 for B1, 8.3 for B3).
  • Redeploy the vNode from the SMO (undeploy + deploy). A kubectl delete pod is not enough: the capability is baked into the Helm chart (BandId0_MaxTxPower) and cached by the xdb service; only a redeploy regenerates them.
C. Verify the chain end to end.
# DU: what EMS sent vs what the RU can do, and the gain pushed
grep -a 'RRHM-030 CALC' /var/log/pw-share/pods/bbu/sv/ornc-*/current | tail -4
#  cfgTxPower=500 (5 dBm) maxRRHPower=7.30 dBm -> txPower=230 (attenuation, 0.01 dB units)
helm get values pw -n pw --all | grep -E 'BandId0_MaxTxPower|rat_split'
# RU: carrier READY, DACs on, gain, sync, alarms
grep -E 'TRX CARRIER_STATE_READY|DAC Channel|is_valid_combined_gain' /run/media/mmcblk0p4/fhgw.log | tail -5
sysrepocfg -X -d running -x /o-ran-uplane-conf:user-plane-configuration/tx-array-carriers | grep -A5 B01C00A0A1
sysrepocfg -X -d operational -x /o-ran-sync:sync | grep sync-state     # LOCKED
sysrepocfg -X -d operational -x /o-ran-fm:active-alarm-list            # empty
# which antenna layers carry signal (digital power at the DUC)
power_monitor 00 ; power_monitor 01 ; power_monitor 02 ; power_monitor 03
Healthy 2-port cell: layers 0/1 at roughly −23 to −25 dBFS, layers 2/3 Val: 0, -inf dBFS. A layer you expect to be live reading 0 means the problem is upstream of RF (carrier/config), so do not start swapping cables.
D. Conducted UE cabling (2-port cell, 1-TX UE).
LinkPurpose / note
FHGW TX (ant 0) → UE SDR RX1DL layer 0
FHGW TX (ant 1) → UE SDR RX2DL layer 1
UE TX → 4-way splitter → FHGW RX ant 0 and ant 1one UE transmitter feeds two eNB receivers; each output ~7 dB down (6 dB split + ~1 dB loss)
every unused TX / RX / Obs port and splitter output50 Ω load — the coloured plastic caps are dust caps, not terminations
The BoB port map is interleaved, not contiguous (on a B1B3 board B1 ant 0 is TX4 and ant 1 is TX1; RX ant 0/1 are RX1/RX2; the B1 ant 2/3 ports are TX8/TX5 and RX5/RX6). A 2-port cell activates only carrier B01C00-A0A1, so the ant 2/3 ports are silent by design. Get the map from the hardware team in writing; never assume port order.
E. Firmware slots. Slot 1 = mmcblk0p2, slot 2 = mmcblk0p3, slot 0 = recovery; boot files BOOT000<n>.BIN/image000<n>.ub on p1; p4 = shared data and logs. Compare fw_printenv -n selected_slot with findmnt -n -o SOURCE / (if they disagree, trust Linux). ru-upgrade.sh <pkg> 0 targets 3 − current slot: it stops the M-plane app, wipes the target slot, unpacks, records an md5, sets selected_slot and reboots (-n no reboot, -x extract only). Rollback = fw_setenv selected_slot <old>; reboot. Exit codes: 89 two slots outside recovery, 90 active slot unknown, 91 auto (0) in recovery, 92 bad slot, 99 target = running slot. Use the script version on the board (ru-upgrade.sh -v), and see CM36 for the redesign. After any upgrade, re-check the midboard flags and BoB values rather than assuming they survived or were reset.
Level 3 — RCAs, misleading numbers and real results
Traps that cost days
SymptomReal causeFix
Cell never activates; ERR_CNF_COMBINED_GAIN_BAND_1, is_valid_combined_gain: Invalid gain per carriercell power does not match the RU capability (e.g. 27.8 dBm cell vs 46 dBm AAU = 18.2 dB attenuation, outside the allowed window)Carrier Tx Power = capability, then SMO redeploy
