Capability change seems ignoredold value cached in the Helm chart / xdbSMO redeploy, not pod delete
Attach OK, DL ≈ 0, DL HARQ almost all NACKUE receiver saturated (rx gain raised to 90 dB while cabling was wrong); MIB/SIB still decode because they are heavily codedrx gain back to ~30: DL BLER 93 % → 4.5 %
"No suitable cell" right after SIB1RSRP genuinely below q-RxLevMin — usually the wrong TX portfix the port map; lowering q-RxLevMin only hides it
UL fine, DL exactly 0.00 Mbpsno traffic source — UDP DL needs the content server, UL is fire-and-forgetstart the content server; judge by throughput counters
Faults 2005 / 25, reboot every ~5 minmidboard declared present on a board without oneis-available false (provisioning script)
RFSoC at 147 °C (normal ~66 °C)fan not running after power worknew power cable; check temperatures after any power change
Two numbers people misread. 0x11cc is the digital DL full-scale gain at the end of the low-PHY — the value attenuation reduces. 0x161, written near the DAC when the carrier is activated, is a constant, not a computed back-off. The log also carries a legacy 41 dBm AAU value marked "not used" — do not chase it. In RRHM-030 CALC, txPower=230 is the 2.30 dB attenuation in 0.01 dB units; the rounded "(attenuation 2 dBm)" text is the same number.
Serial-console hazard. During boot an interactive RFDC menu (DAC current write, DSA attenuation write, ...) reads the console. An automated echo > /dev/ttyUSB0 once landed in it and wrote a DSA value: not persistent, but the RF path is unreliable until reboot. Type only at a shell prompt; script over SSH. Newer Ubuntu-rootfs builds refuse root over SSH (non-root user + sudo, or console) and every upgrade brings a new SSH host key.
Measured on a 10 MHz B1 cell (5 dBm, 2.3 dB below capability): DL 2x2 81.6 Mbps, UL single antenna 21.9 Mbps (16QAM ceiling ~25), BLER ~10 % both ways — the LTE link-adaptation target, i.e. the scheduler is using the link fully. A 64-UE run with forced CQI 15 / RI 2 asking 64 × 2.5 = 160 Mbps from a ~75 Mbps cell gave DL 17 Mbps at 33 % BLER — a test-configuration artefact, not the radio.
Interview Q&A
Q: Cell power is 5 dBm and the BoB advertises 7.3 dBm on B1. What gain does the RU get?
A: Attenuation = 7.3 − 5.0 = 2.3 dB, computed by ornc on the DU; carrier gain = 20.0 − 2.3 = 17.7 dB. Inactive carriers keep 20.0.
Q: You set the correct Carrier Tx Power and deleted the pods, but the carrier is still rejected. Why?
A: The RU capability is baked into the Helm chart and cached in xdb; a pod restart reuses the old values. Only an SMO redeploy regenerates them.
Q: UE attaches, MIB/SIB fine, but DL throughput is near zero with almost all NACKs. First suspect on a conducted bench?
A: Receiver saturation — too much UE rx gain or too little attenuation. Control channels survive because they are heavily coded; PDSCH at high MCS does not.
Q: Why must you delete the cached on-the-fly config and reboot twice after a model change?
A: The cache holds the previous model's data; with it present the unit faults (15/25) and reset-loops. Boot 1 regenerates the cache for the new model, boot 2 uses it.
Q: A power_monitor layer you expect to be live reads Val 0. Do you check cables?
A: No. power_monitor reads digital power at the DUC, before any cable. Zero there means the carrier or antenna layer is not active — look at carrier config.
ORUMAN01 Driving a PW O-RU from a DU with no M-plane client — manual NETCONF carrier activation, sysrepocfg health runbook, and a Fault 16 reboot-loop RCA Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
Some O-RUs are CUS-only: they have no management plane, so the moment the DU starts sending C-plane and U-plane packets they radiate. A full O-RAN O-RU such as the PW AAU / FHGW is different: it runs a NETCONF/YANG M-plane agent and will not transmit until an M-plane client (normally the O-DU or SMO acting as "O-RU controller") has configured its carriers and set them ACTIVE.

This card follows a real bring-up where an open-source DU, whose Open Fronthaul library speaks only C/U/S-plane and has no NETCONF client, was pointed at a PW O-RU in place of a CUS-only radio. The engineer had to play the O-RU controller by hand with netopeer2-cli, and used sysrepocfg on the RU shell as a back door into the same datastores. The cell finally came up, but the week was lost to something completely unrelated to the DU: an RU that could not identify itself (Fault 16) and rebooted forever. The lesson set is: what the M-plane must do, a five-line health runbook, and how to prove a fault is DU-independent before you debug the DU.
Who configures what when the DU has no M-plane
The DU only moves IQ. Everything a production O-DU would do over NETCONF (set frequency, activate carrier, read faults, reset) is done by hand.
Level 1 — what an M-plane O-RU needs before it radiates
CUS-only vs M-plane O-RU. A CUS-only RU is configured locally (a config file on the RU) and starts radiating when C/U-plane arrives. An M-plane O-RU waits for the O-RU controller: no edit-config that sets the array carrier active=ACTIVE means no TX, however good the fronthaul is. See CM42 for how the BBU normally discovers and records the RU, and CM15 for the full RU lifecycle (call-home, sync, configure, activate).

The tools. On the RU: netopeer2-server (NETCONF agent) on top of sysrepo (the YANG datastores: startup, running, operational). From outside: netopeer2-cli is the client. On the RU shell: sysrepocfg reads/writes the same datastores locally, so you can check state even when no NETCONF session is possible.
ItemValue in the worked exampleWhy it matters
Band / BW / SCSn78 / 100 MHz / 30 kHz → 273 PRBRU carrier bandwidth must equal the DU cell bandwidth
DL ARFCN643440 = 3651.6 MHzmust equal the RU center-of-channel-bandwidth (3651600000 Hz)
Antennas4T DL / 2R UL, TDDnumber of eAxC ports the DU uses
eAxC portsDL 0–3, UL 0–1, PRACH 8–9low IDs carry CC-ID 0 → carrier C00
CompressionBFP-9 for DL, UL and PRACHmust match the RU processing-element / carrier config
TransportDPDK on an E810 VF, VLAN 1 for C- and U-planeVLAN and MACs must match the RU interface config
SyncPTP from an external GM, clock-class 6RU must be LOCKED before activation
eAxC picks the carrier, not the frequency. The CC-ID bits inside the eAxC ID select which RU carrier the IQ belongs to. Ports 0–9 all have CC-ID 0, so they feed C00. To drive C01 you add 0x10 to every port ID. A DU tuned to a C01-ish frequency but still sending CC-ID 0 lands on C00 — the RU does not "follow" the DU's ARFCN.
Level 2 — manual NETCONF bring-up and the health runbook
Step 1 — match the RU carrier to the DU (startup XML). In the RU personality startup file under /etc/configs/, set the C00 tx- and rx-array-carriers:
<center-of-channel-bandwidth>3651600000</center-of-channel-bandwidth>  <!-- = dl_arfcn 643440 -->
<channel-bandwidth>100000000</channel-bandwidth>                    <!-- 100 MHz -->
Step 2 — activate the carrier over NETCONF. Carriers ship INACTIVE (some O-RUs boot INACTIVE by design).
netopeer2-cli
> connect <ru-mplane-address>
> edit-config --target running --config=/etc/configs/flavours/n78/ACTIVE_CC0.xml   # rerun until "ok"
# running-only: lost on reboot. Persist with
> copy-config --source running --target startup     # or set active=ACTIVE in the startup XML
Step 3 — bring-up order (each a checkpoint, do not skip ahead):
#CheckpointEvidence
1RU boots with a valid identity and PTP lockedhardware component shows real serial/model; sync-state LOCKED
2No active alarmsactive-alarm-list empty (no 16 / 15 / 25)
3Activate C00edit-config returns ok; carrier active=ACTIVE
4Start the DU/gNBNG Setup to the AMF succeeds, cell up at 273 PRB, OFH initialised with BFP-9
5Soakcarrier stays READY, alarm list stays empty, RU restart time does not change
Health-check runbook (works over NETCONF or locally on the RU shell):
# 1. alarms - the key check; must NOT show fault 16 / 15 / 25
sysrepocfg -d operational -X -x /o-ran-fm:active-alarm-list
# 2. identity - real serial-num + model-name (not "DEFAULT"), oper-state enabled, availability NORMAL
sysrepocfg -d operational -X -x /ietf-hardware:hardware/component
# 3. S-plane - sync-state / lock-state LOCKED
sysrepocfg -d operational -X -x /o-ran-sync:sync
# 4. carrier - C00 active=ACTIVE, state=READY, expected BW and centre frequency
sysrepocfg -d operational -X -x /o-ran-uplane-conf:user-plane-configuration/tx-array-carriers
# 5. no reboot loop - restart date/time must stay constant between reads
sysrepocfg -d operational -X -x /o-ran-operations:operational-info/operational-state
RU logs live on the data partition (fhgw.log, and the alarm history alarms.log). An M-plane reset is a user-rpc with the o-ran-operations <reset/> RPC, but NACM denies it by default — the account needs an explicit rule.
Level 3 — root cause, red herrings and pitfalls
The real blocker: Fault 16 → 15 → 25. On every boot, at every bandwidth, the RU raised
fault 16  "Unit unidentified"   (unit, MAJOR)
  -> fault 15  "Unit out of order"  (FPGA module, CRITICAL)
  -> fault 25  "Reset Requested"   -> reboot loop -> TX never enabled
Root cause: the mid-board identity EEPROM (product number, board revision, serial) did not agree with the backup copy eeprom_data kept on the eMMC data partition (the log shows an "eeprom data not match buffer … backup_buff …" line). The unit could not establish who it was, so it never came into service. The RU team re-provisioned the identity; after that the 100 MHz C00 carrier came up clean and stayed up under the DU. See SERNO01 for the EEPROM identity map and Alarm-16 recovery, CM20 for the fault-ID table, and CM40 for a different root cause of the same 15/25 reboot chain.

How it was proved DU-independent — the most reusable technique here: (1) Fault 16 was present on a bare boot with the DU stopped and nothing configured; (2) alarms.log showed the same fault going back months, long before this integration. Two minutes of reading the RU's own history would have saved days.
Red herringWhy it was not the cause
40 vs 100 MHz bandwidthfailed identically at both widths
"Failed to set WOLA values" logbenign, fires ~13 s after Fault 15; WOLA is not used on n78
A known 100 MHz SSB-placement bugdifferent symptom (no SSB, but no Fault 15/16)
A known false RFFE over-current bugother unit type, raises Fault 26 (absent here); its workaround did not clear Fault 16
Open items worth knowing: the DU's built-in test-mode UE does no RRC/NAS, so it can never attach or answer a ping — you need a real UE for E2E. The OFH timing windows (t1a / ta4 sets) were inherited from another RU's template; under traffic watch for late/early U-plane reception counters and retune (CM19). And with no M-plane controller, carrier activation is a manual step after every boot unless it is persisted to startup.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why does a CUS-only RU radiate as soon as the DU sends IQ, but a PW O-RU stays silent?
A: The PW O-RU is a full O-RAN O-RU with an M-plane: its array carriers are INACTIVE until an O-RU controller configures them and sets active=ACTIVE over NETCONF. A CUS-only RU has no M-plane and takes its carrier config from a local file.
Q: Your DU has no NETCONF client. How do you get the RU on air?
A: Act as the O-RU controller yourself: match centre frequency and bandwidth in the startup XML, connect with netopeer2-cli and edit-config the running datastore with the ACTIVE carrier XML, then persist it with copy-config running→startup because running is lost on reboot.
Q: The DU sends on eAxC ports 0–3 but is tuned to the second carrier's frequency. What happens?
A: The IQ still goes to C00, because the CC-ID bits in the eAxC ID choose the carrier, not the DU's ARFCN. To feed C01 you add 0x10 to each port ID and make sure C01 is configured and active.
Q: Give a quick health check for an O-RU that will not stay up.
A: Read active-alarm-list (must be empty), ietf-hardware component (real serial/model, enabled, NORMAL), o-ran-sync (LOCKED), tx-array-carriers (ACTIVE/READY), and operational-state twice to make sure the restart time is not changing.
Q: How do you show a Fault 16 reboot loop is not caused by the DU?
A: Stop the DU and reboot the RU with nothing configured: the fault still appears. Then read the RU alarm history: the same fault goes back months. Here the cause was an identity EEPROM that did not match its eMMC backup.
OCUDU01 O-RAN 7.2 DU Bring-up Debug Journal — RT host, LLS-C3 PTP, DPDK VF, eAxC maps and the silent failures Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
This card is a debug journal of bringing up an open-source 5G DU (OCUDU — the carrier-grade successor of the srsRAN Project) on a bare-metal Intel Ice Lake server with a third-party O-RAN 7.2 O-RU, an external PTP grandmaster (LLS-C3) and a lab 5G core. The end result was a real n77 cell — 3.9 GHz, 100 MHz TDD, 4T4R DL / 2R UL — with a commercial-style UE attached, DL 256QAM and ~45 Mbps UL at 64QAM. The value is not the install steps but the seven root causes on the way, most of which were silent: no error, no alarm, just a cell that does not work. Any engineer bringing up a 7.2 DU — ours or anyone else's — meets the same classes of fault: real-time host tuning, NTP fighting PTP, a management NIC dying under busy-poll load, hugepages starving RAM, eAxC conventions, TDD pattern mismatch and PA protection trips.
Related: CM35 (LLS-C1..C4 and G.8275 profiles), CM31 (eAxC and C/U-plane packets), CM34 (O-DU internals, Category A/B), PTPSTEP01, DUOPS01, RUEMU01.
Bench topology that finally worked
One E810 port: the PF stays on the kernel driver and owns PTP, a VF on the same port carries DPDK fronthaul. Management and backhaul on an all-Intel NIC.
Level 1 — platform, timing and fronthaul facts
The real-time host
  • PREEMPT_RT 5.15-rt kernel with isolcpus, nohz_full, rcu_nocbs, IRQ affinity to housekeeping cores (0–1 and their siblings), 1 GB hugepages, idle=poll, max_cstate limited, intel_iommu=on iommu=pt.
  • Imaging the server with the existing platform Ubuntu image (via FOCOM, see CM38) was a huge shortcut — the RT tuning is already correct. Never apt upgrade it: ~713 packages are held to protect the RT kernel.
  • Before RAN use: un-blacklist SCTP (N2/NGAP needs it — otherwise a cryptic socket error), stop NTP (timedatectl set-ntp false, mask chrony/timesyncd), no swap; optionally disable kubelet/containerd.
Timing (LLS-C3, G.8275.1 domain 24)
ptp4l   -2 -i <pf> --dataset_comparison=G.8275.x --domain=24 --slaveOnly=1
phc2sys -s <pf> -c CLOCK_REALTIME -w -n 24
# each pinned to its own isolated core with chrt FIFO
# good: port state SLAVE, ptp4l rms 1-8 ns, phc2sys offsets within +/-100 ns
The data path — the same-NIC rule
  • E810 PF stays on the ice driver and owns PTP hardware timestamping; one VF on the same port (sriov_numvfs=1, trust on, MAC set) is bound to vfio-pci for DPDK fronthaul. trust on is needed for the multicast/VLAN handling eCPRI uses.
  • A freshly imaged box shows every port DOWN — admin-down looks exactly like a dead cable.
  • The RU dictates the DU MAC: the VF MAC must equal the DU MAC configured in the RU, or every frame is silently dropped. The C/U-plane VLAN must match on both sides.
  • What a DU must agree with any O-RU: common PTP source, C/U VLAN, accepted DU MAC, eAxC maps (DL / UL / PRACH), compression, and the T1a/Ta4 delay windows.
Level 2 — configuration, pre-flight and attach ladder
DU-side OFH settings that matched this RU
ParameterValueWhy it matters
T1a C-plane window286–535 µsC-plane must reach the RU inside its reception window
T1a U-plane window80–390 µsDL IQ arrival window; outside it the RU drops symbols
Ta4 window25–500 µsUL arrival window at the DU
CompressionBFP 9-bit, all planesmust match the RU (RU calls it "dynamic compressed")
PRACH C-planeenabledRU needs C-plane sections for PRACH
TDD patternDDDSUU + DDDDmust equal the DU tdd_ul_dl_cfg exactly
DPDK EALexplicit CPU map for every PHY worker--lcores alone restricts the whole process (see RCA 7)
OFH busy-waitingonotherwise "woke up late, skipped N symbols"
FAPI log levelerrorwarning floods add lateness, which causes more warnings
Pre-flight checks before every gNB start
grep Huge /proc/meminfo ; free -g        # hugepages vs real free RAM
dpdk-devbind.py -s                        # VF bound to vfio-pci
ip link show <pf>                         # VF MAC = RU's DU MAC, trust on, link UP
pmc -u -b 0 'GET PORT_DATA_SET'           # SLAVE, not LISTENING
timedatectl | grep NTP                    # NTP service inactive
oru_status | grep -E "ORX|Att"            # RU radiating: real ORX power, not -inf
Attach checkpoints — where to look
Stage that failsCheck
No PRACH seenSSB power and ARFCN, TDD pattern RU = DU, RU actually radiating (ORX)
PRACH OK, Msg3 / PUSCH failsUL antenna / eAxC port map, which RU antenna the UE couples into, UL SINR
No authentication answerIMSI, PLMN, TAC, slice in the core
Attached, no dataN3 binding and backhaul capacity (100 MHz 4T4R can exceed 1 Gbps DL — use a 10 G link)
Drops under loadUL quality, RT lateness counters, OOM (dmesg | grep -i oom)
Automation should gate the gNB start behind these checks rather than use Restart=always — see RCA 2 for why.
Level 3 — RCAs and the silent-failure pattern
The seven root causes
#SymptomRoot causeFix / lesson
1phc2sys locks, then periodic excursions to ~16 µsNTP (chrony) still stepping/slewing CLOCK_REALTIME against phc2sys; RT pinning did not helpmask chrony/timesyncd: average 12 ns, max 52 ns
2Management NIC dies ~7 min after starting a busy-poll gNB (TX timeout, firmware command hang); later the whole host hangsBroadcom management NIC driver could not live with busy-poll RT load; SCHED_FIFO 96 PHY workers + reset storm starved journald/jbd2 for > 600 sall-Intel NICs (E810 fronthaul, X550 mgmt/backhaul); never auto-restart a busy-poll gNB against broken fronthaul
3Compiler killed (Error 137), SSH sluggish23 × 1 GB hugepages on a 32 GB host left ~4 GB RAM8 × 1 GB is enough for the gNB
4First RU stuck in PTP LISTENING, no errors; then 100 % U-plane rejectedRU only accepted a master announcing clockClass 6, timeSource GPS and realistic variance; then an eAxC convention mismatch (PW-PHY/FlexRAN puts PRACH on eAxC 8–B, srsRAN/OCUDU on 4–7) on old RU firmwarematch RU firmware to the version the DU vendor tested; check the eAxC convention first
5UE invisible: no PRACH, nothing loggedRU TDD pattern differed from DU tdd_ul_dl_cfg, so RU RX was gated off during PRACHalign patterns; RU config changes need a full RU reboot
6No cell, ORX = -inf, while fronthaul, PTP and gNB look healthyRF cables hot-swapped with RU powered tripped the transceiver TX-PA protection; survives soft rebootpower off, terminate every TX port, power on
7gNB start hangs silentlyDPDK --lcores restricted the whole process; every PHY worker piled onto one coreexplicit per-worker CPU affinity
Why the cell is 2R UL. The second RU streams DL on eAxC 0–3 and UL on 0–3, but PRACH only on eAxC 8 and 9 (plus a muxed copy on eAxC 0). The DU needs one PRACH port per receive antenna, so the cell can only be 2R. eAxC 0/1 are hard-wired to physical ANT1/ANT2. If a shield-box UE couples mainly into ANT3/4, PRACH still detects (via the muxed copy) but Msg3/PUSCH fails almost every time — move the coupling to ANT1/2. Lesson: draw the eAxC ↔ antenna map before blaming the stack.
Pattern across all seven: the failure shows up somewhere other than its cause, and nothing logs an error. Healthy PTP plus healthy fronthaul counters do not prove the RU is radiating; a locked phc2sys does not prove the system clock is stable; an attached UE does not prove the UL antenna map is right. Build the pre-flight to test each link separately.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why put PTP on the PF and fronthaul on a VF of the same E810 port?
A: The PF keeps the kernel driver so ptp4l gets hardware timestamps on the same physical port the RU is timed through; the VF goes to vfio-pci so DPDK can busy-poll the fronthaul without fighting the kernel for the device.
Q: An O-RU sits in PTP LISTENING forever and logs nothing. What do you check?
A: That Announce messages reach it (VLAN, domain 24, multicast) and what they contain: some RU firmware rejects a master that does not announce clockClass 6, a GPS time source and realistic variance.
Q: PRACH is detected but Msg3 never decodes. Name two likely causes.
A: UL eAxC/antenna map wrong (UE coupled into antennas whose UL is not configured), or poor UL SINR / timing. Check which RU antenna the UE is on.
Q: Fronthaul counters and PTP look perfect but the UE sees no cell. What else?
A: Check the RU is actually radiating (ORX power). A PA protection trip from hot-swapping cables, or a TDD mismatch, leaves everything else green.
Q: Why is NTP dangerous on a PTP-timed DU?
A: chrony/timesyncd discipline CLOCK_REALTIME too, so they fight phc2sys and cause periodic microsecond excursions. Only phc2sys should steer the system clock.
NBXG01 NB-IoT Extended Grid on the FHGW — capability rows, config-ids, NPRACH endpoint, eAxC marker, NETCONF apply/verify and the read-backs that lie Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
NB-IoT in guard-band mode uses one 180 kHz PRB that sits just outside the edge of an LTE carrier (see LF34 for the air interface, NBIOT01 for the PHY test vectors). On an O-RAN 7.2 radio, NB-IoT has no RAT of its own: it rides an LTE host carrier. The radio simply widens that carrier's grid by a PRB or two on each side — the extended grid (10 MHz: 50 → 52 PRB) — so the NB-IoT PRB fits in the guard band, and opens a separate narrow NPRACH receive pipe for NB-IoT random access. This card puts three views together: how the RU advertises that it can do this (there is no "NB-IoT supported" flag — it is structural), how the BBU configures it over the M-plane, and how to apply and verify it by hand on an FHGW bench with NETCONF — including the read-backs that lie and the firmware gap that looked like a config error. It ends with the end-to-end bench lessons from getting LTE 4x4 and NB-IoT UEs to attach on the same FHGW.
Related: FHGWBOB01 (the BoB bench and power chain), CM31 (eAxC), CM16 (carrier activation chain), CM42 (RRH DB endpoint types).
The extended grid on a 10 MHz host carrier
M-plane opens the window (wider grid + NPRACH endpoint); C-plane points inside it. Upper guard band shown.
Level 1 — endpoints, config-ids and the capability rule
1. Endpoints. An O-RAN low-level endpoint (o-ran-uplane-conf) is one U-plane pipe per band × TX/RX × antenna × carrier, tagged by an eAxC. FHGW names: B01TxA00C00 (band 1, TX, antenna 0, carrier 0), B01RxA00C00 (RX data), B01RxRachA00C00 (LTE/NR PRACH), B01RxNbiotRachA00C00 (NB-IoT NPRACH). Each carries a combination-configuration with three fields: endpoint-type (read-only capability — on B1B3 data = 3, PRACH = 100, NPRACH = 101), set-id (read-only, 0 data / 1 PRACH) and config-id — the one field you change.
config-idData endpoints (set 0)PRACH endpoints (set 1)
0LTE 15 kHz — default (50 PRB at 10 MHz)LTE format 0, 1.25 kHz
1NR 15 kHzNR format 0, 1.25 kHz
2LTE + NB-IoT 15 kHz — 52 PRB at 10 MHzNR 15 kHz format B4
32GNR 30 kHz format B4
4NR 30 kHzNB-IoT NPRACH, 3.75 kHz, 1 PRB
5—format 1, 1.25 kHz
2. How a radio says "I can host NB-IoT". The YANG has no NB-IoT flag. Under endpoint-types → supported-configuration-combinations → set → config the RU lists rows of carrier type, max-prb-range, filter bandwidth, SCS and center-from-freqoffset. An antenna's endpoint type is NB-IoT-capable when it offers an LTE row with more PRBs than standard LTE (for example 102 or 106 against 100 at 20 MHz). The rule is strictly greater: a row of exactly 100 means no guard-band room. A row without carrier types is a wildcard. Capability can differ per antenna — on one real 4-antenna radio antennas 0/1 used a type with such a row and antennas 2/3 a type without it, so only antennas 0/1 can carry NB-IoT.
Host LTE BWNormal PRBGuard PRB per sideExtended PRB
5 MHz25127
10 MHz50152
15 MHz75279
20 MHz1001102
Extension is symmetric, so the centre frequency never moves (20 MHz example: 102 × 180 kHz = 18.36 MHz occupied around the RU's own centre). config-id does not move the carrier — frequency comes from the array-carrier path. The YANG array-carrier type enum only has NR / LTE / DSS_LTE_NR, so the RAT stays "LTE".
Level 2 — the managed M-plane flow and the manual bench procedure
A. Managed path — what the BBU does (RRH manager + ornc)
  • At Call Home, ornc reads the endpoint-type capability tree and sends one compact record per type to the RRH manager inside the existing capabilities message (no new message, no extra NETCONF). Gated on M-plane YANG version ≥ 18; an older radio simply reports no types.
  • The LTE vNode sends its normal carrier request with configType = 4G_NB ("an LTE carrier that hosts NB-IoT"). Everything else is the normal LTE flow: L1_DONE, then SET_TX_POWER triggers the U-plane push, then RRH_READY. In that push only three leaves change on capable antennas: number-of-prb (100 → 102 at 20 MHz), the combination and the config-id (0 → 2). Incapable antennas are left untouched.
  • The NB-IoT vNode sends configType = NB with no frequency, bandwidth or antenna count — it names its host by RRH/band/carrier. It is accepted only if a 4G_NB host row already exists (a plain 4G carrier never reserved guard room) and is stored inside the host's carrier row, so it dies with the host.
  • For the NPRACH endpoint ornc writes center-from-freqoffset-enabled = true and an occupied bandwidth spanning the whole extended grid. Gate: the RU must declare centre-from-freqoffset at both type and config level, and max-overlapping-instances ≥ 1.
  • NB-IoT UL samples are marked in the eAxC with the top bit of the CC_ID field: 0x0080 (bit 8 counted MSB-first, inside the 0x00F0 ccid mask) — not 1<<8, which is a band-sector bit. Example: eAxC 12 → 140. If the RU's bitmask cannot carry the bit, keep the RU value.
B. Bench path — apply it by hand on an unmanaged FHGW
# 0. firmware first: which slot runs, and does it have type-101 NPRACH endpoints?
sysrepocfg -X -d operational -x /o-ran-software-management:software-inventory \
  | grep -E '<name>|<active>|<running>|build-version'
sysrepocfg -X -d running -x /o-ran-uplane-conf:user-plane-configuration \
  | grep -oE '<name>B[0-9]+Rx[A-Za-z]*Rach[A-Z0-9]*</name>' | sort -u
# 1. deactivate the carrier (running is locked while a carrier is ACTIVE)
# 2. merge a partial XML: config-id 2 on B01Tx/RxA0[0-3]C00, 4 on B01RxNbiotRachA0[0-3]C00
sysrepocfg --edit=/run/media/mmcblk0p4/nbiot_extgrid.xml -d running -m o-ran-uplane-conf
#    (or netopeer2-cli: edit-config --target running --config=...)
sysrepocfg --copy-from running -d startup     # keep both datastores bootable
reboot                                    # transient faults after the edit are expected
# 3. verify
grep -E 'availability:|sync_state:|TRX Carrier|center frequency|Carrier Placement' \
  /run/media/mmcblk0p4/fhgw.log | tail -20
sysrepocfg -X -d operational -x /o-ran-sync:sync | grep sync-state     # LOCKED
sysrepocfg -X -d operational -x /o-ran-fm:active-alarm-list            # empty
Leave the legacy B01RxRach… endpoints at 0. The change persists across reboots and firmware upgrades — reverting means writing config-id 0 back and rebooting. Good read-back: all B01 Tx/Rx C00 endpoints at 2 — especially A00/A01, the antennas of the live carrier B01C00-A0A1 — and the NbiotRach endpoints at 4, identical in running and startup. NPRACH endpoint itself: 16-bit static IQ, SCS 3.75 kHz, 1 PRB.
Level 3 — traps, firmware RCA and bench lessons
Read-backs that lie
  • Wrong user: under a restricted NACM user, sysrepocfg export returns empty with rc 0 — it looks exactly like an unconfigured unit. Read as root.
  • grep window: grep -A2 <name> misses config-id, which sits several lines below the name. Widen the window or parse the XML.
  • Wrong antennas: sampling A02/A03 only can look right while the on-air A00/A01 are still LTE.
  • Two datastores: running (tmpfs, what the low-PHY reads) and startup can disagree; editing startup alone never reaches the low-PHY. With carriers deactivated in startup, an apply + reboot leaves the cell dead.
Firmware RCA. On the first firmware (v1.0.0) the edit applied cleanly, yet the low-PHY still logged RAT LTE: carrier activation silently reset the active antennas' endpoints to config-id 0 (inactive A02/A03 kept 2), and no type-101 NPRACH endpoints existed at all (a workaround put config-id 4 on the legacy PRACH pipe). v1.0.1 fixed both. "A00/A01 at 0, A02/A03 at 2" is the firmware signature, not a half-finished edit — check the software-inventory slot before re-applying anything.
NPRACH detects nothing? The NPRACH endpoint has offset-to-centre 0, so the RU extracts at the carrier centre; the whole guard-band offset (≈ −4.6 MHz at 10 MHz) must come from the PHY's C-plane frequency offset. That is the first suspect — the RU will happily extract noise from mid-carrier.
Admission refusals are silent. The BBU drops a carrier request with a logged reason and the sender retries — there is no NACK; RRH_READY is the only acknowledgement. Reasons: capabilities not received yet, no RRH DB entry, BW not 5/10/15/20 MHz, no capable antenna, extended grid outside the RU filter window, or (for NB) no 4G_NB host. A host reconfiguration, sync loss or RU disconnect must reach both vNodes.End-to-end bench lessons (LTE 4x4 B1 10 MHz + NB-IoT upper guard band on a BoB FHGW)
ObservationCause / rule
Placement in the RU logLTE PRACH static id 0 at re-offset 2880 (PRB 35); host grid 52 PRB; NB-IoT PRACH static id 4 at re-offset 2400, which the FHGW shifts by 45 to 2445 = upper guard band
EMS modelseparate LTE vNode (7.2, has M-plane) and NB vNode (NB-IoT 7.2, C/U-plane only); both must reference the same RRH with the same allocated antenna count — PHY and FHS take HW_ANTS from it
Host-carrier link ignoreda hidden EMS parameter (NB-IoT host carrier) is set only over the EMS API and applied by an EMS reboot of the LTE vNode; a pod restart does not apply it
Two rigs knock each other off S1the NB stack uses its NB cell ID as the Home-eNB ID and ignores the EMS eNB ID — each rig on a shared MME needs a unique NB cell ID
NB S1 never comes backno auto-reconnect: undeploy + deploy the NB vNode (do not delete pods — config may not be re-pushed)
UE sees NPSS but no MIBjust after deploy — wait a few minutes
LTE RAPID = sent + 1, no Msg3UE emulator with global timing advance −1 latched the first RAR's TA; set it to 0
SDR saturatesUE rx gain 30 too high on this path; 15 worked. One emulator instance cannot run LTE and NB-IoT UEs together
Result: LTE DL rank 4, CQI 15, RSRP −54 dBm; NB-IoT MIB/SIB, NPRACH, attach and ping 15/15. Fault 16 on every boot was known and harmless on that build (SERNO01).
Interview Q&A
Q: How does an O-RU tell the DU it can host guard-band NB-IoT?
A: Structurally: an endpoint type offers an LTE configuration row with max-prb-range greater than standard LTE (e.g. 102 vs 100 at 20 MHz). Equal means not capable. It is per antenna type.
Q: Why does widening a 10 MHz carrier to 52 PRB not move its centre frequency?
A: One PRB is added on each side — symmetric — so the centre stays put and the RU's own reported centre is reused.
Q: The NB-IoT vNode request carries no frequency. How does the RU know where NPRACH is?
A: The M-plane only opens a window (centre-from-freqoffset enabled, occupied bandwidth = whole extended grid); the PHY points to the exact position per NPRACH occasion with the C-plane frequency offset.
Q: A00/A01 read config-id 0 while A02/A03 read 2 after your edit. What happened?
A: On the old firmware, carrier activation reset the active antennas to the LTE default. Check the running software slot; v1.0.1 or later is required.
Q: Which bit marks NB-IoT UL in the eAxC, and the classic mistake?
A: The top bit of the CC_ID field, 0x0080 (bit 8 counted MSB-first). Using 1<<8 sets a band-sector bit instead.
M-plane, RRH manager & alarms
ORNC01 M-Plane Field Notes — compression fault 15, TDD pattern change under active carriers, stale carriers and false RRH-ready, PTP master restarts, late alarm clears, supervision drops and sentinel values Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
Most M-plane problems do not look like M-plane problems. A carrier raises a fault half a minute after activation, a cell comes up 20 seconds late, an alarm "clears" for no reason, or the BBU believes a radio is ready when it is running yesterday's configuration. This card collects real field notes from investigating the O-RAN M-plane controller (ornc), its NETCONF library and the option-8 RRH daemon on lab stands — what was seen, how it was isolated, and the general rule that follows. Every rule here applies to any O-RU/RRH integration.

The underlying lesson: YANG validity is not enough. The RU can accept every edit-config with <ok/> and still fail at run time. Isolate by replaying known-good bytes and changing one factor at a time. See CM16 for the carrier-activation chain, CM15 for the RU life-cycle, CM20 for fault ids, and RRHMGR01 for the software components named here.
How the fault-15 cause was found
Capture the daemon's exact NETCONF XML (debug log level), replay it byte for byte through the CLI, then bisect the difference.
Level 1 — the field notes (symptom → cause → rule)
#SymptomCause foundRule
1Carriers accepted and go ACTIVE/BUSY, then fault 15 "error during activation/deactivation of carriers" ~25 s later; RU latches system oper-state DISABLED until rebootEndpoint compression container. Working: compression-type STATIC, iq-bitwidth 9, (deprecated) bitwidth 16, exponent 4. Failing: STATIC + bitwidth 9 onlySome RUs need the full, legacy-ordered compression block; schema-valid is not RU-valid
2TDD pattern replace refused: "Change of active carrier is not supported" (clean refusal, nothing latches)RU forbids changing an active carrier's patternDeactivate → wait until not BUSY (~9 s) → replace → activate. Delete + create races BUSY
3Controller reports L1 done / RRH ready although the RU refused a create ("node already exists")Edit result ignored; stale TxArrayCarrier0/RxArrayCarrier0 from the previous run; readiness matched carriers by name onlyAlways check every edit-config reply; clean stale carriers; with a changed ARFCN the RU would radiate the old one while the BBU hears "ready"
4Option-8 daemon reports RRH ready for an LTE carrier no vNode configured this sessionReady derived from radio state: carrier still CarrierEnable'd from a previous runReadiness must be tied to the configuration actually sent
5RU goes FREERUN "fault 18, radio DPLL unlock" ~1 min after each install for ~25 s; SET_FREQ refused -32010 "RU is not LOCKED or HOLDOVER"; cell ~20 s lateCoincides with the PTP manager restarting the shared master ptp4l when a port is added to the master group (restart proven, causation not)Write all master sections in one configuration update; see PTPGM01
6Sync alarms 5031/5050 arrive ~1 min after in-syncThey are clears ("type": false), queued until capabilities are pushed, which waits for the AISG full scanRead the raise/clear flag, not just the id
7AISG inventory republished after exactly 15 min on a port with no RETsObserve-deadline watchdog treats "no devices" as "not converged"Harmless, but do not count it as a rescan
8Long NETCONF get on a sluggish RU → RU drops the sessionSynchronous RPC blocked the event loop; supervision watchdog not refreshedKeep resetting supervision during long RPCs (wait callback)
Level 2 — lab techniques that made these findable
1. Capture the exact NETCONF XML. Set the controller's log level to debug in its runit env file (trace does not enable the NETCONF message dump). The XML lands in the service log split into NETCONF 1.1 chunks of ~1 KiB, one line per chunk, ending with a ## line. Do not reassemble from the syslog copy — the forward truncates lines at ~1000 characters.
# per-vendor M-plane controller service (runit)
# set ORNC_LOG_LEVEL=debug in /etc/sv/ornc-<VENDOR>/env
sv restart ornc-<VENDOR>
less /var/log/sv/ornc-<VENDOR>/current                  # full chunks; NOT /var/log/messages
2. Keep one CLI session alive (supervision watchdog)
Some RUs reboot if nobody resets their O-RAN supervision watchdog, so one-shot CLI calls are useless for anything that must persist. Keep a single session open and feed it commands from a regular file with tail -f (a FIFO would block the writer or deliver end-of-input between commands):
D=$(mktemp -d); : > $D/in
exec 3<>/dev/tcp/<RU-mgmt-addr>/830          # NETCONF over SSH port
tail -n +1 -f $D/in | ornc-cli --fd 3 --no-init -v > $D/out 2>&1 &
echo "watchdog 60 10" >> $D/in                 # keep supervision alive
echo "show rf"        >> $D/in
3. Make a port a PTP master by hand (stand without the RRH manager)
An RU in FREERUN (fault 18) cannot be configured. If the RRH manager wrote the radio port as disabled, stop its two PTP relay services so it cannot overwrite, then drop a [master] section into the PTP manager's input directory atomically (write a temp file, then mv). The echo appears in the matching output file. It lasts until the pod or PTP manager restarts.
sv down ptp-config-relay ptp-response-relay
t=$(mktemp /run/ptpmanager/rx/.wr.XXXXXX)
printf '[master]
state=ena
port=<fh-port>
hardwareSync=ena
' > $t
mv $t /run/ptpmanager/rx/wrconfig
cat /run/ptpmanager/tx/wrconfig      # OK + echoed section; RU LOCKED within ~1 min
4. Read sentinel values correctly (option-8 RRH status)
FieldValueMeaning
Optical port TX/RX power99.00No SFP in that optical port (not an RF path)
ANTn carrier DL IQ power−99.00 dBFSNo DL stream on that carrier (DL FIFO status 1); real values are e.g. −12 to −25 dBFS
Subframe assignment / special subframe / CP length255"Not set" (valid CP values are only 0 = normal, 1 = extended)
Output power32767No valid reading (see ALARMLC01)
Alarm time0001-01-01T00:00:00ZRaised before the RU had a clock
Power module output voltage (0.1V)48000 / TransRatio 100 = 480.0Units of 0.1 V → 48.0 V; scale and unit live in the name
Level 3 — deeper cases and bug classes
DL FIFO alarm decoded by correlation. An option-8 RRH raised "DL FIFO alarm, ANT=2, Carrier=1, DLFIFO=1, Enable=1". With no vendor definition, correlating with the status values showed DLFIFO=1 = no DL stream, DLFIFO=2 = stream flowing, Enable=1 = carrier switched on at that antenna. Cause: a 2G carrier was enabled on two ports while 2G L1 streamed on one. LTE carriers raise the same alarm on all antennas at SET_FREQ and clear it ~2.5 min later when the stream starts — expected, not a fault.

Bug classes worth testing for:
  • Fixed-width fields with no terminator: a 15-byte antenna/carrier string was read up to the first NUL and picked up the next message's magic bytes in the log. Bound reads by the declared length.
  • RRH date one day behind after GPS lock (time of day correct) — a radio bug, visible because the date is text on the wire.
  • PRB lookup tables: a helper returned 36 PRB for 15 MHz NR at 30 kHz SCS where TS 38.101-1 Table 5.3.2-1 gives 38, and 35/45 MHz fell through to 273 instead of 92/119. Two unit tests asserted the two different answers and both were green. Always test against the spec table, not against the code.
  • Notifications with schema-less (opaque) nodes were silently dropped — no failure, no log.
  • Health statistics flood: per-value status messages were ~97% of the control trace (136 string values every 5 min from one RRH, each repeating the radio identity); names inconsistent ("VSWR level" vs "VSWR Level"). Parse defensively.
  • A legacy "set_freq_finished" notification closes every RF update pass, including one started by a TX-power request — it is a bracket, not an answer to SET_FREQ.
Interview Q&A
Q: The RU accepts all edit-configs with <ok/> but raises fault 15 ~25 s after activation. How do you isolate it?
A: Capture a known-good payload (e.g. from the production daemon at debug log level), replay it byte for byte on a freshly rebooted RU with the same tool. If it works, the cause is in the payload, not the session or RU. Then swap one block at a time (eAxC, activation staging, PRB, compression) until it breaks. In the real case it was the compression container missing iq-bitwidth/exponent.
Q: How do you change a TDD pattern on an RU with active carriers?
A: Deactivate the carriers, wait until they are INACTIVE and not BUSY (~9 s), replace the pattern, re-activate. A replace on active carriers is refused; delete + create races the BUSY state.
Q: Why can the BBU say "RRH ready" while the RU runs an old configuration?
A: If the controller ignores a failed create and matches carriers by name only, a stale carrier from the previous run (same name, maybe different ARFCN) satisfies the readiness check. Always check edit results and clean stale carriers before configuring.
Q: An alarm 5031 "out of sync" arrives a minute after the RU reported in-sync. Is sync broken?
A: Check the raise/clear flag — here it was a clear ("type": false) queued until the controller had pushed RU capabilities, which waits for the AISG full scan.
Q: What does −99 dBFS DL IQ power on an option-8 RRH mean?
A: A sentinel: no DL stream on that carrier/antenna (DL FIFO status 1), not a real measurement. Similarly 99 on an optical port = no SFP, 255 = not set, 32767 = no valid reading.
ORNC02 O-RU Multi-Controller Call-Home via DHCP Option 43 — the 0x81 controller list, the TLV-encoding trap, and how each radio vendor really behaves Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
An O-RAN radio (O-RU) has exactly one way to learn who manages it: the controller address list that the BBU's fronthaul DHCP server hands it in DHCP option 43 while it boots. The call-home NETCONF session, configuration, alarms and software updates all hang off that list, and the radio will not talk to a controller that is not on it.

The O-RAN M-plane spec allows more than one controller in the list, and a radio that honours it calls home to every address in parallel. That would give you a standby controller, a second observer/debug session next to the production one, or a migration path where a new controller is added before the old one is removed. A lab experiment on three radio vendors showed the catch: the spec allows two byte encodings, one vendor's radio goes off the air with one of them, and only one vendor out of three actually uses the second address while the first is healthy. This card explains the encoding, the per-vendor behaviour and how to test it yourself. Discovery in general (vendor classes, RRH DB entry) is in CM42; the call-home step in the RU lifecycle is in CM15.
Figure — how the controller list reaches the O-RU, and the two legal encodings
CA1/CA2 = the two controller IPv4 addresses (4 bytes each). Only the TLV-sequence form is safe across vendors.
Level 1 — the facts you need
Where the list lives. DHCPv4 option 43 (vendor-specific information, RFC 2132 §8.4), filled per vendor class. The current O-RAN prefix is the o-ran-ru2 vendor class (option 60 looks like o-ran-ru2/<VENDOR>). Sub-option types defined in O-RAN.WG4 M-plane §6.2.5:
Sub-optionMeaningNote
0x81O-RU controller IPv4 address(es)length 4 per address
0x82O-RU controller FQDNname instead of address
0x86call-home protocolwhich transport to call home with
0x01 / 0x02legacy (pre-o-ran-ru2) address / FQDNold o-ran-ru class only
Two legal ways to put two addresses in 0x81. The spec says the value encodes "IPv4 address(es)" and that multiple instances are encoded as a sequence of type/length/value fields, so both of these are valid:
81:04:<CA1 4 bytes>:81:04:<CA2 4 bytes>    # two TLVs, one address each   -> SAFE
81:08:<CA1 4 bytes><CA2 4 bytes>            # one TLV, length 8, two addresses -> BREAKS one vendor
What the radio does with it (each vendor offered its existing call-home address plus a second one, then rebooted to re-read the option):
Radio vendor (class)TLV sequenceSingle TLV, length 8
ZILLNK (o-ran-ru2/ZORU)Uses both. Full NETCONF on CA1, a TCP SYN about once per second to CA2 (RST if nothing listens; a full SSH + NETCONF session when something does)Radio off the air: accepts the lease, then DISCOVER/OFFER/REQUEST/ACK every ~5 s forever, no DECLINE, no TCP to 4334
GreenRAN (o-ran-ru2/PW)Parses cleanly, calls home to CA1 only; zero packets (not even ARP) to CA2 even with a listener therenot tested
Sunwave (o-ran-ru2/SUNWAVE)Same as GreenRAN: CA1 only while CA1 is healthynot tested
Comba on LRCP firmwareTakes a lease but never uses option 43 or call-home at all — served by lrcpsrv on TCP 33339n/a
Ports to remember: NETCONF call-home TCP 4334 (RFC 8071), NETCONF direct SSH 830, LRCP (non-O-RAN radio control) TCP 33339.
Level 2 — how to set it up and test it on a lab BBU
0. Confirm the radio really speaks O-RAN M-plane (a unit can be O-RAN-capable on paper and still run LRCP firmware). Three read-only checks on the BBU pod:
# has any O-RU ever announced an O-RAN vendor class here?
grep -rhoE "o-ran-ru2/[A-Za-z0-9]+" /var/log/ | sort | uniq -c
# who holds a call-home session, and who an LRCP one?
ss -tnp | grep 4334      # O-RAN M-plane
ss -tnp | grep 33339     # LRCP
# what do the debug tools list?
orncrrh_dbg              # O-RAN O-RUs
lrcprrh_dbg              # LRCP radios, by serial
If the first grep is empty and every radio shows under lrcprrh_dbg, there is no O-RAN radio to test on that stand.

1. Edit the vendor class in the fronthaul DHCP config (/opt/pw/etc/dhcpd-fh.conf, laid down from the image). Extend the TLV sequence:
option vendor-encapsulated-options 81:04:<CA1>:81:04:<CA2>;
2. Give the BBU the second address. Add CA2 as a /32 on the dummy interface the per-vendor call-home listeners use. Adding the address does not create a listener: each vendor's call-home socat binds only the call-home IP from that vendor's rrh_vendor_data_<VENDOR>.json, so anything on CA2 (for example ornc-cli or a plain socat) has to be started by hand.
3. Validate, then restart dhcpd. /opt/pw/bin/dhcpd -t -cf /opt/pw/etc/dhcpd-fh.conf checks syntax. dhcpd is not under runit: kill it and the BBU entry-script watchdog restarts it with the same command line within about 10 s.
4. Make the radio re-read option 43. A running RU does not re-request it (the lease is 7 days). Reboot it: orncrrh_dbg → pick the RU → item 0 (REBOOT RRH) → confirm. That needs a live ornc client; if the radio is already silent, force a fresh DHCP by flapping its fronthaul link or sending a reset RPC to its NETCONF port.
5. Observe.
tcpdump -ni <fh-if> port 67 or port 68 -v     # see Vendor-Option (43) in OFFER/ACK
#   length 12 = two TLVs of 4-byte addresses (129.4.a.b.c.d.129.4.e.f.g.h in decimal)
tcpdump -ni <fh-if> tcp port 4334             # SYN to CA2 ~1/s, RST if no listener
ss -tnp | grep 4334                              # ESTAB rows per controller
6. Tell "standby" from "discarded" (the open question for the vendors that use only CA1): stop the call-home listener on CA1 so it stops answering and watch whether the radio falls back to CA2. No reboot needed. If it never moves, the rest of the TLV sequence is ignored.
Pass criteria for "multi-controller works": both sessions ESTABLISHED, the second one serves reads (sync/PTP state, active alarms, processing elements, carriers) while the production session stays up with no disconnect.
Level 3 — traps, and what the experiment really proves
  • Spec-legal is not interop-safe. The single-TLV form is valid O-RAN, yet it put one vendor's radio into an endless DHCP loop with no M-plane at all. Rule: always encode multiple controllers as a sequence of 0x81 TLVs, one address each.
  • There is only one option 43 per packet. A config line like option serverip code 43 = string; is an alias for the same option, not a second one. The vendor-class value overrides the pool-scope value, so the alias never reaches the wire. A leftover value using a non-current type byte (0x03) is just dead config. To signal more controllers, extend the TLV sequence; do not add an option.
  • Pod-level edits do not persist. The dummy interface is rebuilt from the per-vendor JSON files and the DHCP config is re-laid from the image at every container start. A permanent change belongs in the image source and the vendor JSON.
  • "Parses fine" is not "uses it". Two vendors accepted the list and simply never sent a packet (not even ARP) to CA2. Do not conclude support from a clean DHCP exchange; look for TCP to 4334 on the second address.
  • Scope. The test proves only the DHCP / call-home side: the radio opens a session to every address. Whether a second controller may configure the radio (NACM privileges, configuration ownership, real failover) is a separate test.
  • LRCP radios are out of scope. A radio on LRCP firmware takes the lease and ignores option 43; its control link is the radio-initiated LRCP TCP session (see RRHMGR01 for the rrhmgr / ornc / lrcpsrv split).
Real outcome: of three O-RAN vendors tested, only one opened the second channel while the primary was healthy. So any feature that needs a second controller alongside a working primary (observer session, e.g. for streaming spectrogram data) works on one vendor in three today, and the standby behaviour of the other two still needs the cheap fallback test above.
Interview Q&A
Q: How does an O-RU learn which controller to call home to?
A: From DHCP option 43 at boot: the BBU fronthaul DHCP server matches the radio's vendor class (option 60, e.g. o-ran-ru2/<vendor>) and returns sub-option 0x81 with one or more controller IPv4 addresses (0x82 for an FQDN). The radio then opens TCP 4334 to each and runs SSH + NETCONF call-home.
Q: Two encodings of two controller addresses are spec-legal. Which do you use and why?
A: The TLV sequence 81:04:<CA1>:81:04:<CA2>. The single TLV 81:08:<CA1><CA2> is also legal, but one vendor's radio accepted the lease and then looped in DHCP every ~5 s with no call-home, i.e. it went off the air.
Q: You added a second address and the radio still talks only to the first. Is the feature broken?
A: Not necessarily. First check the radio re-read the option (it needs a reboot; the lease is 7 days), the BBU owns the address and something listens on it. Some vendors parse the list but use only the first entry while it is healthy. Stop the first listener and see whether it falls back, to distinguish standby from discard.
Q: Why might a dhcpd config change appear to do nothing on a BBU pod?
A: The vendor-class option 43 overrides a pool-scope alias of the same option; the RU does not re-request until reboot; and changes inside the running pod are lost when it restarts because config and dummy interface are rebuilt from the image and vendor JSON.
Q: What would you check to prove a second controller session is genuinely usable?
A: Both ESTABLISHED sessions on 4334, a complete NETCONF hello on the second, reads (sync state, alarms, processing elements, carriers) answered there, and no disconnect or reconfiguration on the production session meanwhile. Write access and failover need a separate test.
RRHMGR01 Inside the RRH Manager Stack — rrhmgr / ornc / lrcpsrv / uidscan in their own pod, interfaces and ports, where every RU config value comes from, start-up order, event ids and field-bug patterns Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
Between the base-station software (one OAM process per vNode: 2G, 4G, 5G or NB-IoT) and the physical radios sits the RRH manager stack. Its job: take "bring up band X, ARFCN Y, bandwidth Z, N antennas, this TX power" from OAM, decide which radio and carrier that belongs to, and drive the radio in whatever language its vendor speaks — the O-RAN M-plane (NETCONF over SSH, split 7.2x) or the LRCP control protocol of option-8 (split-8) RRHs — plus AISG for the antenna tilt motors. It also pushes radio alarms to the fault manager, feeds statistics to the EMS and tells the PTP manager which fronthaul ports need timing.

A tester rarely needs the code, but needs the map: which process owns what, which port each radio connects to, where each configuration value comes from, which restart causes which side effect, and the bug patterns seen in the field. CM16 shows the carrier-activation chain step by step; this card shows the machinery behind it. Field notes on the M-plane controller are in ORNC01, alarm handling in ALARMLC01, timing in PTPGM01.
Where the RRH manager stack sits
Simplified. Process names as used on the vBBU; dashed boxes are Kubernetes pods.
Level 1 — the components and how they talk
All radio-facing processes live in their own rrhmgr pod, beside the bbu pod, built and versioned separately (an M-plane change no longer needs a core build). Inside the main container, runit supervises every service: sv stat /etc/service/*.
ComponentRole
rrhmgrCoordinator: OAM edge, RRH carrier map (which vNode owns which carrier), vNode routing, XDB persistence, alarms to faultmgr, tells the PTP manager which ports have radios
ornc-<vendor>One process per O-RAN vendor family (8 run under runit); NETCONF client for 7.2x O-RUs that call home
lrcpsrvOne process per option-8 RRH connection; speaks LRCP south (control, status, alarms, AISG transparent channel)
libaisg / uidscanHeader-only AISG v2 library (layer-2 device discovery, layer-7 RET commands) built into ornc and lrcpsrv; uidscan is the AISG "full scan" utility
rrhdbgOperator debug client: send a command to one radio process and print the answer (e.g. RET tilt, spectrogram start/stop)
net-init / dhcp-containerFronthaul VF addressing, call-home addresses, FH DHCP server that gives radios their lease and controller list (option 43)

Where every radio configuration value comes from
Three sources feed a radio's configuration — keep them apart when you debug a wrong value:
  • The RU (facts): YANG modules are fetched from the radio at connect time with get-schema (module list parsed from the NETCONF hello) instead of compiled per-vendor bundles; manufacturer from ietf-hardware; band from the module-capability band number.
  • OAM (intent), via SET_FREQ: band, ARFCN, bandwidth, number of TX antennas, TDD pattern, TX power, PRACH start RB, TX/RX feature bitmaps. Other OAM → rrhmgr messages: SET_TX_POWER_REQ, RRH_REBOOT_CMD, RRH_PA_STATUS_REQ, HEARTBEAT, IS_RRH_READY_REQ. rrhmgr answers RRH_READY, L1_DONE, RRH_DISCONNECT, PTP_OUT_OF_SYNC, SYNC_STATE_INFO.
  • Variant JSON (fallback / policy / deployment): TX-antenna fallback (used only if the RU declares no arrays), u-plane mode copy/create/probe, processing-element interface/VLAN/name (fronthaul wiring, not a radio property), TDD wire format, AISG present, a power-gain ceiling (never the gain itself).
Antenna count used = MIN(what OAM asked for, what the radio declares) — the network can ask for less than the hardware, never more.
Level 2 — start-up order, and what to check at each step
  1. Deployment JSON → configuration builder → Helm installs the XDB server with seed rows (RRHs, vNodes, vNode-RRH-carrier, fronthaul NIC names).
  2. Pods wait in init containers (rrhmgr waits for the XDB server and the NATS broker; fails after ~60 s without the broker and the kubelet retries).
  3. net-init gives fronthaul VFs link-local addresses, writes the FH DHCP config and puts the vendors' call-home addresses on a dummy interface.
  4. runit starts rrhmgr (which writes the bbu_is_running flag), lrcpsrv, one ornc per vendor, uidscan, PTP relays, sshd, (s)ftp, chrony, log server.
  5. vNodes see the flag and each sends SET_FREQ — this is how rrhmgr learns carrier ownership.
  6. Radios get a DHCP lease: O-RUs call home to ornc on TCP 4334, option-8 RRHs connect to lrcpsrv on TCP 33339; rrhmgr writes the RRH rows and reports state to the owning vNode.
  7. Statistics: configmgr polls rrhmgr (health every 2 min, full stats per profile period, e.g. 15 min), packs a tarball and uploads it to the ACS through the M-plane aggregator.
kubectl -n pw get pod -l app=rrhmgr
kubectl -n pw exec -it deploy/rrhmgr -c rrhmgr-container -- bash
sv stat /etc/service/*                       # rrhmgr, ornc-<vendor> x8, lrcpsrv, uidscan, relays ...
ls /var/log/sv/<service>/current              # per-service log (empty = daemon never started)
watch bbu-val-tilt.py                        # RET current/min/max tilt + alarms from the XDB dump
helm get values pw -n pw -a | grep -i rrhmgr # no key = rrhmgr module not rendered

No rrhmgr pod and every cell AccLinkStatus DownThe SMO configuration builder did not render the rrhmgr module (check Helm values for the rrhmgr key)
All 2G/4G stacks and 5G DUs restart togetherrrhmgr restarted: it rewrites bbu_is_running on every start and vNodes restart on change — deliberate, because a 5G DU never resends SET_FREQ and rrhmgr would not know who owns which carrier

AISG/RET in the stack
EMS/ACS drives AISG by writing operation rows (scan, full scan, tilt set, tilt get) over TR-069; rrhmgr reacts to the XDB notification — it never starts scans itself except on radio connect. On connect: if the per-radio persist file lists known RET ids, a short scan is enough; with no persist file the device ids are unknown and the slower full scan (uidscan) runs, which is why the first boot of a site takes longer than a reboot (see CM08). Empty tilt in XDB is -500; a raw AISG "no tilt" is -32768. RET alarms are mapped to BBU alarm ids (a RET malfunction is reported as 5017). Lab switch: a flag file disables the automatic scan on connect.
Event idMeaning
5013RRH M-plane disconnected (must be keyed per RU — a regression keyed it per BBU)
5030RU unidentified (invalid capabilities)
5031 / 5050RRH out of sync / in holdover (clears may arrive late, see ORNC01)
5046–5049IEEE 1588 state transitions
5057O-RAN fault-management alarm forwarded from the RU
5068RU in recovery mode (golden image)
Level 3 — field-bug patterns worth testing for
These are real defect classes found and fixed in the RRH manager stack. Each one suggests a test you can run on any radio-control chain.
PatternWhat happenedTest idea
Units mismatch2G DL attenuation sent in 0.1 dB while the radio expects 0.01 dB → a 2G carrier got a tenth of its attenuation and transmitted near full power; on a radio shared with 4G the radio forced 46 dB on both carriersMeasure output power per RAT on a shared radio after every config change
Early-alarm raceAn option-8 RRH sends alarms before its capabilities message, so its RRH id is unknown and alarms were dropped. Fix: queue per connection, flush with RRH id + timestamp once capabilities arriveBoot an RRH with a standing fault; the alarm must reach EMS
Stale alarm after rebootAn RU that rebooted instead of clearing left the alarm on the ACS forever; 5013 was cleared/keyed per BBU instead of per RURaise, reboot RU, check EMS; disconnect two RUs, reconnect one
Success reported on failureFailed user-plane push reported as applied → TX enabled on a carrier that never took its config; firmware upgrade success reported as timeoutInject a refused edit; verify readiness is not reported
Sibling side-effectsMuting one carrier muted its sibling; a multi-band AAU's per-band power ceiling was pulled down to the lowest bandChange one carrier/band, read back all others
Radiating when it should notA shared PA kept radiating during a backhaul outage although every carrier had TX disabledPull backhaul, check RF on a spectrum analyser
Orphaned recoveryAn O-RU requesting a reset (fault 25) while no vNode owned it stayed disabled until a manual reboot; a latched DL-PA failure left a 2G cell silently deadRaise recovery faults with and without an owning vNode
Retry stormsA supervision reset the O-RU kept refusing was retried ~180 times per session; now retried with back-offMake the RU refuse supervision; count retries
Design limits a tester should know
  • Still vendor-gated: a fixed vendor-name map rejects unknown vendors at start-up ("Unsupported RRH Vendor"); the connect-time u-plane wipe and an option-8 power formula (hardcoded max power per port of 46) are keyed on vendor names, not capabilities. A new variant of a known vendor needs no code change; a new vendor does.
  • Capabilities the RU already declares but software ignores: true array element count (rows × columns × polarisations — an array count of 1 on a 4T radio is legal), min/max carrier bandwidth (a bad bandwidth only fails at the RU as a generic config-error alarm), technologies per band, max carriers per band vs a hardcoded constant. Better: detect features from the NETCONF hello capabilities (e.g. the ALD-port module means AISG), not from vendor names.
  • Open issue: probing the running datastore cannot tell a factory u-plane from one written by an earlier SET_FREQ, so second-carrier / second-band rigs can fail.
  • Per-radio statistics are sent one value per message with strings and units in the names, so they dominate traces; EMS per-radio commands (reboot, spectrogram) bypass XDB entirely.
  • Each change needs a sub-system rig test that asserts the new behaviour including the bad path — a green suite that only exercises the happy path proves little (see MPTF01).
Interview Q&A
Q: Which processes sit between OAM and an O-RAN radio, and which between OAM and an option-8 RRH?
A: OAM → rrhmgr (NATS) → ornc-<vendor> (unix datagram socket) → NETCONF/SSH call-home session (RU connects to TCP 4334). For option-8: OAM → rrhmgr → lrcpsrv → LRCP on TCP 33339. AISG RET control goes through libaisg inside ornc or lrcpsrv.
Q: Why does restarting rrhmgr restart every vNode?
A: rrhmgr learns which vNode owns which carrier only from SET_FREQ, and a 5G DU never resends it. So rrhmgr rewrites a bbu_is_running flag on every start and vNodes restart when it changes, forcing fresh SET_FREQs.
Q: A radio reports 4 antennas but the cell uses 2. Is that a bug?
A: Not necessarily. Antenna count used = MIN(OAM request, what the radio declares). Check numOfTxAntennas in SET_FREQ first, then the radio's declared arrays; the variant-file value is only a fallback if the radio declares none.
Q: Why does the first boot of a site take much longer to show RET tilt than a later reboot?
A: With no persist file of known AISG device ids, the stack runs the AISG full scan (uidscan) to discover devices; after that the ids are saved and later connects use a short scan.
Q: Name three bug classes you would deliberately test in a radio-control chain.
A: Units/scale mismatch (e.g. 0.1 vs 0.01 dB attenuation), success reported on a refused configuration, alarms raised before the radio is identified (early-alarm race), stale alarms after RU reboot, side-effects on sibling carriers/bands, radiating with all carriers TX-disabled.
ALARMLC01 RU Alarm Life-Cycle End to End — why a VSWR alarm leaves EMS showing RF Tx UP: alarm path vs state path, lost clears, catalog severity, PHY recovery loop and the validator's matrix Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
An RU detects a high VSWR on one antenna port, raises a service-affecting alarm and stops transmitting. You would expect the EMS to show the cell's RF Tx DOWN, the alarm with the severity the RU sent, and the alarm to disappear once the cable is fixed. In a real investigation none of the three happened: EMS kept showing RF Tx UP, showed a different severity, and the alarm never cleared.

The reason is architectural, not a single bug: the alarm travels on a fault-management path (RU → radio daemon → rrhmgr → vBBU FaultMgr → ACS → EMS) while the RF Tx state is computed by the OAM process from a completely different input ("RRH ready"). The two never meet. On top of that, clears get lost, severity is not carried on the wire, and one alarm id was keyed per BBU instead of per RU. This card walks the life-cycle end to end so a validator knows what to check and where an alarm can disappear. It complements the fault-id reference (see CM20), site alarm triage (see CM28) and the alarm automation suite (see AUTO10).
Alarm path vs. RF Tx path (4G example)
Red boxes: where behaviour diverged from the acceptance criteria. Sanitised; component names as used in the BBU software.
Level 1 — the life-cycle and the five places it breaks
Life-cycle of one RU alarm: raise (with severity and affected port) → classified service-affecting (SA) or not → shown in EMS with the RU's severity → operational state follows (RF Tx DOWN while an SA fault is active) → clear from the RU → EMS entry cleared → RF Tx returns through the normal activation flow. It must also survive an RU reboot, an RU disconnect/reconnect and a BBU pod restart without leaving a stale entry.
Break pointWhat was foundEffect you see
OAM cell state4G rftx = cellOpState && isRrhConnected && isPhyRrhAlarmCleared && cellRfTransmissionState — no RU-fault term; RRH Ready sets "connected" unconditionally. 5G had no RF Tx value at all; 2G only drops a cell for disconnect/sync/fronthaul faults.RF Tx UP while the RU is silent
rrhmgrThe option-8 daemon mapped the RU alarm level to service-affecting, then rrhmgr overrode it to NOT_SA for every alarm; antenna number parsed but not forwarded; several vendor codes collapsed onto one id.Cannot tell which port; wrong classification
Alarm state for option-8 RRHsO-RAN RUs were tracked and swept on disconnect; option-8 (LRCP) RUs were not, on the assumption they have no replay — but the LRCP spec does a full alarm sync on access.Alarms stuck after RU reboot
vBBU FaultMgrA clear with no matching active entry is dropped (raise predates a pod restart); a raise purges any in-flight clear with the same event id + system name regardless of object (another RU!); the "BBU restarted" message had no device id so ACS rejected it.Lost clears, ghost alarms
ACS / EMS / GUINo severity on the wire → EMS uses its static catalog (one VSWR id is Major on the BBU, Critical in EMS); duplicate raise silently dropped; active-alarm sync only adds; GUI default filter hides alarms older than 1 h; sentinel output power 32767 shown as a reading.Wrong severity, alarm "missing" from GUI
Key numbers to remember
  • Option-8 RRH VSWR threshold 2.5 per antenna port, measured only while DL output > 33 dBm; "antenna disconnect" above VSWR 3.
  • PHY-alarm recovery loop re-enables TX about 100 ms after OAM turned it off.
  • Alarm 5013 (RRHMGR M-plane disconnected) was regressed to one slot per BBU instead of per RU.
  • Output power 32767 = "no valid reading" sentinel, not 3276.7 dBm.
  • 19 independent defects found across six components during one investigation.
Level 2 — how to validate an alarm life-cycle (the tester's matrix)
Checking "the RU raised it" is not enough. For each alarm family run every event and verify at the EMS/GUI, not only on the RU or in BBU logs:
EventCheck at RU / BBUCheck at EMS / GUI
RaiseAlarm in RU active list; BBU fault log shows raise with portEntry present, severity = RU severity, antenna/port shown; RF Tx DOWN if SA
ClearRU clears (note: some RUs send the clear with severity WARNING — match on the raise)Entry cleared; RF Tx returns via normal activation, not instantly
Clear after RU rebootRU replays its active list on reconnectNo stale entry; if the fault persists it is re-raised once
RU disconnect / reconnect5013 raise/clear for that RU onlyOther RUs' alarms untouched
BBU pod restart during an active alarmClear after restart still forwardedEntry cleared (this is where clears were lost)
Two RUs, same alarm idRaise on RU-B while RU-A clearsRU-A clear not purged by RU-B raise
Duplicate raise with new severity—Entry updated, not ignored
Reproducing a VSWR alarm in the lab
Insert a removable attenuator / mismatched load in one antenna feeder of an option-8 RRH while it transmits above 33 dBm. Expect: RU raises VSWR on that port and may cut PA. Pitfall: once TX is off the RU no longer measures VSWR, so the alarm cannot self-clear even after you restore the feeder — the recovery procedure is fix + RU reboot. An "under power" alarm that follows a TX-off is a consequence, not a second fault, and must not block re-enable. Also watch the GUI time filter: an alarm older than one hour is hidden by default, which looks exactly like a lost alarm.
Level 3 — the design conflict: who is allowed to turn TX back on?
The PHY-alarm handling design makes OAM re-enable TX as a recovery mechanism: OAM turns TX off → the PHY stops seeing U-plane faults → the PHY clears its alarm after ~100 ms → OAM turns TX back on. Any one-shot "TX off" sent because of an RU fault is therefore undone within a fraction of a second — and again by RRH Ready, by the in-sync re-assert, by the bring-up mask expiry and by rrhmgr recovery. Worse, the M-plane controller's TX-disable also deactivated the matching RX array-carrier, which itself triggers the PHY U-plane alarm and kicks the loop.

The fix is a precedence rule: an active RU fault holds TX off; a PHY clear, RRH Ready or in-sync event cannot re-enable it. That touches 2G/4G/5G OAM and the 5G stack manager, which is why it became a multi-team feature, not a bug fix. Target design: rrhmgr owns RU alarm state and classification and sends a per-RU RRH_FAULT_STATE_IND (fault active, worst severity, band/carrier scope, port) to every vNode on the RU, on change and as a snapshot on L1 Done / RRH Ready; OAM owns the TX action and reports RF Tx DOWN with reason "RF TX fault" — without setting the cell INACTIVE (that would stop L2).
DecisionWhy
Critical / Major = service-affecting; Minor / Warning notSimple, vendor-independent rule
On SA the BBU switches the RU TX off and keeps it off until the RU clearsStops a faulty RU radiating; makes RF Tx truthful
One faulty antenna stream takes the RU off air; alarm shows id + antennaPartial TX on a MIMO cell is worse than none
Per-band TX-off only when bands have separate TX hardwareShared hardware or no port info → whole RU
Sync: HOLDOVER keeps transmitting, FREERUN stopsSync alarms follow sync state, not severity
Option-8 follows the O-RAN life-cycle: clear on disconnect, re-raise from replayRemoves ghost alarms after reboot
Only RU-raised alarms act; no RET/AISG or daemon-internal alarmsAvoid self-inflicted outages
Fault 25 (reset requested) also stops TX; the reboot request staysRU is about to reset anyway
RU behaviours that shape the design
  • Option-8 RRH: about 19 alarm codes; level arrives per message (no fixed severity in the guide); VSWR per port, measured only above 33 dBm → no self-clear with TX off; some older firmware shuts the PA on over-power silently.
  • O-RAN AAU: clears are sent with severity WARNING, so take severity from the raise. The RU itself switches its PA off for fault 2 (over-temperature) and 18 (FREERUN, Critical); 17 HOLDOVER is Minor. Fault 27 PA faulty (Major) cascades to 19 TX out of order (Critical). Some faults never clear until reboot. Actions "RU reset by DU" exist for faults 11, 22, 25, 26 and 2005 (see CM20).
  • The previous requirement said "alarm only" for most faults — no fault asked the DU to stop TX. BBU TX-off for Critical/Major is a new requirement, so old test cases that expect TX to stay on will start failing (correctly).
Real case — summary of the investigation
Symptom: VSWR on one port of an option-8 RRH, RU stopped TX, EMS showed RF Tx UP, a Critical instead of Major severity, and the alarm stayed for days after the cable was fixed. Root causes: (1) OAM never received RU alarms; (2) severity never sent BBU → ACS; (3) VSWR cannot self-clear without TX and no reboot was done; (4) FaultMgr dropped the clear after a pod restart. The fix plan was split into one story per component (rrhmgr, FaultMgr, OAM 2G/4G/5G, 5G stack manager, DU OAM, EMS, GUI, validation) — roughly 20–29 person-weeks across six teams. Lesson for validators: an alarm test passes only when raise, severity, clear, clear-after-reboot and disconnect/reconnect are all correct at the EMS.
Interview Q&A
Q: An RU raises VSWR and stops transmitting but EMS still shows RF Tx UP. Where do you look?
A: The RF Tx value comes from OAM's cell-state formula, which in 4G is fed by RRH Ready, cell op-state, PHY alarms and admin state — not by RU alarms. So the alarm path (FaultMgr → ACS → EMS) and the state path never meet. Confirm the alarm reached EMS, then check whether OAM has any RU-fault input; if not, it is a design gap, not a lost message.
Q: Why can an option-8 VSWR alarm never clear on its own?
A: The RRH measures VSWR only while DL output is above about 33 dBm. Once it (or the BBU) turns TX off there is no measurement, so the alarm stays latched; recovery is fix the feeder, then reboot the RU.
Q: Why did the EMS show Critical when the RU said Major?
A: Severity was not carried on the wire from BBU to ACS; EMS looked it up in its own static catalog, which disagreed with the BBU catalog. The fix is per-instance severity in the fault event, and taking the severity from the raise (some RUs send clears as WARNING).
Q: What is the PHY-alarm recovery loop and why does it conflict with RU-fault TX-off?
A: OAM turns TX off on a PHY U-plane alarm; with no TX the PHY stops seeing faults and clears ~100 ms later; OAM turns TX on again. Any RU-fault TX-off is undone by that loop (and by RRH Ready). A precedence rule is needed: an active RU fault holds TX off.
Q: List five alarm events you would test end to end.
A: Raise (severity, port, RF Tx DOWN), clear (RF Tx back via activation), clear after RU reboot (no stale entry), RU disconnect/reconnect (5013 per RU, other RUs untouched), clear during/after a BBU pod restart; plus two RUs with the same alarm id and a duplicate raise with changed severity.
RRHBW01 RCA: LTE Bandwidth Change Never Reaches the RRH — a lost reboot request after a vNode pod restart (330 s consumer gap, destructive purge), repro and pass criteria Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
An operator changes the LTE downlink bandwidth of a cell from the EMS GUI (say 20 MHz → 10 MHz). For a non-O-RAN RRH this needs the RRH to reboot with the new carrier configuration. In this defect the RRH simply never rebooted: the cell stayed up on the old bandwidth, nothing alarmed, and it happened only sometimes.

The radio was innocent. The "please reboot" request travels across several software pods through a message broker, and right after a vNode pod restart there was a 330-second window in which nobody was listening for it — and when the listener finally appeared it wiped the queue. The lesson for validation: when a configuration change "does not reach the radio", first prove the control message reached the RRH manager before you debug the RRH. Related cards: CM16 (activation chain), CM17 (bandwidth change on an AAU via startup.xml).
Figure — path of the reboot request and where it was lost
Cross-pod messages ride a broker stream; a proxy consumer on the vNode side hands them to oammgr over local UDP.
Level 1 — the failure and the fix
Symptom: DL bandwidth changed and deployed from the GUI; the RRH never reboots; the cell stays Up on the old bandwidth; intermittent, only when a vNode pod restart overlaps the change.
Message path: EMS → northbound → cfgmgr (BBU pod) → cross-pod topic xpod.oammgr on a NATS JetStream stream → BrokerBridge proxy consumer → local UDP → oammgr (vNode pod) → rrhmgr → RRH (LRCP-type protocol).
DefectWhat the code didEffect
A — delayed discoveryDiscovery of late-starting facilities (oammgr starting after BrokerBridge, as on every vNode restart) sat inside the "print a health summary every 30th watchdog cycle" log guard. 30 cycles × ~11 s = ~330 s.No proxy consumer for up to 330 s; any message published in that gap is lost.
B — destructive purgeCreating the proxy consumer always purged the stream subject.Pending messages wiped, including those meant for other vNodes sharing the subject.
C — wrong generation guardA pod-generation check on the proxy callback compared against a value the publisher always sets to 0.Valid cross-pod messages rejected.
Latent limit (not fixed)Durable consumers use DeliverPolicy New.Anything published before the consumer exists is skipped — still ~16 s after the fix.
Fix: run discovery on every watchdog cycle (~10 s), pass "skip purge" on late-discovery and ownership-failover paths, drop the broken generation guard. Consumer now up ~16 s after pod init: the gap fell from 330 s to under 20 s (about 20×).
Level 2 — how to reproduce and what "pass" means
Reusable reproduction for any "config lost during pod restart" race (4G BBU with at least one active cell, BrokerBridge proxy mode i.e. RRHMGR_NATIVE_REX=false):
  • Baseline: all cells Up at DL 100 PRB (20 MHz); all broker consumers Active.
  • Delete the vNode pod: kubectl -n <ns> delete pod <vnode-pod>.
  • Within ~30 s, change the DL bandwidth of one cell in the GUI (100 → 50 PRB) and deploy.
  • Wait ~3 minutes (configuration push + a 60 s fault timer).
Pass criteria (all must hold):
#CriterionEvidence
athe xpod.oammgr consumer exists before the reboot request is publishedBrokerBridge log: re-subscribed ~16 s after init
bno destructive purgezero purge calls in BBU and vNode BrokerBridge logs; every setup shows skip-purge
cRRH accepts the new bandwidthRRH-Ready sent to oammgr
dthe changed cell is Up with the new bandwidthL2 log UL BW=50 DL BW=50 for that cell only
eno collateral changeother cells still UL BW=100 DL BW=100
fconsumer healthy afterwardssequence advanced, 0 outstanding messages, Active
Expected timeline on a passing run: pod deleted → new pod ~25 s later → consumer ~16 s after init → BW change deployed → config push reaches the vNode within seconds → CARRIER_CONFIG with BW=50 to the RRH ~1.5 min later → cells Up → a transient DL FIFO alarm during reconfiguration → RRH Ready. The FIFO alarm is expected noise; do not fail the test on it.

Soak used to accept the fix: 5/5 vNode restarts, 10/10 ownership failovers, 5/5 REX restarts, all with BW changes delivered.
Level 3 — why it hid, how to debug the class, design lessons
Why this kind of bug is hard: each component logs "healthy". The publisher sent the message, the broker accepted it, the consumer that appeared later is Active with 0 outstanding — the lost message simply never existed for it. Only the timing between pod init, consumer creation and the publish time reveals the gap.

Debug checklist for "config change not applied to the radio":
  • Did the change leave the EMS? (deploy status, northbound log)
  • Did cfgmgr publish it, and when? Note the timestamp.
  • Did a consumer for that subject exist at that timestamp? Compare with the consumer creation line after the last pod start.
  • Any purge of the subject around that time?
  • Did oammgr / rrhmgr log the request? Only now look at the RRH (carrier config, RRH-Ready).
Design lessons: never couple functional work to a log rate-limiter; a purge on reconnection must be scoped to the caller's own stale data, never the shared subject; "deliver new" consumers need to be pre-created before publishers start, or switched to a policy that replays from the last acknowledged message. The remaining ~16 s window is a known architectural limit — a test that changes config within seconds of a pod start can still lose the message, so record pod start time in every such test log.

Validation take-away: include "change configuration while a pod is restarting" in the regression plan for every config parameter that needs an RRH reboot (bandwidth, EARFCN, power class), not only the happy path on a stable system.
Interview Q&A
Q: A bandwidth change from the GUI never reaches the RRH. Where do you start?
A: Prove the control path before the radio: was the message published, was there a consumer for the subject at that moment, was the stream purged, did oammgr and rrhmgr log the request. Only then look at RRH carrier configuration.
Q: Why did the message get lost only sometimes?
A: Only when a vNode pod restart overlapped the change: discovery of the late-starting oammgr ran every 30th watchdog cycle (~330 s), so publishes in that window had no consumer.
Q: What is wrong with purging the stream when a consumer is created?
