A: It deletes valid pending messages, including other vNodes' messages on the same subject, turning a reconnection into data loss.
Q: What does DeliverPolicy New imply for a restart?
A: A new durable consumer only sees messages published after it is created; anything published between pod start and consumer creation is skipped. After the fix that window is ~16 s, not zero.
Q: How would you write the regression test?
A: Delete the vNode pod, change DL BW within 30 s, wait ~3 min; pass if the consumer existed before the request, no purge, RRH-Ready seen, only the target cell shows the new BW, consumers have 0 outstanding.
AISGRET01 AISG RET in the Lab — bare-RET calibration trick, full vs internal scan, tilt test design, typical defects and failure triage codes Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
A RET (Remote Electrical Tilt) is a small motor unit on the antenna that turns a phase-shifter shaft, which tilts the beam down or up without anyone climbing the mast. The radio talks to it over the AISG antenna-line bus (an RS485 HDLC link, usually powered over the feeder or a separate AISG cable — basics in CM08). On a PW BBU the command travels a long way: operator GUI → ACS → BBU database → RRH manager → per-radio daemon → AISG scan library → radio → RET.

This card is the lab view of that chain: how RETs are discovered (full vs internal scan), how tilt is read and set, a hands-on trick for calibrating a bare RET that is not mounted in an antenna, how good tilt tests are designed, and the defect and failure classes a real system-test campaign found. Internals of rrhmgr / ornc / lrcpsrv are in RRHMGR01.
Figure — the AISG RET command chain on a PW BBU
Scan and tilt are the only AISG operations ACS can request over TR-069; everything else is on-box tooling.
Level 1 — core facts
Standards. AISG v2.0 (what the PW libaisg implements); the HDLC link layer is 3GPP TS 25.462 (Iuant signalling transport); RET procedures and commands are TS 25.463.
Two layers. L2 = discovering devices on the bus (a unique-ID scan with collision handling and narrowing, so many devices on one bus can be found) and assigning HDLC addresses. L7 = the RET commands themselves: GetInformation, GetDeviceData, GetTilt, SetTilt, Calibrate, SelfTest, GetAlarmStatus, AlarmSubscribe, software download and more (~20 in libaisg).
ItemBehaviour
Northbound opcodes (TR-069)only four: AisgScan, AisgScanFull, AisgTiltSet, AisgTiltGet — written into Device.AisgRetCtrl.{i} / Device.RrhCtrl.{i}, copied into the AisgRetOper / RrhOperation rows that rrhmgr subscribes to
Auto-scan on radio connectthe per-radio daemon scans by itself when the radio connects. If its cache file or the persist file /opt/pw-config/aisg/<radio>.persist lists RETs, it runs the short internal scan of those units; otherwise a full scan of the bus
Who starts scansornc (O-RAN radios, via the O-RAN ALD communication RPC) or lrcpsrv (LRCP radios, via AISG transparent messages). rrhmgr never starts one; it only records it
Switch off auto-scanflag file /opt/pw-config/aisg/disable_aisg_auto_scan
Deleting .persistforces a full scan at the next connect — a standard test step
Inventory persistencerrhmgr writes AisgRet rows; XdbSrv saves them in BBU-Val.xml, so the ACS view survives a pod restart
Tilt unitsdegrees with one decimal (set accepts decimals); range MinTilt..MaxTilt reported per RET after a scan
"No tilt" valuesraw AISG "no value" = -32768; stored as empty in XDB (internally clamped to -500). A blank CurTilt means "no GetTilt reply yet", not 0 deg
Bus sizeup to 18 ALDs per bus in rrhmgr/lrcpsrv (one code path allows only 8 — a known inconsistency); multi-antenna RETs expose several sub-antennas
AlarmsAISG alarm codes relayed from the RET (e.g. 296, 300) and a RET-malfunction alarm 5017 raised by the BBU
Level 2 — hands-on: calibrate a bare RET, then test tilt properly
A. Calibrating a RET that is not mounted in an antenna. Calibration makes the RET drive to both mechanical end-stops and store them as its tilt range. On the bench there is no antenna phase shifter, so there is no end-stop and the unit would turn forever. Trick: give it a fake one.
  • Power the RET and make sure it answers on AISG; select the right antenna/actuator; no mechanical load (or a light fixture).
  • Send AISG Calibrate to that actuator — with the libaisg example tool (aisgmgr) or a handheld AISG portable control unit.
  • Let the shaft turn. After about three full shaft rotations, gently stop it with a tool and hold it still for about one second, then release completely.
  • The RET treats the stall as an end-stop, then drives one way to find a limit, reverses to find the other, stores both and completes.
  • Do not force or hold it longer than needed (gearbox/motor damage). For repeated use build a fixture with controlled resistance instead of pliers.
B. Driving tilt. Normal path: ACS (TR-069 AisgTiltSet / AisgTiltGet). On-box path, bypassing ACS: orncrrh_dbg (O-RAN radios) or lrcprrh_dbg (LRCP radios). Read results back from ACS and from BBU-Val.xml (a small script printing current/min/max tilt and alarms per RET under watch is handy).
C. Test designs that hold up (from an automated nightly on three RET-wired setups):
TestDesign detail that matters
List all RETswait for a confirmed full scan on every RET-bearing radio, poll the ACS antenna total until it settles, compare to a committed per-setup oracle — no more, no fewer
Full scan on restartfrom no RET-IDs in ACS and no .persist file, restart the pods; expect an automatic full scan and BBU-Val.xml listing exactly the declared RETs
Set + verify + restoreread baseline and Min/Max, set a value one degree away inside the range, wait for CurTilt to converge, then restore the baseline best-effort so a restore failure never masks a genuine pass
Range sweepintegers, decimals and out-of-range values: each accepted value must reach CurTilt; each reject must be refused and must not change the current tilt
Range populatedafter a forced full scan every RET shows parseable MinTilt ≤ MaxTilt; an empty MinTilt after a completed scan is a product bug, not a test bug
Persistenceset tilt, restart the BBU pod, read back. The BBU does not replay the setpoint, so this checks RET retention plus GetTilt re-read
Debug-app tilt±2 deg on one sub-antenna; verify every other (RET, sub-antenna) did not move; one-past-the-last sub-antenna index must be dropped with nothing moving
RecoverabilityRET identity and tilt survive a radio reboot; radio reboot raises and clears the M-plane-disconnect alarm and re-initialises AISG
Level 3 — defects found and how to triage failures
Product defect classes found in one integration campaign (43 test cases, 25 pass, 6 product failures):
  • Radio stays down after a radio reboot until the per-radio LRCP daemon is restarted (reconnect not handled).
  • One RET never finishes initialisation — no timeout and no retry, so it hangs forever.
  • Resetting one RET renumbers all ALD and ACS ids on the bus (identity must not depend on discovery order).
  • GetTilt times out on a RET after a good init.
  • A RET alarm never reaches the ACS.
  • A tilt set for a non-existent antenna is not refused and is sent to the RET.
Failure taxonomy used by the nightly triage — classify before you debug:
CodeMeaningFirst action
F-SCANfull scan never completed (inventory marker not seen within 1100 s)RET bus / cabling / power on that setup; each timeout burns ~18 min of stage budget and can overrun the whole stage
F-NORETno live RET on the radio (empty inventory)check AISG power and cable before blaming code
S-NOBASELINERET has blank CurTilt — nothing to move fromoften a mid-scan read: an 18-RET bus fills CurTilt one by one; if the same RETs stay blank every run, they are discovered but never answer — a product signal
S-TRANSPORTradio speaks LRCP, test drives the O-RAN debug app (or vice versa)by design; pick a matching radio
S-DARKradio not transmitting (power reads 32767 / -9900 sentinels)setup state, not an AISG problem
F-CRASHassertions passed but a crash was found at teardownthe test is green, the build is not — open the core
F (tilt did not converge)RET accepted the set but CurTilt stayed oldcheck the RET physically moved, then whether the read path (ACS/XDB) is stale
NRno result — build died or stage timeout hitfix the pipeline first
Lesson: blank is not zero, discovered is not alive, and "set accepted" is not "tilt changed". Assert each separately.
Interview Q&A
Q: How do you calibrate a RET actuator that is not fitted to an antenna?
A: Send AISG Calibrate, let the shaft turn about three rotations, stall it by hand for about a second and release. The unit takes the stall as an end-stop, then finds and stores both limits itself. Do not over-force; use a resistance fixture for repeated work.
Q: What is the difference between a full and an internal AISG scan?
A: A full scan discovers every device on the bus with the L2 unique-ID scan. An internal scan only re-contacts the RETs already listed in the daemon cache or the .persist file. The daemon picks internal when that list exists, full otherwise; deleting .persist forces a full scan.
Q: A test reads CurTilt as blank. Is the tilt 0 degrees?
A: No. Blank means no GetTilt reply has been stored yet (the raw no-value is -32768). It can be a mid-scan read on a large bus; if the same RETs stay blank after a completed scan they are discovered but not answering, which is a product defect.
Q: How do you design a set-tilt test that does not leave the site mis-tilted or hide failures?
A: Read the baseline and Min/Max, move one degree inside the range, wait for convergence, then restore the baseline best-effort in a way that cannot turn a pass into a fail. Separately verify rejects of out-of-range values leave the tilt unchanged.
Q: Resetting one RET changed the ids of all the others. Why is that a bug?
A: RET identity in ACS must be stable (keyed by unique ID/serial), not by discovery order. Renumbering breaks any stored tilt plan or alarm mapping and can apply a tilt to the wrong antenna.
Timing — PTP masters, grandmasters & drift
TSYNC01 PTP Locked but the Clock Drifts — the chrony trap (LTE4G-17898), ptp_manager modes/states, the two boundary-clock servos, FHS event-interval / tp_delta, and reading the timing dashboard Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
A vBBU node that acts as a PTP boundary clock has two clocks to keep right: the network card's hardware clock, steered to the grandmaster, and the Linux system clock, steered to the network card. The fronthaul software and every application read the system clock. If the second loop breaks, the node still reports "PTP locked" while the clock the radios are timed from slowly drifts — and cells go to sleep with no obvious timing alarm.

That is exactly what happened in LTE4G-17898: about three months across several teams ruled out BIOS, TSC frequency, SMI storms and thermal throttling. The real cause was simple: the configuration handoff from rrhmgr to the PTP manager failed, so chrony kept steering the system clock in competition with PTP. The signature was a chronyd started without -x. Every clue was already in the PTP-manager and fronthaul-server (FHS) logs; what was missing was a way to read them together. This card explains those log lines and the dashboard built on them. Background: CM35 (PTP profiles, ptp4l/phc2sys/pmc), PTPSTEP01 (one-step / two-step).
Figure — one hardware clock, two servo loops on a boundary clock
Servo 1 can be perfect while servo 2 is broken; the fronthaul reads the system clock, so servo 2 is the health indicator that matters.
Level 1 — the signals and what each one means
Design point: each timing component (the PTP manager with its chronyd, and FHS/xran) writes one-line key=value events to the node syslog; a shipper sends them to Elasticsearch, ingest parses them, Kibana only displays. No component talks to the dashboard — the log line is the contract, so the same greps work on a log bundle without the dashboard.
SignalLog line (shape)How to read it
Pod startstarted chronyd ... -x, pid: None per PTP-manager start; a trailing -x = chrony may not adjust the system clock. Missing -x = the LTE4G-17898 signature
Pod stopGot signal SIGTERM. Shutting downSIGTERM = orchestrator stop, SIGINT = manual, SIGABRT = crash; lines that just stop = SIGKILL/OOM/reboot
ModeMode changed from INIT to BCINIT → BC (slave to GM, master to RRHs) or GM. Stuck in INIT = never finished configuring; repeated BC↔INIT = config re-applied
Clock statestate=SYNC_LOCKED timeSource=<port> clockClass=6 clockAccuracy=20states SYNC_LOCKED, SYNC_HOLDOVER, LOCAL_HOLDOVER, OUT_OF_SYNC. clockClass 6 locked, 7 holdover, 248 free-run; accuracy 0x20 ≈ locked, 0xfe unknown. No PTP packets → holdover within ~10 s
Servo 1 (network)(port), up, slave, cc=6 ca=20, rms=7 max=19PHC vs GM, ns. Master ports print only cc/ca; a disabled port prints neither
Servo 2 (system)(port - CLOCK_REALTIME), rms=341 max=1445system clock vs PHC, ns — the headline indicator
FHS event intervalevent interval= N is out-of-range [low..high]ns; N > high = slow, N < low = fast. Empty = healthy
FHS tp_deltaRRH_n : tp_delta_<ns>logged only when a gap exceeds 50 µs; > 4 s is flagged
FHS splitRRH_n : 'config_split_option' - split_Opt8 category_A rat_4Gone per RRH at FHS bring-up; an RRH reporting two splits is a config smell
RMS and max exist only in BC mode (GM mode has no slave port to measure). RMS = mean offset over the status period (default 15 s), max = peak in that period; an alarm is raised when max ≥ the RMS threshold (default 300 ns, hysteresis 10); the dashboard highlights RMS above 150 ns.
Level 2 — how to triage, with or without the dashboard
Triage order for a suspected timing sleeping cell (any one pointing the wrong way → suspect clock discipline, not the radio):
#CheckBad sign
1PTP-manager pod lifecycle: how was chronyd launched on the last start?no trailing -x — chrony and phc2sys both steer the system clock
2FHS event-interval out-of-rangecontinuous alternating fast/slow pairs = drifting system clock (the earliest warning; it fired continuously during LTE4G-17898)
3Servo 2 RMS (system clock vs PHC)growing while servo 1 (network side) stays small
4Mode and statenever reached BC + SYNC_LOCKED, stuck in INIT, or flapping BC↔INIT
The same checks from a log bundle, without the dashboard:
grep "started chronyd" messages* | tail -3          # last pod start: trailing -x present?
grep -E "Mode changed|state=" messages* | tail -20   # INIT -> BC ? SYNC_LOCKED ?
grep "CLOCK_REALTIME), rms=" messages* | tail -20    # servo 2 trend (ns)
grep -F "), up, slave, cc=" messages* | tail -20   # servo 1 trend (ns)
grep -c "event interval=" fhs*.log                  # 0 is healthy
grep "tp_delta_" fhs*.log | sort -t_ -k3 -n | tail  # worst per-RRH gaps (ns)
ps -ef | grep [c]hronyd ; pmc -u -b 0 "GET TIME_STATUS_NP"
Reading the panels:
  • Per-servo RMS bars: the solid bar is the average, the lighter cap the worst spike; it turns red when the spike crosses the threshold. The two servos run at very different magnitudes, so each has its own threshold.
  • Spikes right after a re-lock are the RMS window refilling (the buffer resets when the state leaves SYNC_LOCKED) — not a fault.
  • Per-port role timeline (slave, master, listening, uncalibrated, pre_master, passive, disabled, faulty, initializing) and link up/down table: the first "up" after each pod restart is the pod noticing the link, not a flap.
  • A "highlights" strip counts each log family over the whole capture: amber = the software can log it but this capture never did, red = expected and absent. Know what your logs can tell you before trusting an empty panel.
  • FHS pod lifecycle: one row per boot with its timing threads and cores; a clean shutdown shows both shutdown markers, anything else is "unknown".
Level 3 — the two-servo trap, pitfalls and observability lessons
Why "PTP locked" lied. A boundary clock has one PHC shared by both NIC ports, so it runs two servos: ptp4l (PHC ← GM on the slave port) and phc2sys (CLOCK_REALTIME ← PHC). The state machine and clockClass describe servo 1. If phc2sys dies or chrony fights it, nothing in the PTP state changes, while the system clock that FHS uses to pace fronthaul events free-runs or wanders. FHS then sees its event interval outside the allowed window (in one example the window was ~537–617 µs and a sample read ~778 µs) long before cells fail.

Pitfalls
  • Checking chrony on a pod that has since restarted: read the last start line, not the first.
  • A one-sided burst of event-interval messages for more than ~5 minutes is a real out-of-range; isolated blips are noise.
  • tp_delta values are ns in the log; a value like 4 251 638 407 is ~4.25 s, i.e. that RRH lost sync completely.
  • Mixed split options for one RRH (Opt7.2 and Opt8) mean the RRH configuration is not what you think — fix that before timing analysis.
  • Unclean pod exits (SIGKILL, OOM, reboot) leave no exit line; group by PID and take the last timestamp.
Logger gaps found in design review (a useful lesson for any observability work): the boot-time INIT state was never logged, there was no discrete "RMS threshold crossed" event, and there was no port-link event table. If the log line is the contract, missing lines are missing evidence — review the loggers, not only the dashboard.
Interview Q&A
Q: How can a node report SYNC_LOCKED and still cause timing failures?
A: The PTP state reflects the NIC hardware clock against the grandmaster. Applications and the fronthaul read the system clock, steered by a second servo (phc2sys). If that loop fails or chrony also steers the system clock, the system clock drifts while PTP still looks locked.
Q: What does the chronyd -x flag do here and why does it matter?
A: It stops chronyd from adjusting the system clock, leaving phc2sys as the only owner. Without it, chrony and phc2sys fight; that was the LTE4G-17898 signature.
Q: Which log signal gives the earliest warning of system-clock drift?
A: The FHS event-interval out-of-range messages; continuous alternating fast/slow pairs mean the system clock is wandering.
Q: Why do RMS values spike right after a re-lock?
A: The RMS buffer is reset when the state leaves SYNC_LOCKED, so the first samples average over a refilling window. It is not a new fault.
Q: List the four checks, in order, for a suspected timing sleeping cell.
A: chronyd launched with -x on the last start; FHS event-interval firing; system-clock RMS growing while the network side is fine; mode reached BC and state SYNC_LOCKED.
PTPGM01 vBBU as PTP Master — FOCOM port roles (C1/C3, external/internal in, out), daisy-chained timing, PTP on every fronthaul port incl. option-8 RRHs, free-run clock class and ptp4l restarts Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
A vBBU is not just a PTP slave of the site grandmaster (GM); it is a boundary clock. It recovers time on one port and re-transmits it as a master on others: toward its own O-RUs, toward a second NIC in the same server, or toward a neighbouring vBBU that has no GM port of its own. This card covers two related questions:
  1. How do you declare which NIC ports are PTP slaves and masters when the vBBU is deployed through FOCOM (C1 vs C3, "external in", "internal in", "out")? This is how daisy-chained timing between NICs and vBBUs is built.
  2. What happens when the BBU is master on every fronthaul port — including ports with GPS-timed option-8 RRHs — and when the BBU itself loses or regains its time source? A ~14-hour A/B lab study answered this with numbers.
Background on LLS-C1..C4 topologies, G.8275.1 profiles and clock classes is in CM35; RU behaviour on a clock step is in PTPSTEP01; FOCOM cluster provisioning and vBBU bring-up are in CM38 / CM39; a GNSS grandmaster NIC inside the server is covered in PTPGM02.
PTP port roles on a vBBU and a daisy chain
Example: GM feeds the quad NIC; one out-port re-times the dual 100G NIC (internal in), another feeds a second vBBU (external in from its point of view). O-RU-facing ports are masters automatically.
Level 1 — port roles and the rules the deployment API enforces
FOCOM only declares port roles and prepares the ports (role classification, VF handling) into platform-config.json; it does not run PTP. ptp4l / phc2sys are configured downstream by the PTP manager on the vBBU.
Field / roleMeaningFronthaul use
ptp_type = C1Dedicated timing port from the GM, no O-RU traffic on itPort gives up its SR-IOV VFs
ptp_type = C3Combined fronthaul + timing port; PTP comes from a fronthaul switch with an embedded GMPort keeps its VFs
ptp_in_interfaces.externalSlave port fed from outside this vBBU — a GM or an upstream vBBU's out-portOrdered list; first entry = legacy "grandmaster" object
ptp_in_interfaces.internalSlave port fed from an out-port of the same vBBU (NIC-to-NIC jumper)Timing-only, 0 VFs
ptp_out_interfacesMaster (boundary-clock) port toward another NIC or vBBUTiming-only, 0 VFs
O-RU-facing fronthaul portsNot listed anywhere; the vBBU is always master toward its O-RUs (handled by the RRH manager)Normal fronthaul
Rules
  • Legacy XOR new: either the old GM-setup fields or the new PTP fields — never both. Keep the legacy setup null.
  • ptp_type is mandatory as soon as any PTP port is given; at least one external in-port is required — a vBBU cannot be a pure master.
  • One role per port; lists are ordered. The PTP VLAN applies only to the first external in-port (C1 only).
  • Modify semantics per list: omitted = unchanged, a value = overwrite the whole list, __CLEAR__ = blank it (ports return to the fronthaul pool).
  • Interface names are only validated on the worker — a typo surfaces 30–40 min into provisioning.
  • Bring up the upstream vBBU first; the downstream cannot lock until the upstream out-port transmits.
Level 2 — configuring a chain and checking it
Design the chain on paper first, create the deployment (ports come up as fronthaul if you leave the PTP fields empty), read the real Linux interface names on the worker, then assign roles with a Modify and mirror the same values into the stored SMO deployment.
// Modify: quad NIC slave on port A, re-times the dual NIC (port C) and a neighbour vBBU (port D)
{ "ModifyCluster": {
    "ptp_type": "C1",
    "managedelementinfo": {
      "ptp_in_interfaces": { "external": "PORT_A", "internal": "PORT_C" },
      "ptp_out_interfaces": "PORT_B,PORT_D"
    } } }

// later: remove only the out-ports (slaves stay)
{ "ModifyCluster": { "managedelementinfo": { "ptp_out_interfaces": "__CLEAR__" } } }
Topologyexternalinternalout
Single slave from GM (C1 baseline)A——
Single slave via FH switch with embedded GM (C3)A (keeps VFs)——
Daisy chain inside one vBBU (quad → dual NIC)ACB
Chain between two vBBUsvBBU1: A / vBBU2: A—vBBU1: B
Two independent GM feeds (fiber + copper)A,B (A is "primary")——
4 vBBUs on one GM (two feeders + two dual-NIC-only)feeders: Afeeders: own dual NIC lanefeeders: 2 ports
Hardware rules that decide the cabling
  • A GM with 1G outputs cannot feed a dual 100G NIC: its breakout lanes are fixed at 10G. Feed it from a 10G GM output or from a quad 25G NIC out-port (same or neighbouring vBBU).
  • A copper GM output reaches a quad NIC through an SFP copper adaptor; copper cannot reach the dual NIC.
  • Every NIC/vBBU hop is another boundary clock and eats time-error budget (see CM35) — keep chains short and prefer direct GM feeds when spare outputs exist.
  • Port budget example: four vBBUs on one GM — on each feeder vBBU timing consumes 3 of 4 quad ports and 1 of 8 dual lanes, leaving 1 quad port + 7 lanes for O-RUs; the fronthaul server limit was 14 FH ports per vBBU.
Verify: the cluster info returns the lists exactly as sent; platform-config.json carries ptp_type, ptp_in_interfaces[] (external first) and ptp_out_interfaces[]; timing ports are absent from the fronthaul list with 0 VFs. Lock state and clock class are owned by the PTP manager — confirm with its CLI / alarms and pmc, not with FOCOM.
Level 2b — should the BBU send PTP to GPS-timed option-8 RRHs? (method)
The proposal was to make every fronthaul port a PTP master (static masters) instead of enabling a master only when an RU reports it needs PTP (the option-8 daemon always says "not needed"). The test: a 4-port E810 boundary clock with one shared PHC, G.8275.1-style L2 multicast, domain 24, two-step; one 7.2 RU (PTP slave, used as positive control) and two option-8 RRHs, cells at maximum load.
  • A/B windows of 25 min, PTP ON vs OFF on the port under test; first 2 min after each switch excluded.
  • Every 30 s: fronthaul-server late/early/corrupt/duplicate counters and jitter, 38 ethtool -S error counters per port, each RRH's clock source/GPS over its control link; every 15 s pmc port states, offset, announced class.
  • Continuous PTP captures per port; positive control proves the capture works (the 7.2 RU sends Delay_Req ~1/s).
  • Event phases: GPS antenna pulled, GM cable pulled, slave port removed, RRH booted without GPS, fiber pulls.
Message (per master port)IntervalRate
Sync62.5 ms (logSyncInterval −4)16/s
Follow_Up (two-step)with each Sync16/s
Announce (carries clock class)125 ms (logAnnounceInterval −3)8/s
Delay_Responly if the RU sends Delay_Req0/s to option-8, ~1/s to the 7.2 RU
Total~40 frames/s ≈ 28 kbit/s
Level 3 — results, and the three real risks
Option-8 RRHs ignore PTP entirely. They sent 0 PTP frames in every test, their clock source stayed GPS, and an RRH booted without GPS while PTP was on its port from power-on still did not lock: it free-ran at about 1.7 ppm (tp_delta drifting ~1.7 µs per second against the BBU) and its cell stayed off until GPS returned. The option-8 daemon decides sync from the RRH's GPS alarm alone, so PTP can never be a fallback for these radios without software changes.

PTP traffic cannot disturb the U-plane: ~40 frames/s is 0.06% of packets and 0.001% of the bandwidth of a 4x4 option-8 fronthaul (~2.5 Gbit/s, ~70k packets/s). Worst-case added delay to one IQ packet is ~0.08 µs (one 64–82 B frame at 10 Gbit/s), versus a measured baseline fronthaul tick jitter of 1.4 µs average. PTP goes through the kernel driver on the physical function; IQ uses SR-IOV VFs with DPDK on isolated CPUs. A/B: late/early/corrupt/duplicate and all 38 NIC error counters were 0 with PTP ON and OFF; CQI, rank, NACK and UL SNR identical.
Event7.2 O-RU (PTP slave)Option-8 RRH (GPS)
BBU loses GM (OUT_OF_SYNC, class 248): PTP manager stops the master ptp4lRF TX off immediately; fronthaul fault 8 (PTP out of sync); ~3.5 min later RU stops U-plane (fault 5) and raises O-RAN fault 18 FREERUNUnaffected
BBU with no PTP input acting as free-running GMLocks to it — the BBU announces class 6, accuracy 0x20, timeTraceable 1Unaffected
Source returns after 60 min free-runBBU steps clock −414 µs (−78 µs after 37 min) → fault 11 (system time jump) + fault 15 (early U-plane) for ~50 sNot noticed
Dynamic per-RU masters: an RU connects/disconnectsThe shared master ptp4l restarts → every other 7.2 RU on the NIC loses Sync for ~1 sNot noticed
Static "every port is master"No restarts, no gaps; a stranded 7.2 RU (link flapping 106–151 MAC faults / 25 min without PTP, 0 with) registered after one rebootNot noticed
Pitfalls and recommendations
  • Wrong clock class when free-running: an undisciplined BBU advertising class 6 / timeTraceable 1 looks like a primary reference to any PTP-capable RU. It should announce a non-traceable class such as 248 with timeTraceable 0 (see CM35 for the class table).
  • Clock step on restore: the longer the free-run, the bigger the step; 7.2 RUs see a ~50 s fault burst — exactly the scenario studied in PTPSTEP01.
  • Prefer static masters over per-RU masters: one shared ptp4l serves all master ports, so any add/remove restarts it. A workaround seen in the field is to write all master sections in one configuration update.
  • Re-test new option-8 models: a model/firmware with a PTP client could lock to the BBU instead of GPS. The decisive one-hour check: boot it without GPS and see whether it sends PTP frames and whether its tp_delta drifts.
  • NTP is never a fallback in boundary-clock mode; chrony may steer the system clock only with no PTP mode or in GM free-run.
  • Side finding: the fronthaul server picked a free-running option-8 RRH as its S-plane master, causing tp_delta bursts on another GPS-locked RRH — check which RRH the fronthaul server is following.
Interview Q&A
Q: What is the difference between ptp_type C1 and C3 on a vBBU?
A: C1: the slave port is a dedicated timing link from the GM, no O-RU traffic, so it gives up its SR-IOV VFs. C3: PTP arrives on a combined fronthaul port from a switch with an embedded GM; the port keeps its VFs and carries O-RU traffic too.
Q: A second vBBU has no GM port. How does it get time, and how is its port declared?
A: Cable it to an out-port of the first vBBU (a boundary-clock master). On the downstream vBBU that port is an external in-port — it only sees a master on the wire. "Internal" is reserved for an out-port of the same vBBU. Bring up the upstream vBBU first.
Q: Is it safe to send PTP to GPS-timed option-8 RRHs?
A: For the models tested, yes: ~40 frames/s, 28 kbit/s, ≤0.08 µs worst-case added IQ delay, separate kernel vs DPDK paths and CPUs; A/B showed zero counter or KPI difference and the RRHs never used PTP even without GPS. Re-check any new model with a boot-without-GPS test.
Q: Why do 7.2 RUs see 1-second Sync gaps when an unrelated RU reconnects?
A: All master ports share one ptp4l on the shared PHC. With per-RU dynamic masters, adding or removing a port restarts that process, so every other slave loses Sync for about a second. Static "all ports master" avoids the restart.
Q: The BBU free-ran for an hour and then the GM came back. What do you expect on a 7.2 RU?
A: The BBU steps its clock by hundreds of µs (−414 µs measured after 60 min); the RU raises a system-time-jump fault and early U-plane faults for ~50 s. During free-run the BBU should have announced a degraded, non-traceable class (e.g. 248) rather than class 6.
PTPGM02 GNSS PTP Grandmaster inside the DU/CU server — E810 GNSS NIC, ts2phc / phc2sys / ptp4l chain, NIC daisy-chaining, DPLL states and holdover Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
An O-RU needs phase/time sync from PTP before it may transmit. Today a lab or site usually has an external grandmaster box (a GNSS-fed PTP switch or appliance): in LLS-C3 it sits in the fronthaul switch and both DU and RU are slaves; in LLS-C1 it feeds the DU, and the DU acts as boundary clock towards the RU (see CM35).
This design removes that box: a GNSS-capable PTP NIC (Intel E810-XXVDA4T, "GG1" variant with on-board GNSS receiver and OCXO) is fitted in the DU (or CU) server. The NIC's hardware clock is steered by GNSS 1PPS, and the DU itself becomes the grandmaster for its RUs. Benefits: one box fewer on site, lower cost and power, and in C1 a NIC port that used to face the external GM is freed for fronthaul or midhaul.

For a validation engineer the interesting parts are the Linux clock chain (ts2phc → PHC → phc2sys / ptp4l), the NIC's DPLL states, holdover behaviour when GNSS is lost, and the SMA outputs (1PPS, 10 MHz) that can discipline your test equipment.
LLS-C1 with the grandmaster inside the DU
One ts2phc, one phc2sys and one ptp4l master per fronthaul port, all run by the PTP manager pod (ptpmgr). The RUs are ordinary clocks.
Level 1 — core facts
PTP clock roles (refresher): GM = time source, master ports only; OC = one slave port (an RU); BC = slave in, master out (the DU in classic C1); TC = forwards PTP and corrects the residence time (ideal for a switch between CU and DU).
The three linuxptp daemons (see CM35 for ptp4l/pmc basics):
DaemonDisciplinesIn this design
ts2phcNIC PHC from an external time-stamp signal (GNSS 1PPS)One instance per NIC that receives 1PPS (GNSS NIC, and daisy-chained NICs)
phc2sysSystem clock from a PHC (or the other way)One instance, from the GNSS NIC PHC
ptp4lPTP protocol on a port (GM/OC/BC/TC)One master per FH port; masters/slaves on NIC-to-NIC links; masters on MH in the CU variant
The NIC: 4 x SFP28 25G ports; base variant needs an external 1PPS, the GG1 variant has its own GNSS module. The on-board OCXO gives a holdover of roughly ±1.5 µs for about 4 hours after losing the reference — far better than a plain NIC oscillator. 8-port and 12-port E810-based third-party cards with GNSS + OCXO and SMA I/O (antenna, 1PPS, 10 MHz) are alternatives that avoid multiple NICs.
Deployment variants:
VariantHow sync is spreadPriority
One GM NIC in the DUts2phc + phc2sys + ptp4l master on each FH port; DU = GM, RUs = OCMust have
Several GM NICs in the DUFirst NIC has GNSS; 1PPS daisy-chained SMA out → SMA in; one ts2phc per NIC. Max RUs = total portsNice to have
GM NIC + regular NICsRegular NICs synced by PTP over an SFP link from the previous NIC (ptp4l master → slave). Max RUs = P − 2(N−1): 1 NIC 4, 2 NICs 6, 3 NICs 8Nice to have
GM NIC in the CUptp4l masters on midhaul ports; each DU is slave on its MH NIC port and master on FH ports (a BC)Nice to have
GNSS constellations are a local system-defaults setting of the PTP manager (not exposed in the GUI): any of GPS, Galileo, SBAS, GLONASS, BeiDou; default GPS + Galileo.
Level 2 — configure, check and measure
Port roles at deployment. The cluster deployment (FOCOM) auto-detects the NICs and asks how each port is used. Existing categories map naturally:
CategoryMeaningUsed for the GM NIC as
fhinterfacesPTP master ports carrying FH + sync (C1)Ports towards RUs
bhinterfacesBackhaul / midhaul, no PTPBH/MH ports with no PTP role
gminterfacesPTP slave ports facing a GMSlave port on a regular NIC in a PTP daisy-chain
fhgminterfaceSingle FH slave port via a GM switch (C3)Not used when the DU is the GM
new: master-to-NIC categoryPTP master port used only to sync the next NICMaster end of a PTP daisy-chain
If several NICs are present and no PTP daisy-chain ports are defined, 1PPS daisy-chaining over SMA is assumed. The port map flows into the platform config JSON pulled by the BBU pod and then into the PTP manager configuration.

Illustrative linuxptp chain (generic linuxptp syntax; the PTP manager generates the real files):
# 1) PHC from GNSS 1PPS (+ time of day from the GNSS NMEA stream)
ts2phc -f ts2phc.cfg -s nmea -m           # cfg lists the NIC and the GNSS tty, e.g. /dev/gnss0
# 2) system clock follows the NIC PHC
phc2sys -s <fh_port0> -c CLOCK_REALTIME -O -37 -m   # PHC on TAI, system clock UTC
# 3) a master on every fronthaul port (G.8275.1, domain 24, masterOnly)
ptp4l -f ptp4l_fh1.cfg -i <fh_port1> -m

# checks
pmc -u -b 0 -d 24 'GET PARENT_DATA_SET'      # grandmasterIdentity = this NIC
pmc -u -b 0 -d 24 'GET PORT_DATA_SET'        # portState MASTER on FH ports
cat /run/ptpmanager/tx/status                 # DPLL state, satellites seen/used, RMS
DPLL states reported by the NIC (state changes also go to the system log):
StateMeaningExpect the RU to...
uninitialized / invalidDPLL not yet configured or no usable inputStay unlocked, no TX
freerunRunning on the oscillator, never lockedStay unlocked
lockedLocked to GNSS 1PPS, holdover not yet qualifiedLock, normal
locked_ho_acqLocked and holdover data acquiredLock; ready to ride through a GNSS outage
holdoverReference lost, coasting on OCXOStay locked while within spec (about 4 h to ±1.5 µs)
The dashboard keeps the existing counters (time in Locked / Holdover / Unlocked, PTP RMS) and adds GNSS satellites seen and satellites used; the status file is polled about every 10 s and uploaded in 15-minute bulk files. GNSS health can also be read directly from /dev/gnss0 or via gpsd.

Bench use: the NIC can drive 1PPS and 10 MHz on SMA. Feeding the analyser / signal generator reference input from the same NIC that times the RU removes frequency offset between DUT and instrument (useful for EVM and frequency-error tests, see SET2).
Level 3 — expert detail, pitfalls and test ideas
  • Only one GNSS module per server. Further NICs get time via SMA 1PPS (needs one more ts2phc per NIC) or via PTP over an SFP link (costs two ports per extra NIC: that is where P − 2(N−1) comes from).
  • phc2sys source must be the GNSS NIC, not a downstream daisy-chained NIC, or the system clock inherits extra chain error.
  • CU-hosted GM: the DU midhaul must terminate on the NIC (hardware timestamping), not the motherboard port; a switch between CU and DU should ideally be a transparent clock. A non-TC switch still works but acquisition time and accuracy suffer. Distance is not a PTP limit — packet delay variation is.
  • Antenna placement decides everything: a GNSS antenna with poor sky view gives "locked" with few satellites used, then frequent holdover. Trend satellites-used, not just lock state.
  • Holdover is not forever. A cell that rides out a short outage may drift out of the RU's time-error budget during a long one; then RU fault behaviour (holdover / freerun faults, see AUTO10 and SPLANE01) should follow.
  • Time steps: any re-lock that steps the PHC is dangerous for the RU datapath — see PTPSTEP01.

Validation checklist: (1) cold start: time from power-on to DPLL locked and to RU LOCKED; (2) GNSS antenna pull: DPLL goes holdover, RU stays locked, alarms raised as designed, recovery after re-connect without a time step; (3) PTP manager / GM restart: RU re-lock time; (4) 1PPS phase of the NIC SMA output vs a reference GNSS receiver on a scope or time-interval counter; (5) constellation change (GPS only vs GPS + Galileo) and its effect on satellites used; (6) daisy-chain: phase offset between NIC 1 and NIC 2 1PPS; (7) long run: Locked/Holdover/Unlocked counters on the dashboard match the injected events.
Interview Q&A
Q: What do ts2phc, phc2sys and ptp4l each do in a GNSS GM DU?
A: ts2phc steers the NIC hardware clock from GNSS 1PPS, phc2sys aligns the Linux system clock to that PHC, and ptp4l runs PTP master ports on each fronthaul port so the RUs (ordinary clocks) lock to the DU.
Q: Why does the GM NIC have an OCXO and what does it buy you?
A: A stable oscillator for holdover: about ±1.5 µs for roughly 4 hours after losing GNSS, so the cell survives antenna or sky-view outages.
Q: Difference between DPLL locked and locked_ho_acq?
A: Both are locked to the reference; locked_ho_acq additionally means the DPLL has learned enough to enter a qualified holdover if the reference disappears.
Q: You add a second, regular NIC for more RUs. How is it synced and what does it cost?
A: Via PTP over an SFP link from the GM NIC (master on the GM NIC, slave on the new NIC), which consumes one port on each NIC; total RUs = P − 2(N−1).
Q: How can the GM NIC help RF measurements on the bench?
A: Its 10 MHz and 1PPS SMA outputs can be the analyser/generator reference, so instrument and RU share one frequency source and frequency error/EVM are not polluted by reference offset.
FHSVC01 Inside the DU fronthaul service — busy-poll symbol-boundary loop, PHY callbacks, and why a 100%-busy RT thread can freeze Linux Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
On a virtualised DU the fronthaul service (fhsvc) is the program that actually puts IQ packets on the wire to the RU and takes uplink packets off it, through DPDK virtual functions. It has to act on every OFDM symbol boundary — every 71.4 µs in LTE and every 35.7 µs in NR at 30 kHz — with sub-microsecond accuracy, on ordinary Linux, with no hardware timer interrupt to wake it.

The answer is a busy-poll loop that reads the clock non-stop on an isolated core. That meets the timing, but a thread that never lets go of its core collides with a hard fact: even an isolated core still needs a few kernel threads to run now and then. Starve them and the whole server can freeze; let them in at the wrong moment and you get late packets. This card explains the design, why each fix tried so far is a compromise, and what the trade-off looks like from the validation bench: intermittent late/early U-plane faults, sporadic RU faults or throughput dips that line up with kernel activity in long stability runs.
One fhsvc cycle per symbol
At each boundary fhsvc runs the symbol map, writes the symbol config into shared memory and yields to the PHY callbacks, then goes back to polling the clock.
Level 1 — how the fronthaul service keeps time
ItemValue / behaviour
TransportDPDK vfio virtual functions mapped to physical FH NIC ports
Timing threadstwo: opt7.2 (O-RAN split 7.2) and opt8 (CPRI-like); LTE uses both with per-PHY clients, NR drives everything from the opt7.2 thread
Symbol periodLTE 1 ms / 14 = 71.4285 µs; NR 30 kHz 0.5 ms / 14 = 35.7142 µs
How it finds the boundarytight loop on timespec_get(), compensating the ~35 ns cost of the call itself
On each boundarywalk a symbol map: DL processing, UL processing, mid-slot and slot-boundary procedures; also check for received packets (data-driven, not scheduled)
Hand-off to PHYssymbol config written into a shared structure (PBBU_IO), then yield; PHY callback threads at the same RT priority run in turn with no mutex waits, then wake their PHY on another core via a futex
Cost of the plug-in modelcallbacks run one after another, so each PHY is a little later than the last: ~10 µs for a full cycle with 3 PHYs on a 6.4 SUSE kernel, uninterrupted
Why not just use an interrupt? There is no hardware interrupt at symbol rate on a COTS server, and Linux sleeps of a few microseconds are not deterministic. So the service must keep the core 100% busy — which is exactly what the kernel cannot tolerate forever. See CM29 for CPU isolation, huge pages and RT kernel basics, and CM19 for the timing windows the RU enforces on the packets fhsvc sends.
Level 2 — why a 100%-busy RT thread fights Linux, and the options
The core problem. Isolating a core (isolcpus/nohz_full, IRQs moved away) removes most noise, but some kernel work is per-CPU and cannot be moved: scheduler ticks, kernel timers, RCU callbacks, migration threads. Kernel developers confirm complete isolation of one thread cannot be guaranteed. Two bad outcomes follow:
• Push kernel threads below fhsvc priority and they never run → kernel lockout and a freeze of the whole processor, not just that core.
• Let stalld watch for starved threads and boost them → works most of the time, but it is not guaranteed and each boost steals time from fhsvc at an unpredictable moment.
Mitigation triedIdeaResult
CPU hopping (current model)every ~1 s, jump fhsvc and callbacks to another core for ~1 ms so kernel threads on the home core can runworks on the surface when timed well; long-term reliability not proven; does not fix the root need
Sleep and yieldsleep ~5 µs before the next boundary, callbacks told via PBBU_IO to sleep tookernel traces show a 5 µs sleep only relinquishes to the scheduler — wake time already in the past; idle time not deterministic
Mutex shiftcallbacks release a mutex on another core so the tight loop can quiescelarge redesign, not pursued yet
Timing jumphand boundary-watching to a thread on another core for a short periodcross-core hand-over delay is not deterministic
HW timer interrupt / kernel driverinterrupt at every symbol boundarythe ideal; needs a dedicated clock and driver, feasibility on COTS unproven (and very short kernel delays also busy-wait)
What to check on a DU that shows fronthaul glitches (generic commands):
cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/isolated        # fhsvc core really isolated?
ps -eLo pid,tid,psr,cls,rtprio,comm | grep -Ei "fh|xran|phy"   # which core, which RT priority
systemctl status stalld; journalctl -u stalld | tail   # boosts = starvation events
grep -E "LOC|RES|TLB" /proc/interrupts       # timer / resched IPIs still hitting the core
dmesg -T | grep -Ei "rcu.*stall|hung_task|soft lockup"   # kernel-side starvation symptoms
Correlate the timestamps of stalld boosts, RCU stall warnings or CPU-hop events with the DU fault log (XRAN codes 14/15 late/early U-plane, 18/19 callback stall — see MMIMO01) and with the RU's own late/early counters.
Level 3 — conclusions and what to look for in long runs
Conclusion of the investigation: without a hardware or deterministic software interrupt, a busy loop is the only way to hit the symbol boundary — and a COTS Linux kernel, even with RT extensions, cannot give 100% of a CPU to one thread without risking a lockup. Symbol-level determinism and quiescing to the OS are opposing needs; the long-term fix needs a timing/processing change in fhsvc and the PHY callbacks, probably a symbol-rate interrupt from hardware.

What this means for validation and stability runs:
• Expect faults that are rare and time-correlated, not configuration-correlated: a burst of late U-plane packets once an hour, a short throughput dip, an RU fault that clears itself. Long soak tests (AUTO09 self-healing watchdog, AUTO14 crash triage) are the only way to see them.
• More PHYs on one fhsvc = more compound delay per cycle; a 3-PHY LTE configuration has less timing margin than a single NR cell. Test the worst configuration.
• Kernel version, BIOS power settings and background services change the result; record them with every stability run.
• A full-server freeze during a stress test on a DU is a known failure mode of this design, not necessarily a hardware fault — collect stalld and kernel logs before rebooting.
• RU-side timing windows (CM19) decide whether a late fhsvc cycle becomes a dropped packet: a RU with tighter windows exposes jitter that another RU tolerates.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why does the DU fronthaul service busy-poll the clock instead of sleeping?
A: It must act at every symbol boundary (35.7 µs at 30 kHz NR) with sub-microsecond accuracy, and there is no hardware interrupt at that rate on a COTS server. Linux microsecond sleeps are not deterministic, so a tight loop on an isolated core is the only reliable trigger.
Q: How does fhsvc hand work to several PHYs without locks?
A: It writes the symbol configuration into a shared structure and yields; PHY callback threads at the same real-time priority run in turn, check the config and signal their PHY on another core through a futex. It is loosely coupled but delays add up per PHY.
Q: What happens if you lower kernel threads below the fhsvc priority on its core?
A: Per-CPU kernel work such as timers, RCU and migration never runs, which can lock up the kernel and freeze the whole processor, not only that core.
Q: Name the mitigation in use today and its weakness.
A: CPU hopping: about every second the service jumps to another core for about a millisecond so kernel threads can run. It works when timed well, but it does not give guaranteed determinism and its long-term reliability is not proven.
Q: In a 24-hour run you see rare late U-plane faults with no config change. How do you investigate?
A: Line up their timestamps with stalld boosts, RCU stall or soft-lockup messages, CPU-hop events and interrupt counts on the fhsvc core; check isolation and priorities; compare with the RU late/early counters and timing windows.
RU security
RUSEC01 O-RU M-plane & software security — NETCONF over TLS vs SSH, vendor certificates, cert-to-name, WG4 password policy and signed RU packages Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
An O-RU is managed over the O-RAN M-plane: a NETCONF session from the DU (client) to the RU (server). Two security questions follow. Who is allowed to manage the RU? Today the session runs over SSH with one username/password, which proves very little about the client. The O-RAN WG4 M-plane spec also allows NETCONF over TLS, where both ends present X.509 certificates and the RU maps the client certificate to a NETCONF user. Is the software we install genuine? An RU package carries MD5 checksums in a manifest that travels with the package, so anyone who changes a file can change its checksum too. The fix is code signing: the RU verifies a signature with a CA chain it already trusts.

This card explains the PW design for both, the commands used to configure the TLS server in sysrepo, the vendor-certificate provisioning step in production, the WG4 password policy, and the negative tests a validation engineer should run. It pairs with RUSEC02 (locking the physical debug ports) and CM36 (the RU software-update flow).
NETCONF over TLS between DU and RU
Both ends authenticate with certificates. The RU learns the client's NETCONF username from the certificate itself.
Level 1 — SSH vs TLS, client identity, certificates and passwords
AspectNETCONF over SSHNETCONF over TLS
Port8306513
Client proves itself withusername + password (or SSH key)X.509 v3 certificate signed by a trusted CA
Server proves itself withSSH host keyX.509 certificate (the RU vendor certificate)
WG4 requirementspassword policy belowTLS 1.2 and 1.3; certificates not self-signed; CA chains configured on both ends
Software stacklibssh + netopeer2needs libnetconf2 (the old libnetconf has no TLS) + libyang, sysrepo, netopeer2 on DU and RU
Two ways the RU can decide who the client is:
1. Fingerprint (x509c2n:specified): the SHA-256 fingerprint of the DU certificate is configured on the RU and mapped to a username. Every time the DU certificate changes the new fingerprint must be pushed again: the first push out-of-band over SSH, later ones by edit-config on the live TLS session.
2. Cert-to-name from the SAN (x509c2n:san-rfc822-name): the DU certificate carries the NETCONF username in its rfc822-name SAN, and that name must be a valid RU account. No fingerprint to maintain — this is the chosen design; the DU certificate manager adds the rfc822 SAN to DU certificates.

The RU vendor certificate. In production every AAU gets its own certificate, private key and CA chain from the vendor PKI (GUI or REST call, product type "RU"): CN = the AAU serial number, SAN = a DNS name built from the serial (IP SANs are possible; the SAN may be left empty if not known in manufacturing), RSA 2048 or 4096. The bundle is written to a predefined persistent location on the unit, and a copy is kept in a secure vault.

WG4 password policy (for accounts that still use passwords): 8–128 characters from upper/lower case letters, digits and a short list of special characters; the password leaf is absent for certificate-authenticated accounts. The legacy shared default password did not meet it and had to change. The AAU uses the same account for host SSH and NETCONF-over-SSH; the password is changed with the RPC defined in the WG4 YANG over the NETCONF session, with options to mirror it to host SSH or change it from the DU CLI.
Level 2 — configuring and testing NETCONF over TLS
RU side — three sysrepo modules, each imported to startup then copied to running:
ModuleHoldsInput format
ietf-keystoreserver private key + server certificate (the vendor cert)base64 of DER
ietf-truststorecertificate bag with root CA + intermediate CAbase64 of DER
ietf-netconf-serverTLS listen endpoint: keystore reference, client-auth CA bag, cert-to-name ruleXML
ietf-netconf-acmNACM group/rules so the mapped user may edit keystore/truststore/serverXML (disable → add rules → enable)
# prepare base64-DER inputs (never paste real keys into tickets or wikis)
openssl rsa  -in <key>  -outform DER | base64 -w 0 > key.b64
openssl x509 -in <cert> -outform DER | base64 -w 0 > cert.b64
openssl x509 -in <cert> -pubkey -noout | openssl pkey -pubin -outform DER | base64 -w 0 > spki.b64
openssl x509 -in <cert> -noout -fingerprint -sha256      # only for the fingerprint method

# load each module: startup, then running
sysrepocfg --import tls_keystore.xml --datastore=startup --module=ietf-keystore -v3
sysrepocfg --copy-from=startup --datastore=running --module=ietf-keystore -v3
#   ... same for ietf-truststore (tls_truststore.xml) and ietf-netconf-server (tls_listen.xml)
netopeer2-server -d -v3                                   # foreground, verbose

# DU / test client
netopeer2-cli
> connect --host <serial>.<vendor-domain> --port 6513 --tls \
          --cert <client.crt> --key <client.key> --trusted <ca.pem>
> get-config --source running
Host-name trap: the vendor certificate's SAN is a DNS name built from the serial, so the client must connect by that name and it must resolve to the RU M-plane address (a hosts entry in the lab; the DU keeps the serial of every RU). Operator certificates issued with the M-plane IP in the SAN avoid this.
Good evidence in the server log: chain verification at depth 2 (root) → depth 1 (sub-CA) → depth 0 (client cert), then a cert-to-name line saying the username was recognised, then the session starts.
Feature design: a flag enableNetconfTLS (default off) on DU and RU. When on, the DU pushes its CA to the RU first; the RU builds the keystore/truststore/listen XML from its certificate, key and CA, loads sysrepo, and starts the TLS listener. SSH NETCONF stays up concurrently as the fallback. Automated enrolment of operator certificates with CMPv2 is the planned next step.
Level 3 — signed RU packages, trust anchors and the test list
Software integrity: the gap. A RU package (zip/tgz) arrives on the eMMC user partition through the SMO and installs to the standby slot (p1 = shared BOOT.BIN + image.ub, p2 = slot 1 rootfs, p3 = slot 2 rootfs). BOOT.BIN and image.ub are verified at every boot by the SoC secure boot, but rootfs.tar (ext4, all applications and configs) is not, and its MD5 sits in the same manifest an attacker would edit. MD5-in-manifest gives integrity, not authenticity.

The fix: code signing. The package gains a hash container (SHA-256 per file), a build/packaging certificate and a signature file with one RSA signature per file. On install the RU:
#CheckFails if
1verify the packaging certificate against the Software-Signing CA chain already on the RUcert from another CA, or forged
2take the public key out of that certificate—
3hash rootfs.tar itself and verify the signature from the signature fileany byte of rootfs.tar changed
4on units without secure boot, do the same for BOOT.BIN and image.ubboot files tampered
5only then copy to the standby slot and set the slot infoany check above failed → install rejected
Trust-anchor rule: the CA chain must already be on the RU and is never taken from the package being checked. Option 1: provision it in the factory (ATE) with the vendor certificate — changeable without a new BOOT.BIN. Option 2: embed it in BOOT.BIN — protected by secure boot, but the first package that brings it cannot itself be verified, and on non-secure-boot units direct flash tampering is not detected.
Limitation: signing protects the update path, not a box an attacker is already on. That is why JTAG is disabled and the debug Ethernet and UART are locked (RUSEC02). Compare CM36, where the redesigned installer also checks a signed SHA-256 list before writing.

Negative tests a validation engineer should own: TLS 1.2 and 1.3 both negotiate; a self-signed client cert is rejected; a cert from an untrusted CA is rejected; a cert whose rfc822 SAN maps to no RU account is rejected; NACM blocks an unmapped user; breaking TLS falls back to SSH; DU cert rotation works without an RU reboot. For packages: tampered rootfs.tar rejected; packaging cert swapped for one from another CA rejected; editing MD5/manifest alone no longer passes; a valid signed package installs to the standby slot and activates.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why move NETCONF from SSH to TLS?
A: SSH authenticates the client only with a password or key; TLS gives mutual X.509 authentication, so the RU can verify the DU certificate chain and learn the NETCONF username from the certificate. WG4 asks for TLS 1.2/1.3 and certificates that are not self-signed.
Q: Fingerprint vs cert-to-name client mapping: which is easier to operate?
A: Cert-to-name from the rfc822 SAN: the username is inside the DU certificate, so nothing on the RU changes when the DU certificate is renewed. The fingerprint method needs the new fingerprint pushed to every RU after each renewal.
Q: netopeer2-cli fails to connect over TLS by IP address even though the certs are right. Why?
A: The RU vendor certificate names the unit by a DNS name derived from its serial, so host-name verification fails for a bare IP. Connect by that name and resolve it to the M-plane address, or use an operator certificate issued with the IP in the SAN.
Q: Why is an MD5 list in the package manifest not enough?
A: The checksum travels with the file it protects, so whoever changes the file can update the checksum. A signature made with a key whose CA chain the RU already trusts cannot be regenerated by the attacker.
Q: Where must the RU get the CA chain used to verify packages?
A: From something it already trusts: factory provisioning or the secure-booted BOOT.BIN. Never from the package under test, otherwise an attacker simply ships their own CA.
RUSEC02 Locking the AAU's physical debug paths — certificate-only SSH on the eth0/LMT port and over UART, U-Boot/recovery hardening, and the test plan that proves it Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
An AAU on a mast has two physical ways in that do not go through the DU: the 1G LMT/debug Ethernet port (eth0) on the outside of the box, and a UART header inside. (The 10G M-plane port, eth1, is only reachable through the connected DU.) Before hardening, eth0 accepted SSH with one shared account password — the same on every unit, so one leak opens the fleet — and the UART auto-logged in to a root shell. Behind those sit two more doors: the U-Boot prompt (any key stops autoboot) and the recovery image (open console and password SSH).

The design keeps both ports usable for engineers but replaces passwords with short-lived SSH certificates signed by a central SSH CA, checked offline on the AAU. A firewall keyed on the ingress interface leaves only one port open on eth0, the UART carries SSH instead of a login prompt, and the boot-loader and recovery paths get the same treatment. The second half of the card is the test plan that proves it — a reusable template for any security feature. Software-package signing is in RUSEC01.
Physical access paths after hardening
Both physical paths accept only a CA-signed certificate for the normal account; root still needs su and the root password.
Level 1 — threat, design and the certificate model
PathBeforeAfter
eth0 LMT portsshd on 22 with the shared password; NETCONF 830 also reachablesecond sshd on 2222, certificate-only; everything else on eth0 dropped
UART consoleautologin to root shellboot log still printed (for RMA), then SSH over the serial line, certificate-only
U-Bootany key stops autoboot; kernel command line editable (e.g. a shell as init)keyed autoboot with a hashed stop string, limited attempts, no env override of boot command/delay
Recovery imageopen getty + password SSHships the same sshd/firewall/CA files as the main image
Boot counterbootlimit 4 → recovery; power cuts could countpower-on resets must not count, so repeated power cuts cannot force recovery
Why SSH certificates and not just a better password? A certificate names the engineer (Key ID), the allowed login (principal), and a validity window. The AAU verifies it with the CA public key shipped in rootfs, so it works even with the M-plane down. Every login is logged with the Key ID and certificate serial — an audit trail a shared password can never give. The price: no revocation while offline, so validity is kept short (8 h default, up to 30 days for a site visit without network).
What the sshd config enforces: trusted user CA = the debug CA key; a principals file per account; AuthorizedKeysFile none (otherwise a planted plain key would bypass the certificate); password and keyboard-interactive off; no root login; only the normal account allowed; verbose auth logging. Its host key (ed25519) is created per unit at first start on the persistent partition — never in the image, or every AAU would share one host key.
Level 2 — implementing and using it
Firewall by ingress interface, not by destination address. Binding port 22 to the eth1 address is not enough: Linux accepts a packet for eth1's address even when it arrives on eth0, and NETCONF (830) has its own listener. So the rule matches -i eth0. The AAU kernel supports iptables-legacy only (no nftables), and IPv6 must be mirrored because eth0 gets a link-local address:
iptables-legacy  -A INPUT -i eth0 -p tcp --dport 2222 -j ACCEPT
iptables-legacy  -A INPUT -i eth0 -j DROP
ip6tables-legacy -A INPUT -i eth0 -p tcp --dport 2222 -j ACCEPT
ip6tables-legacy -A INPUT -i eth0 -j DROP
# must load at every boot BEFORE eth0 comes up, as one iptables-restore (no flush gap on restart)
Issuing and using a certificate (placeholders only — the CA private key never leaves the CA service):
# CA side: 8 h validity, back-dated 1 h for clock skew, Key ID = who, -n = principal
ssh-keygen -s <ca_key> -I <engineer-or-station-id> -n <login> -V -1h:+8h -z <serial> id_ed25519.pub

# eth0: all AAUs share the same eth0 address, so remember each by serial
ssh -p 2222 -i <key> -o CertificateFile=<key>-cert.pub \
    -o HostKeyAlias=<AAU serial> -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new <login>@<eth0-address>

# UART: same certificate, SSH carried over the serial line
ssh -o CertificateFile=<key>-cert.pub -o HostKeyAlias=<AAU serial> \
    -o ProxyCommand="socat - /dev/ttyUSB0,raw,echo=0" <login>@uart

# AAU auth log then shows: Accepted publickey ... ED25519-CERT ID <key id> (serial N)
How SSH over UART works: after boot a systemd service owns ttyPS0 (serial-getty masked, Conflicts=, Restart=always). For each session it discards stale bytes until the client greeting SSH- arrives, then runs sshd -i (inetd mode: no listening socket, talks on stdin/stdout). Same CA, principals and host key as eth0. ClientAliveInterval 15 × CountMax 2 ends a session ~30–45 s after the cable is pulled, and dmesg -n 1 stops kernel prints from corrupting the SSH stream (they stay in the journal). On the laptop, MobaXterm already has socat; plain Windows needs a small PowerShell serial helper.
Factory and RCT: ATE/RCT stations run release software, so password login is gone there too. Each station has its own key pair; if it cannot reach the CA it gets a 30-day station certificate monthly. Open issue: a brand-new unit may have an old clock before NTP/PTP, making a certificate "not yet valid" — hence the back-dated start.
Level 3 — the test plan, pitfalls and open risks
Test-plan method (reusable for any security feature): requirements R1–R8 (no access by cable alone; PW-issued cert required and logged; short expiry; normal user, root needs su; nothing per-engineer on the AAU; boot log kept for RMA; U-Boot and recovery closed; power cuts cannot force recovery) are traced to test IDs. Three layers: Cat 1 source/pytest/bash checks in CI (including a U-Boot sandbox in Docker), Cat 5 on-target by hand or with an on-unit validation script. Rules: red first (a new test must fail on the old branch), and a throwaway CA generated at test time — the real CA key never enters the repo. Families: SSH, CA, FW, NET, TM (time), SU, PRIV, SEC, BOOT, UART, AUD (audit), UB, REC, BC (boot count).
CheckPass criterion
Full TCP+UDP scan of eth0 (IPv4, IPv6 link-local, any secondary address)only tcp/2222 open
Probe 22 and 830 on eth0 every 100 ms through a reboot and a firewall restartnever connects; 830 times out (dropped, not refused)
Refused certificatesexpired, not-yet-valid, wrong principal, other CA, plain key in authorized_keys
CA rotationold+new CA keys both trusted during the change-over
Tampered CA key inside a packageinstall rejected by the package signature check (RUSEC01)
Host keydifferent per unit; unchanged across upgrade and rollback
Fronthaul fibre pulled and repluggedeth0 certificate login keeps working, debug sshd not restarted
UART robustness30 consecutive logins; garbage bytes do not kill the service; cable pull ends the old session
Pitfalls the test plan caught: (1) Port forwarding goes around the firewall — a tunnel starts inside the AAU, and ssh-keygen grants permit-port-forwarding by default, so a cert login could tunnel to NETCONF or into the eth1 network. The debug sshd now permits a single local tunnel to one internal test service and nothing else; the UART sshd allows none. (2) Config leakage — port 22 drop-ins enable passwords; sshd takes the first value it reads, so the debug config must never include them. (3) Permanent backdoor — port 22 still reads the user's authorized_keys, so an 8-hour cert holder could plant a key; port 22 must not trust the debug CA either. (4) Other services bound to all interfaces (e.g. an unauthenticated LED helper) are exposed if the firewall ever lapses.
Open risks listed honestly: a shared root password in build history; port 22 on eth1 still password-based; certificate validity judged by an untrusted clock after power cuts; rootfs not verified at boot (no dm-verity yet) — see RUSEC01.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why is a strong password on the AAU debug port still not enough?
A: It is the same on every unit, so one leak opens the whole fleet, and it records nothing about who logged in. A short-lived CA-signed certificate identifies the engineer, expires on its own and is checked offline.
Q: Why match the firewall rule on -i eth0 instead of binding sshd to the eth1 address?
A: Linux accepts packets addressed to eth1's IP even when they arrive on eth0, and NETCONF has its own listener. Only an ingress-interface rule guarantees that nothing but 2222 is reachable through eth0.
Q: How do you run SSH over a UART and why bother?
A: A service owns the serial port, waits for the SSH- greeting and runs sshd -i on the line; the laptop uses ProxyCommand with socat. It keeps the boot log for RMA while replacing the root autologin with certificate authentication.
Q: Name two ways a certificate login could still bypass the design.
A: Port forwarding (certificates allow it by default) can tunnel around the eth0 firewall to NETCONF or eth1; and a key planted in authorized_keys gives permanent password-less access on port 22. Both must be closed and tested.
Q: What does "red first" mean in a security test plan?
A: Every new test is run against the old code and must fail there. A test that passes before the fix proves nothing about the fix.
Massive MIMO, energy saving & resilience
MMIMO01 Massive-MIMO (32T32R / 64T64R) O-RU bench & field-trial playbook — GM switch config, manual vs M-plane carrier bring-up, bring-up ladder, beam sweeps, RET over M-plane and the XRAN fault codes 0–19 Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
A massive-MIMO O-RU (32T32R or 64T64R) is a normal O-RAN 7.2 radio with many more transmit/receive chains, an antenna array that forms beams, and a built-in antenna calibration loop that keeps all chains phase- and gain-aligned. That changes the lab work in three ways: the fronthaul is fatter (25G links, BFP-9 compressed IQ for a whole antenna group), every chain must be checked (power, DPD, calibration), and acceptance includes beam sweeps across azimuth and elevation, not just EVM and ACLR on one port.

This card merges the mMIMO bench notes and the field-trial checklist into one playbook: the kit, the two ways to bring a carrier up (RU shell or M-plane), the grand-master switch settings, the step-by-step bring-up ladder from "link up" to "UE attached", RCT on a pod-based DU, RET (remote electrical tilt) over the M-plane, firmware slots and recovery, and the fronthaul-service (XRAN) fault codes you will see in DU logs when something in that ladder breaks.
mMIMO cell bring-up ladder (LLS-C3)
Stop at the first step that fails; every later symptom is usually a consequence of it.
Level 1 — what a massive-MIMO bench needs
Kit for an LLS-C3 field trial or bench: 25GBASE-LR SFP28 optics on the grand-master (GM) switch ports and in the RU, an E810 NIC with SFP28 on the DU, and a 1500 W supply for the RU. In C3 the GM sits in the fronthaul switch and both DU and RU are PTP slaves of it (see CM35).
TopicWhat is different for mMIMOWhat to check
Antenna groups32 or 64 chains handled as one antenna group (e.g. 0–31)carrier config covers the whole group; per-antenna power meter and DPD status for every chain
CalibrationRU runs its own antenna calibration to align chainstrigger the calibration test while tailing the RU radio trace; look for a clean completion
BeamsDU applies precoding/beam weights (PMI / beam index)beam sweeps in RCT and azimuth sweep in E2E
Fronthaul25G optics, BFP-9 compression, VLAN + PCP 7same optic vendor/type/wavelength on both ends, FH counters free of late/early
Powerhigh-power RU, 1500 W PSUno red/orange LEDs before radiating
Bench pre-check (do this before blaming software): power on and every RF cable connected; the RF switch routes the right TRx/RFIO to the analyser (EXM); no red/orange LEDs; SFPs on both ends of each fibre from the same vendor, same single-/multi-mode type, 25G rated, same wavelength; link LED on; the GM web page shows the port Active (not Inactive / Down / Disabled / No SFP — hovering a port shows its state).
RF hygiene before a field transmission: approved centre frequency, correct bandwidth, scan the band with a portable analyser for interference, and confirm both the stack and the UE support that band and ARFCN.
Lab setups you will meet: conducted CI RCT (EXM + RF switch), OTA-chamber RCT, multi-port phase-matrix RCT for fading/MU-MIMO (PXI analyser + vector signal generator), channel-emulator RCT and E2E (TDL models), and RF-cage E2E with real UEs.
Level 2 — GM switch, two carrier bring-up paths, and RCT on pods
Grand-master switch settings (menu names vary by GM model): RU and DU ports set to 25 Gbps and the GM not overloaded; the same VLAN for RU and DU; ports in trunk mode allowing the setup VLAN and the PTP VLAN (100 in this lab); private-VLAN membership for the RU and DU ports; and both ports ticked in the PTP clock instance. A port that is up but not in the PTP clock instance gives you link with no sync.

Path A — manual carrier on the RU shell (quick bench bring-up, no DU M-plane needed):
tail -f /var/log/messages                 # 1. wait for PTP lock messages
ifconfig                                  # 2. fheth0 has its DHCP address
shell                                     # 3. RU internal shell
XorIf set protocol --vlan=1 --ipmode=0 --transport=0
XorIf set vlantag --port=0 --id=<vlan> --dei=0 --pcp=7
# 4. one TX and one RX carrier over the whole antenna group
CarrierProcess active --vlanswitch=on --vlanid=1 --portid=0 --rumac=<ru-mac> --dumac=<du-mac> \
   --tddconfig=[(7,6,2,4),(7,6,2,4)] --tddperiod=5 --freq=3420000 --band=100 \
   --antgrp=[0,31] --comp=bfp9 --cargrp=0 --dir=tx --name=tx0      # repeat with --dir=rx --name=rx0
Ac test on 20                             # 5. antenna calibration
Path B — M-plane with netopeer2-cli (the production-like path; this RU family listens on a non-standard NETCONF port, 9999). Apply three XML files to running in order: (1) interfaces (VLAN/MAC of the FH interface), (2) processing-elements (binds eAxC transport flows to the interface), (3) the active tx/rx-array-carriers (frequency, bandwidth, TDD pattern, compression). Same model as ORUMAN01: nothing radiates until step 3 sets the carriers ACTIVE.

Useful RU shell commands
CommandUse
XorIf clear counters / XorIf get countersfronthaul packet counters — on-time / early / late per direction; clear, run traffic, read
CarrierProcess query processedlist --name=*list carriers and their state; CarrierProcess deactive --name=tx0 to drop one
PowerMeter adc|vca|fft ... 0 63per-antenna power at ADC, VCA and FFT points for chains 0–63
Dpd get status --ant=[0,63]DPD convergence for every PA chain
orutest get carrierconfirms the stack actually set the carrier (bring-up step 8)
tail -f <radio.trace>RU application trace: faults, calibration, ALD/RET messages
RCT on a pod-based DU (RCT ISO on Ubuntu 22.04): the bring-up is driven by /opt/pw/post-install/user-config.json. Key fields for mMIMO: RAT_TYPE 5G, RRH_MASTER_INTF and GM_SLAVE_INTF (the FH NIC port), RRH_ID (RU serial), NETOPEER2_PORT 9999, USE_NETOPEER_DOCKER (true on images where netopeer runs in its own pod), OPT 7, RRH_TOPOLOGY C3, TOTAL_5G_PHYS 1, MIMO_ENABLED 1. After a reboot run run-startup.sh; for RU DHCP stop and disable the distro isc-dhcp-server, disable ufw, then run run-dhcps.sh. PTP state is in /var/run/ptpmanager/tx/status. Shell aliases for the phy, fh-srv, ptpmgr and netopeer containers save a lot of typing. In the BBU pod, arp -n on the FH interface should show the RU's link-local (169.254.x.x) address; that route may need re-adding after a server reboot.
Level 3 — beams, fault codes, RET, firmware and recovery
Beam acceptance. In RCT the RU must pass a sweep over all PMIs on beam index 1; the wide beam must pass a 2-D scan over azimuth −70°…+70° and elevation −10°…+10°; PMI 0 on beam index 1 gets the same 2-D scan. In E2E the check is a sweep over all azimuths. A beam that fails at the edges of the scan usually points at calibration or a weak chain, so re-run calibration and the per-antenna power/DPD checks before suspecting the beam weights.

Fronthaul-service (XRAN) fault codes seen in the DU logs — map each to a ladder step:
CodeMeaningLadder step to re-check
0general / unknown fault—
1 / 2 / 3S-plane out of sync: RRH inactive / GPS unavailable on all RRH / GPS available on all RRHDU and RU PTP lock (3, 5)
4S-plane inactive: >100 consecutive packets discardedPTP VLAN, clock-instance ports
5 / 6one RRH / all RRHs disconnected (>100 consecutive packets missing)links, VLAN, carrier active (1–2, 8)
7 / 8RRH has no GPS signal / no PTP syncGM, sync chain (3, 5)
9inter-cell sync failure (2G only)—
10PHY event discardedDU real-time health (FHSVC01, CM29)
11system time jump detectedphc2sys / clock step (PTPSTEP01)
12UL data from the RRH in a DL subframeTDD pattern mismatch DU vs RU
13PRACH requested in a TDD DL subframePRACH config index vs TDD pattern
14 / 15late / early O7 U-plane packetstiming windows (CM19), FH counters
16no NTP syncserver time source
17connection to the FH service lostfh-srv container / process
18 / 19service callback stalled >2 symbols / >1 slotCPU isolation, RT threads (FHSVC01)
255none (reserved)—
RET over the M-plane (O-RAN ALD port). The antenna tilt motor is an AISG device behind the RU (CM08). Sequence: edit-config ald_off then ald_on, then user-rpc messages: scan → set address → connect → calibrate (poll the response frame) → set tilt (poll) → get tilt. Wait for the response that belongs to the current scan session. Validate in the RU radio trace: the tilt travels in tenths of a degree, so for 11° look for hex(110) = 0x6E in the "Recv data" lines; a calibration acknowledge shows as 0x31 0x0 0x0.

Firmware slots and recovery. list shows the A/B slots and marks the active one with *. Copy the image to the RU media partition, slot-upgrade -f <image.bin> -n <1|2>, then re_boot <slot>. Older units that reboot often: copy the file straight to the media partition with scp, and clear a stale host key with ssh-keygen -R after a re-image. If the RU is unreachable: unplug the management Ethernet, power-cycle, wait up to 15 min until only the SFP0 and RUN LEDs are green, re-plug; otherwise attach the serial debug board, do not press keys during boot, then check list and ifconfig. Always load the vendor-approved firmware and re-validate calibration before a trial.
RU searching for an M-plane VLAN: if the DU serves DHCP untagged, stop the RU scanning VLANs: fw_setenv vlan_mode off and in the o-ran-mplane-int startup XML set the searchable M-plane VLAN range to lowest 2 / highest 1 (an empty range), then reboot.

DU-side tricks: FH container exits silently → copy its entry script out, start fh-srv under stdbuf -oL so the log is unbuffered, copy it back and start the container. Re-load beamforming weights or the test MAC without restarting the PHY: ctrlapp pdu-config false → ctrlapp precoding-72b-db-reinit (or testmac-reinit) → ctrlapp pdu-config true. The L1 debug-data tool extracts SRS channel estimates (CIR/CFR), and L1/L2 pcaps can be turned into PHY test vectors. UE side: screen mirroring, iperf3 started through adb shell, and a 5G-only lock app. Drive tests use the pw-pytest drive-test runner with type 5g_mimo and KPI collection (AUTO15).
Interview Q&A
Q: What is different about validating a 64T64R RU compared with a 4T4R RU?
A: Every chain needs power and DPD checks, the RU must pass its own antenna calibration, the fronthaul carries a whole antenna group at 25G with BFP-9, and acceptance adds beam sweeps (all PMIs on a beam index, a 2-D azimuth/elevation scan for the wide beam).
Q: A mMIMO cell will not come up. How do you work through it?
A: Follow the ladder: RU and DU links active on the GM, DU PTP lock, RU DHCP (link-local address visible with arp in the BBU pod), RU PTP lock, RU in ACS, PHY config sent, carrier set on the RU, no RU faults, cell up, FH counters free of early/late, UE attach. Fix the first step that fails.
Q: The DU log shows XRAN fault 14. What does it mean and what do you check?
A: Late O7 U-plane packets: the IQ arrives after the RU receive window. Check the timing-window settings against the RU, the FH counters, fronthaul path delay, and DU real-time health (callback stalls, CPU isolation).
Q: How do you set and verify antenna tilt through an O-RU?
A: Over the O-RAN ALD port: ald_on, then RPCs for scan, set address, connect, calibrate, set tilt, get tilt. Verify in the RU radio trace that the tilt value (in tenths of a degree, in hex) appears in the received data and that calibration was acknowledged.
Q: Why might a correctly cabled RU never get its M-plane address from the DU?
A: The RU may be scanning tagged M-plane VLANs while the DU serves DHCP untagged. Disable the VLAN search (U-Boot env plus an empty VLAN range in the M-plane startup XML) or configure the matching VLAN on the DU side.
BANDSD01 Carrier vs band shutdown — measured savings, return times and the controls that do not work Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
An Integrity-ME AAU carries two bands per radio, each band with one or two carriers. At night, when traffic is low, the network can save energy in three ways: let the radio blank empty symbols (uSleep, see USLEEP02), switch off one carrier, or switch off a whole band. The question an energy-saving designer actually asks is: which of these is worth doing, how much does it save, and how long does it take to get the band back?

The measured answer is short. Switch the whole band off. Switching off one carrier of a band that is still on air saves almost nothing (0.2 W), because the band's power amplifiers must stay powered for the other carrier. uSleep and band shutdown add together. Restoring a band takes about a minute; deciding to shut it takes 7-20 minutes. Picture a shop: turning off one checkout lane saves nothing if the lights and fridges stay on; closing the whole floor does. CM22 is the O-RAN toolbox this sits in.
The preference ladder
Bars to scale (1.5 px per W). Idle, both radios, two cells per band; the band switched off is B3 on the mid-band radio and B28 on the low-band radio.
Level 1 — what each step saves and how long the band takes to return
Savings (idle). Band shutdown saves about the same share on both radio types (45-48%). uSleep does not: about half the radio on the mid-band unit, about a tenth on the low-band unit, and its value depends on the build. If you can pick only one lever, band shutdown is the predictable one. The two are additive: shutting a band off on a radio that is already in uSleep still took both units to about 84 W.

Under traffic. With a handset on the sibling band: 154.1 W with both bands up, 84.6 W with B28 off, 152.3 W after it returned, a 45% saving while uplink held 8.00 Mbps before, during and after.

Single carrier. Switching off one of a band's two carriers moved input power from 147.84 to 148.06 W, and the PA register block stayed at 0xff.
