That is correct behaviour: the band is still serving, so its amplifiers stay on. The only carrier action worth taking is removing the last carrier of a band.

Return times:
PathMeasuredWhat it covers
ESLS decision7 to 19.5 minA1 policy accepted until the band leaves air. The xApp evaluates on a 5-minute grid and needs about 855 KPM documents before it decides.
ESLS restore48 to 73 sPolicy disarmed until the band carries traffic again, end to end through the product chain
Direct M-plane1.7 s each wayWrites straight at the radio; 40 shutdown/restore cycles, 0 failures (bench timing only)
Carrier READY in RU datastore8 sThe radio's own state change, inside the restore above
Put hysteresis on the decision, not the restore. Restore was under 73 s every time; the decision is slow and variable because it waits for KPM data.

Annual value at 8 h per night (2920 h/year): about 203 kWh per radio with one band off while the radio carries traffic (69.5 W), 428 kWh for an idle mid-band radio (146.5 W) and 230 kWh for an idle low-band radio (78.9 W).
Level 2 — how it was measured so the claim is electrical
• Power from the radio's per-RFFE power objects, not the per-band total. The per-band total still gives an idle band an equal share of the 12 V bus (GRDEV-11737), so it hides the saving.
• Amplifier state read back from the midboard PA registers over I2C (0x1C-0x1F and 0x20-0x23, two-byte addressing) and from the RF_GPIO registers at 0xa0100000 and 0xa0100004, before and after every transition. A shut band reads 0x00 on its register block: both PA and LNA are released, not just the TX half.
• Soak: 2324 samples over 233 transitions with 0 disagreements between the datastore and the registers. Cycle test: 40 shutdown/restore cycles, 0 failures.
• Drive paths: "ESLS" figures were driven end to end from the Near-RT RIC over A1 (ESLS policy type 3); "M-plane" figures were written straight at the radio.
• Residue: a band that is off still draws about 7 W on its RFFEs. The savings above already include that; do not add it back.
• Not covered: EVM, ACLR and radiated power (need an RCT bench; the change never switches an amplifier on or touches waveform generation). The single-band low-power unit was not measured; it switches its amplifiers through RF_GPIO and has no sibling band.
Level 3 — controls that look valid but are not, and a stale-xApp trap
1. The product will not shut a band that is carrying. It waits for the cell to go quiet. A policy armed against a loaded cell is not an error; it simply does not act until traffic stops.

2. A direct M-plane write does not stick. Setting a carrier active = INACTIVE straight at the radio is put back by a healthy O-DU within 60 s. Use it only to time the radio; only an ESLS-driven shutdown holds the band down.

3. active = SLEEP is a silent no-op. The edit returns rc=0, the value does not persist, and the amplifiers stay driven. It exists in the schema only.

4. The ru-module energy-saving leaves are refused. energy-saving-enabled, power-state and availability-state are published, but every write is rejected by nw-manager with "energy saving is not supported" (same on the single-band unit). Do not design on them.

5. Real case: the shutdown that never happened. The ESLS xApp had been running for 26 days and kept its old subscriptions through a bench redeploy and an SMO data-model update. The A1 policy read ENFORCED, the status endpoint answered, no alarm was raised, and the band never shut. The tell was in the xApp log: when healthy it logs a barring check every 5 minutes with a document count climbing towards 855; when stale the count freezes part-way and the evaluation lines stop. A pod restart fixed it and the threshold was reached 16 minutes later. Two runs looked exactly like a broken radio feature. Lesson: before blaming the radio, prove the decision logic is still counting.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why does switching off one carrier of a two-carrier band save almost nothing?
A: The power goes into the band's PAs, and they must stay powered while any carrier on that band is live. The measured change was 0.22 W with the PA block still 0xff. Only removing the last carrier of the band turns the amplifiers off.
Q: uSleep or band shutdown: which would you choose, and why?
A: Band shutdown if I can pick one: it saved 45-48% on both radio types, while uSleep ranged from 51% on the mid-band radio to 12% on the low-band radio and depends on the build. Better still, use both, because they are additive (72% and 52%).
Q: Where would you put hysteresis in an energy-saving loop, and why?
A: On the shutdown decision. Restore takes 48-73 s end to end and is consistent; the decision takes 7-19.5 min because the xApp waits for about 855 KPM documents on a 5-minute grid. Damping the decision prevents flapping without hurting recovery.
Q: How do you prove a band is really off, not just marked off in the datastore?
A: Read the hardware: midboard PA registers over I2C and the RF_GPIO registers before and after each transition, and per-RFFE input power. A shut band reads 0x00 on its register block. In the soak, 2324 samples showed no disagreement with the datastore.
Q: The A1 policy says ENFORCED but the band never shuts. What do you check?
A: Whether the cell is still carrying traffic (the product waits for quiet), then the xApp log: is the KPM document count still climbing towards the threshold every 5 minutes? A frozen count means a stale xApp, for example after an SMO data-model update; restart the pod.
PRACHLEAK01 fh-srv PRACH C-plane slot leak — how a falsely passing retest hid a pool-exhaustion crash Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
The fronthaul server (fh-srv) sits between the LTE cells on a DU server and the radios. When a cell (a "client") joins a radio, fh-srv programs a PRACH C-plane configuration for it into a small pool on that radio: 8 slots. Two cells can share one radio. The bug: when a cell leaves and rejoins with a different PRACH configuration (for example after a bandwidth change), fh-srv takes a new slot and never frees the old one. After enough changes the pool is empty, the allocator returns nothing, and fh-srv crashes, taking down every cell on that server, not just the one being changed.

The more useful lesson is about testing. A first retest "passed" with 28 clean reconnects and zero slots consumed. It looked like a fix. It was not: both cells sat at 5 MHz the whole time, which is the one condition under which slots are shared. The test held the triggering variable constant, so it could not fail. Think of testing a leaking tap by never turning it on. This card is a case study in how to design a retest that can actually reproduce a bug. See CRASH01 for crash triage in general and CM34 for O-DU internals.
Seven bandwidth changes fill the pool; the eighth crashes fh-srv
A and B are the two cells sharing one radio; numbers are cell bandwidth in MHz after each change. Step "B 10" reused a slot because A already held a 10 MHz config. Starting level was 2 of 8.
Level 1 — the allocation rule and the crash
• fh-srv programs config_prach_cp about 0.3 s after "Added Client". A slot is consumed by the client joining, not by any UE: no UE or traffic is needed to reproduce.
• Rule (derived from 7 bandwidth steps, with the 28 same-bandwidth reconnects as the control): a slot is reused only if another live client already holds an identical PRACH config. PRACH numPrbc and frequency offset scale with PRB count, so same bandwidth means same config. Otherwise a new slot is taken, and the slot the client held in its previous session is never freed on disconnect.
• Result: 7 changes (ACS bandwidth write followed by an EMS reboot) took the pool from 2 to 8; the 8th reconnect logged content buffer alloc FAILED, the allocator returned NULL, and xran_config_prach_cp in libxran dereferenced it: SIGSEGV, SEGV_MAPERR, address nil. Same backtrace as the original crash.
• Blast radius: two cells that were never touched by the test restarted about 40 s after fh-srv died. One cell's bandwidth change takes down every cell on that fronthaul server.
• No core dump: the crash directory was empty although the core monitor was running. The backtrace in the fh-srv /var/log/messages was the only artefact; collect it before the pod log rotates.
Level 2 — how to build a retest that can fail
1. Vary the parameter that triggered the original failure. The original crash happened during a bandwidth sweep. The first retest kept both cells at 25 PRB, verified afterwards from the bandwidth line fh-srv logs on every join. Under the rule above, every one of those 28 reconnects had to reuse a slot. Before running a retest, write down the trigger and check the plan actually exercises it.

2. Gate each cycle on the real event. Each cycle waited for the fh-srv client-join log line for that radio port, not for pod readiness, so each cycle was a real reconnect. The join counter advancing monotonically proves the count.

3. Measure the resource directly. A read-only script reported slot count, slot addresses and client events. Addresses marched in +0x40 steps as slots were taken; unchanged addresses at the end show nothing leaked.

4. Make destructive tools hard to misuse. The repro loop lived outside the automation tree so a pytest run could never reach it, refused to start without an explicit confirmation variable (PL_CONFIRM=yes), and refused any target except the two cells sharing the radio. Rebooting a single-client radio proves nothing: its disconnect releases the radio and reinitialises the pool.

5. Know what your restart is equivalent to. Deleting the vnode pod produced the same xran stop + disconnect pair as an EMS reboot (checked against both). It is a valid lab substitute, but the field path is an EMS reboot after a configuration change.

Scripts used (standalone): slot reader (read-only), reconnect loop (destructive, gated), collector for the crash window, slot timeline, cores and blast radius (read-only), and a bandwidth-sweep driver.
Level 3 — red herrings and a configuration side-quest
"RRH is disconnected" is not a release. The original report assumed the radio is never released while a second client holds it. The log did contain "RRH_1 Is disconnected" lines, but the pool was not reinitialised: the allocator kept walking through eight distinct addresses across eight such events. A log line is a claim; the allocator address is evidence.

Check noisy errors against a healthy peer. A sqlite3: not found error in a pre-config script and a "sendRatMode failed after 5 attempts" line both looked suspicious. Both appeared equally on healthy vnodes (the latter exactly 45 times on both), so they were unrelated.

Carrier index rules for the 5-band AAU. Before the retest, three cells had RRHCarrierIdx values that broke the rules: on the B1/B3 radio both carriers use index 1; on the B8/B28 radio B8 uses 1 and B28 uses 2. A wrong index on the B8 cell put it on eAxC 4-7 instead of 0-3. After correction its PRACH config matched its neighbour's and fh-srv logged sharing ("PRACH CP config is of another eAxc"). This is why the same-bandwidth retest looked so clean, and why the correction was mistaken for a fix.

Every parameter exists twice. RRHCarrierIdx and bandwidth live both as a single-instance parameter and as a mirror under AdditionalConfigurations.RRHParameters. Writing one leaves the device inconsistent while looking correct in one view. After the sweep, the mirrors still held old bandwidths (single instance 25 PRB, mirror 50 or 100). The cells used the single-instance value, but sweep automation must write both copies.

Correct the record. The retest page was updated with a withdrawal banner at the top rather than silently edited. A false "fixed" conclusion that stays visible causes more damage than the original bug.

Fixes the evidence points to: free the client's slot on disconnect; reuse an existing slot when an identical config is already in the pool; and check the allocator result in xran_config_prach_cp so exhaustion becomes a handled error, not a crash of every cell.
Interview Q&A
Q: A retest of a crash shows 28 clean cycles. Why might that prove nothing?
A: If the retest never exercises the trigger. Here both cells stayed at 5 MHz, so every reconnect presented an identical PRACH config and reused a slot; a leak was impossible. The original crash came from a bandwidth sweep, so the retest had to vary bandwidth. When it did, the crash reproduced in 8 steps.
Q: Why did changing one cell's bandwidth restart cells that were never touched?
A: All the cells on the DU share one fh-srv process. Pool exhaustion made the allocator return NULL, xran_config_prach_cp dereferenced it, and fh-srv crashed. Every cell depending on that process restarted about 40 s later.
Q: How would you prove a resource leak without waiting for the crash?
A: Read the resource directly after every cycle: slot count and slot addresses. A count that only grows and addresses that keep advancing (+0x40 each) show allocations without frees. Control it with a case that should reuse (same config) and one that should allocate (different config).
Q: The log says "RRH is disconnected". Is the radio released?
A: Not necessarily. Here the pool was not reinitialised after those lines; the allocator kept taking new addresses. Verify release by its effect on state, not by a log message.
Q: There is no core dump. What do you collect?
A: The backtrace from fh-srv's /var/log/messages (signal, si_code, fault address, frames), pod restart counts and container start times to map the blast radius, the slot timeline from the read-only script, and the exact build tags. Collect them quickly, before log rotation.
RUREG01 RU release resilience regression — power-cut soak, fronthaul flip, soft reboot and alarm raise/clear: method, numbers, what fails Common click to expand ▾
In plain English
Before a new RU build is released, someone has to be rude to it: pull the power, unplug the fronthaul, reboot it, and inject every alarm, then check it comes back cleanly each time. That is resilience regression. On the 2026.3.1 AAU build the suite was: a 98-cycle hard power-cut soak, a fronthaul flip (link down 30 s, 20 times), a soft reboot (10 times) and an 18-case alarm raise/clear suite.

The three recovery tests passed cleanly and produced useful numbers: a radio is back on air about 2.5 minutes after power returns, and the time is set by PTP lock, not by the radio. The alarm suite was the interesting part: raising alarms worked, but what happened after the raise (the clear, the service action) often did not match the test matrix. Like a fire drill where every alarm rings, but half the doors do not unlock afterwards. See CM20 for fault IDs and CM02 for recovery behaviour.
Power-cut recovery timeline
Axis scaled 3.7 px per second. Medians over the soak; all five bands within 10 s of each other on carrier-on-air.
Level 1 — what was run and the headline numbers
TestMethodResult
Hard power-cut soakPDU outlet off 30 s every 15 min; 98 cycles over two days; 5 bands on 3 radios100% carrier activation on every band, 0 drops after activation. Median 159 s to carrier on air, 172 s to a camped UE
Fronthaul flipFronthaul port taken down inside the BBU pod for 30 s, then up; 2 runs x 1020/20 recovered. UE back in 0.3-1.8 s, cell listed again in 1.7-4.2 s; the UE never registered loss of service
Soft rebootRU rebooted 10 times in a row10/10. Cell up 138-168 s (mean 150.5 s); UE re-attached in 0.84-1.34 s with the same IP
Alarm raise/clear18 TCM cases, one per fault ID, trigger then clear8 pass, 9 fail, 1 skipped (needs a deliberately corrupted FPGA image). Raises healthy; failures are in post-raise behaviour
Per-stage power-cut timing (from power restored): RU application awake median 94 s (85-99); PTP sync median 146 s (max 280); carrier READY + ACTIVE median 159 s (max 292); UE camped median 172 s (max 1180). Per band, the carrier-on-air medians were 154-164 s; no band is systematically slower.

UE camping is not carrier availability. Every band activated on every boot, but free handsets picked their favourite bands: one band had a camper in 97 of 98 cycles, B28 in only 13. Pin a handset to each band if you want UE-side numbers for all of them.
Level 2 — evidence sources and how to grade the alarm suite
Use each source only for what it can prove.
SourceMeasuresNot valid for
RU transition log (fhgw.log): power-state AWAKE, PTP_UP, TRX carrier stateboot, sync, carrier on air, carrier dropsanything UE-related
DU lteStats showuerate (EARFCN in the UE-rate table)UE camped / in service, throughputcell up/down: the EARFCN only prints while a UE is camped
Collect logs faster than they rotate. fhgw.log rotated faster than the harness collected it, so carrier timing survived for only about 36% of boots (n around 36, not 98). Rotation depends on log volume, not recovery speed, so the sample is unbiased but smaller than the cycle count suggests.

Grade the alarm suite on three separate axes: (1) the raise and its severity; (2) the clear, observed in the alarm log; (3) the service action the matrix specifies (continue, PA shutdown, reset). A single PASS/FAIL hides which part broke. In this run raises were correct in all but two cases; the failures were clears not observed and service actions that did not match.

Do not grade on a noisy metric. UL baseline in this suite ranged 0.92-1.73 Mbps while DL held 28.6-34.8 Mbps, so a 15% tolerance on UL was judging noise. The overheating case was first marked failed on UL alone despite behaving exactly as specified. Percentage checks now need a baseline of at least 5 Mbps; absolute checks (PA shutdown) are unchanged.
Level 3 — what failed, and two defects the soak exposed
Faults that reset the RU when the matrix said "action continues". Fault 14 (configuration file corrupted) and fault 16 (unit unidentified) were raised at the right severity, but the RU reset (back after about 75 s); fault 14 never wrote a clear to alarms.log, and DL after fault 16 fell from about 30 to 11 Mbps. Fault 4 (temperature too low, MINOR) cleared correctly but halved DL during the alarm. Fault 2005 (midboard not responding) expected PA shutdown, yet DL ran at full rate. These are product-or-matrix questions, not harness bugs: someone must decide which side is wrong.

The trigger that tested the wrong thing. The fault-18 (sync error / free-run) case raised fault 17, which cleared 23 s later; o-ran-sync stayed LOCKED, fault 18 never appeared in 2088 s, and there was no PA shutdown, yet DL dropped from 34 to 3 Mbps. The trigger took the fronthaul away instead of the RU's clock source. A test-design flaw: check that the stimulus really creates the condition the fault describes.

Clear never delivered. For faults 26 (power supply, fanned out to all eight RFFE supplies) and 29 (transceiver), the RU stopped answering SSH while the fault was active, so the clear command never arrived and the RU was left dirty for the next case, without any reset. One fix to that management-path drop could change up to eight verdicts.

Fault 2 overheating behaved as specified: CRITICAL, service stopped, RU reset, back in 417.5 s, DL back to baseline.

RTC defect from the soak. Of 5153 boot-time RTC reads, 47% showed impossible years (2051-2103) on all three radios, never 1970. The kernel sets system time from the RTC before ru-init runs, and ru-init then replaces it with a stale placeholder time from a file. Early-boot log lines therefore carry bad timestamps, and the RTC is read before PTP lock. Do not correlate RU logs across a reboot by timestamp alone.

An unexplained cluster. About a third of boots (51 of 163) showed a ~449 s boot. PTP-lock failure and midboard firmware upgrade were tested and refuted; the cluster was kept out of the statistics and logged as open rather than averaged in.
Interview Q&A
Q: After a power cut the carrier takes about 160 s to come back. Where does the time go?
A: About 94 s for the RU application to start, then PTP acquisition (median 146 s, up to 280 s). The carrier follows PTP lock by about 13 s and the UE camps about 13 s later. To speed recovery you work on timing acquisition, not the radio boot.
Q: Why use two evidence sources for recovery, and what can each not tell you?
A: The RU log gives boot, PTP and carrier-state transitions but knows nothing about UEs. The DU UE-rate table shows service and throughput but only prints the EARFCN while a UE is camped, so it cannot prove a cell is down. Each metric must come from the source that can prove it.
Q: An alarm test raises the fault correctly but the case fails. What else do you check?
A: The clear (did it appear in the alarm log?) and the service action (did the RU continue, shut the PA, or reset as the matrix says?). Report the three separately. Also check the RU is still reachable: here SSH dropped during faults 26 and 29 so the clear never arrived.
Q: Your sync-error test raised fault 17, never fault 18, and throughput collapsed. What is wrong?
A: Probably the stimulus. o-ran-sync stayed LOCKED, so the RU never lost its clock; the trigger took the fronthaul away instead. Fix the test so it removes the sync source and confirm the sync state moves to holdover and free-run.
Q: UL baseline is about 1 Mbps. Should a 15% UL drop fail an alarm case?
A: No. At that level the run-to-run spread (0.92-1.73 Mbps) exceeds 15%, so the check grades noise. Require a meaningful baseline (at least 5 Mbps) for percentage checks, or use DL and absolute checks such as PA shutdown.
